p.seg: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Fó was in the state of Mójié at the Shànshèng Bodhimaṇḍa. When he first attained Buddhahood,
he contemplated all sentient beings,
who are entangled in the net of delusion and perverse views,
and are difficult to teach and transform.
"If I remain in the world," [he thought,]
"it will be of no benefit to matters;
it would be better to pass away into the Nièpán without remainder."
At that time, Fàntiān, knowing what the Fó thought,
immediately descended from heaven, went before the Fó,
bowed his head to his feet,
knelt with palms joined, and entreated him:
"Shìzūn! Turn the fǎlún,
and do not enter bānièpán."
The Fó replied to Fàntiān:
"The species of sentient beings are obscured by dust and defilement;
they take pleasure in and are attached to worldly joys, lacking a mind of wisdom.
If I remain in the world,
my efforts will be in vain;
as I have thought, only extinction is pleasant."
At that time, Fàntiān again bowed prostrate
and said to the Fó:
"Shìzūn! Today the fǎhǎi is full,
the fǎchuáng is established;
now is exactly the time to provide relief and guidance.
Furthermore, those sentient beings who should be saved are also very numerous;
why does the Shìzūn wish to enter Nièpán?
This would cause these burgeoning beings to forever lose their protection and shelter.
In the past, throughout countless jié, the Shìzūn
always gathered fǎyào for the sake of sentient beings;
even for a single jì,
you sought it at the cost of your own body, wife, and children.
Why do you not consider this and instead wish to abandon them in solitude?
Long ago in the past, in Yánfútí, there was a great king
named Xiūlóupó,
who ruled this world's eighty-four thousand small kingdoms and cities,
sixty thousand mountains and rivers, and eight hundred billion villages.
The king had twenty thousand wives and ten thousand great ministers.
At that time, King Miàosè
possessed incomparable power of virtue,
protected and nurtured the people and all things,
and the kingdom was limitlessly prosperous and joyful.
The king thought to himself:
'As I am now, I only provide for everyone with wealth and treasures;
I have no dàojiào to establish and settle them.
This is my fault;
how distressing it is!
I must now seek the solid fǎcái
to enable everyone to attain liberation.'
He immediately issued a proclamation
within Yánfútí: 'To anyone who has the fǎ and can speak it to me,
I will grant whatever they require, and I will not dare to go against them.'
The search went out everywhere,
but there was no one who responded.
At that time, the king was sorrowful, grieved, and deeply pained.
King Píshāmén saw him like this
and wished to go and test him.
He suddenly transformed his body into a Yèchā,
with a blue-black appearance,
eyes red as blood,
canine teeth protruding upwards,
hair all standing on end,
and fire coming out of his mouth.
He came to the palace gate and proclaimed:
'Who wishes to hear the fǎ? I shall speak it for them.'
When the king heard these words, he was overcome with joy.
He went out in person to welcome him, stepped forward to pay homage,
arranged a high seat, and invited him to sit.
He immediately gathered his officials, who surrounded them front and back, wishing to listen.
At that time, the Yèchā said to the king:
'The matter of learning the fǎ is difficult;
how can you wish to hear and know it so simply?'
The king folded his hands and said:
'Whatever is required, I do not dare to refuse.'
The Yèchā replied:
'If you give me the Great King's beloved wife and children to eat,
then I will give you the fǎ.'
At that time, the Great King offered his beloved wife and the best of his sons to the Yèchā.
Once the Yèchā received them,
he took them and ate them upon the high seat in the midst of the assembly.
At that time, all the kings, the hundred officials, and the group of ministers, seeing the king act thus,
wept and were distressed;
they rolled on the ground
and entreated the Great King to abandon this matter.
For the sake of the fǎ, the king's heart was firm and did not waver.
When the Yèchā ghost had finished eating the wife and children,
he spoke a jì:
'All formations are impermanent,
Those who are born all have suffering,
The wǔyīn are empty and without marks,
There is no self or what belongs to self.'
Having spoken this jì, the king was greatly delighted,
and in his heart, he had no regret or resentment
even as large as a hair.
He immediately wrote it down
and sent messengers to proclaim it throughout Yánfútí,
causing everyone to recite and practice it.
At that time, King Píshāmén returned to his original form
and praised him, saying: 'Excellent! Most wonderful and extraordinary!
The wife and crown prince are still alive as before.'
The king of that time is none other than the present body of the Fó.
If the Shìzūn acted thus for the fǎ in former days,
why do you now wish to abandon sentient beings,
entering Nièpán early instead of providing relief and salvation?
Furthermore, Shìzūn!
In the remote past, an āsēngqí jié ago,
there was a great king in Yánfútí
named Qiánshéníbólí,
who ruled over the various countries' eighty-four thousand villages,
twenty thousand wives and palace ladies, and ten thousand great ministers.
The king possessed compassion
and pity for all;
the people relied on him,
grains were abundant and cheap,
and they were grateful for the king's kindness,
viewing him as a compassionate father.
At that time, the king thought:
'I am now the most honorable,
holding the position of the supreme leader,
and the people are each peaceful and happy under me.
Although this is so,
it does not fulfill my heart's desire.
I must now seek the wonderful treasure of fǎcái to benefit them.'
Having thought this, he sent a minister to proclaim an order
to inform everyone:
'To anyone who has the wonderful fǎ and speaks it to me,
I shall give them what they need,
according to their desires.'
At that time, there was a Póluómén named Láodùchā
who came to the palace gate, saying, 'I have the fǎ.'
The king rejoiced to hear this, immediately went out to receive him,
stepped forward to pay homage,
spread out a fine mat and cushions, and invited him to take a seat.
The king and his attendants joined their palms and said:
'We only wish the Dàshī! Please have pity on my foolishness and meanness,
and expound the wonderful fǎ, so that we may hear and know it.'
At that time, Láodùchā replied to the king:
'My wisdom was sought in distant lands;
it was not easy to accumulate this learning. How can you wish to hear it so simply?'
The king replied again:
'Whatever is required, please just command me,
and I shall supply it all.'
Láodùchā said:
'If the Great King today can carve a thousand lamps into his body and light them
as an offering,
then I will speak it for you.'
Hearing these words, the king was doubly delighted.
He immediately sent a person riding an elephant that could travel eighty thousand lǐ
to announce to everyone within Yánfútí:
'The Great King Qiánshéníbólí,
seven days from now, for the sake of the fǎ,
shall carve his body to light a thousand lamps.'
At that time, the various lesser kings and all the people, having heard these words,
each harbored bitter sorrow and all came to the king.
Having arrived and finished their bows, they spoke together:
'The living beings of this world now rely upon the Great King,
just as the blind rely on a guide
or a child looks up to its mother.
After the king passes away, what will we have to depend on?
If you carve a thousand lamps into your body,
you will certainly not survive.
Why, for the sake of this one Póluómén,
do you abandon all the sentient beings of this world?'
At that time, the twenty thousand wives, five hundred crown princes, and ten thousand great ministers in the palace
joined their palms and entreated him,
also in the same manner.
The king replied:
'All of you,
must be careful not to discourage my wúshàng dàoxīn.
I vow to seek to become a Fó through this act;
when I attain Buddhahood in the future, I will certainly save you first.'
At that time, the people, seeing that the king's intention was firm,
wept and were distressed, throwing themselves on the ground.
The king's intention did not change, and he said to the Póluómén:
'Now you may carve my body and light the thousand lamps.'
He immediately carved them for him and placed fat and wicks in each.
When the assembly saw this, they fainted and then revived,
throwing their bodies to the ground like a great mountain collapsing.
The king spoke again:
'I only wish the Dàshī! Please have pity and compassion,
and first speak the fǎ for me, and then light the lamps.
If my life should end,
I would not have time to hear the fǎ.'
At that time, Láodùchā then chanted the words of the fǎ:
'What is permanent all comes to an end;
What is high must surely fall;
Meeting ends in separation;
Those who are born all die.'
Having spoken this jì,
he then lit the fire.
At this moment, the king was greatly delighted,
and in his heart, he had no regret or resentment.
He made a vow himself:
"I now seek the Dharma for the sake of attaining the Buddha Way;
when I later become a Buddha,
I shall use the light of wisdom to illuminate and awaken sentient beings from the darkness of their fetters."
Having made this vow, heaven and earth shook greatly,
even the palaces of the various *Jìng Jū* Heavens trembled and moved,
and they all looked down together.
Seeing the *Pú Sà* making an offering of the Dharma,
destroying his own body
and disregarding his physical life,
they all descended together
and crowded the empty space.
Their tears of weeping were like heavy rain,
and they rained down heavenly flowers to make an offering.
At that time, *Tiān Dì Shì* descended to stand before the King,
praised him in various ways, and further asked him, saying:
"Great King! Now your pain is extreme;
is there any regret or resentment in your heart?"
The King immediately said: "No."
*Tiān Dì Shì* spoke again:
"I see your body now, trembling and not at peace;
though you say you have no regret,
who can know this for certain?"
The King then made a vow:
"If from the beginning until now,
my heart has not felt regret,
may the many wounds on my body be immediately restored."
Having spoken these words, they were restored in an instant.
That King of that time is the current Buddha.
The *Shì Zūn* in the past suffered bitter agony to seek the Dharma,
all for the sake of sentient beings;
now that his fulfillment is complete,
why would he abandon them and wish to enter *Niè Pán*,
forever causing all to lose the great light of the Dharma?
"Furthermore, *Shì Zūn*!
In a past age,
in *Yán Fú Tí*, there was a great king named *Pí Léng Jié Lí*,
who governed eighty-four thousand settlements across the various lands,
with twenty thousand consorts and ladies, five hundred princes,
and ten thousand ministers.
The King was compassionate
and looked upon the people as his children.
At that time, the Great King loved the True Dharma in his heart,
and he immediately sent a minister to proclaim to all:
'Whoever has sutras or Dharma to speak for me,
I shall provide whatever they need according to their wishes.'
There was a *Bó Luó Mén* named *Láo Dù Chā*
who came to the palace gate and said:
'I have the Great Dharma. To whoever wishes to hear it,
I shall speak.'
Hearing these words, the King was overjoyed beyond measure;
he personally went out to welcome him, bowed at his feet in greeting,
inquired after his well-being,
led him to the great hall, prepared a high seat,
and invited him to sit.
With palms joined, he said:
'I only wish, Great Master, that you would speak the Dharma.'
*Láo Dù Chā* said:
'What I know,
I pursued and studied in the four directions,
accumulating hardship for many years.
How can the Great King
expect to hear it so simply?'
The King folded his hands and said:
'Whatever is needed, I hope you will favor me with your command;
I dare not withhold anything from the Great Master.'
He immediately replied to the King, saying:
'If you can hammer a thousand iron nails into your body,
then I will give you the Dharma.'
The King agreed to it:
'Seven days from now, this shall be done.'
Then the Great King immediately sent people riding elephants eighty thousand *lǐ*,
to announce everywhere within *Yán Fú Tí*:
'Great King *Pí Léng Jié Lí*
will have a thousand iron nails hammered into his body seven days from now.'
When the ministers and people heard this, they all gathered like clouds and said to the Great King:
'We from the four distant directions have received the King's kindness and virtue,
and each has obtained peace and joy.
We only wish, Great King, for our sake, that you would not have a thousand iron nails hammered into your body.'
At that time, in the palace, the consorts, ladies, princes, and ministers,
and the entire assembly,
all at once pleaded with the King for mercy:
'We only wish, Great King, that for our sake,
you would not take your life for the sake of one person
and abandon all the sentient beings of the world.'
Then the Great King thanked them, saying:
'In the long cycle of birth and death, I have sacrificed my body countlessly;
sometimes for greed, anger, or ignorance.
If one were to count my white bones, they would be higher than *Xū Mí*;
the blood from my decapitations would exceed the five rivers;
my tears of weeping would be more than the four seas.
All such various sacrifices of life were in vain,
for I never did it for the Dharma.
I now hammer nails to seek the Buddha Way;
when I later become a Buddha,
I shall use the sharp sword of wisdom to sever the illness of your fetters.
Why then do you wish to obstruct my resolve for the Way?'
Then the assembly was silent and said nothing.
At that time, the Great King said to the *Bó Luó Mén*:
'I only wish, Great Master, that you would show mercy and speak first,
and then hammer the nails;
if my life should end, I might not hear the Dharma.'
*Láo Dù Chā* then spoke a verse:
'All things are impermanent;
all who are born have suffering.
All dharmas are empty and without birth;
they truly are not what I possess.'
Having spoken this verse, he then hammered a thousand iron nails into the body.
Then the crowd of lesser kings and ministers, and the entire assembly,
threw themselves to the ground like a great mountain collapsing,
rolling about and weeping
until they lost their sense of direction.
At that time, heaven and earth shook in six ways;
the gods of the *Yù* and *Sè* realms, wondering at the cause,
all descended together.
Seeing the *Pú Sà* in such agony for the sake of the Dharma, with his body wounded and destroyed,
they wept at once,
their tears like heavy rain,
and they also rained down heavenly flowers
to make an offering.
Then *Tiān Dì Shì* came before the King
and asked the King, saying:
'Great King! Now
you are brave and diligent,
not fearing bitter pain.
For the sake of the Dharma,
what do you seek?
Do you wish to be *Tiān Dì Shì* or a *Zhuǎn Lún Wáng*?
Or do you wish to be a *Mó Wáng* or a *Fàn Wáng*?'
The King answered him, saying:
'What I do
is not for the pleasure of receiving rewards in the *Sān Jiè*;
all my merit is used to seek the Buddha Way.'
*Tiān Dì Shì* spoke again:
'The King has now destroyed his body
and is in such pain;
do you have any thought of regret?'
The King said: 'None.'
*Tiān Dì Shì* spoke again:
'I see your body now, unable to support itself;
you say you have no regret, but what is the evidence?'
The King then made a vow:
'If I am sincere and my heart has no regret,
may my body now return to its former state.'
Having spoken these words, it was immediately restored.
The gods and people were immeasurably joyful.
*Shì Zūn*, now the sea of Dharma is full
and merit is complete;
why would you wish to abandon all sentient beings
and quickly enter *Niè Pán* without speaking the Dharma?
Furthermore, *Shì Zūn*!
In the distant past, throughout immeasurable *ā sēng qí* kalpas,
in this *Yán Fú Tí*, there was a great king named *Fàn Tiān Wáng*.
He had a prince named *Tán Mó Qián*,
who loved the True Dharma.
He sent messengers to search for it,
traveling everywhere in the four directions,
yet they could not find it at all.
'At that time, the Prince, not having obtained the Dharma,
was distressed and despondent.
*Tiān Dì Shì* knew his sincerity
and transformed into a *Bó Luó Mén* who came to the palace gate
and said: "I know the Dharma;
to whoever wishes to hear it,
I shall speak."
Hearing this, the Prince
immediately went out to welcome him,
bowed at his feet in greeting,
led him to the great hall, prepared a fine seat,
and invited him to sit.
With palms joined, he said:
"I only wish, Great Master,
that you would show pity and speak for me."
The *Bó Luó Mén* said:
"Learning is very difficult!
I followed masters for a long time
before I finally obtained it.
How can you expect to hear it so simply?
It is not reasonable."
The Prince spoke again:
"Whatever the Master needs, I hope you will command it;
I will not spare even my body, wife, or children."
The *Bó Luó Mén* said:
"If you can now make a great fire pit ten zhang deep, fill it with blazing fire,
and throw yourself into it as an offering,
then I will give you the Dharma."
Then the Prince, following his words, immediately made a great fire pit.
When the King, the consorts, the ministers, and the ladies heard these words,
they could not be at peace.
They all gathered together
at the Prince's palace
to advise the Prince
and plead with the *Bó Luó Mén*:
"I only wish you would show mercy;
for our sake,
do not let the Prince throw himself into the fire pit.
If anything is needed,
the kingdom, the wife and children, or even our own bodies, we shall provide as servants."
The Póluómén said:
“I will not coerce you;
it shall be as the Tàizǐ wishes!
If you can do this, I shall speak the Dharma for you;
if not, I shall not speak it.”
Observing his firm resolve, they each remained silent.
At that time, the Dàwáng immediately dispatched messengers, riding elephants that could travel eighty thousand lǐ,
to announce throughout all of Yánfútí:
“Tàizǐ Tánmóqián, for the sake of the Dharma,
seven days from now, will throw his body into a fire pit.
Those who wish to see him should come and gather early.”
Then all the minor kings and the people from the four directions,
the strong and the weak supporting one another, all gathered like clouds
at the place where the Tàizǐ was.
They knelt for a long time with palms joined and, with one voice, spoke to the Tàizǐ, saying:
“We, your subjects, look up to the Tàizǐ as if to our own parents.
If you now throw yourself into the fire,
the world will lose its father, and we will forever have nothing to rely upon.
We pray you have pity on us
and do not, for the sake of one person, abandon everyone to isolation.”
Then the Tàizǐ said to the multitude:
“Throughout the long ages of birth and death, I have lost my body countless times.
Among humans, out of greed, we have slaughtered one another;
in the heavens, when life ends,
there is the sorrow and suffering of losing desires;
in the hells, there is burning by fire and boiling in cauldrons,
axes, saws, knives, and halberds,
the River of Ash and the Forest of Sword-leaves.
Within a single day, the times I have lost my body are beyond calculation;
the pain penetrates to the core of my heart and marrow, and cannot be fully described.
Among hungry ghosts, a hundred poisons pierce the body.
Among animals, there is the suffering of providing one's body for others' mouths,
bearing heavy loads and eating grass; such suffering is also hard to count.
Vainly I have endured all these sufferings,
and in vain have I lost my life,
never once with a virtuous heart for the sake of the Dharma.
Now I take this foul and filthy body
to offer it for the sake of the Dharma.
Why would you all again wish to turn back my Unsurpassed resolve for the Way?
I discard this body to seek the Buddha Way;
when I attain Buddhahood in the future, I shall bestow upon you all the five-fold Dharma-body.”
The multitude remained silent.
At that time, the Tàizǐ stood above the fire pit and said to the Póluómén:
“I only pray that the Great Master will speak the Dharma for me!
Lest my life should end and I fail to hear the Dharma.”
Then the Póluómén spoke this verse:
“Always practice with a heart of kindness,
remove thoughts of anger and harm,
with great compassion, pity all living beings,
and weep tears of sympathy for their wounds.
Cultivate the heart of great joy,
regarding the Dharma one has attained as equal to others’,
and rescue and protect with the resolve for the Way;
only then is it in accord with the Púsà’s practice.”
Having spoken this verse,
he was about to throw himself into the fire.
At that time, Dìshì and Fàntiānwáng each grabbed one of his hands
and again questioned him:
“All living kinds within Yánfútí rely on the Tàizǐ’s kindness;
none have failed to find their place.
If you now throw yourself into the fire pit, the world will lose its father.
Why do you seek your own destruction and abandon everyone to isolation?”
Then the Tàizǐ replied to the Heaven Kings and all the subjects and people:
“Why do you obstruct my Unsurpassed resolve for the Way?”
The gods and the human multitude then each fell silent.
He immediately threw his body into the fire pit.
Heaven and Earth shook greatly,
and all the gods in the void cried out simultaneously,
their tears falling like heavy rain.
Instantly, the fire pit turned into a flower pond,
and the Tàizǐ sat upon a lotus pedestal within it.
The gods rained down flowers until they reached his knees.
At that time, the Fàntiān Dàwáng was the present royal father, Jìngfàn;
the mother at that time was the present Móyé;
the Tàizǐ Tánmóqián at that time was the present Shìzūn.
The Shìzūn at that time sought the Dharma in this way
for the sake of teaching sentient beings.
Now that it has been perfected and fulfilled,
you should moisten those withered and parched kinds.
Why would you then wish to depart into Nièpán and be unwilling to speak the Dharma?
Furthermore, Shìzūn!
Countless asengīya kalpas ago,
at that time in the kingdom of Bōluónài, there were five hundred immortals.
The teacher of the immortals was named Yùduōluó.
He constantly contemplated the True Dharma
and wished to cultivate and study it.
He sought it in the four directions, announcing to all:
‘If there is anyone who possesses the True Dharma
and will speak it for me,
I shall provide whatever they desire.’
A Póluómén came and responded, saying:
‘I have the True Dharma.
For whoever wishes to hear it,
I shall speak it.’
Then the teacher of the immortals joined his palms and said:
‘I only pray that you will show pity and compassion and deign to speak it.’
The Póluómén said:
‘Learning the Dharma is a difficult matter!
It is only obtained after long suffering.
How can you now wish to hear it just like that?
That is not reasonable.
If you are sincere and wish to obtain the Dharma,
you must follow my instructions.’
The immortal said:
‘I would not dare to disobey the Great Master’s commands.’
He then said:
‘If you can now flay your skin to make paper,
break your bones to make pens,
and use your blood to mix ink
to write down my Dharma,
then I shall speak it to you.’
When Yùduōluó heard these words,
he leaped with joy.
Respecting the teachings of the Rúlái,
he immediately flayed the skin from his body,
broke and took his own bones,
mixed ink with his blood,
and looked up to say:
‘Now is the time!
I only pray that you speak quickly!’
Then the Póluómén spoke this verse:
‘Always restrain the actions of the body,
and do not kill, steal, or commit adultery;
do not use double-tongued or harsh speech,
false words or flowery language;
let the heart not crave various desires,
and be without thoughts of anger or poison;
abandon all wrong views;
this is the Púsà’s practice.’
Having spoken this verse,
he immediately wrote it down himself,
and sent people to proclaim and transcribe it,
so that all the people within Yánfútí
were made to recite and read it
and practice according to the teaching.
The Shìzūn at that time sought the Dharma in this way,
without any regret in his heart for the sake of sentient beings.
Why would you now wish to abandon everyone,
enter into Nièpán, and not speak the Dharma?
“Furthermore, Shìzūn!
In the distant past, asengīya kalpas ago,
in Yánfútí, there was a great king
named Shībí.
The city where the king resided was called Típóbátí,
which was boundlessly prosperous and joyful.
At that time, King Shībí ruled over the eighty-four thousand small lands of Yánfútí,
sixty thousand mountains and rivers, and eight hundred billion villages.
The King had twenty thousand queens and maidens,
five hundred princes, and ten thousand ministers.
He practiced great kindness and compassion, pitying all.
At that time, the Heavenly Dìshì’s five virtues left his body,
his life was about to end,
and he was distressed and unhappy.
Píshǒuqiémó, seeing him like this,
came forward and said:
‘Why are you so distressed
and have such a sorrowful countenance?’
Dìshì replied:
‘My life is ending;
the signs of death have already appeared.
In the world today, the Buddha Dharma has already vanished,
and furthermore, there are no great Púsàs.
My heart does not know where to seek refuge;
that is why I am sorrowful.’
Píshǒuqiémó said to the Heavenly Dìshì:
‘Now in Yánfútí there is a great king practicing the Púsà Way,
named Shībí.
His resolve is firm and diligent,
and he will surely attain the Buddha Way.
You should go and seek refuge with him;
he will certainly be able to protect you
and rescue you from your peril.’
Dìshì said again:
‘If he is a Púsà, I must first test him
to see if he is sincere.
You transform into a dove,
and I will change into a hawk, chasing closely behind you.
We will follow each other to the place where that Dàwáng is sitting,
and you will seek his protection.
By this test, it will be sufficient to know whether he is true or false.’
Píshǒuqiémó replied again to the Heavenly Dìshì:
‘A great Púsà should not be subjected to suffering;
one should rather offer him worship,
and there is no need to coerce him with such a difficult matter.’
Then Dìshì spoke a verse:
‘I do not have an evil heart either;
as true gold should be tested,
so I use this to test the Púsà,
to know if he is sincere.’
Having spoken this verse, Píshǒuqiémó transformed himself into a dove,
and Dìshì became a hawk, chasing closely after the dove,
about to seize and eat it.
The dove, terrified, flew toward the Dàwáng,
and the hawk arrived immediately after, standing before the palace.
He addressed the Great King, saying:
“Now, this dove is my food.
It has come to the King’s side.
You should quickly return it to me;
my hunger is most urgent.”
King Shīpí said:
“I originally made a vow that I would deliver all beings.
This one has come to rely on me,
and I will never give it to you.”
The hawk spoke again, saying:
“Great King! Now you say you deliver all.
If you cut off my food, my life cannot be preserved.
Is my kind not part of ‘all’?”
The King then replied:
“If I give you other meat, would you be able to eat it?”
The hawk immediately said:
“Only if I obtain freshly killed warm meat
will I eat it.”
The King thought again:
“To seek freshly killed warm meat now
would mean harming one to save another; logically, there is no benefit.”
He contemplated within himself:
“Except for my own body,
all others that have life protect and cherish themselves.”
He then took a sharp knife, cut the flesh from his own thigh,
and held it out to give to the hawk
to trade for the life of this dove.
The hawk reported to the King:
“The King is a benefactor who views all equally.
Although I am a small bird, logically there should be no bias.
If you wish to use meat to trade for this dove,
it should be placed on a scale to be weighed.”
The King commanded his attendants:
“Quickly fetch a scale.”
They hung it by the middle hook and placed pans at both ends.
They immediately took the dove and placed it on one end,
and placed the flesh cut from his body on the other end.
Though he cut all the flesh from his thighs,
it was still lighter than the dove.
He further cut from both arms and both flanks
until the flesh of his body was exhausted,
yet it still did not equal the dove.
At that time, the Great King lifted his whole body, wishing to get onto the scale pan.
His strength failed him, and he slipped and fell to the ground.
He was unconscious and senseless, and only after a long time did he revive.
He rebuked his own heart:
“From long ago, I have been troubled by you,
wandering through the Three Realms,
tasting all bitterness and poison, yet never having performed such merit.
Now is the time for diligent practice,
not the time for indolence.”
After various rebukes,
he forced himself to stand up
and succeeded in getting onto the scale pan, his heart filled with joy,
considering it a good deed. At that moment, the earth shook in six ways,
and the palaces of the heavens all tilted and rocked.
Even the devas of the Form Realm descended together.
In the void, they saw the Púsà practicing what is difficult to practice,
damaging his own body,
his heart aspiring for the Great Dharma, disregarding his own life.
Each of them wept together, their tears like heavy rain,
and they rained down heavenly flowers as an offering.
At that time, Dìshì returned to his original form,
stood before the King, and said to the Great King:
“Now that you have performed such an unattainable deed,
what do you seek?
Do you now wish to become a Wheel-Turning Holy King, Dìshì, or Mówáng?
What do you seek within the Three Realms?”
The Púsà answered:
“What I seek is not the honor and pleasure of the Three Realms;
through the merit of my actions, I seek the path of the Buddha.”
The Heavenly Lord spoke again:
“You have now damaged your body even to the bone and marrow;
do you have any thoughts of regret?”
The King said: “None.”
The Heavenly Lord said again:
“Though you say you have no regret, who can know it?
I see your body trembling without ceasing,
your words and breath failing.
What evidence is there for saying you have no regret?”
The King then made a vow:
“From the beginning until now,
if I have had no regret even as large as a hair,
then the vow I seek shall certainly be attained.
If my words are sincere and not false,
let my body be immediately restored.”
After he finished making the vow, his body was restored,
even better than before.
The devas and the people of the world marveled at this unprecedented event,
jumping for joy, unable to contain themselves.
King Shīpí is the present body of the Buddha. In the past, the Shìzūn, for the sake of sentient beings,
disregarded his own life
to such an extent.
Now the Shìzūn’s Ocean of Dharma is full, the Dharma Banner is established,
the Dharma Drum is set up, and the Dharma Torch is shining.
The benefits of nourishment are established.
Now is exactly the right time.
How can you wish to abandon all sentient beings
and enter Nièpán without preaching the Dharma?”
At that time, Fànwáng, before the Rúlái, joined his palms in praise
and spoke of how the Rúlái
sought the Dharma in previous lives
for the sake of sentient beings a thousand times.
The Shìzūn then accepted Fànwáng’s request
and went to the Deer Park in the country of Bāluónà to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Because of this, the Triple Gem appeared in the world.
At that time, all the humans, devas, dragons, ghosts, and spirits,
the assembly of the eight departments,
having heard this, were all filled with joy,
and they accepted and practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the Jǐshù Gǐgūdú Garden in the country of Shèwèi.
At that time, when the hour for begging for food had come, the Shìzūn put on his robes, took his bowl,
and accompanied only by Ānán, entered the city to beg for food.
At that time, there was an old mother
who had only two sons. They were excessively thieving.
The owners of the property caught them and took them to the King.
The matter was settled according to the law; their crime warranted death.
They were handed over to the Zhāntuóluó
to be taken to the place of execution. From afar, they saw the Shìzūn!
The three, mother and sons, all turned toward the Buddha, bowing their heads and pleading for mercy:
“We only wish the Heavenly Honored One would condescend to save us from our suffering
and save my sons’ lives.”
Their sincerity was profound
and most piteous.
The Rúlái, with compassion and pity,
immediately sent Ānán to the King to plead for their lives.
When the King heard the Buddha’s instruction, he immediately released them.
Having escaped this disaster, they were deeply grateful for the Buddha’s kindness
and their joy was boundless. They immediately went to the Buddha’s place,
bowed their heads to his feet, joined their palms, and said:
“By the Buddha’s compassionate grace, our remaining lives have been saved.
We only wish the Heavenly Honored One would pity us and allow us to join the ranks of the Path.”
The Buddha consented and said:
“Welcome, Bǐqiū!”
Their hair and beards fell off naturally,
and the clothes they were wearing
transformed into Kāshā robes.
Reverence arose from within,
and their will and faith became even firmer.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them;
all impurities were forever exhausted,
and they attained the path of the Āluóhàn.
When their mother heard the Dharma, she attained the stage of Ānàhán.
At that time, Ānán, seeing this matter with his own eyes, marveled at the unprecedented event
and praised the Rúlái’s various virtuous conducts.
He also sighed in admiration:
“What past blessings did this mother and her two sons have
to encounter the Shìzūn, escape their heavy crimes,
and obtain the peace of Nièpán?
Within a single lifetime, they especially received such benefit;
how delightful!”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“These three people have not only been saved by me today;
in the past, they also received my grace and were saved.”
Ānán said to the Buddha:
“I do not know, Shìzūn, in the past ages,
how the matter of saving these three people occurred?”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“Long ago, in a distant Āsēngqí kalpa,
in this Yánfútí, there was a great king
named Móhēluótánnáng,
which in the language of Qín means ‘Great Treasure’.
He governed five thousand small kingdoms.
The King had three sons.
The first was named Móhēfùnàníng;
the next was named Móhētíbó, which in the language of Qín means ‘Great Heaven’;
and the next was named Móhēsàduǒ.
This youngest son
had practiced compassion since childhood,
pitying all beings as if they were his own infants.
At that time, the Great King, with his various ministers, consorts, and princes, went out to sightsee.
The King became tired and stopped for a short rest.
The King’s three sons went wandering together in the forest
and saw a tigress that had just given birth to two cubs.
She was pressed by extreme hunger and was about to eat them.
The King’s youngest son said to his two elder brothers:
‘Now this tigress is in an extremely bitter and wretched state,
emaciated and on the verge of death.
Moreover, having just given birth,
I see her intent is to eat her own cubs.’
The two elder brothers replied:
‘It is as you say.’
The younger brother then asked his brothers:
‘What should this tigress eat now?’”
The two elder brothers replied:
“If one could obtain the freshly killed warm blood and flesh of a being,
that would satisfy its intent.”
He asked again:
“Is there anyone now capable of performing such a deed to save this living being’s life
and allow it to survive?”
The two elder brothers answered, saying:
“This is a difficult matter.”
At that time, the King’s youngest son
thought to himself:
“Throughout the long cycle of births and deaths, I have sacrificed my body countless times,
giving up my life in vain,
sometimes for greed and desire, sometimes for anger and hatred,
or for ignorance, but never for the sake of the Dharma.
Now that I have encountered a field of merit,
why should I keep this body?”
Having made his plan, they proceeded forward together.
Before they had gone far, he said to his two elder brothers:
“Brothers, please go ahead;
I have a private matter
and will follow you shortly.”
After saying this,
he quickly took the original path
to where the tigress was
and threw himself down before her.
The hungry tigress’s mouth was clamped shut, and she could not eat.
At that time, the Prince took a sharp piece of wood
and pricked his body to draw blood.
The tigress licked it,
and her mouth then opened,
and she immediately ate the flesh of his body.
The two brothers waited for a long time and he did not return;
they followed his tracks to search for him.
Recalling his previous intention,
they knew he must have gone there to feed the hungry tigress.
Reaching the edge of the cliff, they saw Móhē Sàduǒ dead before the tigress;
the tigress had already eaten him, and blood and flesh were smeared everywhere.
They threw themselves to the ground, lost consciousness, and were as if dead.
After a long time, they revived,
weeping and rolling on the ground,
falling into a daze and fainting again, and then reviving once more.
The Queen Consort was sleeping
and dreamed of three pigeons playing together in the forest;
suddenly a hawk caught the smallest one and ate it.
Having awakened, she was terrified
and spoke of it to the King:
“I have heard the proverb:
‘Pigeons represent children and grandchildren.’
Now the little pigeon is gone;
my beloved child will surely meet with misfortune.”
Immediately, messengers were sent in four directions to search for him.
Before long, the two sons arrived.
The parents asked:
“Where is my beloved son now?”
The two sons choked with sobs;
their breath was stifled, and they could not make a sound.
After a long time, they finally spoke:
“The tigress has already eaten him.”
Hearing this, the parents
fell to the ground unconscious and insensible.
After a long while they revived,
and immediately, with the two sons, the Queen, and the ladies-in-waiting, they rushed to the place of the corpse.
At that time, the hungry tigress had finished eating the flesh,
and only the bones remained scattered on the ground.
The mother held his head,
the father took his hand,
and they wailed in grief until they fainted;
they fainted and then revived.
After a long time had passed like this,
after the death of Móhē Sàduǒ, he was born in the Dōushuài Heaven.
He immediately thought:
“By what action have I come to receive this reward?”
With the divine eye, he saw clearly throughout the five realms
and saw his former corpse still in the mountains,
and his parents grieving in deep, agonizing pain,
pitying their delusion and excessive weeping.
“They might lose their lives because of this;
I must go now to counsel and comfort them.”
He immediately descended from heaven and stood in the air,
using various words to console and counsel his parents.
The parents looked up and asked:
“What deity are you?
We pray you tell us.”
The deity immediately replied:
“I am the Prince Móhē Sàduǒ.
Because I gave my body to save the hungry and exhausted tigress,
I was born in the Dōushuài Heaven.
Great King, you should know!
All that exists returns to nothingness; life must have an end.
Evil leads to falling into hell,
while doing good leads to birth in heaven.
Birth and death are the common path;
why are you now solely submerged in the sea of sorrow and affliction,
not awakening to diligently practice all kinds of good?”
The parents replied:
“You practiced great compassion and had pity on all beings,
leaving us to meet your end.
My heart thinks of you;
it is desolate and broken,
and my suffering is immeasurable.
You practiced great compassion;
how could it result in this?”
At that time, the heavenly being
again used various
wonderful and good verses to respond to and thank his parents.
The parents then gained a bit of awakening.
They made a casket of the seven treasures to hold the bones within,
and after the burial was completed,
they built a stupa over it.
The deity then vanished.
The King and the great assembly returned to the palace.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“The Great King of that time, Móhē Luótánnà, was he anyone else?
He is my father, King Yuètóután.
The Queen of that time
was my mother, Móhē Móyē.
He who was Móhē Fùnàníng
is now Mílè.
The second prince, Móhē Tíbó,
is now Póxiūmìduōluó.
The Prince Móhē Sàduǒ of that time, was he anyone else?
It was I.
The mother tigress of that time
is this old woman now.
The two cubs of that time
are these two people now.
Long ago, I saved their lives from urgent distress and peril,
making them safe.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood,
I also save them from distress,
making them forever free from the great suffering of birth and death.”
At that time, Ānán and all the members of the assembly,
having heard what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and followed it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was at Shèwèi Guó in the Qíshù Gěigūdú Yuán.
At that time, during the first watch of the night, two deities came to where the Buddha was;
the light of the heavenly beings’ bodies illuminated the Qíhuán,
all like the color of gold.
The Buddha then, according to what was appropriate, expounded the wonderful Dharma.
Their minds were awakened, and both attained the path;
they bowed their heads to the Buddha’s feet
and returned to the heavens.
The next morning, Ānán said to the Buddha:
“Last night two deities came to see the Shìzūn.
Their majestic appearance was brilliant
and their pure light was radiant.
What merit did they plant in the past
to obtain such a wonderful result?”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“After the Parinirvāṇa of Jiāshè Tathāgata,
when his bequeathed Dharma was coming to an end,
there were two Póluómén who received and upheld the eight precepts.
One of them made a vow to be born in heaven;
the second one sought to become a king.
The first one returned to his home,
and his wife called him to eat together.
The husband replied to his wife:
‘I have just received the Buddha’s precepts;
after noon I do not eat.’
The wife said again:
‘You are a Fànzhì
and have your own rules of conduct;
for what reason do you receive the precepts of another path?
If you now go against me and do not eat with me,
I shall speak of this matter to all the Fànzhì,
and have them drive you out and exclude you from the assemblies.’
Hearing these words, he was deeply terrified,
and so he ate with his wife at the improper time.
According to the length of their lives, each met their end.
The one who wished to be a king had kept the precepts perfectly
and was born into a royal family.
The one who wished to be born in heaven,
because he broke the precepts,
was born among the dragons.
At that time there was a man who tended the garden for the King,
daily offering various fruits and vegetables.
Later, this man found a unique nà fruit in the spring water,
its color and fragrance were very beautiful.
He then thought:
‘Every time I go in or out,
I am often stopped or sent back by the gatekeeper;
I should give it to him.’
As he thought, so he gave it. The gatekeeper, having received it,
thought to himself:
‘Whenever I report matters, I am always held back by the Huángmén;
I should give it to him.’
He then used this nà fruit to present to the Huángmén.
The Huángmén, after accepting it,
turned and presented it to the Queen Consort.
The Queen Consort received the nà fruit and then offered it to the King. The King ate this nà fruit and found it extremely sweet and delicious,
and then asked the Queen:
“Where did you get this?”
The consort immediately replied truthfully according to the facts,
and the matter was passed from one person to another until it reached the garden supervisor.
The King then summoned him and asked, saying:
“In my garden there are such beautiful fruits;
why were they not offered to me,
but instead given to others?”
Thereupon, the garden supervisor recounted the entire story from beginning to end.
The King spoke again, saying:
“From now on, regularly send these *nài* fruits;
do not let the supply be cut off.”
The garden supervisor reported, saying:
“These *nài* fruits have no stock for planting.
They were obtained from a spring.
If I am commanded to send them regularly,
there is no means by which it can be managed.”
The King spoke again, saying:
“If you cannot obtain them, I shall have you executed.”
The garden supervisor went out and returned to the garden,
where he was filled with sorrow and distress, crying out in a loud voice.
At that time, there was a *Lóng* who heard the sound of his crying.
He transformed himself into a man and came to ask him, saying:
“What matter do you have
that makes you weep so sorrowfully?”
At that time, the garden supervisor explained everything.
The *Lóng* returned into the water,
placed many beautiful fruits upon a golden tray,
and gave them to this man,
then told him:
“You may take these fruits to offer to your King,
and also convey my message.
Say that I and the King were originally close friends;
in a former life, we were both *Fànzhì*.
Together we received the *Bāzhāi*
and each sought what we desired.
Your precepts were complete, so you were able to become a king of men;
my precepts were incomplete, so I was born among the *Lóng*.
Now I wish to practice and cultivate the *Zhāi fǎ* to seek to discard this body.
I wish to request the *Bāguānzhāi fǎ* to be sent to me.
If this is refused,
I shall submerge your kingdom
and turn it into a great sea.”
Thereupon, the garden supervisor presented the fruit to the King
and then recounted the instructions and the transformations of the *Lóng*.
When the King heard this, he was extremely unhappy.
Why was this?
At that time, there was no *Fó* in the world, and the *Fǎ*
was also extinguished. The *Bāguānzhāi Wén*
could not be obtained now.
If he did not fulfill it,
he feared he would encounter harm.
Only by contemplating this matter,
was he therefore sorrowful and distressed.
The King had a minister whom he respected most.
The King told the minister:
“A divine *Lóng* has requested the *Zhāi fǎ* from me.
I rely on you, my lord, to obtain it,
and it shall be sent to him.”
The minister replied:
“In the present world, there is no *Fǎ*.
How can it be obtained?”
The King spoke again:
“If you do not find it now,
I shall kill you.”
When the minister heard this, he was very much distressed.
He went to his own home.
This minister had a father who was aged and elderly.
Every time the minister came from outside, he showed a gentle and pleasant countenance
to comfort his father’s mind.
At that time, the father saw that his son’s
facial expression had changed from usual, so he immediately asked him:
“For what reason is it thus?”
Then the minister explained the details to his father.
His father replied:
“The hall pillars of our house often manifest light.
Try breaking them open to see if perhaps there is something extraordinary?”
Following his father’s instructions, he ordered others to fell the pillar,
taking it to be cut and split open.
He obtained two scrolls of sutras:
one was the *Shí'èr Yīnyuán Jīng*,
and the second was the *Bāguānzhāi Wén*.
The minister immediately took them and presented them to the King.
The King was filled with a joy he could not contain.
He then placed these sutras on a golden tray
and personally sent them to the *Lóng*.
When the *Lóng* obtained these sutras, he was greatly delighted.
He then used fine treasures to present as a gift to the King.
He received and upheld the *Bāzhāi*, diligently practicing them.
After his life ended, he was born in a heavenly palace.
The human King also cultivated and practiced the *Zhāi fǎ*.
When his life ended, he was born in heaven in the same place.
Last night, they came together to inquire about and receive the teachings of the *Fǎ*.
They immediately attained the fruit of *Xūtuóhuán*,
forever ceasing the three miserable paths,
and wandering in the ways of humans and heavens.
From now on, they will ultimately attain *Nièpán*.”
When the *Fó* said this,
the entire assembly
rejoiced and followed the teachings.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, at the Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, there was a great elder in the kingdom
who fathered a baby boy.
His face and head were upright and handsome.
A few days after he was born,
he was already able to speak,
and he asked his parents:
"Is the Shìzūn still here or not?"
They answered:
"He is still here."
He asked again:
"Are the Venerable Shèlìfú,
Ānán, and the others
all still here or not?"
They replied:
"They are all here."
When the parents saw that their son could speak as soon as he was born,
they thought he was not human
and were deeply bewildered as to the reason,
so they went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This child has merit;
there is no need to doubt."
The parents were delighted
and returned to their home.
The boy spoke to them again, saying:
"I only wish, my two parents,
that you would invite the Buddha and the Bǐqiū Sangha for me."
The parents told him:
"To invite the Buddha and the Sangha,
one must have offerings and utensils;
this cannot be prepared in haste."
The boy spoke again:
"Just sweep and sprinkle the halls and rooms,
adorn the couches and mats,
and set out three high seats.
Food and drink of a hundred flavors
will arrive naturally.
Furthermore, the mother from my previous life
still exists today,
living in the kingdom of Bōluónài;
summon her for me."
The parents followed his words
and sent a person riding an elephant
to race and summon her.
The reason for setting up three high seats was:
one for the Rúlái,
one for his mother from his previous birth,
and one for the mother of his current life.
After the Buddha and the assembly of monks
had entered the house
and sat down in order,
sweet meals and fine flavors
were naturally abundant.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
The father, the two mothers,
and the whole family, great and small,
heard the Dharma and rejoiced,
and all attained the first fruit of the path.
As this child grew older,
he took his leave to become a monk,
diligently applied himself to the right path,
and attained the state of an Luóhàn.
Ānán said to the Buddha:
"This Shāmén,
what merit did he plant in the past
to be born into a noble and wealthy family,
to be able to speak while small,
and then to study the Way
and attain supernatural powers?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In a previous life, this man
was born in Bōluónài
as the son of an elder.
After his father passed away,
the family business declined
and they gradually became poor.
Although he lived in the time of a Buddha,
he had nothing with which to make offerings.
Distressed by this
and unable to find peace of mind,
he left his noble clan
and sought work as a hired laborer.
After completing a full year,
he asked for a thousand taels of gold.
The nobleman asked:
'Do you wish to take a wife?'
He replied:
'No.'
The nobleman asked again:
'What will you do with the gold?'
He replied:
'I wish to use it to provide a meal for the Buddha and the holy Sangha.'
The nobleman said:
'If you wish to invite the Buddha,
I shall give you the gold and also manage the gathering at my house.'
The poor man agreed,
and so fine food was prepared,
inviting the Buddha and the Sangha.
Because of this cause and condition,
after his life ended,
he was born into an elder's family,
and now he has again invited the Buddha,
heard the Dharma, and attained the Way."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"The poor man of long ago
is this monk, the son of the elder today."
When the Buddha said this,
the whole assembly
was filled with joy,
and they respectfully received and practiced it. (
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, at the Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants in this kingdom
who entered the sea to gather treasures.
They consulted among themselves, saying:
"We should seek a wise person to act as our guide."
They then invited a Yōupósè who kept the Five Precepts to enter the great sea with them.
Once they reached the middle of the sea, the sea god transformed his body into a Yèchā,
with a hideous and loathsome form;
his color was bluish-black,
long fangs protruding from his mouth,
and fire burning on his head.
He came to pull their ship and asked the merchants:
"In the world, is there anything fearsome that surpasses me?"
The virtuous man replied:
"There are things even more fearsome, many times more terrible than you."
The sea god asked again:
"What are they?"
He replied:
"In the world, there are foolish people who perform all kinds of unwholesome deeds,
killing living beings, stealing, and committing licentious and unrestrained acts;
lying, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, frivolous talk, greed, and hatred,
and being submerged in wrong views.
Upon death, they enter hell and undergo ten thousand kinds of suffering.
The hell wardens, the Āpáng, take the sinners and punish them in various ways,
either hacking them with blades or tearing them apart with chariots,
breaking their bodies into thousands of pieces.
Or they are pounded in mortars or ground in mills;
the mountains of knives and trees of swords, the fire chariots and boiling cauldrons,
the freezing ice and boiling excrement—they undergo all of these.
Enduring such suffering for tens of millions of years—
this is more fearsome than you by far."
The sea god let them go
and vanished from sight.
After the ship advanced a few miles, the sea god transformed himself into another person
whose body was emaciated and withered,
with only sinews and bones holding together.
Again he came to pull the ship
and asked the men:
"In the world, is there anyone more emaciated than me?"
The virtuous man answered:
"There are those even more emaciated than you."
The sea god asked again:
"Who is more so?"
The virtuous man replied:
"There are foolish people with evil natures,
stingy, greedy, and envious,
who do not know how to practice generosity.
Upon death, they fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Their bodies are as large as mountains,
but their throats are like the eye of a needle.
Their hair is long and disheveled,
and their bodies are black and withered.
For tens of millions of years, they do not even know the names of water or grain.
Such forms are even more emaciated than yours."
The sea god released the ship
and disappeared.
The ship sailed for a few miles, and the sea god transformed himself again into a person
who was extremely handsome and upright.
He came again to pull the ship
and asked the merchants:
"Among humans, is there any beauty equal to mine?"
The virtuous man replied:
"There are those who surpass you by hundreds of thousands or millions of times."
The sea god asked again:
"Who is superior?"
The virtuous man replied:
"In the world, there are wise people who practice all kinds of goodness,
always keeping the actions of their body, speech, and mind pure.
They have faith and respect for the Triple Gem and make offerings at all times.
When such people die, they are born in the heavens.
Their appearance is bright and pure, uniquely handsome and upright,
surpassing you tens of millions of times.
Comparing you to them
is like comparing a blind macaque to a beautiful woman."
The Hǎishén took a handful of water and asked him,
"Is there more water in this handful, or is there more sea water?"
The Xiánzhě answered,
"The water in the handful is more; it is not the sea water."
The Hǎishén asked again,
"Is what you have just said the utmost truth or not?"
The Xiánzhě answered,
"These words are the absolute truth and are not false.
How can this be made clear?
Although sea water is plentiful,
it must eventually be exhausted.
When the Jié is about to end and two suns rise together,
the spring sources, pools, and streams will all dry up;
when three suns rise,
the various small rivers will all wither and dry;
when four suns rise,
the various great rivers and seas will all be exhausted;
when five suns rise,
the great sea will slightly diminish;
when six suns rise,
two-thirds of it will diminish;
when seven suns rise,
the sea water will be entirely gone,
Xūmí will collapse and be destroyed,
and down to the Jīngāngdìjì,
all will be scorched and burned.
If there is someone who can, with a heart of faith, take a handful of water to make an offering to the Fó,
or use it to give to the Sēng, or serve their parents,
or bestow it upon the poor, or give it to birds and beasts,
the merit of this will not be exhausted throughout successive Jié.
Based on this,
one knows the sea is little and the handful of water is much."
The Hǎishén was delighted
and immediately gave precious treasures to the Xiánzhě,
and also sent wondrous treasures to be offered to the Fó and the Sēng.
At that time, the various merchants, along with the Xiánzhě, had collected sufficient treasures
and returned to their home country.
At that time, the Xiánzhě and the five hundred merchants all went to the Fó's place,
prostrated at the Fó's feet,
and after completing the rites,
each held their treasures along with those sent by the Hǎishén to offer to the Fó and the Sēng.
They all knelt formally with palms joined and said to the Fó:
"We wish to be disciples and receive your pure transformation."
The Fó soon permitted them.
"Welcome, Bǐqiū!"
Their beards and hair fell off spontaneously,
and dharma robes appeared on their bodies.
The Fó spoke the Dharma for them,
responding to their dispositions;
they were instantly awakened,
all desires were completely purified,
and they attained the status of Āluóhàn.
At that time, all those in the assembly,
hearing what the Fó had spoken,
were all greatly rejoiced,
and they received and practiced it with honor.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in Luóyuèqí at the Zhúyuán Jīngshè.
At that time, there was a chief minister in the kingdom
whose family was very wealthy,
but he had no son.
At that time, on the banks of the Hénghé,
there was a shrine to the deity Móníbáluó,
which the people of the whole land
all respectfully worshipped.
Then this chief minister
went to the shrine
and prayed, saying:
"I have no offspring.
I have heard that you, heavenly deity,
have immeasurable merit
and protect all living beings,
being able to grant their wishes.
I now come to seek refuge.
If my wish is granted
and you bestow upon me a son,
I shall adorn the deity's body with gold and silver
and coat the divine chamber with famous incense;
but if there is no proof of your power,
I shall destroy your temple and smear your body with dung."
When the deity heard this,
he thought to himself:
"This man is wealthy and powerful,
and his influence is strong;
he is no ordinary person
who could easily have a son born to him.
My merit is meager and small,
and I cannot grant his wish.
If the wish is not fulfilled,
I will surely be disgraced and insulted."
The shrine deity then went again to inform Móníbáluó.
Móníbáluó's power was also not sufficient for the task,
so he went personally to Píshāmén Wáng to report this matter.
Píshāmén said:
"Neither is it within my power to cause him to have a son;
we should go to the Heavenly Emperor to seek this wish."
Píshāmén Wáng immediately ascended to heaven and addressed Dìshì, saying:
"I have a subordinate named Móníbáluó
who recently spoke to me, saying:
'In Wángshè Chéng there is a chief minister
who seeks a son from him
and has made a solemn vow:
if the wish is fulfilled,
he will double his offerings;
but if the wish is thwarted,
he will destroy my temple and humiliate me.'
That man is powerful and fierce;
he will certainly do as he says.
I hope the Heavenly King
will cause him to have a son."
Dìshì replied:
"This matter is extremely difficult;
we must look for a suitable cause."
At that time, there was a heavenly being
whose five signs of decay had appeared,
and his life was about to end.
Dìshì told him:
"Your life is at its end;
would you be willing to be born into the house of that chief minister?"
The heavenly being answered:
"I intend to leave the household life and pursue correct practice.
If I am born into a noble and honored family,
it will be difficult to leave worldly life;
I fear being caught in the middle and not fulfilling my aim."
Dìshì said again:
"Just go and be born there.
If you wish to study the Way,
I shall assist you."
The heavenly being's life ended,
and his spirit descended to take conception in the house of the chief minister.
After he was born and grew up,
his appearance was upright and handsome.
They immediately summoned a physiognomist
to give him a name.
The physiognomist asked:
"From where did you originally seek and obtain this child?"
The chief minister replied:
"In the past, I sought him from the deity of the Hénghé."
Therefore, he named him
Héngqiédá.
As he gradually grew older,
his will was set upon the Buddha's Law.
He then informed his parents,
seeking to leave the household life.
His parents told him:
"We are now wealthy and noble,
with vast estates.
You are our only son
and must succeed to our lineage.
While we are still alive,
we will never permit it."
Because his wish was not granted, the son felt deep sorrow.
He then wished to discard his body and seek birth in a common place,
thinking that seeking liberation from there
would surely be very easy.
Thereupon, he secretly departed
and threw himself from a high cliff;
having fallen to the ground,
he suffered no injury.
He then went to the riverbank
and threw himself into the water;
the water floated him back out,
and he suffered no harm.
He then took poison
and swallowed it;
the poison did not take effect,
and he had no way to die.
He thought again:
"I should violate the law and be executed by the King."
He encountered the King's consort and various palace ladies
who had left the palace to bathe in a garden pool.
They had all taken off their clothes
and placed them among the trees.
At that time, Héngqiédá secretly entered the woods,
took their garments and ornaments, and walked out clutching them.
The gate guards saw him
and took him to report to Āshéshì Wáng.
When the King heard of this,
his anger flared up greatly.
He took up his bow and arrows
to shoot him with his own hand,
but the arrow turned back
and flew straight toward the King's own body.
This happened up to three times,
and he could not make it hit him.
Terrified, the King dropped the bow
and asked the man:
"Are you a deity, a dragon, a ghost, or a spirit?"
Héngqiédá said:
"Grant me one wish,
and then I shall dare to explain myself."
The King said:
"It shall be granted."
Héngqiédá said:
"I am not a deity,
nor a dragon or a ghost;
I am the son of the chief minister of the kingdom of Wángshè.
I wish to leave the household life,
but my parents will not permit it.
Therefore, I wished to kill myself to be born in another place.
I threw myself from a cliff,
plunged into a river,
and drank poison, yet I did not die.
Thus I violated the King's law,
hoping to end my life.
Now the King tries to kill me,
yet again I cannot be harmed.
Since the situation is thus,
how can it be so cruel!
I pray you show compassion and permit me to follow the Way."
The King immediately said:
"I permit you to leave the household life and study the Sagely Way."
He then took him
to the Buddha's place
and reported to the World-Honored One
what had just occurred.
At that time, the Rúlái
permitted him to become a Shāmén.
With the dharma robes on his body,
he became a Bǐqiū.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him;
his mind became clear and joyful,
and he achieved the path of an Luóhàn,
mastering the Three Insights and Six Supernatural Powers,
and attaining the Eight Liberations.
Āshéshì Wáng then said to the Buddha:
"This Héngqiédá,
in previous lives,
what roots of virtue did he plant,
that he did not die when falling from a mountain,
did not drown when falling into water,
suffered no pain from eating poison,
was not harmed when shot with arrows,
and moreover met the Holy One and gained liberation from birth and death?"
The Buddha told the King:
"Long ago, in countless past ages,
there was a great kingdom
named Bōluónài.
Its king was named Fànmódá.
He took the palace attendants
into the forest to amuse themselves.
The various palace ladies
raised their voices and sang.
Outside, there was a man
who harmonized with them in a loud voice.
The king heard the sound
and immediately became angry and jealous.
He sent men to capture him and ordered his execution.
At that time, there was a great minister
who was coming from the outside.
He saw this man
being held prisoner
and asked those around him:
'For what reason is this so?'
The people nearby
explained the situation in detail."
The Chén said:
“Stop!
Wait for me to see the Wáng.”
The Dàchén entered
and reported to the Wáng, saying:
“That person's crime
is not so severe;
why kill him?
Although their voices were harmonized,
they did not see each other's forms.
Since there was no act of intercourse or illicit lust,
I humbly hope you will bestow compassion
and grant him his life.”
The Wáng could not refuse
and pardoned him from execution.
Having escaped, that man
served the Dàchén
with diligence and caution, never ceasing.
Serving him in this way
for many years,
he then thought to himself:
“Lustful desire harms people,
more sharply than swords and blades.
My current distress
is entirely due to the cause of desire.”
He then said to the Dàchén:
“Allow me to leave the household life to follow and practice the Dàoyè.”
The Dàchén replied:
“I dare not oppose you.
If your studies lead you to attain the Dào,
come back to see me.”
He then went to the mountains and marshes
to focus his thoughts on the profound principles.
His spirit attained enlightenment,
and he became a Bìzhīfó.
He returned to the city
and went to the Dàchén’s house.
The Dàchén was joyful
and requested to make offerings to him
with delicious food and fine robes,
lacking none of the four requirements.
At that time, the Bìzhīfó,
in the midst of the void,
manifested supernatural transformations,
his body emitting water and fire
and radiating great light.
The Dàchén saw this
and was boundlessly delighted;
he then made a vow:
“Because of my kindness,
his life was saved.
May I, in every lifetime, be wealthy, honored, and long-lived,
exceptionally extraordinary,
tens of millions of times over,
and let my wisdom and virtue be equal to his.”
The Fó told the Wáng:
“The Dàchén of that time,
who saved a person
and enabled him to attain the Dào,
is now Hénggádá.
Because of these causes and conditions,
wherever he is born,
his life does not end prematurely.
Now that he has encountered me,
he has attained the state of Yìngzhēn.”
After the Fó said this,
all those in the assembly
were filled with faith, respect, and joy,
and they bowed to receive and practice the teaching.
Thus have I heard:
Once the Fó was at the Zhú-yuán Jīng-shè in Luó-yuè-qí.
At that time, the Shì-zūn was with Ā-nán,
donning their robes and carrying their alms bowls,
entering the city to beg for food.
At that time, there were an old man and an old woman
who were both blind,
poor and suffering in isolation,
having no place to stay,
taking shelter under a city gate.
They had only one son,
just seven years of age,
who often went begging to support his parents.
When he obtained good fruits or vegetables,
the best ones
he would offer to his parents;
the leftover scraps that were sour or astringent,
foul-smelling, and bad,
he would eat himself.
At that time, Ā-nán,
seeing this young child,
though young in years,
was respectful and filial,
and he felt love and admiration in his heart.
After the Fó finished begging for food,
he returned to the monastery.
At that time, the Shì-zūn was expounding the Dharma to the great assembly.
Ā-nán then knelt for a long time with palms pressed together,
stepped forward and addressed the Fó, saying:
"Earlier, with the Shì-zūn,
I entered the city for the alms-round
and saw a young child
who was compassionate and filial.
Together with his blind parents,
he stayed under the city gate.
Of the things he obtained by begging here and there,
whether cooked food, vegetables, or fruit,
the best ones
he first offered to his old parents.
Those that were spoiled, foul-smelling, and very bad,
he would eat himself.
Day after day it was like this,
and he is most worthy of love and respect."
The Fó said to Ā-nán:
"Whether one has left home or is a householder,
to have a compassionate heart and be filial,
providing for one's parents—
when calculating its merit,
it is supreme and immeasurable.
Why is this?
I recall in past lives,
I was compassionate and filial,
providing for my parents,
even to the point of using the flesh of my own body to save my parents from the disaster of a critical crisis.
Because of this merit,
I became Tiān-dì above,
a Sagely Ruler below,
and even achieved Buddhahood as the Peerless Honored One of the Three Realms;
all this is due to such blessings."
Ā-nán addressed him, saying:
"I do not know,
Shì-zūn!
In past lives,
how you were compassionate and filial to your parents,
not sparing your own life,
being able to use the flesh of your own body
to rescue the lives of your parents from danger—
what was that matter like?"
The Fó told Ā-nán:
"Listen attentively and reflect well!
I shall speak of it."
Ā-nán said:
"Yes indeed,
I shall listen well!"
The Fó told Ā-nán:
"In the past, immeasurable, uncountable, countless kalpas ago,
there was a great country in this Yán-fú-tí,
named Tè-chā-shī-lì.
At that time, there was a king
named Tí-pó.
At that time, the king of that country
had ten crown princes,
each governing various lands.
The youngest crown prince
was named Xiū-pó-luó-tí-zhì,
which in the Jìn language is Shàn-zhù.
In the territory he governed,
the people looked up to him,
and it was the most prosperous and joyful.
By the side of the father king,
there was a high minister
named Luó-hóu,
who constantly harbored treacherous and rebellious thoughts
and eventually rebelled and killed the Great King.
The Great King having died,
he seized the government and became king,
then immediately dispatched troops
to go to the various lands
and kill all the crown princes.
This youngest one
was respected by ghosts and spirits.
At that time, as he entered a garden
intending to go for a stroll,
a Yè-chā
emerged from the ground,
knelt for a long time, and said:
'The minister Luó-hóu
has rebelled and killed your father the king,
and has dispatched troops
to kill your elder brothers.
Now he has further dispatched people
who intend to come and kill you.
Your Majesty should devise a plan to avoid this calamity.'
When the king heard this,
his heart collapsed in terror and fear.
When that night came,
he thought over a plan,
wishing to break away and flee.
At that time, he had a son
named Xū-shé-tí,
which in the Jìn language is Shàn-shēng.
He had reached the age of seven,
was handsome and clever,
and was very much beloved.
The king cherished him;
going out and returning again,
he embraced this child,
weeping and sighing in sorrow.
His wife, seeing the king entering and leaving in such panic,
immediately asked him:
'Why are you in such a rush,
appearing as if in terror?'
Her husband replied:
'It is not something for you to know.'
The wife pulled at him again:
'Now I am with you,
our lives joined together, following each other through danger.
Do not abandon me.
What matter is there now
that you should inform me of?'
The king replied:
'Recently, as I entered the garden,
a Yè-chā ghost emerged from the ground
and knelt for a long time to tell me:
"The minister Luó-hóu
has now committed an evil rebellion;
he has already killed your father the king,
dispatched troops
to kill your elder brothers,
and has now also dispatched troops
who are coming to kill the king.
You should avoid them."
When I heard these words,
my heart was filled with terror.
I only fear the troops
will arrive like this,
and for this reason, I must hurry
and wish to leave.'
His wife knelt for a long time
and immediately said to the king:
'I wish to follow and serve you;
do not leave me isolated and abandoned.'
Thereupon, the king took his wife and embraced his son,
and they set off together,
wishing to reach another country.
At that time, there were two paths:
one path took seven days,
the other path took fourteen days.
When they first set out in panic,
they only prepared a seven-day supply of food,
intended for only one person.
Having already left the city,
his mind was in turmoil,
and he thus took the fourteen-day path.
Several days had already passed,
the food was exhausted,
and they were hungry, confused, and desperate.
Having no other plan,
and although he loved his son,
he wished to kill his wife
so that he might save himself and keep the child alive.
He ordered his wife to go in front carrying the child,
while he followed behind, drawing his sword to kill her.
At that time, the child looked back,
saw his father drawing the sword to kill his mother,
and the child pressed his palms together,
reasoning with his father the king, saying:
'I beg of you, Great King!
I would rather you kill my own body
than harm my mother.'
He earnestly pleaded with his father
to save his mother's life,
and said to his father:
'Do not kill me all at once;
cut and eat me piece by piece,
so that it may last for several days.
If you end my life...
"The meat would then smell and rot,
and could not be kept for long."
Thereupon, the parents,
wishing to cut the boy’s flesh,
wept and were filled with anguish,
yet they cut and ate it.
Day after day they cut and ate,
until his flesh was almost gone
and only the bones remained.
Before they reached the other country,
the famine became even more severe.
The father again took up the knife
and at his joints
stripped them in succession,
thereby obtaining a little meat.
At this, the parents
were about to abandon him and go on.
The boy thought to himself:
"My life remains but a little.
I only wish that my parents,
from all the meat they have,
would give a small portion back to me."
The parents did not refuse
and immediately made three portions:
two portions for themselves to eat,
and one portion remained,
which, along with the remnants of muscle, eyes, tongue, and such, they gave entirely to him.
Then they parted.
The boy then made a vow:
"With my body's flesh now
having made offerings to my parents,
I hold this merit
to seek the Fó dào
and universally save all sentient beings of the ten directions,
causing them to leave all suffering and reach the joy of Nièpán."
When he made this vow,
the three thousand worlds shook in six ways.
The gods of the Sèyù realms were all struck with wonder,
not knowing why their palaces were shaking.
They immediately used their divine eyes to observe the world
and saw the Púsà using the flesh of his body to make offerings to his parents,
vowing to achieve the Fó dào
and swearing to deliver sentient beings.
Because of this,
the heavens and earth shook greatly.
Then all the gods
all came down,
filling the void,
weeping and shedding tears
like a heavy rain.
At that time, Tiāndìshì came wishing to test him;
he transformed into a beggar
and came to beg from him.
Holding the meat in his hand,
the boy again gave it away.
Then the god again transformed into a lion, tiger, and wolf,
coming as if to devour him.
The boy thought to himself:
"If these beasts
wish to eat me,
I shall give them all the remaining bones, flesh, marrow, and brain of my body."
His heart gave rise to joy
without any regret.
At that time, Tiāndì
saw that his resolve was firm and his heart did not waver;
he resumed his form as Shì,
stood before the boy,
and spoke to him, saying:
"In your kindness and filial piety,
you were able to use your body's flesh to make offerings to your parents.
With this merit,
what do you seek?
To be Tiāndì, Mówáng, or Fàntiānwáng?"
The boy immediately replied, saying:
"I do not wish to seek the happiness of the Sānjiè.
I hold this merit
to seek the Fó dào,
wishing to deliver all immeasurable sentient beings."
Tiāndì spoke again:
"You were able to use your body to make offerings to your parents;
did you have no regret toward your parents?"
The boy replied:
"I am now perfectly sincere
in making offerings to my parents;
I have no regret even as large as a hair."
Tiāndì spoke again:
"I see you now,
the flesh of your body is already gone,
yet you say you have no regret;
this is difficult to believe."
The boy replied:
"If I have no regret
and am destined to become a Fó,
may my body be restored as it was before."
Once his oath was finished,
his body was immediately restored.
At that time, Tiāndìshì and the other gods,
with different mouths but one voice,
praised him, saying, "Shànzāi!"
The boy's parents and the people of the country
all came to where the boy was
and marveled at this unprecedented event.
At that time, the Guówáng of that country
saw the extraordinary deeds performed by the Tàizǐ
and increased his respect twofold.
With immeasurable joy,
he took the parents and the Tàizǐ
into the palace to make offerings to them,
showing them extreme respect
and pitying this Tàizǐ.
At that time, the Guówáng
personally led his horses and soldiers,
together with Guówáng Shànzhù and Tàizǐ Xūshétí,
back to their original country.
They executed Luóhóu
and established the original king,
with father and son succeeding each other.
The country became abundant and joyful,
eventually reaching great peace."
The Fó said to Ānán:
"The Guówáng Shànzhù of that time
is my current father, Guówáng Báijìng.
The mother of that time
is my current mother, Móhē-móyē.
The Tàizǐ Xūshétí of that time
is my current self."
The Fó said to Ānán:
"Because of his compassionate heart and filial obedience in past lives,
making offerings to his parents
and using his body's flesh
to save his parents from distress,
through this merit,
among gods and humans,
he was always born noble and honored
and received immeasurable blessings.
Through this merit,
he naturally achieved Buddhahood."
At that time, the great assembly,
hearing the Fó himself speak of his past causal origins,
were all moved to sighs of sorrow and admiration,
touched by the Fó's extraordinary deeds of kindness and filial piety.
Among them, there were those who attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn.
Some made the vow for the unsurpassed right and true path,
and some stayed in the stage of non-retrogression.
The entire assembly
was filled with great joy
and received the teachings with devotion.

Translated in Gāochāng Jùn by the Liángzhōu Shàmén Huìjué and others during the Yuán Wèi Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Fó was in the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán in the Kingdom of Shèwèi.
At that time, the chief consort of Guówáng Bōsīnuì was named Mòlì.
She gave birth to a daughter named Bōshéluó, which in the Jìn language means Jīngāng.
The daughter's face was extremely ugly,
her skin and body were rough and coarse like camel skin,
and her hair was coarse and stiff like a horse's tail.
When the Guówáng looked at this daughter, he felt no joy in his heart,
so he commanded those within the palace: "Diligently guard and protect her;
do not let outsiders see her.
Why is this?
Although this girl is ugly and her form does not resemble a human,
she was born of Lady Mòlì.
Though she is ugly and loathsome,
we must secretly send people to protect and nurture her."
As the girl grew older,
she reached the age for marriage.
At that time, the Guówáng was worried and distressed
and had no other plan.
So he told his officials:
"You go and search for someone who was originally of a noble house or a householder clan,
but who is now poor and has no money or wealth;
you may bring him here."
The official followed the instructions,
immediately went to search, and found a son of a noble house who was poor.
The official then called him
and brought him to the Guówáng’s place.
When the Guówáng received this man,
they went together to a secluded place
where the Guówáng told him the circumstances in detail:
"I have a daughter whose face and appearance are ugly and hideous.
I wish to find a place for her to marry,
but no match has been found.
