I have heard that you are of a noble family;
although you are poor now,
I shall provide for you.
If you would be so kind as not to refuse, you should take her in marriage."
At that time, the son of the elder knelt for a long time and said:
"I shall obey your royal command.
Even if the Great King were to grant me a dog,
I would still accept it,
let alone the Great King's own flesh and blood.
If she is now to be granted to me,
I shall obey your command and receive her."
The King then gave his daughter to that poor man as a wife.
He built a palace and residence for them, with gates and inner chambers,
making them sevenfold.
The King commanded his daughter’s husband:
"Hold the door keys yourself.
If you wish to go out, lock them yourself.
My daughter is ugly and hideous, the likes of which have never been seen in the world.
Do not let outsiders see the appearance of her face;
always keep the doors and gates firmly locked, and keep her secluded within."
The King provided wealth and goods,
supplying his son-in-law with everything needed,
so that he lacked for nothing.
The King then appointed him as a Great Minister.
As the man's wealth and treasures increased,
he held banquets with various noble families,
taking turns month by month.
At the time of these gatherings, husbands and wives would go together,
and men and women would mingle, entertaining one another.
All the people who came to the gatherings brought their wives,
except for that Great Minister, who always went alone.
Everyone grew suspicious and wondered:
"That man's wife—
is she perhaps so upright and beautiful that her radiance is peerless?
Or is she perhaps extremely ugly and cannot be shown?
That is why he does not bring her.
Now we should devise a plan to go and see his wife."
They all came to one mind and whispered secretly to each other.
They urged him to drink wine until he lay down in a drunken sleep,
then they untied and took his door keys.
They then sent five men to go to his house
and open the doors.
At that very time, the daughter felt distressed in her heart.
Reproaching herself for her past sins and faults, she said:
"What sin did I plant to be so hated by my husband,
to be constantly kept in seclusion, living in a dark room,
unable to see the sun, the moon, or other people?"
Again she thought to herself:
"Now the *Fó* is in the world, benefiting all sentient beings.
Those who encounter suffering and hardship all receive his salvation."
Then, with a sincere heart, she paid homage to the *Shì Zūn* from afar:
"I only pray that you will show compassion,
come before me, and for a moment grant me your instruction."
The daughter's sincerity was profound, and her heart of reverence was pure and earnest.
The *Fó* knew her resolve and immediately went to her house.
Before the daughter, he emerged from the ground
and displayed the sign of his indigo-colored hair, letting the daughter see it.
The daughter raised her head and saw the sign of the *Fó*’s hair.
Her joy doubled,
and in her joyful emotion and reverence,
her heart of respect became extremely deep.
The daughter’s hair naturally became fine and soft,
like the color of deep indigo blue.
The *Fó* then revealed his face.
The daughter saw it,
and having seen it, she rejoiced; her face also became upright and beautiful.
Her hideous features and coarse skin naturally transformed and vanished.
The *Fó* then revealed his body
from the waist up, shining with a brilliant golden light,
letting the daughter see it.
The daughter saw the *Fó*’s body,
and her joy increased even more.
Because of her joy, her hideous features immediately vanished;
her body became upright and dignified, like that of a heavenly maiden,
extraordinarily wonderful and surpassing the world, with none who could match her.
Out of pity for the daughter, the *Fó* revealed his entire body.
The daughter observed him closely, her eyes not blinking even once.
She leaped with joy, unable to contain herself.
The daughter’s entire body also became upright and beautiful,
her features and marks extraordinary and rare in the world.
All her hideous features vanished,
with none remaining.
The *Fó* preached the *Fǎ* for her,
and she immediately extinguished all evils,
instantly attaining the path of a *Sūtuóhuán*.
Once the daughter had attained the path,
the *Fó* then disappeared.
At that time, those five men opened the door and entered.
They saw that the wife was upright and beautiful, exceptional and with few equals.
They said to one another:
"I wondered why this man did not bring her along;
his wife is actually as beautiful as this!"
Having finished their observation, they closed the doors
and took the keys back to where the man was, tying them back onto his original belt.
When the man woke up,
the gathering ended and he went home.
Entering the door, he saw his wife, upright, beautiful, and wonderful,
her appearance outstanding and rare among humans.
Seeing her, he was delighted and asked who she was.
The wife answered her husband:
"I am your wife."
The husband asked his wife:
"You were extremely ugly before; for what reason are you now so beautiful?"
The wife answered her husband with the full details of what had happened:
"Because of the *Fó*, I have received such a body."
The wife further said to her husband:
"I now wish to see the King.
You should convey my intention for me."
The husband accepted her words and immediately went to tell the King:
"The daughter now wishes to come and see you."
The King answered his son-in-law:
"Do not speak of this.
Quickly and firmly lock her in;
be careful not to let her out."
The daughter’s husband answered the King:
"Why is it so?
The daughter has now received the divine grace of the *Fó*,
and she has become upright and beautiful, no different from a heavenly maiden."
Having heard this, the King answered his son-in-law:
"If it is truly so,
go and bring her quickly."
They immediately prepared a carriage and welcomed the daughter into the palace.
When the King saw that his daughter's body was upright, beautiful, and exceptional,
he leaped with joy, unable to contain herself.
He immediately ordered the carriages to be prepared,
and the King, the Queen, the daughter, and her husband all went together to the *Fó*’s place.
Having finished paying homage to the *Fó*, they stood to one side.
Then King *Bōsīnì* knelt and said to the *Fó*:
"I do not know what blessings this daughter cultivated in her past lives
to be born into a noble and wealthy family,
yet what fault did she commit to receive such an ugly form,
with skin and hair so coarse and harsh, even worse than a beast?
I only pray the *Shì Zūn* will explain this to us."
The *Fó* told the Great King:
"When a person lives in the world,
their beauty or ugliness
are all the retribution of the sins and blessings of their past deeds.
Long ago in the distant past,
there was a great country named *Bāluónài*.
In that country, there was a great elder with immeasurable wealth.
His whole family always made offerings together to a *Pìzhīfó*,
whose body was coarse and ugly,
his form hideous and haggard, making him difficult to look at.
At that time, the elder had a young daughter
who saw that *Pìzhīfó* coming every day.
With an evil heart of disrespect, she scolded and insulted him, saying:
'Your face is hideous and your skin is coarse and ugly.
How can anyone be as detestable as this?'
Later, the *Pìzhīfó* went to her house many times
to receive their offerings.
Having been in the world for a long time, he wished to enter *Nièpán*.
For the sake of his donors, he performed various transformations:
flying into the void,
emitting water and fire from his body,
appearing in the east and vanishing in the west,
appearing in the west and vanishing in the east,
appearing in the south and vanishing in the north,
appearing in the north and vanishing in the south,
sitting and lying in the void—
with various such manifestations,
he let that family witness his divine powers.
He then descended from the void and returned to their house.
Having seen this, the elder was filled with even more joy.
The daughter immediately repented and reproached herself:
'I only pray, Venerable One, that you will forgive me.
My previous evil heart
was a sin of great magnitude.
Fortunately, you do not harbor it in your mind;
do not let me be burdened with this sin.'
The *Pìzhīfó* then accepted her repentance."
The *Fó* told the Great King:
"The daughter of that time is the King's daughter now.
Because of her evil and unwholesome heart at that time
when she slandered the holy *Pìzhīfó*,
she created for herself a fault of speech.
From then on, she constantly received an ugly form.
Because she later saw the divine transformations and repented,
she has now regained a beautiful appearance,
her brilliance surpassing others, with none who can match her.
Because of her offerings to the *Pìzhīfó*,
she has been wealthy and noble in every life,
and this serves as the cause for her liberation."
"Thus it is, Great King! All sentient beings of every kind
should protect their actions and speech,
and not recklessly commit wrongs or treat others with light-hearted mockery."
At that time, King *Bōsīnì*, all the ministers, and the entire assembly,
having heard the *Fó*’s teaching on causes and effects,
all gave rise to faith and reverence and were moved before the *Fó*.
Through this heart of faith,
some attained the first fruit, up to the fourth fruit;
some gave rise to the aspiration for supreme and equal enlightenment;
and others attained the stage of non-retrogression.
All were filled with longing and respectfully followed the *Fó*’s teachings.
With joy and compliance, they all practiced them together.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi, in the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán,
together with a company of twelve hundred and fifty great disciples.
At that time, in the city, there was a great elder.
The elder’s wife gave birth to a boy named Jīncái.
The boy was exceptionally handsome, with few equals in the world.
Because of his past lives, this boy was born with clenched fists.
His parents were startled and thought it was an ill omen.
They immediately opened the child’s two hands
to observe his features,
and saw two gold coins in the child’s two hands.
The parents were delighted
and immediately took them;
once taken, they continued to reappear in the same place.
They took them again, and they reappeared as before;
in this way, they diligently collected the gold coins until the treasury was full,
yet in the child’s hands, they were never exhausted.
As the boy grew older, he spoke to his parents, asking to leave the home life.
His parents did not oppose him and immediately granted permission.
Then Jīncái went to where the Buddha was,
prostrated his head and face at the Buddha's feet, and said to the Buddha:
“I only pray, World-Honored One! Please show me compassion,
permit me to leave the home life, and let me join the ranks of the Path.”
The Buddha told Jīncái:
“I permit you to leave the home life.”
Having received the Buddha’s approval, Jīncái then shaved his beard and hair,
donned the jiāshā robes, and became a Shāmí.
When his age was sufficient, he was ready to receive the great precepts,
and he was ordered by the assembly of monks to receive the full ordination.
Approaching the altar, he paid respects to the assembly of monks in order.
When he prostrated, his two hands touched the ground,
and where his hands touched the ground, there were two gold coins.
In this manner, as he paid respects to everyone in turn,
wherever he prostrated, there were always gold coins.
After the ordination was completed,
he practiced with diligent effort and attained the path of an Āluóhàn.
Ānán said to the Buddha:
“I am uncertain, World-Honored One! What merit did this Jīncái Bǐqiū create in the past,
that since his birth, he has held gold coins in his hands?
I only pray, World-Honored One, that you will provide an explanation.”?
The Buddha told Ānán:
“You should reflect well!
I shall now explain it.”
Ānán replied:
“Indeed, I shall listen well!”
The Buddha said:
“Long ago, ninety-one kalpas in the past,
there was a Buddha named Pípóshī who appeared in the world.
He taught the True Law, delivering and liberating countless sentient beings.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks traveled through the various lands.
At that time, the sons of wealthy elders and such
prepared meals
to make offerings to that Buddha and his group of disciples.
At that time, there was a poor man who lacked wealth and goods.
He often went to the wild marshes to gather firewood and sell it.
At that time, he gathered firewood and sold it for two coins.
Seeing the Buddha and the monks receiving an invitation from the royal family,
with a joyful and respectful heart,
he immediately gave his two coins as an offering to the Buddha and the monks.
The Buddha, taking pity on this man,
immediately accepted them.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“Because that poor man at that time gave those two coins to the Buddha and the monks,
for ninety-one kalpas, he has constantly held gold coins and enjoyed wealth as he pleased,
without any end.
As for the poor man of that time,
he is this Jīncái Bǐqiū.
Even if that person had not attained the Path,
his future rewards would still be immeasurable.
Therefore, Ānán!
All sentient beings should take diligent giving as their practice.”
At that time, Ānán and the members of the great assembly, hearing what the Buddha said,
all believed and understood.
Some attained the fruit of a Xūtuóhuán,
others attained the fruits of a Sītuóhán, Ānàhán, or Āluóhàn.
Some resolved their minds on the unexcelled, truly right Path—some individuals resolving their minds on the unexcelled, truly right Path—
and still others attained the stage of non-retrogression.
The entire great assembly, hearing what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi, in the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán,
together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty Bǐqiū.
At that time in the country, there was a wealthy elder
whose wife gave birth to a son
whose face and features were handsome.
After this child was born,
within the house, heavenly flowers naturally rained down,
filling the house to the brim.
He was then named Fúbōtípó,
which in the language of Jìn is called Huātiān.
As the child grew older,
he went to where the Buddha was.
Seeing that the Buddha’s countenance and marks of excellence were beyond compare,
he was delighted and thought to himself:
“Born into this world, I have been able to meet the Holy Honored One.
I should now invite the Buddha and all the monks.”
He then stepped forward and said to the Buddha:
“I only pray, World-Honored One, that you and the assembly of monks would deign to visit my humble home tomorrow
and accept a simple vegetarian meal.”
Because he saw his auspicious blessings,
the Buddha, knowing his spiritual capacity,
immediately accepted the invitation.
Then Huātiān returned to his home.
The next day at mealtime, the Buddha and the assembly of monks went to his house.
Huātiān immediately manifested jeweled beds and seats
filling the house, arranged and adorned.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks then sat on these seats.
Whatever various foods and drinks Huātiān desired,
were naturally provided through his own merit.
After the Buddha and the assembly of monks had eaten and put away their bowls,
he spoke the various teachings in detail for Huātiān.
Huātiān’s entire family attained the fruit of a Xūtuóhuán.
Then Huātiān took leave of his parents,
asking to leave the home life
to become a disciple of the Buddha.
His parents granted permission.
He went immediately to the Buddha’s place,
bowed at the Buddha’s feet,
and asked to become a Bǐqiū
to receive the Buddha’s teachings.
The Buddha permitted him to enter the Path
and said:
“Welcome, Bǐqiū!”
His beard and hair fell off naturally,
jiāshā robes appeared on his body, and he immediately became a Shāmén.
He followed and practiced the Buddha’s teachings
and attained the state of an Āluóhàn.
At that time, Ānán, having witnessed these events,
went to where the Buddha was,
knelt and said:
“World-Honored One!
What merit did this Huātiān Bǐqiū plant in the past,
to receive such natural heavenly flowers,
and also be able to manifest seats and food?
World-Honored One!
Please resolve this doubt for me.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“Listen well if you wish to know!
In the past there was a Buddha named Pípóshī
who appeared in the world
and delivered sentient beings.
At that time, the assembly of monks traveled through the villages
and came to the noble families,
who all made offerings.
At that time, there was a person who was poor and without money.
Seeing the monks, he was delighted,
but regretted having no offerings to give.
He immediately went to the wild marshes and gathered various wild flowers
and scattered them over the assembly of monks.
He bowed with the utmost sincerity
and then departed.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“The poor person who scattered flowers over the monks at that time
is this Huātiān Bǐqiū. Because in the past he had a heart of faith and respect,
gathering flowers to scatter over the monks and making a sincere vow,
for ninety-one kalpas, in every place he was born,
his body has been handsome,
and whatever his mind required,
whether food, drink, or bedding,
they would immediately arrive naturally as he thought of them.
By virtue of this merit,
he naturally attained the Path for himself.
Therefore, Ānán! All sentient beings should not think lightly of small acts of giving, thinking them to be without merit;
just like Huātiān,
who has now obtained everything for himself.”
At that time, Ānán and the members of the great assembly, hearing what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the Jǐ-shù Gǐ-gū-dú-yuán of Shèwèi Country.
At that time, there was an elder
who had a son.
At the moment of his birth,
the heavens rained down the seven treasures,
filling the interior of his house
and causing them to be piled high and full.
He immediately summoned a physiognomist
to read the boy's features.
When the physiognomist had finished observing
and saw his extraordinary features,
he replied to the elder, saying:
"The boy's appearance is exceptionally rare."
Having heard this, the elder
felt joy in his heart
and said to the physiognomist:
"You should name him."
The physiognomist asked:
"When this child was born,
what auspicious signs were there?"
The elder replied:
"When this child was born,
the heavens rained down the seven treasures,
filling my house."
The physiognomist replied:
"This child possesses great merit;
his name shall be Lènàtípó,
which in the Jìn language means Bǎotiān."
As the child grew older,
his talents and skills became broad and thorough.
Hearing that the Fó's spiritual holiness and extraordinary virtue were matched by few,
his heart felt a yearning admiration,
and he desired to renounce householder life.
He took leave of his parents
and went to the place where the Fó was.
He prostrated himself with his head to the ground
and said to the Fó:
"I only wish, Shìzūn,
that you would permit me to renounce householder life."
The Fó immediately granted his request:
"Welcome, Bǐqiū!"
His hair and beard fell away naturally,
and Dharma robes appeared on his body.
The Fó preached the Dharma to him,
and he immediately attained the stage of Luóhàn.
Ānán said to the Fó:
"I do not know,
Shìzūn,
what merit this Bǐqiū Bǎotiān
originally performed,
such that when he was born,
the heavens rained down various treasures,
and his clothing and food were provided naturally,
without any lack or shortage?"
The Fó told Ānán:
"In a past life,
the Fó Píbóshī
appeared in the world
to deliver sentient beings,
beyond counting.
At that time, the assembly of monks
traveled through the villages.
At that time in a certain village,
there were many lay followers
who together invited the assembly of monks
to provide them with various offerings.
At that time, there was a poor man
who, although his heart was filled with joy,
had no wealth or treasures in his house for offerings.
He then took a handful of white stones resembling pearls
and scattered them over the assembly of monks,
making a great vow."
The Fó told Ānán:
"The poor man who then made the offering of pearls
is this very Bǐqiū Bǎotiān.
Because in the past he used a heart of faith and respect
to take white stones resembling pearls and scatter them over the assembly of monks,
for ninety-one eons
he received immeasurable blessings,
abounding in much wealth and treasure,
with food and clothing provided naturally,
without lack or shortage.
Because of the heart of faith and respect he had at that time,
he has now encountered my time
and attained the realization of the path."
At that time, the great assembly
heard what the Fó had said,
and faith naturally arose within them.
Some attained the first fruit,
up to the fourth fruit,
and others resolved to dwell in non-retrogression.
At that time, the great assembly,
hearing what the Fó had said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó stayed in the Zhúyuán-lín of Luóyuèqí.
At that time, the Shìzūn had just attained the path
and delivered Āruò Jiāochénrú and others.
Next, he delivered the one thousand brothers of Yùbēiluó Kāshè.
As his deliverance of people grew wider, the number of those who received liberation was many.
At that time, the people of Luóyuèqí rejoiced immeasurably
and none did not praise: "The Rúlái's appearance in the world is truly extraordinary!
All kinds of sentient beings
together receive deliverance from suffering."
They also praised Jiāochénrú and others, as well as the Yùbēiluó assembly:
"What past causes and conditions did these Great Virtuous Bǐqiū have with the Rúlái,
that when the Dharma drum first resonated, they were especially the first to hear it,
and the taste of the nectar of the Dharma,
they alone were the first to partake of it?"
When the Bǐqiū heard what the people were proclaiming,
they took the matter and went to tell the Shìzūn.
The Fó told them:
"In the distant past, I made a great vow with this group:
'If I attain the path, I shall deliver them first.'"
Having heard this, the Bǐqiū
again said to the Fó:
"As for the matter of the long-standing vow, how was it?
We only wish you would show compassion
and explain it for us."
The Fó told the Bǐqiū:
"Listen closely, listen closely!
Think on it well.
In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable Āsēngqí eons ago,
in this Yánfútí, there was a great country named Bōluónài.
At that time, the king of the country was named Jiālí.
At that time in the country, there was a great immortal named Chàntípōlí,
who, with five hundred disciples, lived in the mountain forests,
practicing patience.
At that time, the King, with his ministers, wives, and ladies-in-waiting,
entered the mountains for recreation.
The King became tired and weary, and so lay down to rest.
The ladies-in-waiting left the King and wandered about,
observing the flowering forests.
They saw Chàntípōlí sitting upright in meditation.
A heart of respect arose within them,
and they immediately took various flowers and scattered them over him,
then sat before him to listen to the Dharma he spoke.
The King woke up and looked around,
but did not see the women.
Together with his four great ministers, he went to look for them.
Seeing the women sitting before the immortal,
he immediately asked:
'Have you fully attained the four concentrations on emptiness or not?'
He answered: 'Not yet attained.'
He asked again:
'Have you attained the four immeasurable minds or not?'
He answered: 'Not yet attained.'
The King asked again:
'Have you attained the four meditations or not?'
He still answered: 'Not yet attained.'
The King then became angry and said:
'Of all these merits, you say you have none.
You are an ordinary man;
alone with these women in this secluded place,
how can you be trusted?'
He asked again:
'You who are always here,
who are you?
What do you practice?'
The immortal replied:
'I practice patience.'
The King immediately drew his sword and said to him:
'If you are practicing patience,
I wish to test you, to know if you can endure or not.'
He then cut off both his hands and asked the immortal,
who still said he was practicing patience.
He then cut off both his feet,
and asked him again;
he still said he was practicing patience.
Next, he cut off his ears and nose.
His facial expression did not change,
and he still claimed to be practicing patience.
At that time, the heaven and earth shook in six ways.
Then the immortal's five hundred disciples flew into the air
and asked their teacher:
'Having suffered such pain,
has your heart of patience not been lost?'
The teacher replied:
'My heart has not changed.'
The King was startled and terrified,
and asked once more:
'You say you are patient; what is the proof?'
The immortal replied:
'If my patience is real and my sincerity is not false,
my blood shall become milk,
and my body shall be restored as before.'
When his words were finished, his blood immediately became milk,
and his body became whole and complete as before.
Seeing the proof of patience,
the King's fear redoubled.
'Alas, how wicked I am!
To have harmed and insulted a great immortal!
I only hope you will show compassion and accept my repentance.'
The immortal said to him:
'Because of female beauty, you used a blade to cut my form.
My patience is like the earth;'
"When I later become a Buddha,
I will first use the sword of wisdom to sever your three poisons."
At that time in the mountains, the various dragons, ghosts, and spirits,
seeing King Jiālǐ mistreating the Patient Immortal (Rěnrǔ Xiānrén),
were each filled with indignation.
They raised great clouds and mist, thunder and lightning,
wishing to harm that king and his followers.
Then the Immortal looked up and spoke:
"If it is for my sake,
do not distress or harm them."
At that time, after King Jiālǐ repented,
he frequently invited the Immortal to the palace to receive offerings.
At that time, there was another Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) with a thousand followers
who saw the King respectfully treating Chàntípōlí
and were deeply envious.
In a secluded place,
while he was sitting, they took dust, dirt, and filth and threw it upon him.
At that time, the Immortal, seeing them act in this way,
immediately made a vow:
"I now practice patience for the sake of all living beings;
accumulating deeds without ceasing, I shall eventually become a Buddha.
When the path to Buddhahood is completed,
I will first use the water of the Dharma to wash away your dust and grime,
remove your impurities of desire,
and make you pure forever."
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū):
"If you wish to know who Chàntípōlí was at that time,
it was I myself.
King Jiālǐ and the four great ministers of that time
are now the five Bhikṣus including Jiāochénrú and others.
The thousand Brāhmaṇas who threw dust on me then
are now the thousand Bhikṣus including Yùbēiluó and others.
At that time, because of that patience,
I vowed that I would deliver them first;
therefore, when the path was completed,
this assembly was the first to be delivered from suffering."
Then the Bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha said,
marveled at such an unprecedented thing
and joyfully practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the Shèwèi kingdom at Qíhuán.
At that time, the Venerable Ānán,
after the midday meal, was practicing meditation in the forest
and thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata's (Rúlái) appearance in the world is truly extraordinary;
all kinds of living beings receive peace and happiness."
He also thought:
"What roots of goodness did the five venerable Bhikṣus, including Jiāochénrú, plant,
and based on what
causes and conditions
did they enter first when the Dharma gate first opened,
hear it first when the Dharma drum first sounded,
and receive the moistening first when the Dharma rain of nectar fell?"
After having these thoughts,
he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was,
and fully related his thoughts to the Buddha.
The Buddha told him:
"Jiāochénrú and the others indeed have causes and conditions with me from past lives.
In a past life, I used my own blood to satisfy their hunger and thirst,
enabling them to find peace;
therefore in this life, they are the first to obtain my Dharma
and achieve liberation."
The Worthy One Ānán again spoke to the Buddha:
"Regarding how you used your blood to relieve their hunger and exhaustion in the past,
what was that story?
I pray you will fully reveal it
and let all in the assembly gain understanding."
The Buddha told him:
"In the distant past, kalpas ago beyond numbering (Āsēngqí),
in this Yánfútí, there was a great king
named Míqūluóbáluó,
which in the Jìn language means Cílì,
who ruled over eighty-four thousand lesser kings of Yánfútí,
and had twenty thousand consorts and ten thousand ministers.
The king possessed compassion
and was endowed with the Four Immeasurable Hearts (Sì Děng Xīn);
he always pitied all beings and was never weary or negligent.
He constantly taught the people the Ten Good Deeds (Shí Shàn),
and people from all four directions admired him. Under the King's governance,
the land was peaceful and happy,
and everyone rejoiced and relied upon him.
There were various pestilence ghosts (yìguǐ) who constantly consumed human blood and energy
to sustain their own lives.
At that time, the people restrained their bodies, speech, and minds
and diligently followed the Ten Good Deeds;
the various evil pestilences did not dare to approach them,
and thus the ghosts became hungry, emaciated, and exhausted, becoming thin and weak.
Then five Yèchā came to where the King was:
'Our kind relies on human blood and energy
to maintain our lives.
Because of the King's teachings, everyone upholds the Ten Good Deeds,
and as a result, we have no more food or drink;
we are starving, thirsty, and exhausted,
with no way to survive.
Great King, have compassion!
How can you not pity us?'
The King, hearing these words,
was filled with sorrow
and immediately opened his own veins, piercing his body in five places.
Then the five Yèchā each took a vessel,
came forward to receive the blood and drink it;
having drunk the blood until they were full,
they all relied on the King's kindness
and felt immeasurable joy.
The King then told them:
'If you are now satisfied,
remember to practice the Ten Good Deeds.
I now use my body's blood to relieve your hunger and thirst
so that you may find peace;
later, when I become a Buddha,
I shall use the blood of the Dharma-body's precepts, concentration, and wisdom
to remove your hunger and thirst for the three poisons and various desires,
and establish you in the peaceful place of Nièpán.'
Ānán! If you wish to know who King Cílì was at that time,
it is I myself.
The five Yèchā
are now the five Bhikṣus including Jiāochénrú and others.
I have made vows life after life
promising to deliver them first;
therefore, when I first preached the Dharma,
they heard it and were liberated."
Then the Venerable Ānán and the whole assembly,
hearing what the Buddha said,
all felt increased respect and admiration,
and joyfully practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the Zhúyuán of Wángshèchéng,
together with twelve hundred and fifty Bǐqiū.
At that time, King Píngshā had already attained the first fruit,
and his heart of faith and respect was doubly profound.
He constantly provided the four superior necessities
to make offerings to the Fó and the Bǐqiū assembly,
rejoicing in others joining in virtue
and aspiring to encourage and guide them.
In the kingdom, there were six teachers,
such as Fùlánnà and others.
They had appeared in the world earlier,
preaching heterodox views and distorted doctrines,
deceiving and deluding the common people.
Those of confused and darkened minds
believed in and followed their heterodox teachings;
their kind was widespread,
and their evil factions filled the land.
At that time, the King had a younger brother
who reverently served the six teachers.
Believing in and deluded by their heterodoxy and error,
considering them to possess the Way,
he exhausted his household's wealth
to provide for them.
When the Fó-sun first rose
and the stream of wisdom began to moisten the world,
he had no intention of raising himself from error,
being submerged in a heavy net.
His elder brother, King Píngshā,
loved and valued him greatly.
With earnest and skillful means,
he tried to enlighten him and have him serve the Fó.
The brother clung to his heterodox principles
and would not follow the King's instruction.
The King repeatedly ordered him to invite the Fó for an offering.
The brother said to the elder brother, the King:
"I have my own teachers,
and I cannot go again to serve Qútán.
However, since the King has given an instruction, in principle I should not disobey;
I shall prepare a great assembly without limit to the crowd that comes.
If he comes of his own accord,
I shall provide him with food."
After promising the King, he prepared the offering implements,
and set out many seats.
When the preparations were finished and the assembly was set,
he sent someone to call them.
The followers of the six teachers
soon all gathered and arrived.
They sat in the upper seats,
and wondered why the Fó and the monks had not arrived yet.
He immediately went to say to the King:
"Earlier, the King repeatedly ordered me to invite Qútán.
Now that I have prepared the assembly
and the time is approaching,
why has he not come?"
The King told his brother:
"Although you cannot go in person to invite him,
you should send one person to announce that the time has come."
The King's brother followed this instruction and sent a person to announce the time.
The Fó and the great assembly arrived at the place of the gathering.
Seeing the six teachers already seated in the upper seats,
the Fó and the assembly of monks sat down in order.
By means of his divine powers, the Fó
caused these six teachers together with their followers
suddenly to be in the lower rows.
The six teachers felt ashamed;
each stood up to move their seat.
Once seated and settled, they saw themselves
back in the lower positions.
This happened two or three times;
although they moved their seats toward the top,
they still saw their own bodies
at the very bottom.
Lacking any further power,
they sat there, dejected.
The Dányuè distributed water.
When he reached the upper seat,
the Fó told the donor:
"Give it to your teachers first."
Carrying the water, he went before the teachers.
He raised the pitcher,
but the mouth of the pitcher closed by itself,
and the water would not come out.
Returning to the Fó,
he followed the order starting from the Fó;
only then did the water flow out,
and all were able to wash their hands.
After they had finished washing their hands,
next was the time for the prayer of blessing.
The Dányuè took the food
and went before the upper seat.
The Fó said to the Dányuè:
"This was not originally intended for me.
Go before your teachers
and have them perform the blessing."
Following the instruction, he immediately went
to the place of the six teachers.
The six teachers' mouths were clenched shut;
they could not utter a word.
They each only raised a hand
and pointed from afar at the Fó.
The Fó then performed the blessing,
his Brahma-voice clear and resonant.
When the blessing was finished,
next was the distribution of food.
Intending to follow the upper seat
and present it in order,
the Fó said again:
"Give it to your teachers first."
He immediately took the food
and presented it to the six teachers.
The food all suddenly rose
and stayed in the air.
Each portion was high above them,
and they could not reach it.
After the food had been distributed to the Fó and the monks completely,
the food then descended
and was placed before each of them.
The Fó and the monks
all finished eating.
After rinsing their mouths, they returned to their seats.
Next was the time to preach the Dharma.
The Fó said to the Dányuè:
"Have your teachers speak."
He immediately invited the six teachers,
but the six teachers were again silent,
only simultaneously
raising their hands to point at the Fó.
Thereupon, the Rúlái,
for the sake of the great assembly,
produced a gentle voice
and eloquently expounded the nature of the Dharma,
distinguishing the principles and meanings
to suit the inclinations of the crowd.
Hearing the Fó's preaching of the Dharma,
all attained understanding.
King Píngshā’s younger brother
attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Among the rest of the people,
some attained the first fruit,
up to the third fruit.
Some left the household life and ended all outflows,
some gave rise to the unsurpassed mind,
and some dwelled in the stage of non-retrogression.
According to what their hearts yearned for,
all obtained their wishes.
Each recognized the truth
and believed in and respected the Sānbǎo,
while looking down upon the six teachers
and abandoning them, no longer providing offerings.
Thereupon, the six teachers
harbored great distress and anger.
Each went to a secluded place
to seek and learn extraordinary arts.
The heavenly demon Bōxún,
fearing their spirits were cowed
and they would be unable to spread the poison of evil heterodoxy,
immediately descended and transformed himself into the forms of the six teachers.
Before each one of them,
he manifested the arts of the other five:
flying through the air,
emitting water and fire from his body,
dividing his body and scattering his limbs,
and performing a hundred kinds of transformations.
Those foolish followers
again came to rely on one another.
Resentful of their previous humiliation and the loss of offerings,
the six teachers all gathered
and consulted together, saying:
"Our skills and abilities
are not inferior to those of Qútán.
Because of that one previous humiliation,
the hearts of the crowd were scattered.
Recently, the various teachers
have manifested divine arts and transformations.
Examining these marvelous feats now,
they are sufficient to subdue him.
We should go to the King and ask for a contest to decide victory and defeat."
Once their plan was settled,
they immediately went to the King's place
and spoke of their own wisdom, divine transformations, and spiritual arts,
desiring to compete with the Shāmén
in a match of extraordinary transformations.
After the trial against him,
the superior and inferior would be revealed.
The King laughed at them and said:
"How foolish you all are!
The virtue of the Fó is vast and great,
and his divine powers are without hindrance.
You wish to use the size of a firefly to compete for brightness with the sun,
to compare the water in a cow's footprint with the vastness of the great ocean,
to pit the insignificance of a jackal against the ferocity of a lion,
or to make an anthill equal in height to Mount Xūmí.
Between the great and the small forms,
the distinction is perfectly clear.
Deluded and reaching too high,
how extreme is your folly?"
The six teachers spoke again:
"The proof of the matter is in the end.
The Great King has not yet seen our extraordinary transformations,
which is why you are biased and regard him as great.
After the decisive contest,
the magnitude of our abilities will be naturally determined."
The King further spoke, saying:
"If you wish to test him, you may do so,
but I fear you will only bring ruin and humiliation upon yourselves.
If there is truly to be a contest of supernatural powers with the Buddha,
I should let us all witness the extraordinary transformations."
The Liù Shī said:
"Seven days from now,
we request that the King level and prepare the ground for the contest."
After the Liù Shī departed,
the King immediately prepared his carriage
and went to the Buddha’s place.
He reported the matter to the Buddha:
"The Liù Shī are causing a commotion,
wishing to have a contest of skills.
I rebuked them with reason,
but their intentions do not cease.
I only pray, Shì Zūn!
Exert your divine power
to transform and subdue this evil,
so they may follow what is good,
and thereby allow us all to witness your transformations."
The Buddha told Píng Shā:
"I myself know the time."
Píng Shā thought the Buddha had agreed to the contest of powers,
so he immediately ordered his officials
to level and prepare a vast place,
set up seats and couches,
erect various banners and streamers,
and decorate them with ornaments,
making it exceedingly beautiful and wondrous.
When the day of the assembly arrived,
everyone looked forward to it with anticipation.
At that time, the Rú Lái and the assembly of monks
from Wáng Shè Chéng
went to Pí Shè Lí.
Within Pí Shè Lí,
the Lǜ Chāng and their peers,
along with the people,
all came to welcome him.
On the following day, the people
looked for the Buddha but he was not there.
Upon inquiry, they learned the truth,
that he had gone to Pí Shè Lí.
The followers of the Liù Shī
spread the word and proclaimed:
"We have long known that Qú Tán’s wisdom and skills are shallow.
You people were hesitant
and did not believe our words.
Now that a date was set for the contest,
he recognized his own inferiority and has fled away,
going to Pí Shè Lí."
The Liù Shī
became even more arrogant and haughty.
Leading one another,
they vowed to pursue him to the end.
At that time, King Píng Shā
prepared offerings,
filling five hundred chariots.
The King, with his officials and a multitude of 1.4 billion,
each prepared provisions
and all followed after the Buddha,
arriving in a continuous stream,
and gathered at Pí Shè Lí.
The Liù Shī again went and told the Lǜ Chāng:
"Grant us permission
to compete with this Qú Tán
to test our supernatural powers
and discuss the true nature of things.
If you grant us permission,
let us set the date seven days from now."
At that time, the Lǜ Chāng
again went to report to the Buddha:
"The deluded group of Liù Shī
claim to possess the Way
and seek to contest supernatural powers with the Rú Lái.
I only pray, Shì Zūn!
Bestow your divine power to subdue them."
The Buddha again told them:
"The Buddha himself knows the time."
The Lǜ Chāng
gathered their officials and people
and prepared the grounds
just as King Píng Shā had done.
All of them looked forward to it with longing,
expecting it to be on the morrow.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks
went to Jū Shǎn Mí.
The King of Jū Shǎn Mí,
named Yōu Tián,
leading his officials,
also came to welcome him.
The people of Pí Shè Lí
inquired about the Buddha the next morning
and were told the Buddha had already gone to the state of Jū Shǎn Mí.
When the Liù Shī heard this, their arrogance grew even greater.
Gathering their disciples and the crowd,
they planned to corner and pressure him.
The Lǜ Chāng
prepared offerings
loaded onto five hundred chariots
to be used for offerings.
Leading a multitude of seven hundred million people of the state,
along with King Píng Shā,
they gathered at Jū Shǎn Mí
to watch the Buddha and the Liù Shī contest their supernatural powers.
The roads were filled from front to back
as they arrived in a continuous stream.
Once the Liù Shī arrived,
they saw King Yōu Tián and spoke of the situation as they had before,
saying that the Shā Mén had recognized his own state:
"Internally, I have nothing to rely on."
"So he empty-handedly flees and avoids us,
and cannot be pinned down.
We need the King to set a fixed time and command him to contest with us."
Yōu Tián reported to the Buddha,
recounting the words of the Liù Shī:
"Shì Zūn!
Is it possible to have a contest with them?"
The Buddha again replied:
"I myself know the time."
Yōu Tián hoped the Buddha would hold the contest in his state,
so he prepared the grounds
just as King Píng Shā had done.
Everyone came to the assembly.
But the Buddha departed again,
with the Bǐ Qiū monks,
and went to the state of Yuè Qí.
The King of the state of Yuè Qí, Tún Zhēn Tuó Luó,
leading the people,
came to welcome the Shì Zūn.
The people of Jū Shǎn Mí inquired the next day
and heard that the Buddha had already gone toward Yuè Qí.
The followers of the Liù Shī
followed closely behind.
At that time, King Yōu Tián and his eight hundred million people,
along with Píng Shā and the people of other states,
all went together
and gathered in the state of Yuè Qí.
The Liù Shī saw the King
and extensively proclaimed:
"You must command Qú Tán to have a contest with us."
Tún Zhēn Tuó Luó again went to report to the Buddha,
but the Buddha still replied:
"The Buddha himself knows the time."
The King also prepared the grounds.
When the day of the assembly was about to arrive,
the Buddha and the assembly of monks
immediately headed toward Tè Chā Shī Lì.
The King of this state was named Yīn Tuó Pó Mí,
who, with his officials and people,
also came to welcome him.
Tún Zhēn Tuó Luó and five hundred million people,
along with King Píng Shā and other kings, officials, and people,
all followed the Buddha
toward Tè Chā Shī Lì.
Once the Liù Shī arrived,
they told Yīn Tuó Pó Mí,
being extremely deceitful
and speaking with lofty and grand words:
"Let us contest supernatural powers with Qú Tán."
Yīn Tuó Pó Mí again went to report to the Buddha,
but the Buddha still replied:
"I myself know the time."
When the day of the prepared assembly arrived,
the Buddha departed again,
together with the assembly of monks,
and went to Bō Luó Nài.
The King of Bō Luó Nài was named Fàn Mó Dá,
who also, with a crowd of people,
came in person to welcome the Buddha.
The people of Tè Chā Shī Lì
learned the next day that the Buddha had departed.
The Liù Shī pursued him,
racing along his tracks.
Yīn Tuó Pó Mí and six hundred million people,
along with King Píng Shā and others,
all followed after him.
Once the Liù Shī arrived,
they reported to the King as before.
The King, following the previous accounts,
went to report to the Buddha,
and the Buddha also replied:
"I myself know the time."
When the day of the prepared assembly arrived,
the Buddha departed again,
with the Bǐ Qiū monks,
and went to the state of Jiā Pí Luó Wèi.
The Shì Zhǒng of Jiā Pí Luó Wèi,
leading a large crowd,
all came to welcome the Buddha.
The people of Bō Luó Nài
learned of it the next day.
The followers of the Liù Shī
continued to race in pursuit.
King Fànmódá and eight hundred million people,
King Píngshā and the people of six kingdoms,
all gathered before and behind,
following the Buddha.
When the Liù Shī arrived,
they spoke to the Shìzhǒng,
clamoring among themselves, saying:
"Summoning vast skills and abilities,
let Qútán
compete with us in divine power."
The Shìzhǒng went again to tell the Buddha,
reporting the matter in detail.
The Buddha replied again, saying:
"I myself know the time."
Preparations were strictly made,
and as the appointed day approached,
the Buddha and the assembly of monks
went to Shèwèiguó.
The King of Shèwèiguó, named Bōsīnnì,
together with his ministers and people,
all came to welcome the Buddha.
Only on the following day did the Shìzhǒng realize the Buddha had left.
The Liù Shī led their disciples
and pursued from behind.
The Shìzhǒng led nine hundred million people,
King Píngshā, and the people of various nations,
filling the valleys and fields,
following toward Shèwèiguó.
When the Liù Shī and others arrived
and saw Bōsīnnì,
they recounted the entire matter from beginning to end:
"We desired to compete in divine power with Qútán,
but when the time came, he fled
and could not be held to the appointment.
Now with the great assembly,
we have pursued him to your kingdom.
Great King!
You must make him compete with us."
King Bōsīnnì
laughed at them,
saying that the Buddha’s extraordinary transformations are inconceivable,
and how could they, who are lowly and ordinary,
compete in power with the Great Dharma King?
The Liù Shī were aggressive,
and their tone grew louder.
King Bōsīnnì
then went to see the Buddha and said:
"The Liù Shī are so persistent;
I only wish, Shìzūn,
that you would display your divine power to subdue them,
so that everyone may distinguish the false from the true."
The Buddha told the King:
"I myself know the time."
King Bōsīnnì
then ordered his officials
to level the ground,
accumulate many incense and flowers,
arrange seats,
and erect banners and streamers.
When the preparations were complete,
the great assembly gathered.
On the first day of the twelfth month,
the Buddha arrived at the trial ground.
King Bōsīnnì
provided a meal that day;
in the early morning, he personally handed a willow twig to the Buddha.
After the Buddha finished chewing it,
he threw the remains on the ground, where they immediately grew,
rising up luxuriantly.
The roots and stems surged forth,
reaching five hundred yóuxún in height.
The branches and leaves spread like clouds,
and it was the same all around.
Gradually, flowers blossomed,
as large as chariot wheels,
and then there were fruits,
as large as five-dǒu jars.
The roots, stems, branches, and leaves
were all made of the seven treasures of various colors,
brilliant and magnificent.
They emitted light according to their colors,
eclipsing the sun and moon.
Those who ate the fruit
found its taste superior to gānlù,
and its fragrance filled the four directions;
those who smelled it felt joy in their hearts.
When the fragrant wind blew
and the parts brushed against each other,
the branches and leaves all produced harmonious and elegant sounds,
proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma,
which the listeners never tired of.
All the people,
seeing the transformation of this tree,
had their hearts of respect and faith
doubled in purity and sincerity.
The Buddha then taught the Dharma,
suiting their inclinations;
their minds were all enlightened.
Those seeking the Buddha,
those attaining the fruit or being born in heaven,
were very numerous.
On the second day,
King Yōutián invited the Buddha.
At that time, the Rúlái
transformed both sides
into two jeweled mountains,
magnificent and impressive to behold.
Composed of various treasures,
five colors shone brightly,
and the radiance was brilliant.
Various kinds of trees
were lined up on the mountains,
with flowers and fruits in abundance,
emitting a subtle fragrance.
On the summit of one mountain
was ripe jīngmǐ,
smooth and delicious with a hundred flavors,
sweet to the palate.
All kinds of people
ate as they pleased.
On the other mountain,
there was soft grass,
rich and sweet,
to provide for the animals;
those that needed it went to eat,
and being satiated, they were joyful.
The entire assembly,
seeing the mountains' extraordinary display,
were delighted after eating,
and their admiration grew deep.
The Buddha further suited them
by preaching the wonderful Dharma;
each attained enlightenment,
gave rise to the unsurpassed mind,
attained the fruit or was born in heaven,
and their number was also great.
On the third day,
Túnzhēntuóluó
invited the Buddha for an offering,
presenting pure water to the Buddha
for washing and rinsing.
The Buddha spat out the water,
and it transformed into a jeweled pond,
with its four sides
each being two hundred lǐ.
It was purely interspersed with the seven treasures,
their various colors reflecting each other,
and the light was blazing.
The water in that pond
possessed the eight virtues,
and the bottom was covered with seven-jewel sand.
There were eight types of lotus flowers,
as large as chariot wheels,
blue, yellow, red, and white,
mixed with crimson, green, and purple.
Their fragrance was sweet and pervasive,
reaching far in all directions.
According to the color of the lotus flowers,
each emitted light,
and the light shone brilliantly,
illuminating heaven and earth.
The great assembly, seeing this wonderful jeweled pond,
joyfully praised the Buddha's boundless merit.
The Buddha then observed
according to the people's minds,
and skillfully preached the Dharma,
causing each to be enlightened and give rise to the unsurpassed mind,
to attain the fruit and be born in heaven,
and all to increase their merit;
the number was too great to count.
On the fourth day,
King Yīnduópómí invited the Buddha.
On that day, the Buddha
caused the jeweled pond
to naturally have on its four sides
eight channels of water,
which flowed into each other
and naturally circulated.
The flowing water had a sound,
and that sound was clear and wonderful,
all proclaiming various Dharmas:
the five roots and five powers,
the seven factors of awakening and the eightfold path,
the three insights and six supernatural powers,
the six perfections and four immeasurables,
great kindness and great compassion.
Encouraging and guiding,
it spoke of various Dharmas.
All who heard and saw it
were enlightened in their hearts,
set their minds on seeking the Buddha,
attained the fruit or were born in heaven,
and increased their accumulated merit and wisdom;
the number was very many.
On the fifth day,
King Fànmódá
invited the Buddha for an offering.
On that day, the Buddha
emitted light from his mouth,
which was brilliant and golden.
pervading the Great Thousand-fold World.
Wherever the light touched,
all sentient beings’
three poisons and five aggregates
were all naturally stilled;
they were joyful in body and mind,
like a Bǐqiū attaining the Dì-sān Chán.
The assembly marveled
and aspired to the Buddha's virtue.
He then preached the Dharma for them;
each attained understanding,
aroused the mind of the Great Way,
attained fruits and was born in the heavens;
those who advanced in merit and cultivated wisdom
were very many in number.
On the sixth day,
Zhū Lǜchāng and his group
next invited the Buddha.
On this day, the Buddha
caused all sentient beings in the great assembly
to know each other's minds;
each single person knew the minds of all others,
the thoughts of good and evil,
and their intentions and karmic actions.
All were surprised and delighted
and admired the Buddha's virtue.
The Buddha then preached various subtle Dharmas for them;
all attained understanding,
and those who vowed to seek Buddhahood,
attained fruits and were born in the heavens,
were very many in number.
On the seventh day,
the Shìzhǒng invited the Buddha.
On this day, the Buddha
transformed all those in the assembly,
causing them all to see themselves as Zhuànlúnwáng,
with the seven treasures and a thousand sons;
various kings, officials, and citizens
solemnly and respectfully served them,
attending and looking up to them without end.
Each was surprised and marveled,
with immeasurable joy and celebration.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for them,
suiting their inclinations;
they also aroused the mind of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment,
attained fruits and were born in the heavens,
in numbers difficult to count.
On the eighth day, he accepted the invitation of Dìshì,
who made a lion throne for the Buddha.
The Rúlái ascended the throne;
Dìshì attended on the left,
and Fànwáng attended on the right.
All those in the assembly
sat quietly in settled meditation.
The Buddha slowly extended his arm
and touched the throne with his hand;
suddenly there was a great sound
like the roar of an elephant.
Immediately, five great spirits
destroyed and dragged down
the high thrones of the Liùshī.
Jīngāng Mìjì grasped a Vajra pestle;
fire emerged from the tip of the pestle,
and he raised it toward the Liùshī.
The Liùshī were terrified and fled in all directions;
ashamed of this heavy humiliation,
they threw themselves into the river and died.
The followers of the Liùshī,
a crowd of nine hundred million people,
all came to take refuge in the Buddha,
seeking to be his disciples.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bǐqiū!"
Their hair and beards fell off naturally,
Dharma robes appeared on their bodies,
and they all became Shāmén.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them
and showed them the essentials of the Dharma;
their outflows were exhausted and fetters untied,
and they all attained the state of Luóhàn.
Then the Rúlái,
from eighty thousand pores,
all emitted light
that filled the empty space.
At the end of each ray of light,
there was a great lotus flower;
on each flower,
there was a transformed Buddha with a great assembly
surrounding him and preaching the Dharma.
The assembly, seeing this unsurpassed transformation,
their hearts of faith and respect
increased manifold.
The Buddha then preached for them,
according to what was appropriate;
some aroused the Great Mind,
attained fruits and were born in the heavens,
and advanced in merit and increased in goodness;
their numbers were very many.
On the ninth day,
Fànwáng invited the Buddha.
The Buddha transformed his body to be as high as the Fàntiān;
his majesty was lofty and manifest,
towering beyond limit.
He emitted great light,
illuminating heaven and earth.
Everyone looked up and gazed
and all heard his words.
The Buddha displayed various essentials of the Dharma,
also causing many in the multitude to arouse the mind to seek Buddhahood,
attain fruits and be born in the heavens;
their numbers were also difficult to calculate.
On the tenth day,
the Sì Tiānwáng invited the Buddha.
At that time, the Shìzūn
caused the great assembly to see the Buddha's physical body
throughout all the heavens;
from the Sì Tiānwáng
to Sèjiūjìng,
all saw the Buddha's body
emitting great light,
each preaching for the great assembly
the subtle and wonderful Dharma.
They all looked up from afar
and saw it clearly.
All those in the assembly
greatly increased their respect and admiration.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them
according to their inclinations;
they all aroused the Great Mind
and stayed in the stage of non-retrogression;
those who attained fruits and were born in the heavens
were incalculable.
On the eleventh day,
Xūdá invited the Buddha.
On this day, the Buddha,
while on the high throne,
concealed his body;
he was silent and did not appear,
only emitting light
and producing a soft voice,
expounding and explaining the essentials of all Dharmas.
Those in the assembly
heard the Dharma and attained understanding;
some aroused the Great Mind
and stayed in non-retrogression;
those who attained fruits and were born in the heavens
were also very many.
On the twelfth day,
the layman Zhìduō invited the Buddha for an offering.
On this day, the Buddha
entered the Samādhi of Kindness,
emitting golden light
that shone throughout the Great Thousand-fold World.
When the light touched sentient beings,
the heart of the three poisons ceased,
and kindness naturally arose;
they viewed all sentient beings equally,
as father and mother,
or as elder and younger brother;
their hearts of love and compassion
had no increase or decrease.
Then he preached various subtle Dharmas for them;
they also aroused the Great Mind
and stayed in the stage of non-retrogression;
those who attained fruits and were born in the heavens
were difficult to measure.
On the thirteenth day, King Túnzhēntuóluó
next invited the Buddha
to receive offerings.
On this day, the Buddha
ascended the high throne
and emitted light from his navel,
which divided into two branches,
seven rèn away from his body;
each had a flower at the tip,
upon which was a transformed Buddha
no different from the Buddha himself.
From the navel of the transformed Buddha,
light emerged again,
also dividing into two branches seven rèn from the body,
with lotus flowers at the tips,
upon which were transformed Buddhas;
in this way, they rotated throughout the Great Thousand-fold World.
All who gazed
were startled and delighted.
Responding to the time, the Buddha
preached the Dharma as he wished;
they also aroused the Great Mind
and stayed in non-retrogression;
those who attained fruits and were born in the heavens
were very many in number.
On the fourteenth day,
King Yōutián invited the Buddha.
At that time, King Yōutián
scattered flowers over the Buddha.
The Buddha then immediately
transformed the scattered flowers
into one thousand two hundred and fifty-seven precious high carriages,
rising as high as the Fàntiān,
their brilliance surpassing the golden mountains.
Various treasures of many colors,
their brilliance and beauty shining upon one another resplendently,
the golden light vibrating with clarity, extraordinary and difficult to measure.
Divine pearls and necklaces
were interspersed among them.
Within the many high carriages,
there were buddha-bodies
emitting great light
pervading the three thousand worlds.
The assembly witnessed the transformation
and were filled with both joy and reverence.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma,
administering medicine according to the illness.
All resolved for the Great Mind,
some abiding in non-retrogression,
while those who attained the Way or were born in heaven
were also very numerous.
On the fifteenth day,
Píngshā Wáng invited the Buddha.
The Buddha pre-instructed the king:
"You only need to prepare eating utensils."
The king merely prepared the vessels and objects with solemnity,
making them extremely abundant.
When the mealtime arrived,
all the vessels were completely full
with sweet delicacies of a hundred flavors,
various extraordinary delicacies,
making the entire assembly fully satisfied with leftovers.
Having eaten, their bodies and minds were naturally peaceful and happy.
At that time, the World-Honored One
pointed to the ground with his finger,
and the eighteen hells all appeared.
Immeasurable as the number of dust motes,
various people suffering for their sins
each spoke for themselves:
"In my original time,
I committed such evils,
and now I suffer this pain."
The entire assembly
fully heard and saw this,
and were deeply moved with compassion,
their hair standing on end in horror.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for them,
suiting it to their intentions.
Those who resolved for the Great Mind
and stayed in non-retrogression,
or attained the fruit and were born in heaven,
could not be numbered.
Because the sentient beings of the hells
saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma,
reverence and admiration arose in their hearts;
they all took refuge from afar,
and in the end, they were all born in heaven or among humans.
At that time, Píngshā Wáng
knelt long and addressed the Buddha:
"The World-Honored One has thirty-two
extraordinary marks.
The various marks of your body and hands
I have previously seen,
but I have not yet beheld the wheel-marks beneath the Tathāgata's feet.
I wish you would show them to the assembly
so we may all reverently observe them together."
The Buddha then extended his feet
and showed them to the entire assembly.
Everyone saw the wheel-marks on the soles of the Buddha's feet,
upright, solemn, bright, and clear,
the patterns and lines like a painting,
distinct and evident.
Observing them, they never grew weary.
The king's joy increased,
and he addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I do not know, World-Honored One!
What virtues did you cultivate in the past
to attain the excellence of these wheel-marks?"
The Buddha then told the king:
"Because in the past I cultivated the ten good deeds myself
and further taught others to do so,
I attained these marks, as clear and evident as this."
The king again addressed the Buddha:
"I do not know,
World-Honored One!
Self-cultivation of the ten good deeds
and further teaching others to do so,
how was that matter?
I wish you would demonstrate and explain it."
The Buddha told the king:
"Listen well and keep it in your heart.
Countless asamkhyeya eons ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Shītuónímí,
who ruled eighty-four thousand kingdoms,
eighty trillion villages,
and ten thousand great ministers.
The king had twenty thousand consorts,
but none had a son.
The king was very worried,
fearing the end of the state's succession;
thus he widely performed sacrifices and prayed to the various heavens.
The king's first consort,
named Xūlìbōluómǎn,
after some time,
realized she was pregnant.
After she became pregnant,
her mind and nature were clever and clear;
she was benevolent, compassionate, and pitying,
and she encouraged people to do good.
When the months and days were fulfilled,
she gave birth to a male child,
upright and extraordinary,
with a bright and beautiful appearance.
Every pore on his body
emitted light.
The king was very happy and celebratory
and never grew weary of beholding him.
He immediately summoned a physiognomist
to divine whether he would be auspicious.
The physiognomist, having examined him,
sighed and said:
"How wonderful!
The marks of this child
are exceptionally extraordinary.
His virtue will pacify the four regions,
and the world will reverently support him."
The king's joy increased,
and he ordered a name to be established.
The physiognomist said to the king:
"What unusual omens were there?"
The king said:
"Since this child was conceived,
his mother has been wise, benevolent, and compassionate, encouraging good.
Though other omens were many, I find this particular change most strange."
The physiognomist was pleasantly surprised
and said to the king:
"Since the mother was eloquent and wise beforehand,
and he himself has bright light,
we should establish his name as Nàbōluómǎn,
which in the Jìn language means Huìguāng."
The prince grew up,
and his wisdom surpassed others.
When the father king passed away
and the funeral rites were completed,
the kings and ministers gathered and urged him to succeed to the throne.
The prince firmly declined, saying he was not capable.
The ministers each said:
"The Great King has passed away,
and there is only the prince,
with no other brothers.
Now that you say you are unwilling,
to whom would you yield?"
The prince replied:
"The people of the world act wickedly
and will certainly not maintain obedience.
If I apply punishments,
my sins will not be few.
If you can lead the people to universally practice the ten good deeds,
then I shall be able to accept the state's affairs."
The ministers said:
"Very well!
We only wish you to ascend the palace;
as for the way of the ten good deeds,
we shall certainly order them to be practiced."
At that time, the prince
then ascended the royal throne
and announced to the people
to universally practice the ten good deeds.
Everyone reverently obeyed,
changing their hearts and modifying their conduct.
The Demon King was jealous
and wished to ruin the king's transformation.
He secretly made a sealed letter
and announced it to all the kingdoms:
"The previous order to practice good
has neither benefit nor proof;
it is a vain toil,
practicing useless matters.
From now on,
allow the people to follow their hearts' desires
and commit the ten evil deeds,
and do not let their minds be fearful anymore."
The kings of the various lands received the letter
and were surprised by this strange decree:
"For what reason has he violated principle
and encouraged people to follow evil?"
Each sent a trusted envoy
to re-inquire about the reason.
The king heard these words,
and in shock and surprise said:
"I have given no such order;
for what reason could it be so?"
He immediately ordered his carriage prepared
and personally traveled through the various kingdoms
to meet the ministers and people
and proclaim against the deviant transformation.
The Demon by the roadside
transformed into a man
whose body was in a great fire,
with intense flames blazing,
crying and shouting within.
The sound was sorrowful and piercing.
The King immediately went forward and asked:
“Why are you like this?”
The person addressed the King, saying:
“Because in the past I encouraged people to practice the shí shàn,
I now suffer this agony;
the pain is poisonous and unbearable.”
The King replied again, saying:
“How can this be?
You encouraged people to cultivate virtue,
yet in return you suffer pain.”
Again he asked:
“If encouraging the practice of the shí shàn
causes you to suffer;
did the people who were previously encouraged
and practiced the shí shàn
receive a good reward or not?”
The reply was:
“The people before me only received good fortune;
but because I taught others, I alone suffer this pain.”
Hearing this, the King joyfully replied:
“If it only results in those people gaining good fortune,
I will willingly suffer the pain
and bear no resentment.”
The mó, hearing these words,
immediately vanished and left.
Traveling throughout all the kingdoms,
the King proclaimed the practice of the shí shàn;
the people were transformed by his influence,
being careful with their bodies, speech, and minds.
Righteous transformation spread widely,
and all looked up to him with reverence.
The King's virtue was magnificent and glorious,
and auspicious omens descended.
The jīn lún appeared first in response,
and the qī bǎo all arrived.
He traveled and transformed the four regions,
making it his business to guide others toward virtue.
Thus it is, Great King!
If you wish to know who the Shītuónímǐ Wáng was at that time,
it was my current father, Jìngfàn Wáng.
The mother at that time
was my current mother, Móhē Móyé.
That Huìguāng Wáng who transformed the people with the shí shàn
is my current self.
Because I myself practiced the shí shàn in that lifetime,
and also encouraged the people to practice the shí shàn,
I have thus today attained these thousand-spoked wheel signs beneath my feet.”
Then Píngshā Wáng
again addressed the fó, saying:
“The deluded followers of the liù shī,
not knowing their own measure,
were greedily attached to gain and offerings
and gave rise to jealousy.
They sought to challenge the Shìzūn in spiritual power,
saying that if the fó performed one feat,
they would perform two.
The fó manifested divine transformations,
wonderful and inconceivable.
The liù shī were cowed and diminished,
possessing not a single skill.
Ashamed of their forms and shadows,
they threw themselves into the water and died.
Their followers dispersed and dissolved,
bringing calamity upon themselves.
Thinking of their delusion,
how extremely severe was it!”
The fó told the Great King:
“Not only today have
the followers of the liù shī,
for the sake of fame and gain,
sought a contest with me
and lost their own assembly.
In a past life,
they also contended with me,
and I also harmed them
and took away their assembly.”
The King then knelt for a long time
and immediately addressed the fó, saying:
“I do not know,
Shìzūn!
In that past life,
when you fought with the liù shī and took their followers,
how did that happen?
I wish for you to explain it in detail.”
The fó told the King:
“Listen attentively.
Countless, immeasurable āsēngqí jié ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a King
named Móhē Shēchóulì,
who governed five hundred lesser kings.
He had five hundred consorts,
but had no crown prince to succeed him.
The King thought to himself:
‘I am growing old,
yet I have no son to continue the national throne.
If one day after I pass away,
the various kings, officials, and people
do not accept one another,
they will then raise armies and cruelly harm the lives of the people.
The country will fall into chaos;
how severe this suffering will be!’
Having thought this,
his heart sank into a sea of worry.
At that time, Tiāndì Shì,
knowing the King's worry from afar,
immediately descended from heaven,
transformed into a physician,
and came to the King's place,
asking about the cause of the King's worry.
The King then told him the matter as it was,
explaining it to the physician.
The transformed physician said to the King:
‘Worry no more!
I shall, for the King,
go into the Xuěshān,
gather and compound various medicines,
and give them to the consorts to take.
After taking the medicine,
they will all become pregnant.’
The King, hearing these words,
was somewhat relieved of his worry,
and immediately said to the physician:
‘If you can do this, it is well.’
At that time, the transformed physician
immediately went to the Xuěshān,
took various medicinal herbs,
carried them back to the royal palace,
boiled them with milk,
and gave it to the Chief Consort.
The Consort disliked the smell
and in her heart she did not believe in it.
The transformed physician returned to heaven,
and afterward she refused to take it.
The other lesser consorts
all shared and took it together.
Not long after taking it,
they soon realized they were pregnant.
Each informed the Chief Consort of the situation.
Having heard this, the Consort
felt worried and regretful,
and immediately asked:
‘Is there any left of what was taken?’
They replied:
‘It is all gone.’
She asked again:
‘Are the herbs from before still here?’
They replied:
‘They are still here.’
She immediately ordered milk to be brought,
and used it to boil the herbs again.
It was brought to the Consort,
and the Consort then took it.
After taking it for several days,
she also realized she was pregnant.
The various lesser consorts,
when their months were full, each gave birth.
They were all boys,
upright and exceptionally handsome.
The King, seeing the sons,
leaped for joy,
yet he felt uneasy and anxious thinking of the Chief Consort.
When the Consort's months were full,
she also gave birth to a boy,
but his appearance was extremely ugly,
his form like a tree stump.
When the parents saw him,
they were not pleased in their hearts,
and thus they jointly named him Duōluóhóushī,
which in the Jìn language means Zhūwù.
He was ordered to be raised.
As he gradually grew older,
all his other elder brothers
had already taken wives,
but only Zhūwù
was not concerned with this.
Later it happened that a border kingdom
raised an army and entered the territory.
The five hundred princes
led troops to resist them,
but at the start of the battle their army was defeated,
and they retreated toward the city.
Prince Zhūwù
asked his brothers:
‘Why are you retreating as if in terror?’
The brothers said:
‘The battle did not go well,
and the other army is pursuing us,
so we are fleeing in retreat.’
Zhūwù said:
‘How dare such army bandits
come to invade and insult us?
Bring the great bow and conch shell from the celestial temple of my ancestors,
and I will go to attack them.’
His ancestor was a Zhuànlún Wáng.
Immediately many people were sent
to fetch them.
And he gave it to him.
He took the bow and drew it open;
the sound of the bow was like thunder.
The sound of the twanging bow
was heard for forty lǐ.
Carrying the bow and clutching the conch,
he then went forth alone to attack.
Upon arriving, he first blew the conch;
its sound was like a thunderclap.
When that army heard the sound,
they were terrified and scattered,
and he returned only after the enemy had retreated.
His father the King treated him with extraordinary favor
and cherished him from then on;
thinking deeply of a means,
he wished to arrange a marriage for him.
At that time, there was a king
named Lǜshībácuō.
Hearing that he had a daughter
of peerless beauty,
the King immediately sent an envoy
to go and propose marriage.
He pointed to one of his brothers and showed his appearance to them,
saying that it was for this son
that he sought the noble's daughter.
The envoy received the instructions and arrived,
relating the King's words in full.
Lǜshībácuō
immediately consented to the marriage.
The envoy returned and informed the King,
and the King was greatly delighted.
Soon he dispatched carriages and horses
to go and welcome her.
He personally instructed Zhūwù:
"Do not see your wife during the day;
from now on,
always at nightfall
shall you meet and unite."
Later, the various daughters-in-law
were talking together,
each praising her husband's various talents and virtues.
At that time, Zhūwù’s wife also praised her husband, saying:
"My husband has the might of a fierce and robust warrior,
and his body is refined and supple;
he is very much to be respected and loved."
The other wives said:
"You need not speak;
your husband's appearance
is exactly like a gnarled stump.
If you were to see him by day,
it would be enough to terrify you."
Zhūwù’s wife heard this
and kept it in her heart.
She prepared and concealed a lamp,
hiding it behind a screen.
Waiting until her husband had finished lying down,
she brought out the lamp to look.
Seeing his physical form,
she was extremely terrified;
that very night she prepared her carriage
and returned to her home country.
At dawn he realized it
and was extremely sorrowful.
Grasping his bow and holding his conch,
he followed her tracks and pursued her.
Arriving in her country,
he stayed with a certain official.
Later, the kings of six countries
heard that Lǜshībácuō had an exceptionally wonderful daughter;
each was greedy to possess her,
so they raised armies and gathered multitudes,
vying with each other to come and demand her.
At that time, Lǜshībácuō
was extremely troubled
and ordered his various ministers to broadly deliberate the matter:
"If I wish to give her to just one,
the others will be resentful.
What means can be devised
to repel these fierce enemies?"
One minister said:
"You should divide this daughter
into six portions,
giving one to each army;
then their intent may be pacified."
Another minister said:
"Instead, offer a great reward:
whoever is able to repel the armies,
give him the daughter as a wife,
divide the kingdom to rule together,
and add further great rewards."
The King agreed with this
and proceeded to announce the reward.
Then Duōluóhóushī immediately took the bow and conch,
went out of the city toward the rebels,
and blew the conch and struck the bow.
The six armies were startled and horrified,
too frightened to move.
He then entered the armies,
beheaded the six kings,
seized their crowns and ornaments,
and took control of their multitudes.
Lǜshībácuō
was extremely joyful
and presented his daughter to him,
honoring him as the Great King
to govern the seven kingdoms.
With all the military forces
and leading the various troops,
he returned to his own country with his wife.
When the father king heard he was coming,
he went out to the border to welcome him.
Seeing that the troops led by his son were extremely grand,
he abdicated the kingdom to his son,
urging him to become the Great King.
His son would not agree,
saying that while his father was still alive,
by principle it should not be so.
Returning to the palace,
he questioned and reproached his wife:
"Why did you previously abandon me and flee in the night?"
His wife answered, saying:
"Your body was extremely ugly;
when I first saw it, I was startled and terrified,
thinking you were not a human being."
Duōluóhóushī
grasped a mirror to look at himself
and saw that his body and head
deeply resembled a gnarled stump.
He was disgusted by and loathed his body,
and did not like seeing himself;
he then went into a forest
intending to kill himself.
Dìshì knew from afar
and immediately descended to his side,
asking for the reason.
He consoled his mind,
gave him a precious jewel,
and told him:
"Always keep this jewel
upon the crown of your head,
and you shall become exceptionally handsome like me."
He soon joyfully received it
and placed it upon the crown of his head;
he felt his body become doubly extraordinary.
He returned to the palace,
took the bow and conch himself,
and wished to go out to play.
His wife saw him but did not recognize him,
and soon spoke to him, saying:
"Who are you?
Do not touch these things;
if my husband comes,
he might harm you."
He soon spoke to his wife, saying:
"I am your husband."
His wife did not believe him at all
and said to him:
"My husband is extremely ugly,
while your form is handsome.
Who are you
to claim to be my husband?"
The husband then removed the jewel
and showed again his former appearance.
The wife was then startled and delighted,
asking how this could be.
The husband then explained everything in detail,
telling of how he obtained the jewel.
From then on, the wife
respected and loved her husband;
the name Zhūwù
was thereafter abolished,
and they changed his name,
calling him Xūtuóluóshàn.
Later, he thought to himself:
"I should lead the troops to build a palace and city wall anew."
He then went out to observe and travel to a flat and broad place,
and ordered the multitudes:
"It can be built here."
There were four dragon kings
who came in human form to ask:
"You who wish to build a city,
what materials will you use?"
