Xūtuóluóshàn said:
"I shall use earth to build it."
The dragons spoke again, saying:
"Why not use jewels?"
He answered:
"The city is large,
where can I get so many jewels?"
The dragons spoke again, saying:
"We shall provide them to you."
Soon, on the four sides they transformed,
creating four great springs,
and told him:
"Use the water of the eastern spring
to make the moats,
and they shall become lapis lazuli;
use the water of the southern spring
to make the moats,
and they shall become gold."
"By using the water of the western spring
to create a moat,
it can become silver;
by using the water of the northern spring
to create a moat,
it can become crystal."
He immediately ordered it to be made,
and as spoken, the treasures were formed.
Then he ordered the city to be built,
four hundred lǐ square.
He further ordered the palace to be built,
forty lǐ square.
The palace walls, streets, and paths,
the towers, pavilions, and houses,
the groves of trees and bathing ponds,
were all adorned, purified, and marvelous with the four treasures,
appearing much like those in the heavens.
After the palace and city were completed,
the seven treasures appeared in response.
He governed the four regions,
transforming the people to practice goodness.
"In this way, Great King!
If you wish to know who Mōhé Shìchóulí was at that time,
he is now my father, King Jìngfàn.
The mother at that time
is now my mother, Mōhé Móyé.
That Prince Duōluóhóushī the Ugly
is now my very self.
The wife of that time
is now Qúyī.
The father-in-law of that time
is now Mōhé Jiāshè.
The six kings who wished to use military force to demand the woman
are now the Six Teachers.
In that world at that time,
they vied with me over beauty;
I harmed them
and seized their troops.
Even until today,
because they are jealous of fame and profit,
they seek to compete with me,
but having no skills to satisfy their hearts,
they threw themselves into the water and died.
I have gathered nine hundred million of their followers
as my disciples."
Then King Píngshā
spoke to the Buddha again:
"What actions did Duōluóhóushī
perform in the past
that his meritorious power was so strong,
yet his form was so ugly?"
The Buddha again told the King:
"Everything has its causes and conditions.
In the past, immeasurable, uncountable, and incalculable kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great kingdom
named Bāluónài.
In that kingdom was an immortal mountain
named Lǜshī.
At that time, in the immortal mountain,
there was a Pìzhīfó
whose body had a wind ailment
and needed to take oil.
He went to the house of an oil master
to beg for it.
The oil master became angry
and rebuked him:
'Your head is like a tree stump,
and your arms and legs are like axles.
You refuse to make a living and instead wait upon other households;
you do not intend to buy with money,
but only want to get it for nothing.'
Although he scolded and rebuked him,
he nevertheless gave him oil dregs.
The Pìzhīfó's heart was full of reverence;
after receiving them, he prepared to carry them away.
The wife of the oil master
came from outside,
and seeing the Pìzhīfó,
her heart was full of reverence.
She asked,
'Noble man!
Where have you come from?
Holding these oil dregs,
what do you intend to do with them?'
Then the Pìzhīfó told her the truth.
The wife felt deep regret
and called him back.
She took his bowl and filled it with oil.
She complained and blamed her husband, saying:
'You are truly wrong!
Why did you give him oil dregs?
You should quickly repent
to remove your verbal transgression.'
The oil master felt regret in his heart
and apologized roughly.
Husband and wife were of one mind
and said to the Pìzhīfó:
'If you need oil,
come and take it every day.'
Later, the Pìzhīfó
returned many times to take oil.
Moved by the power of their kindness,
in front of the oil master,
he manifested his supernatural powers.
He flew up into the empty sky,
his body emitted water and fire,
he divided and merged his body,
manifesting various transformations.
The oil master and his wife
saw his divine transformations
and were doubly delighted,
their reverence greatly increasing.
After the husband saw this,
he spoke to his wife:
'The oil you gave
shall bring a common blessing, and when we receive the retribution,
let us be husband and wife together.'
The wife said to the husband:
'You uttered evil words
toward a noble man,
and then gave him oil dregs
without a pure heart.
Wherever you are born,
you shall be extremely ugly.
Why should I be a wife with you?'
The husband replied:
'I always work hard
to gather the tools for oil;
how can you give it alone
and not share it with me?
I will never allow you not to be my wife.'
The wife said again:
'If I am your wife
and see your ugly form, I will abandon you and flee in the night.'
The husband replied to her:
'Even if you flee,
I shall pursue you
and will only stop when I have found you.'
After the husband and wife finished speaking,
they turned toward the Pìzhīfó
and took refuge with body and mind,
sincerely repenting their errors.
Then the Pìzhīfó spoke to the oil master and his wife:
'Because you gave me oil,
my illness has been cured.
Now, husband and wife,
what wish do you seek?
Whatever you ask for,
I shall cause you to obtain it all.'
The husband and wife were joyful
and knelt for a long time to make a vow:
'Let the places where we are born,
whether in the heavens or among humans,
be entirely according to our wishes.'
In this way, Great King!
If you wish to know who the oil seller was at that time,
it was Duōluóhóushī.
The wife of the oil master at that time
was the wife of Duōluóhóushī.
Because at that time he saw the Pìzhīfó
and said he was like a tree stump with arms and legs like axles,
and although he gave oil dregs,
he spoke with an angry expression,
due to these causes and conditions,
wherever he was born,
his initial form was extremely ugly,
just like his former evil words.
Because he later repented and joyfully gave good oil,
wherever he was born,
he returned to being upright and handsome.
Because he gave oil as a gift,
he always possessed great strength,
and among millions of people,
none dared to oppose him.
Due to the retribution of his merit,
he became a Wheel-Turning King,
enjoying blessings across the four regions,
with the five desires following his heart.
The karma of good and evil
does not decay in its retribution.
Therefore, all
should contemplate the essentials of the Way,
be careful with body, speech, and mind,
and follow the practice of the Way."
When the Buddha said this,
King Píngshā and others,
all the kings, ministers, and people,
the four assemblies of followers,
and the devas, dragons, and spirits,
hearing what the Buddha said,
some attained the stage of Sūdàhuán,
Sīdàhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
some planted the good roots of a Pìzhīfó;
some gave rise to the mind of the supreme great Way;
or some attained the stage of non-regression.
Everyone was filled with joy.
Respectfully practice.
*Xiányú Jīng*, Fascicle Two
*Xiányú Jīng*, Fascicle Three
Translated in Gāochāng Jùn by the Shāmén Huìjué and others of Liángzhōu during the Yuán Wèi.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was at Luóyuèqí on Mount Qíshéjué.
At that time, the Shìzūn!
His body had an affliction of wind.
Jǐyù, the King of Physicians,
prepared medicinal ghee for Him,
using thirty-two kinds of various medicines mixed together,
ordering the Buddha to take thirty-two ounces daily.
At that time, Típódá always harbored jealousy;
his heart was arrogant, wishing to be equal to the Buddha.
Hearing that the Buddha Shìzūn was taking the medicinal ghee,
his mind became greedy and envious,
desiring to take the same as the Buddha.
He then commanded Jǐyù:
“You must prepare it for me.”
At that time Jǐyù
prepared it for him as well,
and consequently said to him:
“Take four ounces daily.”
Típódá asked:
“How many ounces does the Buddha take?”
Jǐyù replied:
“Thirty-two ounces daily.”
Típódá said:
“I too shall take thirty-two ounces.”
Jǐyù replied:
“The body of the Rúlái
is not the same as yours;
if you take too much,
it will surely cause more suffering.”
Típódá said:
“If I take it,
I am certainly able to digest it.
My body and the Buddha’s body,
what difference is there?
Just give it to me to take.”
He immediately imitated the Buddha,
and also took thirty-two ounces every day.
The medicine flowed through his body into all his channels,
but his physical strength was weak and could not process it.
Throughout his body and limbs,
he suffered extreme pain,
groaning and crying out,
tossing and turning in agitation and distress.
The Shìzūn felt pity
and immediately reached out His hand from afar to rub his head.
The medicine was immediately digested and the pain was instantly removed.
When the illness was healed,
he recognized the Buddha’s hand
and consequently said:
“Xīdá’s other skills
the world does not accept or use,
but he has also studied the way of medicine
and is well able to make it known.”
At that time Ānán,
hearing these words, felt regret and resentment,
and knelt and said to the Buddha:
“Típódáduō
does not recognize kindness and care.
The Shìzūn’s compassionate mercy
removed the suffering for him,
yet he instead utters these unwholesome words.
What kind of mind does he have,
that he can give rise to such a thought,
harboring jealousy through the long night
toward the Buddha Shìzūn?”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“Típódá
not only today harbors an unwholesome heart and wishes to harm me;
in past lives, he also always had an evil mind to kill and harm me.”
Ānán said to the Buddha:
“I do not know the details of the harm in the past,
what were the causes and conditions?”
The Buddha said:
“Listen well!
I shall tell you.”
“Yes, Shìzūn!
I shall listen with a single mind.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“In the distant past,
uncountable Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí, there was a great city
named Bōluónài.
At that time the king
was named Fànmódá;
he was violent and without compassion,
extravagant, licentious, and fond of pleasure,
always harboring evil and jealousy,
and fond of doing harm.
At that time, this king
suddenly in a dream
saw a beast
whose fur was golden.
From the tips of its hairs
there came a golden light,
shining all around,
making everything also golden.
After waking, he thought to himself:
‘According to my dream,
such a thing must exist in the world.
I must order the hunters to seek its hide.’
Having had this thought,
he summoned all the hunters
and said to them:
‘In my dream there was a beast
whose fur was golden,
the tips of its hair emitting light,
extraordinarily beautiful and bright.
I think that within the borders of this kingdom
there must be such a creature.
I rely on you all to go far and wide to seek and capture it.
If you obtain its hide,
I shall grant you great rewards,
allowing your children and grandchildren
to have enough for seven generations.
If you do not apply your hearts
and fail to find it,
I shall execute all of your clans.’
Then the hunters,
having received the king’s command,
were filled with worry and distress.
Having no other plan,
they gathered in one place
to discuss this matter together:
‘The beast of the king’s dream
we have never seen in our lives.
Where should we go to find this?
If we do not get it now,
the king’s law is hard to violate;
our group and kind
will forever have no way to live.’
Having discussed this matter,
their frustration and distress increased further.
And then another said:
‘In these mountains and marshes,
poisonous insects and evil beasts
are also very numerous.
If we go far to seek it,
we will certainly not be able to get it,
and we will surely lose our lives,
dying in exhaustion in the wilderness.
Let us instead privately recruit one person
and send him to search for it.’
Everyone said it was good,
and after selecting among themselves,
they persuaded one man, saying:
‘You should exert your strength to seek it far and wide.
If you return safely,
we will pool our goods
and reward you handsomely.
If you encounter harm in the mountains or marshes and do not return,
we shall also give goods to your wife and children.’
The man heard this
and thought to himself:
‘For the sake of these people,
I will risk my life.’
Once his decision was made,
he immediately set out.
He prepared his travel equipment,
and went into danger.
He traveled for a long time,
his body grew thin and his strength was exhausted.
The weather was midsummer,
and arriving at a hot sandy path,
his lips were parched and he was parched with thirst.
The stifling heat made him feel like dying.
In extreme distress and bitterness,
he said sadly and dejectedly:
‘Who has compassion
and pity for me?
Please come and rescue me,
save my life!’
At that time, in the mountains and marshes,
there was a wild beast
named Jùtuó,
whose fur was golden
and the tips of its hair emitted light.
Hearing his words from afar,
it felt great pity for him.
It entered a cold spring,
came to where he was,
and embraced him with its body.
When he regained a little strength,
it took him to the water,
washed him,
went and gathered fruits,
and brought them for him to eat.
Once his body had recovered,
he thought to himself:
‘I see this extraordinary beast;
its fur and color are bright and shining.
This is exactly what my Great King requires.
However, I was on the verge of death
and relied on it to save my life.
I feel and recognize its kindness,
and have not yet been able to repay it.
How could I give rise to the thought
that I should harm it?
Yet if I do not obtain it,
all those hunters,
“My clan and relatives
will be executed.”
Having thought of this matter,
his grief was unbearable.
Jùtuó asked:
“Why are you unhappy?”
He shed tears and spoke of the matter held in his heart.
Jùtuó said:
“Do not worry about this matter!
My skin is easily obtained.
Considering my past lives,
I have sacrificed my body countless times,
yet never before for the sake of merit
was I able to give up my life.
Now, by using the skin of my body
to save the lives of those many people,
my heart is filled with joy,
as if I have gained something.
Just flay and take the skin,
but do not end my life immediately.
I have already given it to you,
and in the end, there will be no regret.”
At that time, the hunter
then slowly flayed the skin.
At that time, Jùtuó
then made a vow:
“Now I take my skin
to give to this person,
to save the precious lives of those many people.
With this merit,
I extend it to all living beings,
to achieve the unsurpassed, true Path of the Buddha,
to universally deliver all from the suffering of birth and death,
and to place them in the dwelling of Nièpán, the place of eternal bliss.”
After making this vow,
the three thousand worlds
shook in six ways.
The palaces of the various heavens
swayed and were not at peace;
each was filled with shock
and sought out the cause of this omen.
Seeing the Púsà flaying his skin as an offering,
they immediately descended from the heavens to the place where he was,
scattering flowers in offering
while their tears fell like rain.
After the skin was removed,
the flesh of his body was bare and red;
blood flowed and spread,
a sight painful to behold.
Furthermore, there were eighty thousand flies and ants of their kind
that gathered on his body
and bit and ate him at the same time.
He then wished to head towards his burrow,
but feared he might cause them harm;
enduring the pain and maintaining self-control,
his body did not move.
He offered his body to them,
and died among them.
At that time, the flies and ants
that had fed on the Púsà's body,
after their lives ended,
all attained rebirth in the heavens.
At that time, the hunter
carried the skin to the kingdom
and offered it to the king.
The king saw it and was delighted,
marvelling at its unprecedented rarity.
Pleased with its fineness and softness,
he used it constantly as bedding;
his heart then became tranquil
and his feelings joyful.
“Thus, Ānán!
If you wish to know who the beast Jùtuó was at that time,
it is my current self.
That King Fànmódá
is the current Típódá.
The eighty thousand insects
are those who, when I first became a Buddha
and began to turn the Wheel of Dharma,
were the eighty thousand heavenly beings who attained the Way.
This Típódá
harmed me in that lifetime,
and even to this day,
he still lacks a virtuous heart;
through the long night, he thinks of harm,
wishing to slander and injure me.”
The Worthy Ānán
and all those in the assembly,
hearing what the Buddha said,
were filled with both sorrow and grief.
Each was inspired
to diligently seek the essence of the Dharma.
Some attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
some planted the causes and conditions for becoming a Pìzhīfó;
some gave rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed Buddha-Way;
and some reached the stage of non-retrogression.
All were filled with joy,
and they reverently honored and practiced the teachings.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the Shèwèi kingdom at the Qítuó monastery.
After the passing of King Bōsīnuò,
Crown Prince Liúlí
assumed the regency as king.
He was tyrannical and unprincipled,
driving drunken elephants
to trample and kill the people,
beyond counting.
At that time, many women of noble families,
seeing things such as this,
were brokenhearted and distressed.
Finding no joy in worldly life,
they immediately left the home-life together to become Bǐqiūnís.
The people of the kingdom,
seeing these women—
some of the Shì clan,
some of royal lineage,
noble and upright,
the foremost in the kingdom—
all abandoning their desires
to leave home for the Way,
totaling five hundred people,
there was no one who did not praise them,
and they vied with one another to offer them support.
The Bǐqiūnís
said to each other:
"We now,
although called renunciants,
have not yet taken the medicine of the Dharma to eliminate lust, anger, and delusion.
Should we not go together to the place of the Bǐqiūní Tōuluónántuó
to consult her and receive the teachings of the Sūtras,
hoping to attain what we seek?"
They immediately went to her place,
paid their respects and inquired after her,
and each stated:
"Although we have taken the path of the Way,
we have not yet attained the sweet dew.
We wish for you to grant us awakening."
At that time, Tōuluónántuó
thought to herself:
"I should now teach them to break their precepts.
If I take their robes and bowls,
would that not be delightful?"
She then said to them:
"You are of noble and great families,
with fields, estates, and the seven treasures,
elephants, horses, and servants—lacking nothing you need.
Why did you abandon them?
To uphold the Fó's restrictive precepts
and be Bǐqiūnís
is toil and suffering such as this.
It would be better to return home,
where husbands, wives, and children
can enjoy one another
and you can give charitably as you please;
thus you could be honored for a lifetime."
The Bǐqiūnís,
hearing these words,
felt bewildered in their hearts.
Each then wept
and left her.
They then went to the place of the Bǐqiūní Wēimiào,
went forward to pay respects,
and inquired after her according to the Dharma.
They then each declared:
"When we were at home,
we were long lost in worldly habits.
Now, although we have left home,
our minds are unsettled and flighty,
and our passions burn fiercely such that we cannot release ourselves.
We wish for your compassion;
please speak the Dharma for us
and explain how to remove our sins and hindrances."
At that time, Wēimiào
told them:
"Regarding the three periods of time,
what do you wish to ask about?"
The Bǐqiūnís said:
"Setting aside the past and future for now,
we wish for you to speak of the present
and untie our knots of doubt."
Wēimiào told them:
"As for carnal desire,
it is like a raging fire burning through mountains and marshes;
its spreading and growth are extreme,
and the harm it causes is ever more widespread.
Because people dwell in carnal desire,
they harm one another;
as days and months increase,
it leads them to fall into the three miserable paths,
with no time of escape.
As for those who delight in home life,
they are greedy for coming together and meeting;
due to the causes and conditions of affection, honor, and pleasure,
there is birth, old age, sickness, death, and separation,
and the troubles caused by officials.
They turn to one another in weeping and longing,
their hearts and livers are wounded and destroyed,
they faint and revive again.
Longing for home is deep and firm;
the mind is bound and entangled by it,
more so than in a prison."
I was originally born into a family of Fànzhì.
My father was noble,
the foremost in the land.
At that time, there was a son of a Fànzhì,
intelligent and wise, who heard of my beauty.
He immediately sent
marriage gifts through a matchmaker
to take me as his wife.
We thus established a household,
and later gave birth to children.
My husband's father and mother
subsequently passed away.
At that time, I was pregnant,
and I said to my husband:
“Now that I am pregnant
and filled with impurities,
as the months are nearing completion,
should there be any danger or exhaustion,
I should return to my home to see my parents.”
My husband then said it was well.
He then sent me to return,
but when we were halfway on the road,
my body began to ache.
I stopped beneath a tree,
while my husband slept apart from me.
I gave birth during the night,
and the lochia flowed out in great quantities.
A venomous snake, smelling the scent,
immediately came and killed my husband.
During the night, I called out several times but there was no sound.
As the sky turned toward dawn,
I forced myself to rise
and went to pull my husband's hand.
I realized he had been poisoned by a snake;
his body was swollen and rotten,
and his limbs and joints were falling apart.
When I saw this,
I immediately fainted from grief.
At that time, my eldest son,
seeing his father's body dead,
cried out with a wailing voice.
Hearing the child's voice,
I immediately revived.
I then took the eldest son,
carrying him upon my neck,
and held the infant in my arms.
Weeping, I proceeded on the road.
The road was again vast and perilous,
with no people at all.
Arriving at the middle of the way,
there was a great river,
both deep and wide.
I then left the eldest son
sitting on the riverbank,
and first carried the infant
to cross to the other side.
I then returned to fetch the older one.
Seeing me from afar, the child
immediately came into the water and was swept away by the current.
I hurried to pursue him,
but lacked the strength to save him,
and he floated away and submerged.
I then immediately returned,
wishing to go to the infant,
but a wolf had already finished eating him.
I saw only his blood,
scattered upon the ground.
I collapsed again,
and only after a long while did I revive.
I then proceeded forward on the road
and encountered a Fànzhì,
who was a close friend of my father.
He immediately asked me:
“Where have you come from,
to be so distressed and haggard?”
I then told him in detail all the bitter and poisonous events I had undergone.
At that time, the Fànzhì,
pitying my isolation and suffering,
wept with me.
I asked the Fànzhì:
“Are my parents and relatives
all safe and well?”
The Fànzhì replied:
“Your parents and household members, great and small,
recently suffered a fire
and all died at once.”
When I heard this,
I again fainted from grief,
and only after a long while did I revive.
The Fànzhì pitied me
and took me to his home,
providing for my needs without lack,
looking after me like a daughter.
Then another Fànzhì,
seeing my beauty,
asked to take me as his wife.
Consent was given,
and we became a household together.
I again became pregnant,
and the months were completed.
At that time, my husband went out
to drink wine at another house.
He returned home at dusk.
I was then about to give birth,
and was closed alone inside.
Before the birth was finished,
the Fànzhì hammered on the door and shouted loudly.
Since no one went to open it,
the Fànzhì grew furious,
broke down the door and entered.
He immediately began to beat me.
I explained the situation,
but the Fànzhì became even angrier.
He immediately took the child and killed it.
He fried it in ghee
and forced me to eat it.
I was extremely distressed and anguished,
and could not bear to eat it,
so I was beaten again.
After eating the child,
my heart was knotted with bitterness.
I reflected that my merit was exhausted,
to have met such a man.
I then abandoned him and fled,
arriving at Bōluónài.
Outside the city,
I sat beneath a tree to rest.
At that time, in that country,
there was the son of an elder
who had just lost his wife.
He had buried her in a garden outside the city.
Longing for his wife,
he left the city every day
to weep at the tomb.
He then saw me
and immediately asked me:
“Who are you,
sitting alone by the roadside?”
I told him the events as they had happened.
He spoke to me again, saying:
“Now I wish to enter that garden with you; would you agree?”
I then consented,
and so we became husband and wife.
After several days passed,
the son of the elder
fell ill beyond recovery
and suddenly his life ended.
At that time, the law of that country was
that if during one’s life
there was someone one loved and held dear,
on the day of the burial,
they would be buried together in the tomb.
Although I was buried,
my life had not yet ended.
At that time, a group of thieves
came to open the tomb.
Then the leader of the thieves,
seeing my beauty,
immediately took me as his wife.
Within several weeks,
he went out again to plunder and rob,
but was caught by the owner,
who then cut off his head.
The followers among the thieves
immediately took the corpse
and brought it back to me.
They then buried him together,
and according to the custom of the land,
I was buried along with him.
While I was in the tomb,
after three days passed,
various wolves, foxes, and dogs
came again to open the tomb,
wishing to eat the dead.
I was again able to come out.
I again reproached myself:
“What past calamities have I committed
that within a few days
I encounter such sinful suffering?
Having died and come back to life,
what should I serve to preserve my remaining life?”
I then thought to myself:
“I have often heard in the past
that the son of the Shì clan
abandoned his home to study the Path.
When the Path was attained, he was called Fó,
who understands both the past and the future.
I should go to him and take refuge with my body and mind.”
I then went directly,
hurrying toward Qíhuán.
From afar, I saw the Rúlái,
like a tree in full bloom or the moon among the stars.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
with his untainted triple knowledge,
perceived that I should be saved
and came to welcome me.
At that time, my body was exposed,
and I had nothing to cover myself.
I immediately sat on the ground,
covering my breasts with my hands.
Fó told Ānán:
“Take a robe and go cover that woman.”
At that time I received the robe,
and then I prostrated myself at the feet of Shìzūn,
fully detailing my sins and misfortunes,
praying for his compassion
and to be allowed to follow the Path.
Fó told Ānán:
“Take this woman
and give her to Jiāotánmí,
to have her be taught the precepts.”
Then Dà’àidào
immediately accepted me
to become a Bǐqiūní,
and she spoke to me of the essentials of the Four Truths: suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
Hearing this Dharma,
I concentrated my mind with diligence
and achieved the state of Yìngzhēn,
attaining knowledge of the past and future.
Now in my present life,
the hardships I have undergone
are difficult to fully detail;
but as for what was created in previous lives,
not even a hair’s breadth is different.”
Then the Bǐqiūnís
asked once more:
“What fault was there in your past life
that you received such calamities?
We only wish for you to speak of it.”
Wēimiào replied:
“Listen quietly.
In the distant past,
there was an elder
with countless wealth
but no children.
He took a younger wife;
although she was from a minor family,
she was upright and without peer.
The husband loved her dearly
and she subsequently became pregnant.
When ten months were full,
she gave birth to a boy.
The husband and wife respected him
and looked at him without tire.
The senior wife thought to herself:
‘Although I am of noble family,
I have no children who can serve as heirs.
Now this child,
when he grows up,
will lead the household,
and the fields, wealth, and all things
will all be managed by him.
My vain labor and hardship
in accumulating property
will not be at my own disposal.’
Jealousy immediately arose;
it would be better to kill him early.
Having settled the inner plan, she took an iron needle
and pierced it into the child’s fontanel,
making it sink in and not be seen.
The child gradually wasted away,
and within ten days,
he subsequently died.
The younger wife was devastated,
losing her breath and then reviving.
Suspecting the senior wife had killed her son out of jealousy,
she asked the senior wife:
‘You have no decency;
you have resentfully killed my son.’
The senior wife immediately
swore an oath of curse, saying:
‘If I killed your son,
let me in every life
have my husband killed by a venomous snake;
if I have sons,
let them be swept away by water or eaten by wolves;
let me see myself buried alive;
let me eat my own children;
let my parents and family
die in a fire.
Why do you slander me?
Why do you slander me?’
At that time,
she thought there was no retribution for sin or merit,
but the previous oath
is now all being received,
with no one to take my place.
If you wish to know who the senior wife was,
it was none other than myself.”
The Bǐqiūnís
asked again:
“What merit was there
that allowed you to see the Rúlái,
have him welcome you,
and remain in the hall of the Path to escape birth and death?”
Wēimiào replied:
“Formerly, in the kingdom of Bōluónà,
there was a great mountain
called Xiānshān.
Within it, there were always Pìzhīfó, Shēngwén,
and outer-path immortals,
without vacancy.
At that time, a Yuánjué
entered the city for alms.
The wife of an elder
saw him and was delighted,
and immediately provided offerings.
After the Yuánjué had eaten,
he flew up into the void,
his body emitting water and fire,
and he sat and lay in the air.
When the wife saw this,
she made an oath, saying:
‘May I in a future life attain the Path like this.’
The wife at that time
was none other than myself.
Because of this cause,
I was able to see the Rúlái,
my mind was opened and awakened,
and I achieved the way of the Luóhàn.
Although my body today
has attained the state of Luóhàn,
a hot iron needle constantly
enters from the top of my head
and exits from the soles of my feet.
Day and night I suffer from this,
without end.
Such are calamity and blessing;
they do not decay.”
At that time, five hundred Bǐqiūnís from noble families,
hearing this Dharma,
were filled with awe.
Observing the root of desire
as being like a blazing fire,
their hearts of greedy desire
were never again produced.
The suffering of domestic life
was worse than a prison.
All defilements were exhausted,
and they simultaneously entered samadhi,
achieving the way of the Āluóhàn.
Each with a unified mind,
they said to Wēimiào:
“We were entwined and bound by sexual desire
and could not pull ourselves out.
Now, receiving your compassionate guidance,
we have crossed over birth and death.”
Then the Fó praised:
“Splendid, Wēimiào!
One who follows the Path,
being able to use the Dharma
to teach and admonish one another,
can be called a child of the Fó.”
When the assembly heard this,
there were none who were not delighted,
and they prostrated and put it into practice.
Thus have I heard:
Once the Fó was in the kingdom of Shèwèiguó, in the Jǐshù Jǐgūdúyuán.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
in the morning with Ānán,
entered the city to beg for food.
They saw a group of young children playing in the middle of the road,
each gathering earth from the ground,
using it to make palaces and houses,
as well as granaries, treasures, and the five grains.
There was one young child
who saw from afar the Fó coming;
seeing the Fó’s radiant marks,
a heart of reverence arose within him,
and he leaped for joy.
Having given rise to a mind of giving,
he immediately took what was called "grain" from the granary,
scooped it up with his hands,
and wanted to use it as an offering to the Fó.
Since his body was small and could not reach,
he said to another young child:
"I will climb on top of you
to offer the grain."
The young child was happy
and replied:
"It is possible."
He then stepped onto his shoulders
and offered the earth to the Fó.
The Fó then lowered his bowl,
bowed his head to receive the earth,
and after receiving it, he handed it to Ānán,
saying:
"Take this and smear it on the walls of my room."
Having finished begging for food,
they returned to Jǐhuán.
Ānán used the earth
to smear the floor of the Fó’s room,
evenly coating one side,
until the earth was exhausted.
Having finished the coating,
he adjusted his robes
and fully reported it to the Fó.
The Fó told Ānán:
"The young child from before,
who joyfully offered the earth—
the earth was enough to coat one side of the Fó’s room.
By virtue of this merit,
one hundred years after my Bānnièpán,
he shall become a great king
named Āshūjiā.
The other young child
shall become a great minister.
They will together rule over Yánfú-
tí and all its lands,
making the Sānbǎo flourish,
widely providing offerings,
distributing Shèlì
throughout Yánfútí,
and shall build eighty-four thousand pagodas for me."
Ānán was delighted and again addressed the Fó:
"What merit did the Rúlái perform
in the past
to receive this reward of so many pagodas?"
The Fó said: "Ānán! Listen carefully with single-minded attention.
Long ago in the past, incalculable Āsēngqí eons ago,
there was a great king
named Bōsàiqí,
who ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms in Yánfútí.
At that time, there was a Fó in the world
named Fúshā.
King Bōsàiqí,
along with his ministers and people,
made offerings to the Fó and the Bǐqiūsēng,
with the four types of offerings,
and their reverence was boundless.
At that time, the king
thought to
himself:
'In this great kingdom today,
all the people
constantly get to see the Fó, bow to him, and make offerings.
But in the other small kingdoms,
located in remote and secluded places, the people
have no way to cultivate merit.
I should have the image of the Fó painted
and distributed to all the kingdoms,
so that everyone may make offerings.'
After having this thought,
he immediately summoned painters
and ordered them to paint the image.
Then the painters
came to the Fó’s side
to observe the Fó’s excellent marks,
wishing to paint them.
Just as they painted one part,
they forgot the other parts;
they looked again and again,
and then set to work once more,
but if they remembered one they forgot another,
and they could not complete it.
Then Fúshā Fó
mixed the various colors,
and painted it himself with his own hand
to serve as a model,
painting one standing image.
From this, the painters
were then able to paint
all eighty-four thousand images,
making them extremely pure and wondrous,
as upright and dignified as the Fó himself.
They were distributed to all the kingdoms,
one for each kingdom.
He also issued a decree
ordering the people to prepare flowers and incense for the purpose of making offerings.
The kings, ministers, and people of all the kingdoms,
having received the Rúlái image,
joyfully and reverently worshipped them
as if they were looking at the Fó’s actual body.
Thus it is, Ānán!
King Bōsàiqí
was my previous self.
Because in that lifetime I had eighty-four thousand Rúlái images painted
and distributed to all the kingdoms for people to worship,
by virtue of this merit,
I have received blessings life after life,
whether in the heavens or among humans,
I have always been a monarch.
In every place I was born,
I was upright and exceptionally wonderful,
with the thirty-two marks
and eighty secondary signs.
By virtue of this merit,
I have attained Buddhahood myself,
and after my Nièpán,
I shall further receive the retribution of these eighty-four thousand pagodas."
The Worthy Ānán
and all those in the assembly,
having heard what the Fó said,
joyfully took it to heart and practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
Once the Fó was in the kingdom of Shèwèiguó, in the Jǐshù Jǐgūdúyuán.
At that time, various Bǐqiū were in different kingdoms,
undertaking the summer retreat as they chose;
after ninety days, the retreat being concluded,
they each went to the Fó's place to consult and receive the holy teachings.
At that time, the Shìzūn had been separated from the Bǐqiū for a long time,
and with a heart of compassion and pity,
he raised his divine hand with the thousand-spoked wheel mark and consoled them,
lowering his mind to inquire after them:
"All of you! Living in remote places,
were you without lack of food and offerings?"
The Rúlái's merit is without peer in the world,
yet now he humbles himself to look upon the Bǐqiū,
specially maintaining a spirit of humility and respect.
Ānán, seeing this,
was greatly surprised by the reason and said to the Fó:
"The Shìzūn's appearance in the world is most extraordinary,
his merit and wisdom are rare in the world.
Now he humbles his mind to console and inquire after the assembly of Bǐqiū,
how excellent is that!
I wonder, Shìzūn! Is the cause for such humble words
from the distant or recent past?"
The Shìzūn told him:
"Do you wish to know?
Listen clearly and reflect well! I shall tell you."
"I shall follow your instruction and listen well."
The Fó told Ānán:
"Long ago in the past, countless, immeasurable, and inconceivable Āsēngqí eons ago,
in this Yánfútí, there was a great kingdom named Bōluónài.
At that time, there was a man who enjoyed cultivating his family business,
but his mind was particularly fond of gold.
He worked hard to accumulate it,
exhausting his body,
managing business in all directions.
Whatever money he obtained, he used it all to buy gold.
Once he got a jar full,
he dug into the ground inside his house to hide it.
In this way, through various means, toiling with his body and suffering in his person,
over many years, he never spent on clothes or food.
He accumulated it without ceasing until he had seven jars,
and buried them all. Later, the man fell ill and died.
Because of his love for gold,
he was reborn with the body of a venomous snake,
returning to the house to guard these gold jars.
Years passed and the house fell into ruin;
no one lived there anymore.
As the snake guarded the gold jars, its life span was again coming to an end.
After shedding its body, its craving did not cease,
so it took the same form again,
coiling its body around the gold jars.
In this manner, revolving through births, tens of thousands of years passed.
During its final birth, a feeling of revulsion arose;
it thought to itself: "It is because of this gold that I have received this evil form
without end.
Now I should use it as an offering in a field of superior merit,
so that I may receive its blessings life after life."
Having made its decision,
it went to the side of the road and hid its body in the grass,
concealing itself while watching.
Suppose a person comes,
I shall speak to them.
At that time, a poisonous snake saw a person passing by along the road,
and the snake called out to him.
The person heard the calling voice and looked around to the left and right,
but seeing no one and hearing only the voice,
he continued along the road.
The snake appeared again
and called out, saying: "Hey, person! You may come close to me."
The person replied to the snake, saying:
"Your body is poisonous and evil;
why do you call me?
If I come close to you,
I might be harmed."
The snake replied to the person:
"If I harbored evil intent,
even if you did not come, I could still cause you harm."
The person was terrified
and went to where it was.
The snake said to the person:
"In this place where I am, there is a jar of gold.
I wish to entrust it to you to make offerings and create merit;
can you do this?
If you will not,
I shall harm you."
The person replied to the snake:
"I can do it."
Then the snake led the person to the place of the gold,
brought out the gold and gave it to him,
and further told him:
"You take this gold and make offerings to the assembly of monks.
On the day the meal is prepared, remember to bring an Āshūtí
and carry me there."
The person carried the gold to the Sēngqiélán
and handed it over to the Sēng Wéinà,
relating the above matters in detail to the monks,
saying that the poisonous snake wished to make offerings
and fixing the day for the meal.
The monks accepted the gold and prepared a fine meal.
When the day of the meal arrived,
the person took a small Āshūtí and went to the snake's place.
The snake saw the person,
felt joy in its heart,
and comforted him with greetings.
It immediately coiled its body and climbed into the Āshūtí.
Thereupon, the person covered the top with a cloth
and carried it toward the Fótú.
On the way, he met a person who asked the man carrying the snake:
"Where have you come from?
Are you in good health?"
The person remained silent and did not answer the question.
Although he was asked three times,
he did not utter a single word.
The poisonous snake he was carrying immediately became angry,
and its pent-up venom became intense.
It wanted to kill the man,
but then restrained itself.
It thought to itself again:
"What is wrong with this man? He does not know what is appropriate.
The other person greeted him with good intentions,
and asked three times with solemnity,
yet he did not answer with a single word.
How could he be so offensive?"
After having this thought,
its poisonous intent arose again,
boiling up fiercely within,
and it again wanted to harm him.
Just as it was about to spit its venom, it thought again:
"This person is creating merit for me,
and I have not yet repaid his kindness."
This happened three times,
and each time it subsided.
"This person has already shown great kindness to me.
Although he has committed a fault,
it is proper for me to endure it."
Arriving at an open space ahead,
the snake said to the person:
"Put me down on the ground."
It rebuked him most severely
and exhorted him with the Dharma.
Thereupon, the person felt remorse and reproached himself,
giving rise to a humble mind
and showing compassion to all.
The snake exhorted him again: "Do not do that again!"
The person carried the snake to the Sēngqiélán
and placed it before the assembly of monks.
At that time, the mealtime for the monks had arrived,
and they stood in a row.
The snake had that person distribute incense in sequence,
and with a heart of faith, the snake watched those who received the incense.
Thus it went to the very end,
watching intently without turning away.
The monks filed out and circumambulated the pagoda,
and the person took water to wash the monks' hands.
The snake, with a respectful heart, watched the person washing the hands,
without any weariness.
When the monks finished eating,
they again spoke the Dharma extensively for the snake.
The snake was doubly joyful,
and its mind of generosity increased further.
It led the Sēng Wéinà to the original place of the gold,
where the six remaining jars of gold were all given to the monks.
After it had finished creating merit,
its life came to an end,
and due to its merit, it was born in the Dāolì Tiān."
The Fó told Ānán:
"If you wish to know who the man carrying the snake was then,
could it be anyone else?
It was I myself.
The poisonous snake of that time
is now Shèlìfú.
When I was carrying the snake in those past days and was rebuked by it,
I felt shame and made a vow
to give rise to a humble mind,
to view all beings equally,
and I have never regressed
even until today."
At that time, all the Bǐqiū, Ānán, and the others,
having heard what the Fó had said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus I have heard:
At one time the Fó was staying in Luóyuèqí at the Zhúlín Jīngshè,
together with an innumerable multitude of honored disciples.
At that time in the kingdom,
there was a Póluómén
who lived in poverty and hardship,
lacking money and grain.
Although he worked diligently without slackening,
his misfortunes became extreme.
Having exhausted all means and methods,
he could not provide for food and clothing.
He then went and asked people:
"In this world today,
what kind of deeds should one perform
to enable a person to receive the benefits of such blessings in the present life?"
Someone answered, saying:
"Do you not know?
Now the Fó has appeared in the world
to bless and deliver sentient beings,
helping and benefiting all,
and none fail to be delivered.
The Rúlái also has four honored disciples,
Móhē Jiāshè,
Dàmùjiánlián,
Shèlìfú,
and Ānàlǜ; these four virtuous men
always pity the poor and destitute,
and they constantly perform deeds to benefit sentient beings in suffering and distress.
If you can now, with a heart of faith and respect,
prepare food to make offerings to these virtuous men,
then your wishes can be fulfilled in this current life."
At that time, the Póluómén,
after hearing the people say these things,
his heart was filled with joy.
He went throughout the kingdom,
everywhere offering his services,
toiling with his body.
Having obtained a small amount of wealth,
he carried it to his home,
prepared food and drink,
invited the virtuous and holy ones,
and made offerings for one day.
Setting his mind with great diligence,
he hoped for a reward in his current life.
The Póluómén’s wife,
named Chāimó
(which means "Peace and Tranquility" in the language of Jìn),
after the meal for the Sēng was finished,
the honored disciples
exhorted Chāimó
to receive the Bā Guān Zhāi.
After she had received the precepts,
they each returned to the monastery.
At that time, King Píngshā,
while returning to the city from an excursion to the forests and marshes,
saw a man on the road
who had committed a serious crime against the king.
He was bound to a stake
set upright by the roadside.
Seeing the king, he cried out in sorrow,
begging for a little food.
The king’s heart felt pity and compassion,
and promised to give it to him,
but just then he departed.
Though the king spent the whole day,
he suddenly forgot the previous matter.
Suddenly at night, he thought to himself:
"I previously promised food to that criminal;
how could I have forgotten so suddenly?"
He immediately sent someone to take food to him,
but within and without the palace,
there was no one who wished to go.
They all said:
"It is now midnight;
there may be fierce beasts, evil ghosts, and Luóchà on the road,
and many disasters and difficulties.
We would rather die here
than go there."
At that time, the king,
thinking of that man’s suffering,
was troubled in body and mind
and filled with great compassion.
He immediately ordered throughout the kingdom:
"Whoever can deliver food to that man’s location
will be rewarded with a thousand taels of gold."
Among the people of the kingdom,
no one accepted the offer.
At that time, Chāimó,
who had often heard people say:
"If there is a person in the world
who observes the Bā Guān Zhāi,
then all evil spirits, wicked ghosts,
poisonous beasts,
and all kinds of calamities
will be unable to harm them."
When Chāimó heard this,
she had this thought:
"My family is poor,
and I have also received the precepts.
The king’s current recruitment
must be intended for me.
I should now go and accept the reward for his recruitment."
Having finished her deliberations,
she went to respond to the king’s recruitment.
At that time, the king
said to Chāimó:
"Carry the food for me
to that man’s location.
If you arrive and return,
I will certainly give you a thousand taels of gold."
Chāimó immediately,
as commanded, carried it and went.
Sincerely keeping the precepts
without any lapses,
she walked along the road.
As she moved further from the city,
she encountered a Luóchà
named Lánpó.
At that time, that ghost
had given birth to five hundred children.
Having just finished giving birth,
she was extremely hungry and thirsty.
Seeing Chāimó coming,
she hoped to make a meal of her.
However, because Chāimó
kept the precepts without lapse,
when the Luóchà saw her,
she instead felt fear.
Pressed by hunger,
she revealed herself and begged for the food she was carrying:
"Please give a little of it to me."
Chāimó did not refuse
and gave her a little.
Although what was given was little,
because of the ghost’s power,
she was made full and satisfied.
Then the Luóchà
asked Chāimó:
"What is your name?"
The woman replied:
"My name is Chāimó."
The Luóchà rejoiced
and said to Chāimó:
"Now that I have given birth,
I have found peace and tranquility.
Because you saved my life,
you have benefited me greatly.
Since I have been saved,
and have also heard such a good name,
in the place where I live,
there is a cauldron of gold.
I will use it to repay you;
remember to take it when you return."
She asked again:
"Where are you going?"
Chāimó replied:
"I wish to take this food to that person."
Lánpó spoke again:
"I have a younger sister
living further ahead
named Ālánpó.
If you see her,
please give her my greetings.
Tell her that I have given birth,
bearing five hundred children,
and that my body is at peace and tranquility.
Relate my situation in full,
so that she may know the news."
Chāimó did as she was told
and went on her way.
She saw Ālánpó,
and immediately stepped forward to greet her,
telling her of Lánpó’s
detailed circumstances:
that she had given birth to five hundred children,
and all were at peace and tranquility.
At that time, Ālánpó
was delighted to hear this
and asked the woman:
"Now, what is your name?"
The woman replied:
"My name is Chāimó."
When the Luóchà heard this,
she also became joyful.
"My older sister has given birth
and has found peace and tranquility again.
Your name is also good;
how excellent!
In this place where I live,
there is a cauldron of gold.
I will grant it to you;
remember to take it when you return."
She also asked her:
"Where are you going?"
Chāimó replied:
"I am carrying food for the king
to that man’s location."
Ālánpó said:
"I have a brother,
named Fēn-nà-qí,
who lives on the road ahead.
Inquire after his health for me,
and pass along my regards."
They then took leave of each other
and proceeded along the path.
Arriving at the destination as they wished,
they saw Fēn-nà-qí.
For the sake of his two sisters,
they fully explained the situation and their intent,
saying that his eldest sister
had given birth to five hundred sons,
was physically light and at peace,
and there were no ill omens.
At that time, Fēn-nà-qí,
hearing the news of his two sisters' safety,
was joyful in heart.
He again asked Chā-mó:
"What is your name?"
The woman replied:
"My name is Chā-mó."
The ghost replied:
"Your name means 'Peaceful and Content.'
Furthermore, you have brought news of my sisters' safety;
how much more joyful could I be?"
He then said to Chā-mó:
"In this place where I live,
there is a cauldron of gold.
I give it to you as a gift.
Remember to take it when you go."
After the farewell was finished,
they set out on the road.
Remembering the former place,
they went to where the people were.
Having finished eating,
they returned to their original place,
took three cauldrons of gold and brought them home.
Furthermore, from the king's household,
they received a reward of one thousand taels of gold.
Because of this, the family
was pulled out of poverty and became wealthy.
The common people in the country saw the abundance of treasures in the house and each admired them,
delighting in serving them.
They came to the house
to offer their services.
The king heard that this person had such merit,
so he summoned them to the palace
and appointed them as a high official.
Having received the king's emolument,
and with the family being wealthy,
their faith was sincere and firm, and they widely cultivated meritorious deeds.
They invited the Buddha and the Sangha
to set up a great dāna.
The Buddha and the assembly of disciples
all accepted the invitation.
After eating,
the Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
Their minds were enlightened,
and they achieved the stage of Xū-tuó-huán.
At that time, those in the assembly,
such as Ā-nán and others,
hearing what the Buddha spoke,
joyfully followed his teachings.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the country of Shè-wèi, in the Jǐ-shù Jǐ-gū-dú-yuán.
At that time, there was a woman in the country named Nán-tuó,
who was poor and alone,
supporting herself by begging.
Seeing the kings, ministers, and people, great and small,
each making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha,
she thought to herself:
"Due to my past sins, I was born poor and lowly.
Although I have encountered the field of merit,
I have no seeds to sow."
Gripped by sorrow and grief,
she deeply reproached and regretted her past.
She then went begging
to wait for a meager offering.
Not resting the whole day, she obtained only one coin.
She took it to an oil shop
to buy oil.
The oil merchant asked:
"Buying oil with one coin
gets you very little;
what will you use it for?"
Nán-tuó told him all that was in her heart.
The shop owner felt pity for her
and gave her twice the amount of oil.
Having received it, she was joyful.
It was enough to make one lamp.
Carrying it to the vihara, she offered it to the Shì-zūn,
placing it among the many lamps before the Buddha.
She made a vow:
"I am poor now,
and use this small lamp to make an offering to the Buddha.
By this merit, may I obtain the light of wisdom in future lives
to eliminate the darkness of the defilements of all sentient beings."
Having made this vow, she bowed to the Buddha and departed.
When the night ended, all the other lamps went out,
but this one alone continued to burn.
At that time, Mù-lián, whose turn it was for the day's duty,
saw that it was dawn.
As he was clearing away the lamps,
he saw this one lamp burning alone, bright and beautiful,
the oil and wick not depleted, as if it were a newly lit lamp.
He thought to himself:
"Burning a lamp during the day serves no purpose.
I wish to extinguish it
and relight it in the evening."
He then raised his hand to fan out the lamp,
but the flame remained as before,
without diminishing or going out.
He then fanned it with his robe,
but the light was not damaged.
The Buddha saw that Mù-lián wanted to extinguish the lamp
and said to Mù-lián:
"This lamp
is not something you, a Shēng-wén, can move.
Even if you took the water of the four great oceans
and poured it over it,
or if the Suí-lán wind blew on it, it could not be extinguished.
Why is this?
This is an offering from a person who has made a great vow for universal salvation."
After the Buddha said this,
the woman Nán-tuó came again to the Buddha and bowed her head to his feet.
At that time, the Shì-zūn immediately bestowed a prediction upon her:
"In a future life, after two ā-sēng-qí and one hundred kalpas,
you shall become a Buddha named Dèng-guāng,
complete with the ten titles."
Thereupon, Nán-tuó was joyful at receiving the prediction.
She knelt and spoke to the Buddha,
requesting to leave the household life.
The Buddha immediately granted it, and she became a Bǐ-qiū-ní.
Huì-mìng Ā-nán and Mù-lián,
seeing the poor woman escape her suffering, leave the household life, and receive a prediction,
knelt with palms together and spoke to the Buddha:
"What past deeds did the woman Nán-tuó perform
to live in poverty and beg for so long?
And what deeds led her
to meet the Buddha and leave the household life,
so that the four classes of disciples admire her
and compete to provide offerings for her?"
The Buddha said to Ā-nán:
"In the past, there was a Buddha named Jiā-shè.
At that time, there was the wife of a householder
who personally went to invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks.
However, the Buddha had already accepted a poor woman's invitation
to receive her offerings.
This woman had already attained the path of an Ā-nà-hán.
At that time, the elder's wife, prideful of her wealth, looked down on the poor woman
and was annoyed that the Shì-zūn had accepted her invitation first.
She then said:
'Why does the Shì-zūn not accept my offering
but instead responds first to that beggar's invitation?'"
"Because of those evil words, looking down on a sage,
from then on, for five hundred lifetimes,
she was always born into poor and lowly families of beggars.
Because on that day she offered to the Rú-lái and the assembly of monks
with a respectful and joyful heart,
she has now met the Buddha's era, left the household life, and received a prediction,
and the whole country admires her."
At that time, after the assembly heard the Buddha say this,
they were all greatly joyful.
The king, ministers, and people, hearing that this poor woman had offered a single lamp and received a prediction of Buddhahood,
all felt great admiration.
They each gave her excellent clothes
so that she lacked none of the four necessities.
Men and women of the whole country, noble and humble, great and small,
competed to prepare various fragrant oil lamps
and brought them to Qǐ-huán to offer to the Buddha.
The people were so numerous
that the lamps filled Qǐ-huán.
In the groves of trees, they were filled in all four directions,
like stars arrayed in the sky.
It was like this every day for seven nights.
At that time, Ā-nán was very joyful,
praising the various virtuous deeds of the Rú-lái.
He came forward and spoke to the Buddha:
"I do not know, Shì-zūn, what good roots were planted in the past
to bring about this infinite retribution of lamp offerings?"
The Buddha told Ā-nán:
"Long ago in the past, two ā-sēng-qí and ninety-one kalpas ago,
in this Yán-fú-tí, there was a great king named Bō-sài-qí,
who ruled over eighty-four thousand small lands in this world.
The king's primary consort gave birth to a crown prince.
His body was purple-gold in color,
with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
Upon his crown, there was a natural jewel,
and his various features were radiant,
shining brightly in people's eyes.
They then summoned physiognomists to tell his fortune
and to name him."
The Xiàngshī (Physiognomist) opened the swaddling clothes to look,
and seeing his wondrousness,
he raised his hands and proclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!
This current Tàizǐ (Prince), among all devas and humans in the world,
has no equal.
If he remains in the home life,
he will become a Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng (Wheel-Turning Sage King).
If he leaves the home life,
he will become a naturally awakened Buddha."
The Xiàngshī said to the King:
"When the Tàizǐ was born, were there any unusual occurrences?"
The King answered him, saying:
"A bright jewel atop his head naturally appeared with him."
Thereupon, he was given a name;
his name was Lènàshíqí, which in the language of Jìn is Bǎojì.
As he grew older,
he left the home life to study the Way and succeeded in becoming a Buddha.
He taught and transformed the people, and those he saved were very many.
At that time, his father the King invited the Buddha and the Sangha
to receive offerings for three months.
There was a Bǐqiū (Bhikṣu) named Ālímìluó, which in the language of Jìn is Shèngyǒu.
During the three months, he undertook the duty of being the lamp tányuè (patron).
Every day he entered the city,
going to the various elders, householders, and people,
At that time, the King had a daughter named Móuní.
From a high tower, she saw this Bǐqiū entering the city daily,
managing what was required.
Respect arose in her heart,
and she sent someone to ask him:
"Venerable one, you are always toiling so.
What are you managing?"
The Bǐqiū replied:
"For these three months, I am acting as the lamp tányuè for the Buddha and the Sangha.
Therefore, I enter the city
to go to various virtuous ones and seek butter oil, lamp wicks, and equipment."
The messenger returned and reported this.
The Princess was delighted
and spoke further to Shèngyǒu:
"From now on, do not go begging anymore.
I shall provide you with the equipment for making the lamps."
The Bǐqiū agreed to this.
From then on, she constantly sent butter oil, lamp wicks, and equipment
to the vihara.
Bǐqiū Shèngyǒu managed them every day, lighting lamps as an offering.
He resolved to save others broadly, and his sincerity was profound.
The Buddha gave him a prediction:
"In a future life after an asaṃkhyeya of kalpas, you shall become a Buddha named Dìngguāng, complete with the ten titles."
Princess Móuní, hearing that Bǐqiū Shèngyǒu had received the prediction of becoming a Buddha,
thought to herself:
"The items for the Buddha's lamps were all provided by me.
The Bǐqiū only managed them,
yet he has already received the prediction,
while I alone have not."
Having had this thought, she went to the Buddha's place
and expressed her feelings.
The Buddha then gave her a prediction,
saying to Móuní:
"In a future life after two asaṃkhyeyas and ninety-one kalpas,
you shall become a Buddha named Shìjiāmóuní, complete with the ten titles."
Thereupon, the Princess, hearing the Buddha's prediction,
felt joy arise from within.
She transformed into a man,
prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and asked to become a Śramaṇa.
The Buddha then permitted it.
He was diligent and courageous,
cultivating tirelessly without rest."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"At that time, who was the Bǐqiū Ālímìluó?
Could he be anyone else?
He was the Dìngguāng Buddha of the past.
And who was Princess Móuní? Could she be anyone else?
She was my very self.
Because of that past offering of lamp light,
from then until now, throughout countless kalpas,
I have naturally received blessings in the heavens and the world.
My physical body is extraordinary and surpasses all others.
Until now, having attained Buddhahood,
I receive these rewards for those offerings of lamp light."
At that time, the great assembly, hearing what the Buddha said—
some attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit,
some planted the roots of goodness for Pratyekabuddhahood,
and some made the resolve for the supreme, correct, and true Way.
The Huìmìng Ānán and the entire assembly
all bowed their heads in reverence
and joyfully practiced accordingly.
Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish, Volume 3
There are people of wisdom and skill
who, due to small conditions,
can generate the great mind to aspire toward the Buddha-Way;
as for indolent and lazy people,
even though they have great conditions,
they still do not generate the intention to aspire toward the Buddha-Way.
Therefore, practitioners
should strengthen their hearts, establish their resolve, and courageously pursue good conditions.
How is this known to be so?
At that time, the Shìzūn
was in the Kingdom of Shèwèiguó, in the Jǐshù Jǐgūdúyuán,
with the fourfold assembly, various kings, ministers, and people,
surrounding him from front and back,
making offerings and paying respects.
Among this assembly,
there were many who had doubts:
"Shìzūn,
originally by what causes and conditions
did you first generate the mind of Unsurpassed Pútí,
achieving Buddhahood yourself,
and bringing much benefit?
We also ought to generate the mind to achieve the Way and bring benefit and peace to all sentient beings."
The Venerable Ānán,
knowing what the assembly was thinking,
immediately rose from his seat, straightened his robes,
stepped forward and said to the Buddha:
"Now this great assembly
all have doubts:
'By what causes and conditions did the Shìzūn in the past
generate the mind of the Great Way?
We only wish you would speak of it,
to widely benefit all.'"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Excellent, excellent!
That which you have asked
will bring much benefit.
Listen attentively and contemplate well!
I shall speak for you."
At that time, the great assembly
was silent and without a sound;
the wind, the rivers, and the river waters,
the hundred birds and the walking beasts,
were all silent and without a sound.
Then the great assembly,
the Tiān, Lóng, Guǐ, and Shén,
were in awe and happy to hear,
contemplating the Buddha with a single mind.
The Buddha said to Ānán:
"In the far distant past,
immeasurable and boundless Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Dàguāngmíng,
who possessed great merit,
was intelligent, courageous, and wise,
and was fully endowed with the marks of a king.
At that time, on the border,
there was a king
who was close and friendly with him.
Whatever that country lacked,
King Dàguāngmíng
would send as gifts at the appropriate times;
whatever was precious in that country
was also offered to King Guāngmíng.
At that time, that king,
while hunting on a great mountain,
obtained two elephant calves
that were upright and beautiful,
white as the Pō
lí
Mountain,
with seven points touching the ground,
extremely lovable and respectable.
With a joyful heart, he thought:
'I shall now give these to King Dàguāngmíng.'
Having thought this, he decorated them
with gold, silver, and various jewels,
the rarest treasures in the world,
and sent people to deliver them.
When King Dàguāngmíng
saw these elephants,
his heart was greatly delighted.
There was then an elephant trainer
named Sànshé,
and the king told him:
'You shall teach these elephants,
nurturing and taming them.'
Sànshé received the command and before long they were tamed and submissive;
draped in various jewels,
he went to tell the king:
'The elephant I trained
is now well-tamed and good;
I wish the king would observe and test it.'
The king was happy to hear this
and was eager to see it;
he immediately struck the golden drums,
assembled his ministers,
and ordered them to observe the testing of the elephant.
Once the assembly had gathered,
the king mounted this elephant;
just as when the sun first emerges from the mountains with radiant light,
the king’s first mounting of the elephant
was also like that.
With his ministers and people,
he went out of the city for recreation,
approaching the testing ground.
At that time, the elephant's vigor was strong,
and it saw a herd of elephants in a lotus pond eating lotus roots;
seeing them, its desire arose and it rushed to chase the female elephants,
eventually reaching a deep forest.
At that time, the king’s crown and robes
all fell off,
tearing his clothes and wounding his body,
causing bleeding and pulling at his hair.
The king was then dizzy and dazed;
thinking he would surely die,
he was extremely terrified,
and immediately asked the elephant trainer:
'Will I have any life left?'
Sànshé said to the king:
'Among the trees in the forest,
if there is one that can be grasped,
I wish the king would grab it,
then you may be saved.'
The king grabbed a tree branch,
the elephant left and the king remained;
he climbed down the tree and sat on the ground,
seeing himself no longer having robes or crown,
his body wounded and broken,
he felt great distress.
Confused and troubled, he left the forest,
not knowing where his followers were.
The elephant trainer, slightly ahead,
had grasped a tree and stayed there;
he returned to look for the king and saw him sitting alone in sorrow.
The elephant trainer kowtowed
and said to the king:
'I wish the king would not be in great sorrow and suffering;
this elephant’s lustful heart will soon subside;
it will come to loathe the foul grass
and find the muddy water unpleasant,
longing for the clean, rich, and delicious food of the palace;
in this way it will return on its own.'
The king then said:
'I no longer think of you or the elephant;
because of this elephant,
I nearly lost my life.'
At that time, the various ministers
each had the thought
that the king had already been harmed by the mad elephant.
Searching everywhere along the path,
they sometimes found the royal crown and clothes,
or saw fallen blood;
they eventually saw the king,
who mounted another elephant
and returned to the city.
The people in the city
all saw the Great King suffering such hardship,
and none were not filled with sorrow.
At that time, the mad elephant,
in the wild marshes,
ate foul grass
and drank muddy, filthy water;
its lustful intent subsided,
and it immediately longed for the cool, sweet meals of the royal palace.
Moving like a swift wind,
it went back to its original dwelling place.
When the elephant trainer saw it,
he went to tell the king:
'The Great King should know!
The elephant previously lost
has now returned;
I wish the king would look at it.'
The king said:
'I do not need you,
nor do I need the elephant.'
Sànshé addressed the king:
'If the king does not need me or the elephant,
I only wish you would observe my method of training the elephant.'
The king then ordered a seating area to be prepared on a flat ground.
At that time, the people of the country,
hearing that this elephant trainer wanted to show the king his method of training the elephant,
all gathered like clouds.
Then the king left the palace,
with the great assembly leading and following,
he went to the seat and sat down.
The elephant trainer Sànshé
brought the elephant to the gathering,
and immediately ordered a craftsman
to make seven iron balls,
and heat them until they were glowing red.
Having done so, he thought:
'If the elephant swallows these balls,
it will certainly die;
the king might later regret it.'
He said to the king:
'This white elephant treasure,
only a Zhuǎnlúnwáng
can obtain it.'
"Now there is a minor fault,
and it should not lead to its loss."
Guāngmíng Wáng told him:
"If the elephant was not tamed,
you should not have let me ride it;
if it was tamed,
how could such an incident occur?
Now I do not need you,
nor do I need the elephant."
The mahout said again:
"Even if you do not need me,
the elephant is truly a great pity!"
Guāngmíng Wáng's anger surged,
and he told him to get far away!
Sànshé arose
and said with weeping tears:
"The King has no sense of intimacy or distance;
his heart is like poison,
though he falsely speaks sweet words."
At that time, everyone in the assembly, great and small,
wept upon hearing this
and gazed intently at the elephant.
The mahout then signaled to the elephant:
"Swallow this iron ball.
If you do not swallow it,
I shall split your skull with an iron hook."
The elephant knew his intent
and thought to itself:
"I would rather die from swallowing this hot ball
than be unable to endure the pain of being killed by an iron hook.
Just as when people face death,
they would rather be strangled than burned to death."
It knelt before Guāngmíng Wáng,
shedding tears and hoping to be saved.
Guāngmíng Wáng's anger was still surging;
after seeing this, he looked away.
Sànshé said to the elephant:
"Why do you not swallow this ball now?"
The elephant looked in all four directions
and realized that in this assembly,
there was no one who could save its life.
Using its trunk, it took the ball,
placed it in its mouth and swallowed it.
It scorched and rotted its belly,
passed straight through, and the elephant died.
+ Like a Jīngāng chǔ striking a Bōlí mountain,
the iron ball fell to the ground,
still red with heat.
When the assembly saw this,
there was none who did not weep in sorrow.
"Guāngmíng Wáng, seeing this matter,
was startled and terrified.
He then gave rise to a heart of remorse
and immediately summoned Sànshé,
saying:
'Since your elephant was so tamed and submissive,
why, when in the forest,
could you not control it?'
At that time, the Jìngjūtiān,
knowing that Guāngmíng Wáng should give rise to the Unsurpassed Bodhi-mind,
used their divine power
to make the mahout kneel and answer Guāngmíng Wáng:
'Great King!
I can only tame the elephant's body,
but I cannot tame its mind.'
Guāngmíng Wáng then asked:
'Is there anyone
who can tame the body
as well as the mind?'
He replied to Guāngmíng Wáng:
'There is the Fó Shìzūn!
He can tame the body
and also tame the mind.'
When Guāngmíng Wáng
heard the name of Fó,
his heart was startled and his hair stood on end.
He said to Sànshé:
'This one called Fó—
from what lineage was he born?'
Sànshé replied:
'The Fó Shìzūn
is born from two lineages:
the first is Wisdom,
and the second is Great Compassion.
He diligently practiced the six matters,
namely the Liù Bōluómì.
Having perfected both merit and wisdom,
he is
called Fó.
He can tame himself
and also tame all sentient beings.'
When Guāngmíng Wáng heard this,
he trembled with joy.
He immediately went into the palace,
bathed in fragrant water,
changed into new clothes,
and went up to a high pavilion.
He bowed in all four directions,
gave rise to a heart of great compassion for all sentient beings,
and burned incense, making a vow:
'May all the merit I possess
be dedicated to the path of the Fó.
Once I have become a Fó,
I shall tame my own mind
and also tame all sentient beings.
If for the sake of even one sentient being
staying in Ābí Dìyù
for the duration of an eon
would be of benefit,
I shall enter that hell
and never abandon the Bodhi-mind.'
After making this vow,
the earth shook in six ways.
The mountains and great oceans
tossed and surged.
Within the empty sky,
there was spontaneous music.
Countless devas
performed celestial music
and sang in praise of the Púsà,
saying:
'By what you have done,
you shall soon attain Buddhahood.
Once you have attained the path of the Fó,
we pray that you will deliver us;
we also should have a share
in this pure Dharma assembly.' "
Fó told the Bhiksus:
"If you wish to know, the white elephant that swallowed the iron ball at that time
was Nántuó.
The mahout at that time
was Shèlìfú.
Guāngmíng Wáng
was I myself.
At that time,
because I saw how the elephant was tamed and submissive,
I first gave rise to the aspiration for the path
and sought the path of the Fó."
At that time, the great assembly,
hearing of Fó's austerities such as these,
some attained the four stages of fruit,
some gave rise to the aspiration for the Great Path,
and some left home to practice the path.
There was none who was not joyful
and who did not uphold and practice it.
Because of these causes and conditions,
through strength of will and courage,
great things can be accomplished from small causes;
whereas through laziness and negligence,
even if one encounters great opportunities,
nothing can be achieved.
Therefore, practitioners
should be diligent and energetic in advancing toward the path of the Fó.

Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was at the Qíhuán monastery in the kingdom of Shèwèi,
with a great assembly of bǐqiū,
who surrounded him with reverence.
At that time, the Fó praised those who practice with wisdom, saying:
"Those who wish to attain the path of the Fó
should delight in the sūtra-dharma, praising, reciting, and expounding it.
Even if a layperson preaches the Dharma,
all the heavenly beings, ghosts, and spirits
will all come to listen and receive it,
how much more so for those who have left the household life?
When those who have left the household life,
even while walking on the road,
recite sūtras and chant gāthās,
there are always heavenly beings
who follow them to listen and receive it.
Therefore, one should diligently recite and preach the sūtra-dharma."
How is this known?
When the Fó first arrived at the Qíhuán monastery,
his merit spread abroad,
and there was no one who did not hear of it.
At that time, all virtuous people,
hearing of the Fó's name and virtue,
were boundlessly joyful
and praised him.
Why was this?
Wicked people in the world,
hearing the names of virtuous people,
feel hatred and jealousy in their hearts,
and rejoice upon hearing of evil;
worthy and virtuous people
suppress evil and promote good,
wishing for it to be heard far and wide.
When they see someone commit evil,
they understand it is due to defilements
and feel pity and forgiveness.
Such virtuous people,
hearing that a Fó has appeared in the world,
praise and spread the word,
making it known throughout all kingdoms.
At that time, King Bōsīni
had a small border country
named Píniǔqián.
Within this settlement at that time,
many people held wrong views,
and there was no Fó, Dharma, or Sangha.
In this village at that time,
there was a woman
named Móhē Yōubōsīnà.
At that time, she had business
that took her to King Bōsīni in the kingdom of Shèwèi.
When her business was finished,
from some devout yōupósaì,
she heard of the Fó's merit.
Wishing to see the Fó,
she went immediately to Qíhuán.
Seeing the Fó's extraordinary and majestic marks and signs,
she bowed her head to his feet
and withdrew to one side.
At that time, the Shìzūn
preached the Dharma of the five precepts to the great assembly:
"Namely, not killing leads to long life,
not stealing leads to great wealth,
not committing sexual misconduct leads to being respected and loved by others,
not lying leads to one's words being trusted,
and not drinking alcohol leads to being wise and clear-minded."
At that time, Yōubōsīnà,
having heard this Dharma,
was greatly delighted.
She went forward and addressed the Fó, saying:
"I only pray, Shìzūn!
Grant me the five precepts.
I shall purely uphold them for as long as I live.
Even if I were to lose my life,
I would never violate them.
Just as a hungry person cherishes food
and a thirsty person loves water,
or as a sick person takes care of themselves,
my protection of the prohibitive precepts
shall be just like that."
Then the Fó immediately granted her the five precepts.
Having received the five precepts,
she said:
"Shìzūn!
The place where I live
is remote and distant.
I must now return to where I reside.
I pray you grant me some small thing
that I may revere and honor it."
All Buddhas of the past,
as numerous as the sands of the Hénghé,
have all preached the Fǎjù.
All Buddhas of the future,
as numerous as the sands of the Hénghé,
will also preach this sūtra.
At that time, the Shìzūn
gave the Fǎjù Jīng
to Yōubōsīnà
and commanded her to recite and practice it.
Having received it, she bowed,
circumambulated the Fó three times, and departed.
She returned to her original settlement,
contemplating and remembering the sūtra given by the Fó.
At that time, in the middle of the night,
atop a high building,
she was contemplating the Fó's merit
and reciting the Fǎjù.
At that time, Heavenly King Píshāmén,
wishing to go to the place of Pílóulèchā in the south,
was leading a thousand yèchā
and passed over Yōubōsīnà.
Hearing the sound of the sūtra recitation,
they all immediately stopped in the air
to listen to her recitation,
and he praised her, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Sister!
You speak the essentials of the Dharma well.
If I were now to give you heavenly treasures as a gift,
it would not be appropriate for you.
I will now gift you with a piece of good news:
the Honorable Shèlìfú
and Dà Mùjiánlián
have come from Shèwèi
and will stay in this forest.
Tomorrow morning, go and invite them to your house to make offerings.
When they recite the prayer of blessings,
mention my name as well."
When Yōubōsīnà heard these words,
she looked up into the air,
but could not see his form.
Like a blind person,
she could see nothing at all in the darkness of the night.
She then asked:
"Who are you?
I do not see your form,
but only hear a voice."
A voice replied from the air:
"I am the Ghost King Píshāmén Tiān.
Because I was listening to the Dharma,
I stopped here."
The yōupóyí said:
"Heavenly beings do not speak falsely.
You are a heavenly being and I am a human;
we have no connection at all.
For what reason do you call me sister?"
The Heavenly King replied:
"The Fó is the King of Dharma
and also the father of humans and devas.
I am a yōupósaì,
and you are a yōupóyí.
We share the same flavor of the Dharma,
therefore I said sister."
At that time, the yōupóyí
felt joy in her heart
and asked:
"Heavenly King!
When I make offerings
and call your name,
what benefit is there?"
The Heavenly King replied:
"As I am a Heavenly King,
my heavenly ears hear from afar.
Those who call my name,
I hear them all.
Because they call me,
it increases my power, majesty, and retinue.
I, in turn, using my divine power
and commanding the ghosts and spirits,
will protect that person,
increase their fortune and blessings,
and cause them to be free from decline and calamity."
Having said this,
he immediately moved on.
At that time, the yōupóyí
