was leaping for joy
and thought to herself:
"Through a hundred kalpas, the Fó
diligently performed ascetic practices
solely for my sake.
Because of the Fó's kindness,
he even caused the Ghost King to be my sister."
She then did not sleep,
and as dawn was about to break,
she finally got a little sleep.
In her household,
she usually ordered a servant to go into the forest to gather firewood.
At that time, the servant
went early to the forest
and climbed a tree to gather wood.
From a distance, he saw the Honorable Shèlìfú,
Mùlián, and five hundred other bǐqiū
in the forest.
Those who were diligent
sat in meditation and recited sūtras;
those who were lazy
lay on the sand and grass.
At that time, that servant had followed the master
to the kingdom of Shèwèi,
and for that reason, seeing them from afar, he recognized the two Honorables.
Then he thought to himself:
"The one whom my mistress
respects
is now in this forest.
My mistress does not know this.
If I slowly finish gathering firewood
and only then return to tell her,
perhaps some other person
might accidentally invite them away first,
and I would then be at fault.
To make the matter most efficient,
I should first handle this essential task
and only afterwards gather the firewood;
in this way, there will be no trouble for the matter."
He immediately climbed down from the tree,
went to the place where the Zūnzhě were,
bowed his head to their feet, and said to the Zūnzhě:
"My mistress Yōubōsīnà
pays her respects and sends her greetings."
The Zūnzhě replied:
"May Yōubōsīnà find peace and happiness, and be liberated from birth and death."
He said:
"Zūnzhě!
My mistress Yōubōsīnà
invites you to a meal tomorrow;
she only hopes you will deign to come."
The Zūnzhě replied:
"You return home
and tell Yōubōsīnà:
'Excellent, Yōupóyí!
You know the proper time and what is long-term appropriate.
The Fó praises five types of giving that earn immeasurable merit:
giving to those who have come from afar,
giving to those who are going afar,
giving to those who are sick and emaciated,
giving food and drink in times of hunger,
and giving to those who know the Fǎ.
These five kinds of giving
result in merit in the present world.'"
The messenger received the instruction,
took his leave, and exited the forest.
He hurried back home,
and upon arriving, asked a maid where the mistress was.
She replied:
"Up on that high building;
during the early and middle night,
she could not sleep,
and has only just now begun to sleep."
The messenger said he would wake her,
but the others all said they did not dare to.
"If you cannot," he said,
"I shall wake her myself."
They all said, "As you wish."
The messenger went up to the building
and snapped his fingers to wake her.
Once awake, she asked:
"What do you wish to say?"
He said:
"Mistress!
Zūnzhě Shèlìfú,
Mùjiànlián, and the others
are in the forest."
Yōubōsīnà leaped with great joy
and immediately took two gold rings from her ears
to reward him.
He then spoke again:
"The Zūnzhě has good teachings for the mistress."
She said:
"What good teachings?
You may speak them now."
He then fully explained the five types of giving to her.
At that time, the Yōupóyí
felt joy even greater than before,
just as a lotus flower opens when it sees the sun;
her moment of awakening and understanding
was just like that.
She immediately untied the various precious necklaces from her neck
and gave them to him as a further reward.
The messenger said:
"Mistress, please rise now,
wash your hands, and prepare the food and drink for the offering.
I have just taken the mistress's word
to invite the two Zūnzhě and five hundred disciples
to come for a meal today;
please prepare it in time."
Having heard these words,
she leaped with even more joy
and said:
"What I wished to do,
you have already done for me;
it is inexpressibly pleasant.
I now set you free;
you no longer belong to me.
As you are good and kind,
whether as a householder or having left home,
in villages or cities,
you shall be glorious and good everywhere."
Then Yōubōsīnà
immediately rose, washed her hands,
and spoke to her family and neighbors:
"You should prepare the food,
you should light the fire,
you should fetch water,
you should spread the mats,
and you should get flowers."
In such various ways,
after assigning all the tasks,
she herself took medicines
and ground them into powder.
When the offerings were prepared,
she sent that man
back to announce that the time had come
and the meal was ready,
and to request that they know it was the proper time.
Then the two Zūnzhě and the monks
put on their robes and took their bowls,
went to her home,
and sat on their seats.
Then Yōubōsīnà
personally poured the water
and served various foods
complete in color, fragrance, and flavor.
For all actions,
one receives retribution according to one's karma:
by giving food with good color,
one obtains a beautiful complexion;
because the food has good fragrance,
one obtains a far-reaching reputation;
because the flavor is complete,
one obtains the reward of food that is exactly as one desires
and obtains great strength.
After the assembly of monks had eaten,
Zūnzhě Shèlìfú
immediately gave a blessing.
At the time of the blessing,
Yōubōsīnà said:
"Zūnzhě!
I wish for you to call upon the name of Píshāmén Tiān."
When Shèlìfú finished the blessing,
he immediately asked:
"Regarding the Heavenly King Píshāmén,
what is the reason
you called his name?"
She replied:
"Zūnzhě!
There is a rare matter.
Because I recited the Fǎjù last night,
it caused that Heavenly King to stay in the air to listen to my recitation of the Jīng.
He praised me, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!
Sister!
You explain the wonderful Fǎ well.'
I then looked up and asked:
'Who are you?
I do not see a physical form,
yet there is a voice?'
He replied to me:
'I am the Ghost King Píshāmén.
I heard you reciting the Jīng, so I stayed to listen.
I wish to give you heavenly treasures,
but they are not suitable for you.
Now I gift you with good words.'
I then asked:
'What do you wish to tell me?'
He then said:
'Zūnzhě Shèlìfú
and Mùjiànlián
will arrive at a certain forest tomorrow.
You may invite them to your home to provide offerings,
and at the time of the blessing, remember to call my name.'
I then asked him:
'By calling your name,
what benefit is there?'
He then replied to me,
fully explaining the matters mentioned above.
For this reason,
I called it today."
Shèlìfú said:
"It is indeed extraordinary!
You are a human and he is a god,
yet he was able to humble himself
to speak with you
and call you his sister."
The Yōupóyí said:
"I have yet another extraordinary matter.
There is a spirit in this house
who is close and friendly with me,
like women who come and go together.
When I give alms,
this spirit tells me:
'This is an Āluóhàn,
this is an Ānàhán,
this is a Sītuóhán,
this is a Xūtuóhuán,
this is an ordinary person,
this one maintains the precepts,
this one breaks the precepts,
this one has wisdom,
and this one is foolish.'"
Although I have heard this teaching,
my mind remains equanimous and undivided
toward ordinary people
and those who break the precepts,
viewing them as if they were Āluóhàn."
Shèlìfú said,
"You are truly extraordinary!
To be able, within this,
to give rise to a mind of equality."
Móhēsīnà said,
"I have another extraordinary and good thing.
Having a woman's body
and moreover being a householder,
I was yet able to eliminate the twenty views of the self
and attain the stage of Xūtuóhuán."
Shèlìfú said,
"Sister!
You are very extraordinary
to be able, in a woman's body,
to become a Xūtuóhuán."
The Yōupóyí said,
"I have something even more rare and extraordinary!
I have four sons,
all of whom hold wicked and false views.
My husband follows wicked and false ways
even more excessively,
and toward the Fó, Fǎ, and Sēng,
he is ignorant and disrespectful.
If I make offerings to the Sānbǎo
or give to the poor,
they give rise to jealousy and anger,
all saying,
'We work laboriously at the family business,
and yet you make such useless expenditures.'
Despite these words,
regarding my aspiration for the Way,
practicing goodness and giving,
I never shrink back
nor do I feel any resentment."
Shèlìfú said,
"The way of women
is that at all times,
they are usually not autonomous.
When young, they are protected by parents;
when mature, they are protected by their husbands;
and when old, they are protected by their sons.
Yet you are not constrained by husband or sons
and practice goodness as you wish.
Sister!
I now instruct you,
you should take this well to heart.
What is this good thing?
It is that the Fó, the World-Honored One, will arrive this evening at the Píniǔqiántè Forest.
I use this news
as a gift in return to you."
Having spoken, he took his leave and returned to his dwelling.
The Yōupóyí said,
"What the Honorable One has told me
is indeed very good!
After the Honorable One leaves,
I shall prepare offerings
to await the World-Honored One."
Thus the World-Honored One
arrived at that forest.
Móhēsīnà was greatly delighted;
she immediately gathered various Yōupóyí
and that very evening went to the Fó's place.
Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, his radiant appearance being remarkably wonderful,
her five senses were filled with joy,
and her happiness was immeasurable.
Having arrived, she prostrated,
and with various incense and flowers
finished making offerings to the Fó.
She then sat to one side,
and the Fó preached the Dharma for her—discourses on giving, discourses on the precepts,
on being born in heaven and ending desire,
and discourses on Nièpán.
After hearing the Dharma,
she was about to return home,
so she joined her palms and said to the Fó:
"The people of this village all generally hold false views,
not recognizing the Fó's Dharma,
not knowing the Fó's virtue,
and not being fond of giving.
Therefore, when Shāmén and Póluómén
enter this village to beg, they always come to my house.
I only wish, World-Honored One,
that for however long you
stay in this village and town,
the Fó and his disciples would always accept my invitation
and my offering of the four necessities."
Having spoken, she bowed at his feet and withdrew.
She then observed the various Bǐqiū's lodgings one after another.
Finally, she saw a sick Bǐqiū lying in a grass hut
and immediately asked:
"Great Virtuous One!
From what illness do you suffer?"
The Bǐqiū replied,
"Having traveled on the road,
my four elements are out of balance,
leaving me weary and with little to rely on."
The Yōupóyí said,
"For the Great Virtuous One's ailment,
what food is appropriate?"
He replied,
"The doctor prescribed that I should take fresh, warm meat broth."
The Yōupóyí said,
"Look no further;
I shall send some tomorrow."
He replied,
"That would be fine."
The Yōupóyí bowed at his feet and returned home,
thinking to herself:
"I have gained great benefit
from seeing the Fó, the World-Honored One, as well as Shèlìfú and the other great honorable ones."
She was deeply joyful,
yet she did not recall that the next day was the fifteenth.
At that time, the law of that country
was that on the fifteenth day, no killing was allowed;
anyone who killed would be violating the law.
On the following morning,
she ordered a servant to take money
to buy fresh, warm meat.
The servant followed the instruction
and went to the market, searching everywhere,
but could not find any and returned empty-handed.
He said to the mistress,
"Today is the fifteenth;
there is no slaughtering in the market."
Then the Yōupóyí told the servant,
"Take a thousand coins
to buy a hundred coins' worth of meat.
Someone who seeks profit
might be able to give it to you."
The servant took the money
and went again to search,
but because the king's restriction was severe,
no one dared to give him any.
The servant returned and reported
everything as it was.
When the Yōupóyí heard this,
her heart was worried and distressed, and she said,
"Take gold coins
and search for a purchase of equal weight."
At that time, the servant,
although carrying gold coins and searching as ordered,
found that all the butchers,
though greedy for the profit,
feared the king's law which was very severe
and were afraid of losing their lives;
thus no one dared to give him any.
After going back and forth like this,
he could get none at all.
Then the Yōupóyí's worry and distress doubled,
as she thought:
"The sick Bǐqiū has already accepted my invitation,
and if I should fail to provide what he needs,
he might lose his life,
and that would be my fault.
What plan should I devise?"
Having thought of this,
she further reflected to herself:
"In the past, the Púsà,
for the sake of a single dove,
still cut and carved himself,
not sparing the flesh of his own body.
How much more so for this Bǐqiū,
who is superior to a dove?
Could I not cherish my own flesh and fail to save him?"
After she made this reflection,
she took a trusted servant whom she usually employed,
retired into a quiet room,
washed her body clean,
sat upright on a bed,
and ordered the servant, saying,
"You now cut and take the meat from inside my thigh."
At that time, the servant followed the instruction
and immediately cut it out with a sharp knife.
While the meat was being cut,
the pain was so intense
that she fainted and fell to the ground.
Then a maidservant immediately wrapped it with white woolen cloth.
Having taken the meat,
she mixed it with various medicinal herbs
and boiled it to make broth,
which she sent to the sick Bǐqiū.
After the Bǐqiū received the food sent by this faithful donor,
his illness was immediately cured.
Her husband, the Póluómén,
was not there at the time.
Having returned from a distance, he asked,
"Móhēsīnà,
where is she?"
They replied,
"In a certain room."
Her husband went to see her
and her complexion had changed,
not being the same as usual.
He immediately asked:
"For what reason are you now
so haggard?"
She replied:
"I am currently afflicted by an illness."
Her husband, filled with worry,
soon gathered various physicians
to diagnose her ailment.
The physicians gathered and asked:
"What disease do you have?
When your ailment flares up,
how long has it been like this?
Are there periods of relief?"
She answered:
"My illness causes pain at all times;
now the pain and suffering are without any relief."
At that time, the physicians examined her pulse
but did not know the cause of the pain,
and they left in silence.
Her husband wept
and asked his wife:
"What is your illness?
Please tell me the truth."
The wife answered him:
"If even the skilled physicians do not know,
how could I know?"
Then the Póluómén
asked the people of the household:
"Do you know what is troubling Móhésīnà?"
The servants then said:
"Master!
We do not know;
you should ask those who are trustworthy and close to her."
Then the Póluómén summoned her maidservant
and asked her in a private place:
"Why does my wife have this illness?"
The maidservant answered with the truth:
"Master should know!
For the sake of a sick Bǐqiū,
she cut her own flesh to feed him."
After the husband heard this,
toward the Fó, Fǎ, and Sēng,
he conceived a heart of anger and malice.
He then went to the streets and alleys
and shouted in a loud voice:
"The Shāmén Shìzǐ
eat human meat,
just like Bózú Wáng!"
At that time, the faithful Yōupósè,
hearing the Póluómén reviling the Fó, Fǎ, and Sēng,
were worried and unhappy.
They went to the place of the Shìzūn
and prostrated at his feet.
The Shìzūn said to them:
"Why are you all
sorrowful and unhappy?"
They said:
"Shìzūn!
There is a Póluómén
in a crowded place
shouting in a loud voice,
reviling the Fó, Fǎ, and Sēng, saying:
'In the past Bózú Wáng
ate human meat;
now the Shāmén Shìzǐ
eat human meat
in just the same way.'
We pray that the Fó Shìzūn
will command the Bǐqiū
not to eat human meat."
At that time, the Shìzūn, because of this matter,
assembled the community of Bǐqiū
and called for the sick Bǐqiū.
When the sick Bǐqiū
heard the Shìzūn's instruction,
his heart was filled with joy:
"The Shìzūn's great compassion
has even reached me!"
Although his body was weak and emaciated,
he came by his own strength.
Having arrived, he bowed at his feet
and sat to one side.
The Fó said:
"Noble son!
What is your ailment?"
The Bǐqiū said:
"I am tormented by illness,
but seeing the Shìzūn now,
I have found a little relief."
The Shìzūn further asked:
"What did you eat today?"
He answered:
"Today I ate a meal of meat broth."
The Fó said:
"Was the meat you ate fresh
or was it dried meat?"
He answered:
"Fresh meat.
The land of Tiānzhú is hot,
so meat does not last overnight."
"Whether the meat eaten was fresh or dried—
Good son!
When you ate the meat,
did you ask whether it was pure or impure?"
He answered:
"Shìzūn!
I have been distressed by illness for a long time;
when I obtained it, I ate it
and indeed did not ask."
The Fó said:
"Bǐqiū!
How could you receive impure food?
According to the law of the Bǐqiū,
when a Tányuè gives food,
one should first ask:
'What meat is this?'
If the Tányuè says:
'This is pure meat,'
one should observe it again;
if he is trustworthy, one should eat it;
if he is not trustworthy,
then one must not eat it."
At that time, the Shìzūn
immediately made a rule for the Bǐqiū:
"All impure meats
should not be eaten.
Meat that was seen, heard, or suspected—
these three kinds of impure meat
should also not be eaten."
In this way, he distinguished what should and should not be eaten.
When the Yōupóyí
heard that because of her
the Fó Shìzūn
had prohibited the Bǐqiū
from eating meat,
she felt great distress,
because her actions
had caused the Bǐqiū never to eat meat again.
She then said to her husband:
"If you can, for my sake,
invite the Fó and the Sēng
to come here tomorrow
to receive offerings,
that would be very good!
If you cannot,
I shall give up my life.
I even gave my own body's flesh to someone—
what regret do you have
that you should cause such an incident?"
This Póluómén,
who normally toward the Sānbǎo
had no heart of faith or respect,
heard his wife's words
and, because of his wife,
entered the grove to go to the Fó.
Having reached the Fó's place,
he said:
"Shāmén Qútán!
And all your disciples,
please accept my invitation
to have a meal at my house tomorrow."
The Fó accepted in silence.
The Póluómén,
knowing the Fó had accepted the invitation,
returned home and told his wife:
"The Shāmén Qútán
has accepted your invitation."
Then the Yōupóyí
immediately ordered the household
to prepare various foods, incense, flowers, and seats.
When the time came the next day,
she sent someone into the grove
to go and inform the Shìzūn:
"The food and utensils are prepared;
may the Sage know the time."
The Fó and the Bǐqiū,
wearing their robes and holding their bowls,
went to the house
and took their seats.
Having sat, he asked the Póluómén:
"Where is Móhésīnà
now?"
He answered:
"She is sick in a certain room."
The Fó said:
"Call her here!"
The Póluómén
then went and told her:
"Your teacher is calling you."
She replied:
"I, Móhésīnà,
pay homage at the feet of the Fó, Fǎ, and Sēng.
I am suffering from illness
and am unable to rise."
Her husband went and spoke to the Fó, saying:
“Yōupósīnà,
pays homage to the feet of the Fó, the Fǎ, and the Sēng.
I suffer from the pain of illness
and am unable to rise and come.”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Go and tell Yōubōsīnà,
‘Rise and come see the Fó.’”
Ānán immediately went
and told Yōubōsīnà:
“The Shìzūn calls for you;
you should go and see Him.”
At that time, Yōubōsīnà,
while still on her bed,
pressed her palms together and said:
“I now pay homage to the Fó, the Fǎ, and the Sēng.
My longing to see the Shìzūn
is like the hungry needing food,
like the thirsty needing drink,
like the cold longing for warmth,
like the hot longing for coolness,
and like those who have lost the way finding the way.
My longing to see the Fó
is also just like this.
Although my heart desires to go,
my body refuses to follow.”
Ānán returned and told the Fó
what Yōubōsīnà had said.
The Fó commanded Ānán:
“Carry her here along with her bed.”
Ānán followed the instruction,
having people carry her there,
and they arrived before the Fó.
At that time, the Rúlái
emitted a great radiance.
All those who encountered the Fó's light and were touched by it—
the insane regained their sanity,
the disturbed gained concentration,
and the sick were healed.
At that time, when Yōubōsīnà
had encountered the Fó's light,
her pain was immediately removed.
At that time, the Shèshén
washed the sores with water
and applied medicine to them,
and she was restored to her former state.
At that time, Yōubōsīnà
immediately rose and got off the bed.
Holding a golden vessel in her hands,
she personally offered water for washing
and served various kinds of food,
complete in color, fragrance, and taste.
After the Fó had eaten,
he washed his hands and cleansed his bowl.
For Móhēsīnà,
he spoke the subtle and wondrous Fǎ,
namely, on giving and keeping the precepts,
the karmic rewards of humans and heavens,
the faults and suffering of birth and death,
the harm caused by greedy desires,
the bliss of renunciation and cessation,
and how the twelve links of dependent origination revolve without ceasing.
At that time, Yōubōsīnà,
having heard what the Fó said,
was able to sever stinginess and jealousy
and attained the stage of Ānàhán;
her family members and relatives
all received the five precepts;
that Póluómén abandoned false views,
believed in and revered the Sānbǎo,
and received the precepts of a Yōupósuì.
At that time, among the gathered Sìzhòng,
there were those who attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
those who attained Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
and Āluóhàn;
there were those who gave rise to the aspiration for the Great Way.
Everyone, great and small,
was filled with joy.
At that time, there were many people who feared birth and death;
each had this thought:
“Now, if this woman
is able to do this—
cutting her own flesh
to offer it to a Shāmén—
it is truly extraordinary!
If we were to give up our villages, fields, and houses,
how could that be considered difficult?”
They then each abandoned their villages and families,
left the household life to seek the Way,
diligently practiced with vigor,
severed all fetters and outflows,
and attained the stage of Āluóhàn.
At that time, in this village,
the faith and practice of the Fófǎ
was widely proclaimed and spread.
For this reason,
if those with strong will,
even women,
recite the scriptures and Fǎ
and do not begrudge their own flesh,
they obtain the various fruits of the Way;
how much more so for men who diligently apply their minds to the work of the Way—
how could they not succeed?
For this reason,
all you Shànnánzǐ!
You should be diligent in the good Fǎ and fear birth and death.
Then the fetters and afflictions will become thin and you will leave birth and death.
Although you cannot attain liberation within this Mòfǎ period,
by virtue of these merits,
you shall receive infinite blessings among humans and heavens.
The Shìzūn Mílè,
in no long time—after fifty-six billion and one hundred million years—
will come here to attain Buddhahood.
He shall widely speak the wondrous Fǎ for you.
Within that time,
following what you seek according to your vows, you will achieve the path of the Sānchéng
and all will obtain liberation.”
They received the teaching with reverence and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the country of Mójiātuó, in the city of Wángshè, in the Jiālántuó Zhúyuán.
At that time the Shìzūn
praised leaving the household life,
saying that its merit, causes, and conditions bring very many blessings.
If one allows sons or daughters,
if one allows male or female servants,
if one permits the people,
or if one's own self
leaves the household life to enter the Path,
the merit is immeasurable.
The retribution for giving
results in receiving blessings for ten lifetimes;
among the Six Heavens and human realms,
one goes and returns ten times;
yet this is still not as superior as the merit of allowing others to leave the household life or doing so oneself.
Why is this?
The retribution for giving
has blessings that are limited and finite;
the blessings of leaving the household life
are immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, the fruit and retribution of maintaining the precepts
leads to the five supernatural powers of the Shénxiān,
and the reception of heavenly blessings
reaching up to the Fànshì;
within the Fófǎ,
the fruit and retribution of leaving the household life
is inconceivable,
reaching even to Nièpán,
and thus the blessings are never exhausted.
Suppose there is a person
who builds a pagoda of the seven treasures
reaching as high as the Sānshísāntiān;
the merit they obtain
is not equal to that of leaving the household life.
Why is this?
A pagoda of the seven treasures
can be destroyed and broken
by greedy, evil, and foolish people;
but the Dharma of leaving the household life
cannot be destroyed.
If one wishes to seek the good Dharma,
aside from the Fófǎ,
there is nothing more superior.
It is like a hundred blind people
who have one wise physician
who can treat their eyes,
and all at once they see clearly.
Or like a hundred people
whose crimes merit having their eyes gouged out,
and there is one person with the power
to save them from their punishment so they do not lose their eyes.
Although the blessings of these two people
are immeasurable,
they are still not as vast and great as the blessings of permitting others to leave the household life or doing so oneself.
Why is this?
Although one can give eyes to these two kinds of people,
these people only receive the benefit for a single lifetime,
and the nature of the physical eye
is to perish and decay;
but permitting others to leave the household life,
or doing so oneself,
successively guides and shows sentient beings the supreme wisdom-eye for eternal kalpas,
and the nature of the wisdom-eye
remains undestroyed through successive kalpas.
Why is this?
The retribution of its blessings allows one to freely enjoy happiness among humans and devas,
at one's will,
without end or limit,
until one ultimately attains the Fódào.
Why is this?
It is because the Dharma of leaving the household life
destroys the followers of Mó,
increases the seeds of the Buddha,
annihilates evil dharmas,
nurtures good dharmas,
eliminates the defilement of sins,
and gives rise to supreme meritorious karma.
Therefore, the Buddha said the merit of leaving the household life
is higher than Xūmí,
deeper than the great ocean,
and broader than empty space.
If there is a person who creates various obstacles for one who wishes to leave the household life,
preventing them from following their aspiration,
their sin is extremely heavy,
like the darkness of night where nothing can be seen;
the retribution for this person's sin
is also like this,
as they enter deep hells of darkness without eyes.
It is like the great ocean,
where a hundred rivers and streams
all flow into it;
the retribution for this person's sin
is also like this:
all evils
gather within their person.
Like Mount Xūmí being burned by the fires at the end of a kalpa,
with nothing remaining,
this person is also thus;
burned by the fires of hell,
without ever coming to an end.
It is like the Jiāliúlóuxīní medicine,
which is extremely poisonous and bitter;
if an equal weight
is compared to rock honey,
the retribution for that good and evil
is also like this.
Permitting others to leave the household life
or doing so oneself
has the greatest merit,
because one who has left the household life
takes the Xiūduōluó as water
to wash away the defilement of the fetters,
can eliminate the suffering of birth and death,
and create the cause for Nièpán;
they take the Píní as their feet
to walk upon the ground of pure precepts,
and take the Āpítán as their eyes
to see the good and evil of the world,
walking freely upon the path of the Bāzhèng
to reach the wondrous city of Nièpán.
For this reason,
allowing others to leave the household life,
or doing so oneself,
whether old or young,
its blessings are most superior.
At that time the Shìzūn
was in the city of Wángshè, in the Jiālántuó Zhúyuán.
At that time in the city of Wángshè,
there was an elder
named Shīlìbìtí
(in the language of Qín, this means Fúzēng),
who was a hundred years old.
Hearing that the merit of leaving the household life was thus immeasurable,
he thought to himself:
"Why do I not now leave the household life and practice the Path within the Fófǎ?"
He then took leave of his wife, children, male and female servants, young and old, saying:
"I wish to leave the household life."
This man was very old and frail;
the young and old in his household
all felt weary and annoyed by him,
they held his words in low esteem,
and none would follow them.
Hearing that he wished to leave the household life,
they all joyfully said:
"You should have gone long ago;
why are you so late?
Now is exactly the right time."
Shīlìbìtí
then left his home
and went toward the Zhúlín,
wishing to see the Shìzūn and seek the Dharma for leaving the household life.
Having arrived at the Zhúlín,
he asked the Bǐqiū:
"The Buddha, the Shìzūn, the Dàxiān,
who with great compassion extensively benefits devas and humans—
where is He now?"
The Bǐqiū replied:
"The Rúlái Shìzūn
has gone elsewhere to teach and transform,
to bring benefit, and is not here."
Shīlìbìtí asked again:
"Who is the foremost disciple in wisdom next to the Buddha, the Great Teacher,
who is he?"
The Bǐqiū pointed out that it was the Honorable Shèlìfú.
He then leaned on his staff and went to the place of Shèlìfú,
set aside his staff, bowed,
and said:
"Honorable One!
Permit me to leave the household life."
At that time Shèlìfú,
having looked at this man,
considered that he was old
and lacking in the three things:
he would be unable to study,
sit in meditation,
or assist in the various affairs of the community.
He said:
"Go away.
You are too old, past the age,
and may not leave the household life."
Next, he went to Móhējiāshè,
Yōubōlí,
Ānòulóutuó, and others,
following in order through the five hundred Great Āluóhàn.
They all asked:
"Have you approached anyone else before?"
He replied:
"I first approached the Shìzūn,
but the Shìzūn was not here;
next I approached the Honorable Shèlìfú."
They asked again:
"What did he say?"
He replied:
"He told me:
'You are too old, past the age,
and may not leave the household life.'"
The Bǐqiū said:
"That Shèlìfú is foremost in wisdom;
"...still does not accept you,
we also will not accept you.
It is like a skilled physician
who well understands how to look after the sick,
but abandons them and does not provide treatment;
then all the other minor physicians
will also fold their arms.
You should know that this person
must have the signs of death."
Because Shèlìfú, who possesses great wisdom, did not accept him,
the rest of the Bǐqiū
likewise did not accept him.
Shīlìbiètí,
having sought out all the Bǐqiū
but being unable to leave the household life,
returned and went out from the Zhùyuán,
stood upon the threshold of the gate,
and in sorrowful weeping and distress,
raised his voice and wailed loudly:
"Since my birth,
I have committed no great offense.
For what reason do they specifically not allow me to leave the household life?
Like Yōubōlí,
a lowly person who shaved hair;
Nítí,
a person of low filth who cleared away excrement;
Āngjuémóluó,
who killed countless people;
and Tuósèjī,
a great thief and wicked man—
people such as these
were still able to leave the household life.
What sin do I have
that I cannot leave the household life?"
When he spoke these words,
the World-Honored One suddenly appeared before him,
emitting great light,
with majestic and adorned features,
like the seven-jeweled lofty chariot of Dāolì Tiānwáng Dìshì.
The Buddha asked Fúzgēng:
"For what reason are you crying?"
Then the elder,
hearing the Buddha's Brahma-voice,
felt joy in his heart,
like a son seeing his father.
He prostrated his whole body to the ground,
paid homage to the Buddha,
and weeping, spoke to the Buddha:
"All sentient beings—
those who have killed people or acted as thieves,
those who have spoken falsely or slandered,
and people of lowly birth—
all have been able to leave the household life.
What sin do I alone have
that I am specifically not allowed to leave the household life in the Buddha's Dharma?
My family, great and small,
because of my old age,
no longer have use for me.
Now, in the Buddha's Dharma,
I am unable to leave the household life.
If I were to return home now,
they would certainly not let me in.
Where should I go?
I am now determined to cast away my life here."
At that time, the Buddha told Shīlìbiètí:
"Who can raise their hand in the empty sky
and make a definitive statement, saying,
'This person should leave the household life,'
or 'This person should not because he is old'?"
The elder spoke to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The son of the Dharma-Wheel Turning King,
foremost in wisdom,
second to the Buddha,
the world's second guide,
Shèlìfú,
is the one who did not allow me to leave the household life in the Buddha's Dharma."
Then the World-Honored One,
with great compassion,
comforted Fúzgēng,
just as a kind father comforts a filial son,
and told him:
"Do not be distressed!
I will now cause you to be able to leave the household life.
It was not Shèlìfú who for three Ānsēngqí jié diligently practiced bitter austerities
and for a hundred kalpas cultivated merit.
It was not Shèlìfú who in life after life performed difficult deeds,
splitting his head and gouging out his eyes,
giving his marrow, brain, blood, and flesh,
his skin, bones, hands, and feet,
and his ears and nose as gifts.
It was not Shèlìfú who threw his body to a hungry tiger,
entered pits of fire,
had a thousand nails driven into his body,
or had a thousand lamps carved into his flesh.
It was not Shèlìfú who gave away his kingdom, city, wife and children,
servants, elephants and horses,
and the seven treasures.
It was not Shèlìfú who, in the first Ānsēngqí jié,
made offerings to eighty-eight thousand Buddhas;
in the middle Ānsēngqí jié,
made offerings to ninety-nine thousand Buddhas;
and in the final Ānsēngqí jié,
made offerings to one hundred thousand Buddha World-Honored Ones,
leaving the household life to keep the precepts,
and perfecting the Shī bōluómì.
It was not Shèlìfú who attained mastery over the Dharma.
How can he issue a decree saying,
'This one should leave the household life,
and this person should not'?
Only I alone
have mastery over the Dharma.
Only I alone ride the precious chariot of the Six Pāramitās,
wear the armor of patience,
and beneath the Bodhi tree,
sat upon the Vajra throne,
subdued the enmity of the Demon King,
and alone attained the Buddha-way.
None are equal to me.
Come and follow me;
I will let you leave the household life."
In this way, the World-Honored One gave various comforts,
and Fúzgēng's distress was immediately removed.
With great joy in his heart,
he then followed behind the Buddha
and entered the Buddha's Vihāra.
The Buddha told Dàmùqiánlián:
"Let him leave the household life.
Why is this?
Sentient beings are saved according to their conditions.
There are some who have a connection with the Buddha,
whom other people cannot save;
and some who have a connection with other people,
whom the Buddha cannot save.
Some have a connection with Shèlìfú,
but Mùlián,
Jiāshè,
Ānàlǜ,
Jīnbīluó, and all the other disciples
cannot save them.
And so it goes in turn:
depending on who has the connection,
others cannot save them."
Then Mùlián also thought:
"This person is advanced in age and elderly;
in chanting the sūtras,
sitting in meditation,
and assisting with various tasks,
he is deficient in all three matters.
However, the Buddha, the Dharma King, has commanded him to leave the household life,
and in principle, this cannot be disobeyed."
He then let him leave the household life
and receive the full precepts.
In a previous life, this person
had already planted the causal conditions for being saved.
Having swallowed the hook of the Dharma,
like a fish swallowing a hook,
he would surely be pulled out without doubt.
He had already practiced and accumulated various virtuous merits,
and day and night he was diligent
in practicing, reading, and chanting the Xiūduōluó,
Pínì,
and Āpítán,
becoming broadly conversant with the treasure of the scriptures.
Because of his old age,
he could not always respectfully welcome, escort, or pay homage to the elders.
All the young Bǐqiū,
because they had left the household life earlier
and were thus elders,
often spoke to him with harsh and cutting words:
"This elderly Bǐqiū
relies on his advanced age,
his chanting of sūtras and his learning,
to be arrogant and self-important,
and does not show proper respect."
At that time, the old Bǐqiū
thought to himself:
"When I was at home,
I was pricked and distressed by my family, both great and small.
Now that I have come to leave the household life,
hoping to find rest,
I am again being provoked and criticized by these younger ones.
What sin have I committed for it to be like this,
only increasing my suffering and distress?"
Again, he had this thought:
"I would rather die now."
At that time, near that forest,
there was a great river,
both deep and swift.
He immediately went to the riverbank,
took the Jiāshā from his body,
placed it on a tree branch,
knelt before the robe,
and with falling tears,
made a vow:
"I am not now abandoning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha.
I only wish to cast away my life.
This robe upon my body
is offered to those who maintain precepts, are diligent, and chant the Xiūduōluó.
If there be any retribution..."
"I wish that after I cast off this body,
I may be born into a wealthy and joyful family,
with relatives who are harmonious and compliant,
and who, regarding my good Dharmas,
do not create obstructions.
May I always encounter the Triple Gem,
leave home to practice the Path,
meet a virtuous teacher,
and be shown the realization of Nirvāṇa."
Having made this vow,
at a place in the river where the deep, swift currents and whirlpools surged over,
he intended to throw himself into it.
At that time, Mùlián,
observing his elderly disciple with the divine eye
to see what he was doing,
immediately saw the disciple
casting his body into the water.
Before he reached the water,
using supernatural powers,
Mùlián caught him and placed him on the bank,
asking him:
"Son of the Dharma!
What are you doing?"
Shīlìbìtí felt great shame and remorse,
and immediately thought to himself:
"How should I answer?
I should not now use false speech to deceive my teacher.
If I were to deceive my teacher,
I would incur guilt for lifetime after lifetime,
and would be without the organ of the tongue.
Furthermore, my Preceptor
has profound supernatural insight.
Even if I were to lie,
he would know it himself.
If there is someone in the world
whose wisdom is clear and penetrating,
and whose nature is honest and upright,
the devas should respect them.
If one has wisdom
but harbors flattery and deception,
although they could be a teacher of others
whom people should respect and provide for,
if one lacks wisdom
yet is upright and honest,
though they cannot benefit others,
their conduct is sufficient to save themselves.
If a person is foolish
and harbors deception and flattery in their heart,
then among all assemblies,
they are despised as base and inferior.
Should they have something to say,
everyone would know it,
and all would say:
'This person is flattering and deceptive, without truth.'
Even if they spoke the truth,
people would cast it aside and not trust it.
Therefore, if I were to deceive my Preceptor,
it would not be appropriate for me;
I must speak the truth."
He then said to his teacher:
"I renounced my home because I was weary of it,
seeking rest and ease.
Now, I am once again unhappy,
and thus I wished to end my life."
When Mùlián heard this,
he immediately had this thought:
"If I do not use matters of the terrors of birth and death to frighten this man,
then regarding the benefits of leaving home,
he will gain nothing at all."
He then told him:
"You must now with a sincere heart
grasp the corner of my robe
and do not let go midway."
He followed the teacher's instruction.
Just as the nature of wind lightly lifts and blows dust and grass
up into the void,
so did his supernatural feet travel through the air;
if one but grasped a single hair,
they would go wherever he wished.
At that time, Mùlián,
like a fierce eagle clutching a small bird,
flew up into the void.
Mùlián's supernatural power
was also like this.
His body ascended into the void,
and in the time it takes to bend and stretch an arm,
they reached the shore of the great ocean.
By the seashore, there was a recently deceased woman,
whose facial features were upright and whose body was exceptionally beautiful,
complete with all fine marks.
They saw a worm
coming out of her mouth,
then entering through her nose,
then coming out of her eyes,
and entering through her ears.
Mùlián stood and observed,
and having observed, he moved on.
Shīlìbìtí
said:
"Preceptor!
Who is this woman?
Why is her state like this?"
Mùlián told him:
"When the time comes, I shall tell you."
They went forward a little further
and saw a woman
carrying a copper cauldron on her back.
She set the cauldron down and filled it with water,
lit a fire and blew on it.
Once it boiled,
she took off her clothes and entered the cauldron herself.
Her hair and nails fell off first,
and her flesh was cooked and separated from the bones.
The boiling water blew the bones out to the outside;
the wind blew, and she immediately became a person again,
and she took her own flesh and ate it.
Fúzéng saw this,
and his heart was alarmed and his hair stood on end.
He said:
"Preceptor!
This person eating their own flesh,
who are they?"
Mùlián told him:
"When the time comes, I shall tell you."
Next, they went forward a little further
and saw a large body
with many worms
surrounding and biting it,
even to the joints,
leaving no empty space even as small as the point of a needle.
At that time, there was a great sound
of crying and wailing
that shook the far and near,
like the sounds of hell.
He said:
"Preceptor!
This great and terrible sound,
who is it?"
Mùlián told him:
"When the time comes, I shall tell you."
Next, they saw a large man
surrounded by many beings with beast heads and human bodies,
various evil ghosts and spirits,
holding bows and crossbows,
and poisonous three-pronged arrows
with heads that were all ablaze.
They vied with each other to shoot him,
and his body was entirely scorched.
He said:
"Preceptor!
Who is this person
who suffers this bitter poison,
with nowhere to flee?"
The teacher said:
"Wait a moment!
When the time comes, I shall tell you."
After continuing for a long time,
they saw a great mountain
with knives and swords placed below.
They saw a person
throw themselves down from above;
knives, halberds, swords, and spears
broke and pierced their body.
They immediately pulled themselves out,
set them back in their original places,
and returned to the top of the mountain,
repeating this without ceasing as before.
Having seen this, he said to the teacher:
"Who is this person again who suffers this bitterness?"
He told him:
"Stop!
When the time arrives, I shall tell you."
Next, they saw a great mountain of bones,
seven hundred yóuxún high,
which could block the sun
and cast a dark shadow over the sea.
At that time, Mùlián,
upon a great rib of this mountain of bones,
walked back and forth in meditation.
The disciple followed him
and soon thought to himself:
"My Preceptor
is now free of business;
can I perhaps ask about the things from earlier?"
Having thought this, he said:
"I only wish that the Preceptor
would explain to me the things I saw earlier."
Mùlián told him:
"Now is precisely the time."
He then said to the Preceptor:
"Regarding the one seen first,
who was that woman?"
Mùlián replied:
"If you wish to know,
she was the wife of a great Sàpó in the city of Shèwèicheng.
Her appearance was upright and beautiful,
and her husband loved and respected her greatly.
At that time, the Sàpó
wished to enter the great ocean..."
Deeply infatuated with this woman
and unable to leave her,
he was about to go to sea;
with five hundred merchants,
they boarded a ship and entered the sea.
At that time, the woman frequently used wood of three wonders
to hold up a mirror and gaze at her face.
Observing her own upright beauty,
she then gave rise to pride
and deeply developed attachment.
At that time, there was a great turtle
that struck the ship with its legs.
The ship broke and sank into the sea;
the Sàbó, his wife,
and the five hundred merchants
all died.
According to the law of the great sea,
it does not tolerate dead corpses;
if the water's waves churn,
Yèchā and Luóchà
bring them out and place them on the shore.
When sentient beings' lives end,
following that which they love and dwell upon,
they are immediately born into its midst.
Some may find it difficult to say:
if following that which one is attached to,
one then goes to be born there,
who would love Hell and thus enter Hell?
The people answered, saying:
"If there is a sentient being
who steals the property of the Sānzūn or the belongings of their parents,
or even commits murder,
for such great sins,
they should fall into the Chìhuǒ Dìyù.
When this person is oppressed by the illness of wind and cold,
they then think of fire
and desire to enter into it."
Having had this thought, their life ends,
and they then fall into this hell.
If a person steals the light of a Buddha lamp or its value,
or steals the lamps, candles, firewood, or grass of the Sēngqí;
or if they destroy, dismantle, or remove Sēngqí houses or lecture halls;
or if during the winter cold,
they strip people of their clothes;
or if using power and influence
during the freezing ice,
they pour water on slaves or other people;
or if during a raid
they strip people of their garments—
for such karmic retribution of sin,
they should fall into the Hánbīng Dìyù.
This person is oppressed by a feverish illness
and constantly thinks of a cold place;
at the moment of this thought,
they then fall into this hell.
The Yōubàluó,
Bátuómó,
Jūmùtóu,
and Fēntuólì hells
are also like this.
Within the cold hells,
those receiving punishment
have their body's flesh frozen and parched,
like scattered scorched beans;
their brains and marrow burst white,
their skulls are shattered into millions of pieces,
and their body bones are split,
+ like hooked arrows.
If a person is stingy and greedy,
and cuts off the timely food and drink of hungry sentient beings,
they should fall among the Èguǐ.
They contract an illness of reflux
and cannot swallow food.
Friends who attend to the sick,
using various foods,
strongly urge them, saying:
'This is sweet, this is sour;
this is delicious and easy to digest;
you should force yourself to eat.'
Then the person gives rise to a heart of anger:
'When will my eyes finally not see food?'
At that time, their life ends,
and they are born among the Èguǐ.
If a person is foolish
and does not believe in the Sānbǎo,
slandering and destroying the Dào,
they should fall among animals.
Beset by illness,
they can only lie face down
and cannot turn over.
They do not delight in good words.
Those around them, knowing for certain this person will die,
then urge them, saying:
'You should listen to the Dharma, receive the fast, and take the precepts;
you should see the Buddha image,
see the Bǐqiū Sēng;
you should practice charity.'
In that person's heart and mind,
there is no joy at all.
Because they are being strongly exhorted and instructed,
they then increase their evil thoughts:
'I wish I could reach a place where I do not hear the good name of the Sānbǎo;
the pleasure would be unspeakable.'
At that time, their life ends,
and they are born among animals.
If there is a person who cultivates the good causes for being born as a human or a celestial being,
this person is not beset by great illness.
When their life is about to end,
their mind is not confused or disturbed.
Their relatives and those around them,
knowing they are about to die,
each urge them, saying:
'Do you delight in hearing the Dharma?
Do you wish to see the image?
Do you wish to see the Bǐqiū
or hear the sūtras and gāthās?
Do you happily wish to receive the fast and precepts?
Do you wish to give your wealth and goods to the Buddha image?'
They answer all of them, saying:
'Good.'
Furthermore, the people say to them:
'Giving to the Buddha's image
will allow one to attain the Buddha Way;
those who make offerings to the Dharma
will, in the places where they are born,
attain deep wisdom
and penetrate the understanding of the marks of dharmas;
if one gives to the Sēng,
in the place where they are born,
they will obtain great treasures,
according to their wishes without lack.'
After the sick person hears this,
they joyfully vow, saying:
'May I, wherever I am born, always encounter the Sānbǎo and hear the Dharma to become enlightened.'
At that time, their life ends,
and they are born among humans.
If a person widely plants the good causes for birth in heaven,
purely practicing charity and the precepts,
delighting in hearing the sūtras and the Dharma,
and practicing the ten virtues,
when that person is about to die,
they lie face up in tranquility;
they see Buddha images,
celestial palace maidens, and hear celestial music.
Their expression is harmonious and pleased,
and they raise their hands upward.
At that time, their life ends,
and they are immediately born in heaven.
This wife of the Sàbó,
who was attached to her own body,
was reborn after her life ended in her former body as a worm.
Shedding this worm body,
she fell into the Great Hell,
suffering immeasurable pain."
Shīlìbìtí said:
"Héshang!
Who is this woman
who eats her own flesh?"
Mùlián told him:
"She was a maid of an Yōupóyí in Shèwèi Guó.
That Yōupóyí
invited a pure, precept-keeping Bǐqiū
for ninety days of summer,
to provide offerings.
At the end of her own lane,
she built a room for him to reside in,
and she personally prepared various fragrant and delicious food and drink.
When the time came, she sent the maid to bring the food as an offering.
When the maid reached a secluded place,
she selected the best and most delicious parts,
took them and ate them herself,
giving the remainder to the Bǐqiū.
The mistress noticed that the maid's complexion was pleasant and moist, showing signs of having eaten well,
and asked her:
'Have you perhaps defiled the Bǐqiū's food?'
She replied:
'Mistress!
I also have faith
and am not a person of wrong views;
for what reason would I eat first?
After the Bǐqiū has eaten,
if there are leftovers given to me,
only then do I eat them.
If I ate first,
may I eat my own body's flesh for generation after generation.'
Because of this cause and condition,
she first received the flower reward of this minor retribution of being bound,
and when her life ends, she shall fall into the Great Hell
to receive the full fruit reward,
with immeasurable suffering and poison."
Fúzēng said:
"The one seen with a great body,
eaten by various worms,
letting out a great and terrible sound—
who is that again?"
He told Fúzēng:
"That was the Bǐqiū Tàlìzhà who managed affairs;
because of his self-indulgence,
he took the Sēngqí's flowers, fruits, food, and drink
and gave them to laypeople."
"Having received this initial flower retribution,
when life ends here,
he will fall into the great hells;
the various insects nibbling and eating
are the people who obtained the items at that time."
Fú Zēng said:
"Preceptor!
That person crying out loud,
while many arrows vie to shoot him
and fire burns throughout his body—
who is he again?"
Mùlián told him:
"In this person's previous life,
he was a great master hunter
who harmed many birds and beasts.
Because of this sin,
he receives this bitter suffering.
When life ends here,
he will fall into the great hells
and will find it difficult to escape for a long time."
He asked again:
"Preceptor!
That person throwing himself down from that great mountain,
while knives, swords, spears, and lances
pierce and cut his body,
only to go up again after throwing himself—
who is this?"
Mùlián told him:
"He was a robust combat general of the King of Wángshè Chéng.
Due to his fierce bravery,
he was at the vanguard,
and injured or killed living beings with knives, swords, spears, and lances;
thus he receives this retribution.
After dying here,
he will fall into the great hells
and suffer pain for a long time."
Fú Zēng spoke again:
"Now this mountain of bones,
to whom does it belong?"
Mùlián told him:
"If you wish to know,
these are the bones of your own former body."
After Shīlìbìtí heard these words,
his heart was startled and his hair stood on end.
Terrified and drenched in sweat,
he said:
"Preceptor!
While I am still here,
before my heart splits apart,
please explain the origin and causes to me."
Mùlián told him:
"The cycle of birth and death
has no limit,
yet the karma of good and evil
never decays or fails in the end;
one must receive its retribution.
Whatever karma one creates,
one receives retribution according to those actions."
Mùlián continued:
"In a past age,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a king
named Tánmóbìtí
(called Fǎ Zēng in the language of Qín),
who delighted in giving, keeping precepts, and hearing the Dharma.
He had a heart of compassion,
his nature was not violent or evil,
and he did not harm living beings.
Possessing the marks of a king,
he ruled the country with the True Dharma
for a full twenty years.
When his affairs were simple and he had leisure,
he played games of chance with others.
At that time, there was a man who broke the law and killed someone.
The ministers said to the King:
'Outside there is a man
who has violated the King's law.
How should he be punished?'
The King was engrossed in the game at the time
and answered carelessly, saying:
'Punish him according to the laws of the country.'
Following the prescribed laws
that a killer should die,
they quickly killed this man.
After the King finished the game,
he asked the ministers:
'That criminal from before,
where is he now?
I wish to make a judgment.'
The ministers told the King:
'He was punished according to the laws of the country
and has now already been killed.'
When the King heard these words,
he collapsed to the ground in a faint.
The ministers and attendants
sprinkled cold water on his face,
and after a long time he revived.
Weeping, he said:
'The palace ladies and musicians,
the elephants, horses, and seven treasures—
where will they all be?
Only I alone,
solitary in the midst of hell,
will receive various pains and sufferings.
Before I was king,
there was also a king ruling in this palace;
after I die before long,
there will also continue to be a king ruling here.
I am called a king,
yet I have harmed a person's life;
know then that I am a Zhāntuóluó King.
I do not know where I shall go through successive lifetimes.
I have now decided:
I have no need to be king.'
He immediately abandoned the royal throne
and entered the mountains to live in solitude.
When that King's life ended,
he was born in the great ocean
as a Mójé fish.
His body was long and large,
seven hundred yóuxún in size.
Kings and great ministers
who rely on their own power
to oppress the common people,
separate families,
and strip sentient beings bare,
mostly become great Mójé fish when their lives end.
There are many insects
that nibble and eat their bodies;
just like the fibers of Jūzhí and Qūdéng rugs,
the insects attached to their bodies
are also like that.
Because his body was itchy,
he rubbed against a crystal mountain,
crushing and killing the insects.
The blood flowed and polluted the sea,
and for a hundred lǐ it was all red.
Due to the cause of this sin,
when life ended there,
he fell into the great hells.
At that time, the Mójé fish
would sleep for a hundred years at a time.
After waking up, he was hungry and thirsty,
so he opened his mouth,
and the seawater flowed in
like a pouring great river.
At that time, there happened to be five hundred merchants
who had entered the sea to gather treasures.
They encountered the fish opening its mouth,
and as the ship traveled swiftly,
it plunged toward the fish's mouth.
The merchants were terrified
and cried out loudly,
each saying:
'Today we
shall certainly die.'
Each followed what they revered:
some called upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
some called upon the heavens, mountains, rivers, ghosts, and spirits,
or parents, wives, children, brothers, and kin.
They all said:
'Today
is the last time we see Yánfútí;
we shall never see it again.'
As they were about to enter the Mójé fish's mouth,
all at once with one voice,
they called out, 'Nánmó Fó.'
When the fish heard the sound of 'Nánmó Fó,'
it immediately closed its mouth.
The seawater stopped flowing,
and the group of merchants
attained life from the brink of death.
This fish, pressed by hunger,
then ended its life
and was born in Wángshè Chéng.
Yèchā and Luóchà
took out its body
and placed it here on the seashore.
Exposed to the sun and drenched by rain,
the flesh rotted away and the bones remained;
this is that mountain of bones.
Fú Zēng, you should know!
That King Fǎ Zēng of that time
is your very person.
Because of the cause of killing a person,
you fell into the great ocean
as a Mójé fish.
Now that you have already regained a human body,
if you do not become weary of birth and death,
if you die here,
you will fall into hell,
and to wish to get out will be extremely difficult."
When Shīlìbìtí had seen his former body
and heard this teaching,
he feared birth and death.
Regarding the Dharma he practiced,
he recalled it in sequence,
tethered his mind and fixed his attention,
contemplating his former body,
and understanding that all things are impermanent, he sought to leave birth and death behind.
Having exhausted all fetters and taints,
he attained the path of an Āluóhàn.
Mùlián was filled with joy
and said:
“Dharma son!
That which you ought to do
has now all been completed.
You came here
by my power;
now you may return by your own spiritual power.”
At that time, Mùlián
soared into the empty sky,
and Shīlìbìtí
followed behind his preceptor
like a young bird following its mother,
returning to Zhúlín.
At that time, the young monks,
not knowing he had attained the Path,
provoked and mocked him as before.
Shīlìbìtí's mind was already tamed and compliant,
his bearing was serene,
and he remained silent without saying anything.
The Buddha, knowing this and wishing to protect the Bhikṣus so they would not give rise to evil karma,
and also wishing to manifest the virtue of this old Bhikṣu,
in the midst of the great assembly,
called out to Fúzēng, saying:
“Come here, Fúzēng!
Did you go to the shore of the great ocean today?”
Fúzēng replied:
“I did indeed go, Shìzūn!”
“That which you saw,
you may now speak of it.”
Bhikṣu Fúzēng
fully related to the Shìzūn the things he had seen.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
Bhikṣu Fúzēng!
The matters as you saw them are indeed so.
You have now escaped the suffering of birth and death
and attained the bliss of Nièpán;
you should receive the offerings of all humans and devas.
That which a Bhikṣu should do,
you have already fulfilled.”
The young Bhikṣus,
hearing these words of the Buddha,
were deeply filled with regret and remorse:
“Regarding such a wise and virtuous person,
we, lacking wisdom,
mocked and provoked him with evil hearts.
How shall we receive the retribution for this sin?”
At that time, the Bhikṣus
immediately rose from their seats,
went to Fúzēng's place,
prostrated themselves with five limbs on the ground,
and spoke these words:
“When good people are born,
they are born with compassion.
Since the Great Virtuous One is now born into the Dharma,
he should also be born with great compassion.
We only pray that you give rise to a heart of pity for us
and accept our repentance.”
Fúzēng answered:
“Toward all of you,
I have no ill will.
I accept your repentance.”
Shīlìbìtí,
seeing that the young ones were fearful in their hearts,
immediately spoke the Dharma for them.
The Bhikṣus, hearing it,
felt aversion for the laws of birth and death
and diligently practiced and cultivated.
They severed their fetters and exhausted their taints,
attaining the path of an Āluóhàn.
Due to these circumstances, Fúzēng’s good name spread throughout Wángshè Chéng.
Everyone said:
“How marvelous and extraordinary!
This elder,
who in this city
was aged and useless,
has now within the Buddha-Dharma
left the household and attained the Path,
and clearly explains such rare and wondrous Dharma.”
At that time, the people in the city
mostly gave rise to pure minds.
Some permitted their male and female servants and people to leave the household;
some left the household themselves.
There were none who did not joyfully encourage each other to leave the household.
Because of these circumstances,
the merit of leaving the household
is immeasurable and boundless.
Fúzēng was a hundred years old
before he finally left the household,
yet he accomplished such great merits.
How much more so for those in their prime
who wish to seek wondrous and superior great rewards?
They should diligently practice the Dharma, leave the household, and study the Path,
and joyfully put it into practice.
Xiányú Jīng, Volume 4
Xiányú Jīng, Volume 5
Translated in Gāochāng Jùn by the Shāmén Huìjué and others of Liángzhōu during the Yuán Wèi dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the country of Ānduó.
At that time the Shìzūn
earnestly praised those who uphold the precepts,
who protect and maintain the prohibitions,
preferring to sacrifice their bodies and lives
rather than ever violating them.
Why is this?
Precepts are the initial foundation for entering the Way,
the wonderful destination for exhausting defilements,
and the level path to the peace and happiness of Nièpán.
If one upholds the pure precepts
and calculates their merit,
it is immeasurable and boundless.
It is like the great ocean,
which is immeasurable and boundless;
the precepts are also like this.
Just as the great ocean contains many Āxiūluó,
soft-shelled turtles, turtles, and aquatic creatures,
Mójié fish, and other large sentient beings dwelling within;
the ocean of precepts is also like this,
containing many large sentient beings of the Sānchéng dwelling within.
Just as the great ocean
contains many treasures such as gold, silver, and liúlí;
the ocean of precepts is also like this,
producing many wholesome dharmas,
having the four marks of impermanence,
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
and various meditative concentrations, sānmèi, and such treasures.
Just as the great ocean
has jīngāng as its base
and is surrounded by jīngāng mountains,
and the four great rivers
flow and pour into it,
neither increasing nor decreasing;
the ocean of precepts is also like this,
having the Píní as its base
and being surrounded by the mountains of Āpítán,
with the rivers of the four Āhán pouring into it,
remaining eternally tranquil and as such,
neither increasing nor decreasing.
Why is it that the pouring in does not cause increase or decrease?
Below, the fires of Ābí
surge upward toward the great ocean,
causing the ocean water to evaporate and dry up;
for this reason it does not increase.
Because it constantly flows in,
for this reason it does not decrease.
In the ocean of precepts of the Fófǎ,
because of non-negligence it does not increase,
and because it is complete with merit it does not decrease.
Therefore, one should know
that for one who can uphold the precepts,
their virtue is extremely great.
After the Fó’s Nièpán,
in the land of Ānduó,
there was at that time a mendicant bǐqiū who delighted in solitary and quiet places
and was complete in dignified deportment.
The mendicant bǐqiū,
praised by the Fó,
was not one who lived among the assembly.
Why is this?
Mendicant bǐqiūs
have few desires and are easily satisfied;
they do not store or accumulate possessions,
they beg for food in order,
they sit in the open upon whatever is spread,
and they have one meal and three robes;
matters such as these
are worthy of respect and esteem.
Bǐqiūs who stay within the Sēng community
often have many desires and are never satisfied,
storing and accumulating possessions,
greedy in seeking and stingy in giving,
full of jealousy and attachment;
for this reason they cannot attain great fame.
That mendicant bǐqiū
was pure and complete in virtuous conduct,
possessing the fruits of a shāmén,
the six supernatural powers and the three types of knowledge,
dwelling in the eight liberations,
with composed and orderly deportment,
and his fame spread widely.
At that time in the country of Ānduó,
there was a yōupósè
who reverently believed in the Sānbǎo
and upheld the five precepts:
not killing,
not stealing,
not committing sexual misconduct,
not lying,
and not drinking alcohol;
practicing giving and cultivating virtue,
his name was known throughout the cities and towns.
He invited this mendicant bǐqiū
to receive offerings for the rest of his life.
Regarding the merit of making offerings,
one receives retribution according to the cause.
If one invites the assembly of Sēng
to come to one's house to receive offerings,
then it obstructs and halts their practice of the Way,
and they suffer the hardships of the road's cold and heat;
later, when receiving the retribution,
one must labor with thoughts and concerns
and go out to seek and pursue
before one can obtain it.
But if one goes to where they are to present offerings,
later, when receiving the karmic reward of blessings,
one will then receive it naturally while sitting still.
This yōupósè,
whose faith was pure and deep,
prepared various types of beautiful, fragrant, and delicious food
and sent people to deliver them,
doing so day after day.
There are four kinds of shāmén,
whose goodness or badness is difficult to discern,
just as it is hard to know if an ānluó fruit is ripe or unripe.
There may be a bǐqiū
whose deportment is composed and orderly,
walking slowly and looking attentively,
yet internally he is full of greed, anger, and delusion, breaking the precepts and acting against the dharma,
like an ānluó fruit that is ripe on the outside but raw on the inside.
There may be a bǐqiū
whose external behavior is coarse and careless,
not following the formal rules,
yet internally he is complete in the virtuous conduct of a shāmén, in meditative concentration and wisdom,
like an ānluó fruit that is ripe on the inside but raw on the outside.
There may be a bǐqiū
whose deportment is coarse and rough,
who breaks the precepts and creates evil,
and internally he also possesses greed, anger, delusion, stinginess, and jealousy,
like an ānluó fruit that is raw both inside and out.
There may be a bǐqiū
whose deportment is composed and careful,
who upholds the precepts and guards himself,
and internally is complete in the virtuous conduct of a shāmén, in precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation,
like an ānluó fruit that is ripe both inside and out.
That mendicant bǐqiū
was complete both inside and out,
just like this;
because his virtuous conduct was full,
he was honored and respected by all.
At that time in the country,
there was an elder
who believed in and respected the Sānbǎo.
He had a son,
and thought to himself:
“I wish for him to leave home;
I must seek a good teacher to entrust him to.
Why is this so?
By being near a good spiritual friend, wholesome dharmas increase;
by being near an evil spiritual friend, unwholesome dharmas then arise.
For example, although the nature of wind is empty,
if it blows through a zhāntán forest
or a zhānbó forest and brings fragrance,
the wind possesses a wonderful scent;
but if it passes through excrement, filth, or foul corpses and comes,
that wind then becomes foul.
Furthermore, it is like a clean garment placed in a fragrant chest;
when the garment is taken out, it smells of fragrance.
If it is placed in a foul place,
the garment also becomes foul accordingly.
By being close to good friends, one's goodness prospers daily;
by associating with evil friends, one's evil increases.
Therefore, I now
should give this child to this Venerable One to let him leave home.”
Having had this thought, he immediately went there
and said to the bǐqiū:
“This only son of mine,
I now wish him to leave home.
I only pray, Great Virtue!
That you will compassionately accept and deliver him;
if you cannot accept him,
I shall take him back home.”
At that time, the bǐqiū,
observed with the eye of the Way.
Seeing that if this person left home
he would be able to uphold the pure precepts
and cause the Fófǎ to grow,
he then accepted him
and ordained him as a shāmí.
At that time, the yōupósè had a close lay friend
who invited the yōupósè, along with his wife, children, and the household servants,
to a gathering of guests on the following day.
At that time, the yōupósè
thought in the early morning:
“We should all go to the gathering today,
but who will stay behind to guard the house?
If I use force
to order one person to stay,
regarding the portion they should have received,
I would then be indebted to them.
If there is someone who can willingly decide to stay,
when I return from the gathering,
I shall reward them separately.”
The daughter of the yōupósè then said to her father:
“I only pray, parents!
May you and all the servants simply go to answer the invitation;
I am capable of staying behind to guard it.”
Her father said happily:
"Very good, very good!
Now that you are staying to guard the house,
you and your mother are to me
exactly the same.
Regarding the household's gains and losses,
my heart has no doubts or worries."
Thereupon the whole family went to receive the invitation,
and the girl firmly closed the doors
and stayed inside the house alone.
At that time, the Yōupósaì,
being in a great hurry that day,
forgot to send the food.
At that moment, the Zūnzhě thought to himself:
"The day is turning toward evening,
and laypeople have many affairs;
perhaps he forgot to send the food.
Should I now send someone to fetch it?"
He then told a Shāmí:
"Go and fetch the food.
Carefully maintain your dignified bearing,
just as the Buddha said:
when entering a village to beg for food,
do not give rise to greed or attachment.
Be like a bee gathering from a flower,
taking only its nectar without damaging its color or fragrance.
You now should do the same:
when you arrive at the house to take the food,
restrain your sensory faculties
and do not covet sights, sounds, smells, tastes, or touches.
If you maintain the restrictive precepts,
you will certainly attain the Path.
Just as Típó dádduō,
although he recited many sutras,
because he committed evil and violated the precepts,
he fell into the Ābí Hell;
just as Qūjiā lì,
because of his slander and breaking the precepts,
also entered hell;
while Zhōulì pántè,
although he recited only one verse,
because he maintained the precepts,
became an Āluóhàn.
Furthermore, the precepts are the gate to entering Nièpán
and the cause for receiving joy.
For example, according to the laws of the Póluómén,
if they hold a long fast
for three or four months,
they invite many brilliant, precept-holding, and pure-living Póluómén.
Because they select those to be invited
and cannot invite everyone universally,
Chóuliú was used as the seal for those invited.
One Póluómén,
although highly learned in the scriptures,
was not incorruptible by nature.
Because he was greedy for the sweetness of honey,
he licked the seal clean.
The next day, when he reached the assembly,
he had to present the seal to enter.
Next was a Fànzhì
who wished to enter without a seal.
The official in charge said:
'Do you have a seal?'
He answered:
'I had one,
but because it was sweet, I licked it all away.'
The official said:
'What you have had is already enough for you today.'
He was then unable to go forward.
Because he coveted a small sweetness,
he lost the sweet and fragrant flavors of the four months
as well as the various precious treasures of the final Dáčèn.
You now are like this;
do not break the seal of the pure precepts for the sake of small matters,
thus losing the five delicious desires of the heavens and the human realm, as well as the thirty-seven factors of Nièpán, peace, joy, and the measureless treasures of the Dharma.
Do not violate the precepts of the Buddhas of the three ages,
or defile the Triple Gem, your parents, or your teachers."
The Shāmí received the instruction,
bowed at his feet, and departed.
Arriving at the house,
he knocked on the door.
The girl asked:
"Who is it?"
He answered:
"A Shāmí,
here to fetch food for my teacher."
The girl was delighted in her heart, thinking,
"My wish is finally fulfilled!"
She then opened the door for him.
This girl was beautiful,
her appearance was extraordinary,
and she was sixteen years old.
Burned by the fire of lust,
in front of the Shāmí,
she performed many seductive charms,
swaying her shoulders and glancing at her reflection,
deeply manifesting signs of desire.
Seeing this, the Shāmí thought:
"Does this girl have a wind-illness, madness, or epilepsy?
Or is she being driven by the fetters of lust
and wants to harass and destroy my pure conduct?"
He firmly maintained his dignified bearing,
and his expression did not change.
Then the girl prostrated herself on the ground
and said to the Shāmí:
"What I have always wished for
has now come at the right time.
I have always
wanted to speak to you,
but never had a quiet opportunity.
I imagine that you
also always had feelings for me;
you should grant my wish.
In this house of mine,
there are many storehouses of precious treasures, gold, and silver,
like the treasures in the palace of Píshāmén.
Yet they have no master.
You could humble yourself to become the master of this house,
and I will be your wife
to serve you.
Please do not refuse me,
and fulfill my wish."
The Shāmí thought to himself:
"What sin have I committed
to encounter this evil circumstance?
I would rather give up this body and life
than violate the restrictive precepts established by the Buddhas of the three ages.
In the past, when a Bǐqiū went to the house of a courtesan,
he would rather throw himself into a fire pit than commit adultery.
Also, there were Bǐqiū
who were robbed by thieves
and bound with grass;
though blown by the wind and scorched by the sun,
and bitten by insects,
because they protected the precepts,
they did not break the grass to leave.
Like the goose that swallowed a pearl,
although the Bǐqiū saw it,
because he held the precepts,
he would not speak even under extreme suffering.
Like when a ship was destroyed at sea,
a junior Bǐqiū,
because he kept the precepts,
gave his plank to a senior Bǐqiū
and died by drowning in the sea.
All these people
were uniquely disciples of the Buddha
who could maintain the restrictive precepts.
Am I not also a disciple?
Can I not also maintain them?
Is the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
only their teacher
and not my teacher?
Like Zhànbù flowers pressed with sesame seeds,
the oil will have the fragrance of Zhànbù;
if mixed with foul flowers,
the oil will also become foul.
I have already met a virtuous friend;
how can I today commit an evil act?
I would rather give up my body and life
and never break the precepts
or defile the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, my parents, or my teachers."
He thought again:
"If I try to escape,
her lustful heart is so strong
that she will cast aside shame
and run out to grab me.
She might also slander me,
and if people in the streets see us,
I will not escape disgrace.
I must certainly give up my life here."
He used an expedient means and said:
"Lock the doors firmly.
I will enter a room
to do what must be done,
and then I will join you."
The girl then closed the door.
The Shāmí entered the room,
bolted the door,
and found a razor.
His heart was very joyful.
He took off his robes
and placed them on a rack.
With palms joined, he knelt toward the city of Jūshīnà, the place of the Buddha’s Nièpán,
and made a vow:
"I now do not abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha;
I do not abandon my Héshang or Āshé lí;
nor do I abandon the precepts.
It is precisely to maintain the precepts
that I give up this body and life;
I vow that wherever I am reborn,
I shall leave the home life to study the Path,
purely cultivate brahma-conduct,
and exhaust all taints to realize the Path."
He then cut his throat and died,
the blood flowing profusely,
staining his body.
The girl, surprised by the delay,
went to the door to look
and saw that the door was not open.
She called out, but there was no response.
She found a way to open the door
and saw that he was already dead.
His original appearance was lost.
Her lustful heart immediately ceased,
replaced by the knots of shame and anguish.
She tore out her own hair
and scratched her face with her nails.
Wallowing in the dust and ashes,
she wailed in grief and wept tears,
fainting in a state of confused distress.
Her father then returned,
knocked on the door and called for his daughter,
but the daughter remained silent and did not respond.
The father, wondering at her silence,
sent someone to climb over and enter.
They opened the door and looked;
seeing the daughter in such a state,
he immediately asked her, saying:
"Why are you like this?
Did someone violate or dishonor you?"
The daughter remained silent and did not answer,
thinking to herself:
"If I now answer with the truth,
it would be deeply shameful.
But if I say the *shāmí* violated and dishonored me,
then I would be slandering the virtuous,
and I would surely fall into hell to suffer endless punishment.
I must not deceive."
She then answered with the truth:
"While I was guarding this place alone,
a *shāmí* arrived,
seeking food for his teacher.
My lustful heart grew intense,
and I sought to seduce the *shāmí*,
hoping he would follow my desires.
Yet he upheld the precepts,
and his heart did not waver.
He found a way to enter the room
and took his own life.
Because of my defiled form,
I wished to destroy a pure vessel.
Such is my sin and transgression,
and thus I am not happy."
When the father heard the daughter's words,
his heart felt no alarm or fear.
Why was this?
Because he knew the nature of the fetters of affliction.
He then told his daughter:
"All phenomena
are entirely impermanent;
do not be grieved or fearful!"
He then entered the room
and saw the body of the *shāmí*.
The blood was all red and stained,
like a *zhāntán* desk.
He immediately stepped forward and bowed,
praising him, saying:
"Excellent!
You protected the Buddha's precepts
and were able to give up your life."
At that time, the law of that country was:
if a *shāmén* or a layperson died in one's house,
one must pay a fine of one thousand gold coins to the officials.
The *yōupóscè*
placed one thousand gold coins on a bronze tray,
carried it to the royal palace,
and said:
"Great King!
I have a penalty
that should be paid to the King;
I pray you will accept it."
The King answered him, saying:
"In my kingdom,
you respect and believe in the Triple Gem,
you are loyal and upright in following the Way,
and your words and deeds never conflict.
Of everyone, only you—
what fault could you have committed to pay a fine?"
The *yōupóscè* then
detailed the circumstances mentioned above,
disparaging his own daughter
and praising the merit of the *shāmí* in upholding the precepts.
When the King heard of the matter,
his heart was struck with awe,
his sincere faith grew even stronger,
and he told him:
"The *shāmí* protected the precepts
and gave up his own life.
You have no guilt or blame;
how could there be a fine?
Simply take it back home.
I now wish to personally go to your house to make offerings to the *shāmí*."
He then beat the golden drums
and proclaimed to the people of the country.
With a retinue leading and following,
he went to the house.
The King himself entered within
and saw the body of the *shāmí*,
red like *zhāntán*.
