He stepped forward to pay his respects
and praised his merit.
Using various jewels,
he adorned a high carriage,
placed the deceased *shāmí* upon it,
and went to a level ground.
They piled up various fragrant woods
and performed the *shéwéi* offerings.
He adorned the daughter
with beauty surpassing all in the world,
placed her in a high and prominent place
so that everyone in the assembly could see her,
and said to the crowd:
"This girl is exquisite;
her radiant beauty is like this.
For those who have not yet left desire,
who would not have a defiled mind?
Yet this *shāmí*,
though he had not yet attained the Way,
with his body of birth and death,
honored the precepts and gave up his life.
This is truly extraordinary and rare!"
The King then sent someone
to invite the *shāmí*'s teacher
to extensively preach
the subtle and wonderful Dharma for the great assembly.
Everyone in the assembly at that time,
having seen and heard of these events,
some sought to leave home and uphold the pure precepts,
and some gave rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed Bodhi.
There were none who were not joyful,
and they received and practiced it with the highest respect.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the country of *Shèwèiguó*, at the *Qǐtuó* Monastery,
preaching the Dharma to the great assembly of *bǐqiū*.
At that time, in that country, there was a great *zhǎngzhě*
of immeasurable wealth.
Gold, silver, the seven treasures, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, male and female slaves, and people filled his storehouses to overflowing.
He had no sons, only five daughters,
who were upright, intelligent, and perceptive.
While his wife was pregnant, the *zhǎngzhě* died.
According to the law of that country at the time,
if one died and the family had no sons,
all property and goods were to be confiscated by the state.
The King sent high officials to record the wealth
so it could be taken. The daughter thought to herself:
"My mother is pregnant, and we do not yet know if it is a boy or a girl.
If it is another girl, the wealth should belong to the state;
if it is a boy, he should be the owner of the wealth."
Having thought this,
she went to the King and said:
"My father has died,
and because there is no son, the wealth should go to the King.
However, my mother is now pregnant.
We must wait for the birth.
If it is indeed a girl, it will not be too late to take the wealth;
if it is a boy, he should be the owner of the wealth."
At that time, King *Bōsīnì* upheld the law with fairness and equity,
and he immediately granted her request, listening to her words.
Not long after, the mother reached her full term and gave birth to a child.
His body was a shapeless mass, lacking ears and eyes,
possessing a mouth but no tongue, and also lacking hands and feet.
However, he had a male organ.
He was then given a name: *Màncípílí*.
At that time, the daughter, with all these facts, went to ask the King.
When the King heard this,
he contemplated its meaning:
"One does not become the owner of wealth because of eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, or feet;
rather, because he is male, he becomes the owner of the wealth.
Since the child has a male organ, he should receive his father's wealth."
He then told the daughters:
"The wealth belongs to your younger brother;
I shall not take it."
At that time, the eldest daughter went to marry into another family.
She served her husband with humility, reverence, and diligence.
She dusted the bed and mats, prepared and served food and drink,
welcomed him when he arrived and saw him off when he left,
bowing and inquiring after him
just as a servant girl serves a great master.
A neighboring *zhǎngzhě*, seeing her like this,
was surprised and asked her:
"The way of husband and wife exists in every household;
why do you alone change your conduct in such a manner?"
The woman replied:
"My father passed away, leaving immeasurable family wealth.
Although there were five daughters,
it was still due to be taken by the King.
Then my mother gave birth to my one younger brother.
He has no eyes, ears, tongue, or hands and feet;
he has only a male organ,
and thus he could become the owner of the wealth."
"For this reason,
although one may have many daughters, they are not as good as having one son.
That is just how it is."
When the elder heard this, he marveled that it was so,
and immediately took his daughter to the place of the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One! For what causes and conditions
does that elder's son lack eyes, ears, a tongue, and limbs, yet was born into a wealthy family
and became the owner of such riches?"
The Buddha told the elder:
"An excellent question!
Listen carefully and reflect well!
I shall explain it for you."
"Indeed, I joyfully wish to hear."
The Buddha told the elder:
"In the distant past, there were two elder brothers,
the elder named Dānruòshìzhì,
and the younger named Sīluóshìzhì.
From his youth, the elder brother was loyal, trustworthy, and sincere.
He always loved giving and rescuing the poor and needy.
Because of his faithfulness and goodness, he was praised throughout the kingdom.
The king appointed this man as the state Píngshì,
to settle disputes and decide right from wrong.
All final decisions depended on him.
At that time, the laws of the land
for lending and borrowing had no written contracts or records;
everyone went to the Píngshì
Dānruòshìzhì, considering him a man of clarity.
At that time, there was a merchant who wished to go to sea.
He borrowed a large amount of money and goods from the younger brother, Sīluóshìzhì, to provide for his needs.
At that time, the younger brother elder had only one son,
who was young in years.
He then took his son and the money he was lending out to the Píngshì’s place,
and said: 'Elder brother!
This merchant's son is borrowing money from me.
When he returns from the sea,
I should receive such-and-such an amount.
Brother, you are a man of clarity.
If I should die,
witness so that my son receives it.'
The Píngshì elder pointed and spoke in agreement.
The younger brother elder died not long after.
At that time, the merchant's son set sail to sea.
Winds and waves arose,
the ship was destroyed and lost.
At that time, the merchant's son grabbed a plank and survived,
returning to his home country.
At that time, the elder's son heard that his ship was destroyed and he had returned empty-handed.
Seeing only this man,
he thought to himself:
'Although he owes me,
he is now empty-handed and destitute; how can I obtain it?
I must wait until he has means to collect the debt.'
Later, he saw this merchant elder join other traders and set out to sea again,
obtaining great treasures and returning safely and successfully.
He thought to himself:
'That elder's son, although he saw me before,
did not ask me for the debt.
When I borrowed the money, this person was a child; perhaps he does not remember?
Or because I was destitute before,
he did not demand the debt?
Now I shall test him.'
He then prepared fine horses and various treasures, dressed in jeweled robes,
and rode a horse into the market.
The elder's son saw
his clothing and mount were like this,
and thought to himself: 'This person seems to have wealth again;
I should try to collect the debt.'
He immediately sent someone to say:
'You owe me money,
and you should repay it now.'
He replied: 'That may be so.
I should think about how to settle it.'
The merchant thought to himself:
'The amount borrowed was very large, and with interest accumulating,
there is no way I can finish paying it.
I must devise a plan to settle it.'
He then took a precious pearl to the Píngshì’s wife and said:
'Madam!
I originally borrowed a small amount of wealth from Sīluóshìzhì.
His son has come to collect the debt from me.
I now offer a pearl worth one hundred thousand.
If he tries to collect the debt,
please instruct the Píngshì not to be a witness.'
His wife replied:
'The elder is honest and faithful; he will surely not be willing to do that.
But I shall try to speak to him.'
Then she accepted the pearl.
When the Píngshì returned in the evening,
she told him everything.
The elder replied:
'How could such a thing be?
Because of my loyalty, trust, and lack of false speech,
the king appointed me as the state Píngshì.
If I speak even one lie,
this matter would be unacceptable.'
When the merchant came and explained the situation,
he then returned the pearl to him.
Then the merchant offered another pearl
worth two hundred thousand,
and again said:
'I hope you can instruct him.
Since this is a small matter,
just by saying one word, you get three hundred thousand.
If he wins,
although he is your nephew, he will not have a single penny's share.
This logic is acceptable.'
At that time, the woman was greedy for the precious pearls
and accepted them.
In the evening, she again spoke to her husband:
'What I said yesterday is also reasonable.
Please keep it in mind.'
The elder replied:
'There is absolutely no such logic.
Because I am trustworthy, I became the Píngshì.
If I speak even one lie,
in the present life I will not be trusted by the world,
and in future lives I will suffer measureless kalpas of pain.'
At that time, the elder had a son who could not yet walk.
His wife wept and said:
'Now you and I are husband and wife.
If there were a matter of life and death,
I would still hope you would not refuse.
I ask for this small matter,
just to say one word,
but you will not follow me.
What is the use of my living?
If you do not follow me,
I will first kill the child and then kill myself.'
When the elder heard this,
it was as if he were choking;
he could neither swallow nor spit it out.
He thought to himself:
'I have only this one son.
If he should die,
there would be no one to entrust my wealth to.
If I follow her words,
then today I will not be trusted by people,
and in the future I will suffer measureless suffering and distress.'
Hard-pressed and unable to stop,
he then agreed to it.
His wife was delighted and said to the merchant:
'The elder has already agreed.'
When the merchant heard this, he returned home with joy,
prepared a great elephant, adorned with various treasures,
wore great precious robes,
and rode the elephant into the market.
The elder's son saw him and thought happily:
'This person is certainly wealthy,
having such clothing and mount.
I shall get my wealth!'
He immediately went and said:
'Sàbáo, you should know! The money you owed before
should be repaid now.'
The merchant said in alarm:
'I do not remember at all; when did I owe you?
If I owe you,
who is the witness?'
The elder's son said:
'On such-and-such a date, my father and I personally handed you the money.
The Píngshì was my witness.
Why do you say no?'
The merchant said:
'I do not recall now.
If there is indeed a fact, I should repay it to you.'
They immediately went together to the Píngshì’s place.
The elder's son said:
'In the past, this person personally borrowed such-and-such an amount from my father.
Uncle was the witness,
and I saw it at that time.
Is that not the case?'
He replied: 'I do not know.'
His nephew was shocked and said:
'Uncle, if at that time you truly did not see or hear,
and did not speak those words, that would be one thing;
but did you not use your hands and feet to point out this wealth?'
He replied: 'It was not so.'
The nephew said in anger:
'Because Uncle was loyal and good, the king appointed you Píngshì,
and the people of the country trusted you.
To me, your own nephew, you are still this unjust;
how much more so toward outsiders?
Are those who have been wronged few?
The truth or falsehood of this will be known in the next life.'
The Buddha told the elder:
'If you wish to know, the Píngshì elder of that time
is the present Màncíbìlí, who has no eyes or ears and is formless.
Because of that one lie,
he fell into the great hells and suffered much bitter poison.
Since emerging from the hells, for five hundred lifetimes,
he has always received this formless body.
Because he loved to give at that time,
one will constantly be born into wealth and grandeur and become a wealthy lord.
The retribution for good and evil does not fail, even after a long duration of time.
Therefore, all of you! You should strive with diligence,
restrain the body, speech, and mind,
and do not recklessly commit evil."
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Fó had said,
included those who attained from the first fruit to the fourth fruit
and those who gave rise to the unsurpassed Pútíxīn;
there was no one who was not filled with joy,
and they paid homage and practiced it faithfully.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the Shèwèi Guó, at the Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán, Jǐhuán Jīngshè,
together with a great assembly of Bǐqiū,
who surrounded him as he preached the Dharma.
At that time in the kingdom,
there was an elder
whose wife was pregnant.
When the months were full, she gave birth to a daughter,
who was upright, beautiful, and wonderful,
her appearance having few equals.
At the time of her birth,
a fine and soft white cotton cloth
wrapped her body as she was born.
Her parents found this strange
and called for a master to divine her physiognomy.
The master said:
“It is very auspicious!
She possesses great merit and virtue.”
Therefore, they gave her a name,
calling her Shūlí
(which in the language of Qín means “White”).
As Shūlí grew up,
the cotton cloth grew along with her body.
This girl was extraordinary and precious,
and from far and near within the kingdom,
suitors competed to come and seek her in marriage.
Her parents thought:
“Our daughter is already of age;
it is appropriate that she be married off.”
They then commissioned craftsmen to make necklaces and ornaments for her.
Shūlí asked her father:
“Forging this gold and silver,
what is it to be used for?”
Her father told her:
“You are already of age,
and we wish to marry you off,
so we are making rings and bracelets.”
The daughter said to her father:
“I wish to leave the household life;
I do not take joy in being married.”
Out of love and consideration,
her parents did not oppose her will
and immediately brought out cotton cloth,
intending to make the five robes.
Seeing this, the daughter asked again:
“What do you wish to make?”
They told her:
“We are making robes for you.”
She said to her parents:
“What I am wearing now
is already complete and sufficient;
there is no need to make more.
I only wish for you to allow me to go at once to where the Fó is.”
Her parents then led her to the place of the Fó,
where they bowed with their heads at his feet
and requested that she leave the household life.
The Fó said:
“Welcome (Shànlái)!”
Her hair fell off by itself,
and the white cotton cloth she was wearing
immediately became the five robes.
She was entrusted to Dà Àidào
to become a Bǐqiūní.
Not long after her diligent practice,
she attained the path of an Āluóhàn.
Ānán said to the Fó:
“As for the Bǐqiūní Shūlí,
what merit did she plant in the past
to be born in the house of an elder,
to be born appearing together with a cotton cloth,
and not long after leaving the household life,
to attain the path of an Āluóhàn?”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Listen attentively and consider it well!
I shall now speak of it.”
Ānán said:
“Indeed.”
The Fó said:
“In the distant past,
there was a Fó who appeared in the world
named Pípóshī,
who, with his disciples,
widely liberated all beings.
At that time, the king, ministers, and people
provided many offerings
and performed the Bānzhēyúshè ceremony.
There was a Bǐqiū
who constantly went about encouraging and transforming others,
leading them to the place of the Fó to hear the Dharma and practice giving (bùshī).
At that time, there was a woman
named Tánnìjiā,
who was extremely poor.
The husband and wife, the two of them,
shared only one cotton cloth.
If the husband went out,
he would wear it and go,
while the wife remained naked, sitting on a grass mat;
if the wife wore the cloth and went out to seek alms,
the husband would sit naked on the grass mat.
The Bǐqiū who was encouraging others reached their house in turn.
Seeing this woman,
he encouraged her, saying:
‘A Fó appearing is hard to encounter,
the sūtra teachings are hard to hear,
a human body is hard to obtain.
You should hear the Dharma,
and you should practice giving.’
He spoke extensively on the retributions of greed and the rewards of giving.
The woman said:
‘Great Virtuous One (Dàdé), stay a moment.’
She went back inside the house
and spoke to her husband, saying:
‘Outside there is a Shāmén
encouraging me to see the Fó, hear the Dharma, and practice giving.
Because we did not
practice giving in our previous lives,
we have come to this poverty.
Now, what shall we use as provisions for our future lives?’
The husband replied to her:
‘Our house is destitute like this;
although we may have the intention,
what can we give?’
The wife said:
‘Because we did not give in former lives,
we have now come to this distress.
If we do not plant seeds now,
where will we go in the future?
You just listen to me;
I am determined to give.’
The husband thought to himself:
‘Perhaps this wife has a small amount of private property;
I should allow it.’
He then agreed, saying:
‘If you wish to give, then give.’
She immediately said:
‘My intention is to give this cotton cloth.’
The husband said:
‘You and I share this one cloth
to go out and seek alms
to keep ourselves alive.
Now if we use it for giving,
we shall both wait for death.
What plan do you have?’
The wife said:
‘In human life there is death.
If we do not give it now,
we will eventually die anyway; if we do not give it now,
we will eventually die.
It is better to give and die,
for there is hope for future lives;
to die without giving
will lead to even greater suffering.’
The husband joyfully said:
‘I accept death to make the gift.’
The wife then went back out
and said to the Bǐqiū:
“Great Virtuous One!
Please stay below the eaves of the house;
I shall practice giving.”
The Bǐqiū replied:
“If you wish to give,
you should give it in person,
so that I may say a prayer for you.”
Shūlí said:
“I have only this cotton cloth covering me,
and no other clothes underneath.
My female form is impure,
and it is not appropriate to remove it here.”
She then went back inside,
and from a distance through an opening,
she took off the cloth from her body
and handed it to the Bǐqiū.
The Bǐqiū said a prayer
and carried it to the place of the Fó.
“The Fó said to the Bǐqiū:
‘Bring that cotton cloth here.’
The Bǐqiū handed it to the Fó,
and with his own hand the Fó received this dirty and soiled cotton cloth.
At that time, the king and the assembly
slightly felt disdain that the Fó would receive such a dirty cloth.
The Fó knew the minds of the assembly
and told them:
‘I see that in this assembly, of the pure and great gifts,
none surpasses the one who gave this cloth.’
After the great assembly heard this,
there was none who was not awestruck.
The queen, filled with joy,
immediately took off the ornaments, necklaces, and precious robes she was wearing
and sent them to Tuónìjíjí;
the king was also delighted.
She took off her clothes,
gave them to her husband,
and ordered him to go to the assembly.
Pípóshī Fó broadly addressed the great assembly,
preaching the subtle and marvelous Dharma.
Among the assembly at that time,
those who attained liberation were many.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"If you wish to know who the poor woman Tuónìqūqū was at that time,
she is the current Shūlí Bǐqiūní.
Because at that time she offered cotton cloth with a pure heart,
for ninety-one kalpas, in whatever place she was born,
she was always born with cotton cloth,
lacking nothing
and obtaining everything as she wished.
Because of her connection to that Buddha,
hearing the deep and marvelous Dharma
and vowing to be liberated,
she has now met me
and become an Āluóhàn.
Therefore, all of you
should diligently persevere in hearing the Dharma and practicing giving."
When the Buddha said this,
those who attained the Path were many;
none were not joyful,
and they reverently accepted and practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the country of Ālǐtí.
In that country at that time, there was an Elder
with much wealth and many treasures,
but he was stingy, greedy, violent, and wicked,
having no heart of compassion.
He had a slave girl who served him day and night,
never finding a moment's peace.
For the slightest mistake, she would receive lashings and beatings;
her clothes did not cover her body,
her food did not nourish her frame.
Aged, exhausted, and weary,
she wished for death but could not attain it.
Once, while carrying a jar
to the river to fetch water,
she contemplated this suffering
and raised her voice in loud weeping.
At that time, Jiāzhānyán came to her place and asked:
"Old mother!
Why are you weeping in such sorrow and distress?"
She replied:
"Honorable one!
I am already old,
always performing hard labor,
and on top of that, I am poor,
with insufficient food and clothing.
I wish for death but cannot attain it;
that is why I weep."
Jiāzhānyán said:
"If you are poor, why do you not sell your poverty?"
The mother said:
"How can poverty be sold?
Who would buy poverty?"
Jiāzhānyán said:
"Poverty can indeed be sold."
When he said this a third time,
the woman said:
"If poverty can truly be sold,
I should ask for the method."
She then said:
"Great Virtuous One! How is poverty sold?"
Jiāzhānyán said:
"If you truly wish to sell it, follow my words
and answer with agreement."
He told her:
"First, bathe yourself."
After she bathed, he told her:
"You should practice giving."
She replied:
"Honorable one!
I am extremely poor and destitute;
as for my current body, there is not a hand-span of intact cloth.
Although I have this jar,
it belongs to my master.
With what shall I give?"
He then handed his bowl to her
and said, "Take this bowl and fetch a little clean water."
She took it as instructed
and presented it to Jiāzhānyán.
Jiāzhānyán accepted it
and immediately made a prayer of blessing for her.
Next, he taught her to receive the precepts,
and then he taught her to contemplate the various merits of the Buddha.
He then asked:
"Do you have a place to stay?"
She answered: "No.
When it is time to grind grain,
I lie down beneath the millstone;
when pounding or cooking or serving,
I lie down in those places.
Sometimes when there is no work,
I stay on a dung heap."
Jiāzhānyán said:
"Keep your heart well,
work diligently and respectfully,
and do not harbor resentment.
Wait until your master and everyone else
have finished lying down to sleep,
then secretly open the door,
and inside the corner of the doorway, spread a clean grass mat.
Contemplate and visualize the Buddha, and do not let evil thoughts arise."
At that time, the old mother followed the teaching and returned.
She acted as she was instructed,
and during the latter part of the night, she passed away
and was born in Dāolì Tiān.
When the master rose early and saw the slave girl had died,
he was angry and said:
"This slave was never allowed to enter the house;
why did she die here last night?"
He then sent someone to tie her feet with grass ropes
and drag her to the cold forest.
At that time in that heaven, there was a Son of Heaven
who had five hundred Sons of Heaven as his followers,
and his palace was grand and beautiful.
At that time, that Son of Heaven's merit was exhausted and he passed away;
this old woman immediately took his place.
According to the law of birth in heaven,
those with sharp faculties know the causes of their arrival,
while those born with dull faculties only know how to receive pleasure.
At that time, this woman, having been born in the heaven,
enjoyed pleasure with the five hundred Sons of Heaven
and did not know the causes of her birth.
At that time, Shèlìfú was in Dāolì Tiān
and knew the causes and conditions of this Son of Heaven being born in heaven.
He asked: "Son of Heaven! By what merit were you born in this heaven?"
He answered: "I do not know."
Then Shèlìfú lent him his divine eye
to see the causes and conditions for his former body's birth in heaven,
which were due to Jiāzhānyán.
He then led the five hundred Sons of Heaven to the cold forest,
scattering flowers and burning incense
to make offerings to the corpse.
The light of the devas illuminated the village and the forest.
When the master saw this transformation,
he wondered at its cause
and sent word far and near to go to the forest and watch.
Seeing the Sons of Heaven making offerings to this corpse,
he asked the deva:
"This slave girl was ugly and filthy;
when she was alive, people even loathed to see her,
let alone now that she is dead.
Why do the devas make offerings to her?"
At that time, the Son of Heaven related in full the beginning and end of the causes for being born in heaven.
Then everyone turned and went to the place of Jiāzhānyán.
At that time, Jiāzhānyán spoke broadly of the various Dharmas for the devas and humans,
namely, discourse on giving, discourse on precepts, and discourse on being born in heaven,
explaining that desires are impure and that transcendence is joy.
At that time, that deva and the five hundred Sons of Heaven
were far removed from dust and separated from defilement,
attaining the purification of the Dharma Eye,
and they flew back to the heavenly palace.
When the assembly heard this Dharma,
each attained the stages of the Path, even up to the four fruits.
None were not joyful,
and they reverently accepted and practiced it,
paying their respects and departing.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the Jǐshù Gǐgūdúyuán in the country of Shèwèiguó.
In this country at that time, there was an Elder
whose family was very wealthy
with countless treasures.
A son was born to him, whose body was golden in color.
The Elder rejoiced and immediately held a feast
and invited various physiognomists to predict his fortune.
Then the physiognomists held the child and examined him,
saw his extraordinary appearance,
and were overcome with joy.
They immediately gave him a name,
naming him Xiūyuènàtípó
(which in the Jìn language is Jīntiān).
This child's merit and virtue were extremely pure and abundant.
On the day he was born, a well naturally appeared in his house,
eight feet wide
and the same in depth.
When water was drawn from it, it could satisfy a person's wishes:
if they needed clothes, it produced clothes;
if they needed food, it produced food;
gold, silver, precious treasures, and everything needed
could be taken by making a wish,
and it would be obtained just as desired.
As the child grew older,
he became broadly proficient in arts and talents.
The Elder loved him
and never dared to go against his wishes,
and he thought:
"My son is upright and his appearance is peerless."
"I must search for and select a famous girl,"
"whose appearance and form are exceptional and surpass the crowd,"
"with a golden countenance and a marvelous body, like my son,"
"and I should go and seek her."
Thereupon, he recruited various merchants
to search for her everywhere.
At that time, in the country of Yánbō, there was a great elder
who had a daughter
named Xiūbánàpósū (in the Jìn language, Jīnguāngmíng).
She was of extraordinary uprightness,
and her body was golden in color,
radiant and shining upon people,
fine, smooth, and lustrous.
On the day of her birth, there also naturally appeared an eight-foot well of water;
that well could also produce various precious jewels,
clothing, food, and drink according to one's wishes.
That elder also thought to himself:
"My daughter is upright
and the most excellent among people;
I must find a worthy man whose form, color, and radiance
are comparable to my daughter's,
and only then shall I give her in marriage to become his spouse."
At that time, the girl's fame spread far to Shèwèi,
and the reputation of Jīntiān was also heard by the girl's family.
Then the two elders were each filled with joy
and immediately visited one another to seek the marriage.
After the marriage was completed, they returned to Shèwèi.
At that time, the family of Jīntiān prepared a superior offering
and invited the Buddha and the Sangha to be presented with offerings for one day.
The Buddha accepted the invitation and went to their house to eat.
After eating, he put away his bowl
and for the sake of the elder,
Jīntiān, and his wife, he extensively expounded the marvelous Dharma
to open and awaken their minds.
Jīntiān, his wife, and their parents
immediately destroyed twenty billion evils of the burning hells;
their minds were opened and awakened,
and they attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán.
Then the World-Honored One returned to the vihara.
Thereupon, Jīntiān and Jīnguāngmíng
both spoke to their parents, seeking to leave the household life.
Their parents immediately granted permission,
and they went together to the Buddha's place, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and after completing the rites and circumambulation, sought to enter the Way.
The Buddha immediately granted permission
and praised them, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikshus!"
Their hair and beards fell off naturally,
Dharma robes appeared on their bodies,
and they became Shāmén.
Thereupon, Jīntiān
joined the assembly of monks,
and the Bhikshuni Jīnguāngmíng was entrusted to Dààidào;
they were gradually taught and transformed,
and both became Luóhàn,
possessing the three types of knowledge and the six supernatural powers,
endowed with the eight liberations,
and all merits were fully perfected.
Ānán said to the Buddha:
"I wonder, World-Honored One,
what actions did Jīntiān and his wife perform in the past, such that since their birth, they have had much wealth and abundant treasures,
golden bodies,
supreme uprightness,
and obtained this single well capable of producing everything?
I only wish the Tathagata would fully proclaim and show this."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha in the world named Píbáshī.
After that Buddha entered parinirvana, his remaining teachings were in the world.
Later, there were several Bhikshus traveling and teaching,
and they arrived at a village.
There were people, prominent and worthy elders,
who, seeing the assembly of monks arrive,
each competed to provide offerings of clothing, bedding, food, and drink,
without any lack.
At that time, there was a husband and wife who were poor, hungry, and destitute.
They constantly thought to themselves:
'When my father was alive, wealth and treasures were accumulated to the full,
overflowing and immeasurable;
but now my own body is extremely poor and destitute,
sitting and lying on grass mats,
with clothes that do not cover my form
and the house lacking even a small measure of grain.
Why is it so bitter?
Back then, although we were wealthy
and our treasures were immeasurable,
we did not encounter such
a Sangha of holy ones;
now that we have met them,
we have no money to make offerings.'
After thinking this,
he wept sorrowfully,
and in his distress, tears fell,
dropping onto his wife's arm.
The wife, seeing her husband weeping,
questioned him, saying:
'What is wrong
that you are so distressed?'
The husband answered his wife:
'Do you not know?
Now an assembly of monks has just passed through this village,
and the prominent and worthy householders have all raised offerings.
My family is poor and lacks even a small measure of grain;
with this assembly of monks, we cannot plant good roots.
We are poor and destitute now,
and in future lives it will be even more severe.
I thought of this,
and that is why I weep.'
The wife answered her husband:
'What should we do now?
Though we truly wish to make offerings,
we have no wealth or treasures;
although we have this empty intention,
we cannot fulfill our wish.'
The wife said to her husband:
'Now you may go to our original home
and search within the old storehouse for wealth or treasures;
if you happen to find something,
we should use it for an offering.'
At that time, the husband did as she said and went to the old storehouse.
He searched everywhere
and found one gold coin,
which he brought to his wife's place.
At that time, his wife had a bright mirror;
they immediately united their hearts
to use them for an offering.
They took a new bottle,
filled it with pure water,
placed the gold coin into the water in the bottle,
placed the mirror on top,
and carried it to the monks' place.
Having arrived, with a sincere heart, they used it as an offering to the monks.
At that time, the assembly of monks accepted it;
each took some water to wash their bowls,
and some took water to drink.
Then the husband and wife were joyful and delighted in spirit.
After completing the act of merit,
they encountered illness and died, being born in Dāolì Heaven."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"The poor person who held a bottle of water to offer to the monks back then
is this present-day Jīntiān and his wife.
Because in their former life they offered this one gold coin,
one bottle of water, and this bright mirror
to the assembly of monks,
in every life they have been upright,
their bodies have been golden in color,
and their appearance and demeanor have been radiant and incomparably marvelous.
For ninety-one kalpas, it has always been like this.
Because at that time they had faith and respect,
they were able to leave birth and death
and attain the state of a Luóhàn.
Ānán, you should know
that one must not fail to perform any act of merit.
Like that poor person,
by means of a small offering,
they obtained such immeasurable karmic rewards."
At that time, Ānán and the various members of the assembly,
hearing what the Buddha had said,
all gave rise to the mind of generosity,
diligently added to their meritorious deeds,
and joyfully put the teachings into practice.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the country of Shèwèi, in the Qí Shù Gěigūdú Yuán.
At that time, in the country,
there was a wealthy Zhǎngzhě
whose riches were immeasurable,
yet he had no offspring.
He was often filled with melancholy,
praying and making offerings to the deities,
seeking a single son.
Because his sincerity was earnest and devoted,
his wife became pregnant.
When the months and days were fulfilled,
she gave birth to a baby boy.
This boy was handsome
and rare in the world.
His parents and kinsmen,
happening upon the occasion of a banquet,
gathered together
and went to the bank of a great river
to drink wine and enjoy themselves.
The parents held the child
and went to the gathering place.
The father loved this child;
while sitting in order, he carried him and danced.
After the father finished dancing,
the mother also carried him.
Passing through the seats, she held him up and bounced him,
delighting and amusing themselves.
As they approached the riverbank,
her mind suddenly became distracted,
her grip was not firm,
and she lost the child, who fell into the water.
Immediately she tried to grab him,
but in the end, she could not.
At that time, the parents,
piteously thinking of this child,
were heartbroken with attachment and grief;
they fainted and then revived.
Due to the child’s merit and virtue,
he did not die after all.
Entering into the river water,
he drifted with the current.
At that time, there was a fish
that swallowed this small child.
Although he was in the fish’s belly,
he still did not die.
There was a small village downstream,
where a wealthy family also had no offspring.
They had sought one in various ways,
but were frustrated and unable to obtain one.
That wealthy family
always ordered a slave to catch and sell fish,
and the servant would deliver them to the master.
That slave caught fish daily as his profession.
It happened that he caught the fish that had swallowed the child.
Upon cutting open its belly and looking inside,
he found a small child
with a handsome appearance.
Having found him, he was joyful
and carried him to the master.
The master looked at him
and said in celebration:
"My family has always prayed and made offerings to the deities,
seeking an heir.
Through the response to my sincerity,
heaven has thus given him to me."
He then stroked and took him in,
nursing and raising him.
Then the parents from the village upstream
heard that a Zhǎngzhě in the village downstream had found a child in a fish's belly.
They immediately went to his place
to pursue and claim him,
and said to him:
"This is my child.
In that river,
I lost this son.
Now that you have found him,
I wish that you return him."
Then that Zhǎngzhě
answered them, saying:
"My family has always
prayed and made offerings seeking a son.
Now the deity has responded,
bestowing a child upon me.
As for your lost child,
where would he be?"
The dispute was unsettled,
so they went to the Wáng to seek a judgment.
Thereupon, the two families
each presented their arguments.
The child's parents said:
"He is my child.
At a certain time,
I lost him in the river."
But that Zhǎngzhě
also said:
"I found him in a fish's belly within the river.
This is truly my son;
he was not born of you."
The Wáng heard their statements
and did not know how to proceed.
He then spoke with the two families
to deliberate on this matter:
"You two Zhǎngzhě,
each claim this child.
If he were given to only one now,
it would not be reasonable.
You shall raise him together in turns
until the child grows up.
Each of you shall take a wife for him
and establish his household and livelihood
in two separate residences.
The children born of this wife
shall belong to this family,
and the children born of that wife
shall belong to that family."
Then the two Zhǎngzhě
each followed the Wáng's instruction.
When the child grew up,
they both took wives for him
and provided for all his needs,
so that there was no lack.
At that time, the son
said to his two sets of parents:
"Since my birth,
I have encountered hardships;
falling into the water and being swallowed by a fish,
I was saved when near death.
Now it is my sincere intention
that I wish to leave the home life.
I only hope my parents
will grant me permission."
At that time, the two sets of parents,
loving this child in their hearts,
could not refuse him,
so they granted him permission.
The son then took his leave,
went to the Fó's place,
bowed his head at the Fó's feet,
and sought to enter the Way.
The Fó then permitted it
and praised him, saying:
"Welcome, Bǐqiū!"
His hair and beard fell off naturally,
and he immediately became a Shāmén,
named Zhòngxìng.
The Fó preached the Dharma for him,
and he brought an end to all suffering,
immediately while on his seat,
becoming an Āluóhàn.
Ānán said to the Fó:
"I wonder,
Shìzūn!
what deeds did this Bǐqiū Zhòngxìng
perform in the past
and what roots of goodness did he plant,
so that in this present life,
he fell into the water and was swallowed by a fish,
yet still did not die?"
The Fó told Ānán:
"Listen carefully!
I shall tell you.
In the distant past,
there was a Fó, a Shìzūn,
named Pípóshī.
He gathered the great assembly
and preached the wondrous Dharma for them.
At that time, there was a Zhǎngzhě
who came into the assembly.
Hearing that Rúlái extensively preach the Great Dharma,
the blessings of giving
and the blessings of keeping the precepts,
having heard this, he was joyful.
With intense faith,
he then received the three self-refuges from that Fó
and received the precept against killing.
Furthermore, he gave one coin as an offering to that Fó.
Because of this,
in life after life, he received blessings,
with wealth and treasures at his disposal,
and never any lack."
The Fó told Ānán:
"If you wish to know who that Zhǎngzhě's son was then,
it is this Bǐqiū Zhòngxìng.
Because he gave one coin to the Fó at that time,
for ninety-one kalpas,
he has always been wealthy with money and treasures,
even unto this present life,
where two sets of parents
provided for his needs.
Because he kept the precept against killing,
he did not die when falling into the great water and being swallowed by the fish.
Because he received the three self-refuges,
he has now encountered my age, was bathed in pure transformation,
and attained the path of an Āluóhàn."
At that time, Ānán
and the great assembly,
having heard what the Fó said,
followed and practiced good deeds.
Respectfully revere Fójiào,
joyfully believe and accept,
and carry it out with the highest reverence.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the kingdom of Shèwèi, in the Jǐ Shù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time the Shìzūn
was together with twelve hundred and fifty disciples.
At that time in the kingdom,
there were five hundred beggars
who constantly relied on the Rúlái,
followed the assembly of monks,
and sustained their lives by begging.
As the years passed,
a feeling of weary disgust arose within them,
and they spoke these words:
“All of us!
Although we have received the merit of the monks and had our remaining lives prolonged,
our hardships are still many.”
They all had this thought:
“We now,
should perhaps request to leave the household life from the Fó.”
Together they went to the Fó’s place,
and then these people
together spoke to the Fó:
“The Rúlái has appeared in the world,
which is very difficult to encounter.
All of us
were born into a lowly and mean state.
Having received the leftover kindness of the Shìzūn,
and had our lives saved,
having received such exceptional nourishment,
we desire to leave the household life.
We do not know, Shìzūn!
If this may be granted or not?”
At that time the Shìzūn
told the beggars:
“My Dharma is pure,
and there is neither noble nor lowly.
It is like pure water,
which washes away all impurities.
Whether noble or lowly,
whether beautiful or ugly,
whether male or female,
where the water washes,
none remain impure.
Moreover, it is like fire;
wherever it reaches,
mountains, rivers, and stone walls,
all that exists in heaven and earth,
whether great or small,
all the myriad things
that are burned by it,
none are not scorched and consumed.
Moreover, my Dharma
is like the empty sky;
men and women, great and small,
poor and rich, noble and lowly,
those who enter into it
may act freely as they please.”
At that time, when the beggars heard what the Fó had said,
they were all universally joyful.
Their faith became twice as strong,
they turned with sincere devotion toward the Fó,
and requested to enter the Path.
The Shìzūn told them:
“Come, Bǐqiū!”
Their beards and hair fell off naturally,
Dharma robes appeared on their bodies,
and the appearance of a Shāmén
was thus complete.
The Fó preached the Dharma for them,
their hearts opened and their minds understood,
they immediately exhausted all defilements,
and became Āluóhàn.
At that time in the kingdom,
the powerful elders, commoners, and others
heard that the Fó had allowed the beggars to enter the Path.
They all gave rise to arrogance
and spoke these words:
“How can the Rúlái allow these lowly beggar people to be in the rank of the monks?
When we
cultivate meritorious karma
and invite the Fó and the monks,
at the time of food offerings,
how can he allow these lowly fellows
to sit on our couches and mats
and handle our eating vessels?”
At that time the crown prince,
named Jǐtuó,
prepared offerings,
invited the Fó and the monks,
and sent a messenger to say to the Fó:
“I only wish that the Shìzūn will accept my invitation tomorrow, along with the Bǐqiū monks.”
He also had him say to the Fó:
“Regarding the beggars who have been ordained
and become Bǐqiū,
I do not invite them.
Be sure not to bring them along.”
The Fó then accepted the invitation.
The next day at the time for the meal,
the Fó and the assembly of monks,
when it was time to respond to the invitation,
told the beggar Bǐqiū:
“We have received an invitation,
but you are not included.
You may now go to Yùduōluóyuè,
take the naturally ripened non-glutinous rice,
return to his house,
and sit in order according to your will and eat the rice yourselves.”
At that time the Bǐqiū,
as commanded, immediately used their Āluóhàn psychic powers
to go to that world,
each took for themselves,
and returned with their bowls full.
Maintaining their dignified bearing
and following their own order,
they came traveling through the air
like flying king geese,
arrived at Jǐtuó’s house,
sat in order,
and each ate for themselves.
At that time the Prince,
seeing the assembly of Bǐqiū,
their dignified bearing and movements,
and their psychic powers and merit,
was joyful in his respectful heart,
praised it as unprecedented,
and said to the Fó:
“I do not know,
Shìzūn!
This assembly of holy ones and virtuous ones,
with majestic psychic power and all the marks complete,
from what direction did they come to reach here?
They are very worthy of admiration and respect.
I only wish the Rúlái
would now explain for me the beginning and end of the causes and conditions for this group.”
The Fó told Jǐtuó:
“If you wish to know,
listen well and reflect!
I shall speak for you.
These Bǐqiū
are exactly those you did not invite yesterday.
When I and the monks
were about to come to respond to the Prince’s invitation,
these Bǐqiū,
because they were not invited,
went to Yùduōyuè,
took naturally ripened non-glutinous rice,
and ate it themselves.”
At that time Jǐtuó,
hearing these words,
was filled with deep shame,
and distressed, rebuked himself:
“How was I so foolish and clouded
as to not distinguish between light and darkness?”
Moreover he said:
“The Shìzūn’s merit
is inconceivable!
These beggars,
within this kingdom,
were the most lowly.
Today they have received the pure transformation
and the greatest immense nourishment.
Since they have received the peace, happiness, and bodily merit of the present life,
they have also obtained the eternal joy of Wúwéi.
The reason the Rúlái today
appeared in the world
is solely for this class of people
and none other.
Furthermore,
Shìzūn!
I do not know what this group,
in ages past,
planted what good deeds
and cultivated what merit,
that they have now encountered the Shìzūn and specially received such exceptional nourishment?
And what fault did they commit,
that since their birth,
they have sustained themselves by begging
and been so destitute and miserable?
Shìzūn in your compassion!
Please reveal this to me.”
The Fó told him:
“If you wish to know,
you should listen well!
I shall fully explain for you the beginning and end of this matter.
Agreed, you should listen well!”
At that time the Shìzūn
then told Jǐtuó:
“In the remote past,
immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable Āsēngqí Jié ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great kingdom
named Bōluónài.
In the kingdom there was a mountain
named Lìshī
(in the Jìn language it means Xiān Shān),
which many Fó of the past
mostly dwelt within.
When there was no Fó,
there were Bìzhīfó
who relied on it for their residence.
Even if there were no Pratyekabuddhas,
there would be disciples of the immortals who have mastered the five supernatural powers,
who would also reside there;
it would never be empty or abandoned.
At that time, there were more than two thousand Pratyekabuddhas in the mountains,
who constantly dwelled within them.
In those days, in that country,
the star Huǒxīng appeared,
which was an omen of an evil disaster.
Once this star appeared,
for twelve years,
the country would suffer drought without rain from the heavens;
planting would be impossible,
and the country would surely be destroyed.
At that time, within the country,
there was an elder
named Sàntuóníng.
His family was immensely wealthy,
with limitless riches and grain.
He constantly prepared offerings
to provide for various practitioners.
At that time, a thousand noble beings
went to his house
to seek offerings,
and said this:
"We
live in those mountains.
We have encountered a drought in the land,
and it is impossible to obtain food through begging.
If the elder can provide us with food,
we shall stay here;
if you cannot give it to us,
we shall go to other regions."
The elder then
immediately asked the granary steward:
"In my granary now,
is all the grain and rice
sufficient to feed these great beings?
I wish to invite them."
The steward replied:
"I only wish you would invite them immediately;
as for the grain and food,
there is an abundance more than sufficient."
The elder then invited the thousand Pratyekabuddhas
and provided them with food and offerings.
The other thousand people
also went to his house
and also sought offerings.
The elder again asked his steward:
"The granary you manage,
how much grain and food is there?
There are another thousand people
for whom I also wish to provide offerings.
Is it sufficient to manage?"
The steward said:
"The grain and food under my management
will surely be sufficient.
If you wish to provide offerings,
you should invite them immediately."
Then the elder
immediately invited them.
He assigned five hundred servants
to provide and prepare the meals.
These servants
handled the cooking utensils
for many years.
Weariness and resentment arose in their hearts,
and they all spoke in this way:
"The reason we
suffer such hardship
is all because of these beggars."
At that time, the elder
always ordered one person to inform the monks when it was time for the meal.
This servant
raised a small dog.
Whenever he went to give the notice,
the dog would follow along;
it was like this every day.
Then one day, the servant
suddenly forgot to go and give the notice.
When the time arrived, the dog
went alone to the usual place
toward the great beings
and barked loudly.
The Pratyekabuddhas,
hearing the dog's bark,
knew they were being invited.
They went to his house
and received their food according to the Dharma.
They then told the elder:
"It will rain today;
you should plant your crops."
The elder did as they said
and immediately ordered the workers to take their tools
and diligently plow and sow:
barley, wheat,
and all kinds of edible grains;
they planted them all.
After some time,
the things they had planted
all turned into gourds.
When the elder saw this,
he wondered and asked about it.
The great beings said:
"There is no trouble in this;
just continue your diligent work
and irrigate them according to the season."
He diligently irrigated them as told.
Later, when they ripened,
the gourds were all large
and extremely abundant.
When they split them open to look,
according to whatever had been planted,
it had become processed and pure,
and the wheat filled them.
The elder rejoiced.
His whole family stored it away,
until his house was overflowing.
He also shared it with his relatives
and everyone in the whole country;
all were graced by his kindness.
At that time, the five hundred people who prepared the food thought:
"The reward of this fruit we have obtained
is surely due to the grace of these great beings.
Why did we speak evil words toward them?"
They immediately went to where they were
and sought to repent and reform.
The great beings listened to them.
After their repentance was completed,
they made a vow:
"May we, in future lives,
encounter sages
and receive liberation."
Because of this,
for five hundred lifetimes,
they were always beggars.
Because they repented and made a vow,
they have now encountered my era
and have been delivered.
Crown Prince, you should know!
Who was the wealthy elder Sàntuóníng at that time?
Was he someone else?
He was myself.
The granary official
is now Xūdá.
The person who went daily to announce the time
is King Yōutián.
The little dog at that time,
because of its barking,
has had a beautiful voice in every lifetime;
he is the elder Měiyīn.
The five hundred people who prepared the food at that time
are these five hundred Āluóhàn."
Then Qǐtuó
and the members of the assembly,
having witnessed these spiritual transformations
and being moved by the Buddha's merit,
applied themselves with diligent focus.
Some attained the first fruit or the fourth fruit,
while others specialized in the practices of the noble beings,
and others gave rise to the aspiration for the Buddha-way.
Each person was diligent,
seeking to fulfill their original intent.
They rejoiced greatly,
accepted the teaching respectfully, and put it into practice.
*Xiányú Jīng*, Volume 5
*Xiányú Jīng*, Volume 6
Translated in Gāochāng Prefecture by the monks Huìjué and others from Liángzhōu during the Yuán-Wèi dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Fó was in the Ānluó tree garden in Píshèlǐ.
At that time, the Shìzūn
addressed the worthy Ānán:
"One who has attained the four Shénzú
can remain alive for one jié.
I have cultivated the four Shénzú extremely well;
how long should the Rúlái remain alive now?"
Thus he spoke up to three times.
At that time, Ānán was deluded by Mó;
hearing the Shìzūn's teaching,
he remained silent and did not respond.
Again he said to Ānán:
"You may arise and go to a quiet place to contemplate."
The worthy Ānán
arose from his seat
and went into the forest.
After Ānán had left,
the Mó Bōxún came to where the Fó was
and said to the Fó:
"The Shìzūn has been in the world teaching and transforming for a long time,
and the work of delivering people is complete.
Those who have received liberation from birth and death
are as numerous as the sands of the Héng.
Your years are now advanced;
you may enter Nièpán."
At that time, the Shìzūn
took a small amount of earth from the ground and placed it on his fingernail,
and said to the Mó:
"Is the earth of the ground more,
or is the earth on the fingernail more?"
The Mó replied to the Fó:
"The earth of the ground is extremely much,
not the earth on the fingernail."
The Fó said again:
"The sentient beings who have been delivered
are like the earth on the fingernail;
those remaining who have not yet been delivered
are like the earth of the great ground."
Again he said to the Mó:
"After three months,
I shall enter Bānnièpán."
At that time, Bōxún,
hearing this, departed joyfully.
At that time, Ānán,
sitting in the forest,
suddenly fell asleep
and dreamed of a great tree that covered the entire sky.
Its branches and leaves were lush and dense,
its flowers and fruits were flourishing,
and all living beings
depended on it for protection.
The tree's virtues were varied and wondrous,
beyond counting.
A whirlwind suddenly arose,
buffeting the tree;
its branches and leaves were shattered like fine dust,
perishing in the land where the Lìshì dwelt.
All sentient beings
were filled with grief and mourning.
Ānán woke up startled,
terrified and unsettled.
He then thought to himself:
"The tree in my dream
was extraordinarily wondrous and immeasurable;
all under heaven relied on its kindness.
By what cause did it meet such wind and become shattered like this?
Now, the Shìzūn
protects and nurtures all like that great tree;
could it be that the Shìzūn is about to enter Bānnièpán?"
Having had this thought,
he was extremely fearful and trembling.
He came to where the Fó was,
bowed to the Fó,
and said to the Fó:
"The dream I just had was such as this;
could it be that the Shìzūn is about to enter Bānnièpán?"
The Fó said to Ānán:
"It is as you say.
In three months,
I shall enter Bānnièpán.
I just asked you:
'If one has attained the four Shénzú, they can remain alive for one jié.
I have cultivated the four Shénzú extremely well;
how long can the Rúlái remain alive today?'
Thus it was three times, yet you did not respond.
After you left,
the Mó came to urge me to take Nièpán,
and I have already promised him."
Ānán, hearing this, was grief-stricken and dazed;
overwhelmed with anguish and confusion, he could not compose himself.
All the disciples
told one another,
and each carrying grief and mourning, they came to where the Fó was.
At that time, the Shìzūn
said to Ānán and all the disciples:
"All things are impermanent;
who can remain forever?
For your sake,
what should be done has been done,
and what should be said has been said.
You should only diligently and vigorously cultivate and assemble;
why be sorrowful?
It offers no benefit and is not proper practice."
At that time, Shèlìfú, hearing that the Shìzūn would enter Bānnièpán,
was deeply moved and sighed,
and consequently said:
"The Rúlái's Nièpán—
why is it so soon?
The eye of the world will be extinguished,
and we will forever lose our reliance and protection."
Again he said to the Fó:
"I cannot now bear to see the Shìzūn enter extinction;
I now wish to enter Nièpán before you.
Only I pray, Shìzūn,
that you will grant me permission."
Thus he spoke up to three times.
The Shìzūn said:
"You should know the time;
all worthy and holy ones
always enter quiet extinction."
At that time, Shèlìfú,
having received the Fó's approval,
immediately adjusted his robes, knelt, and moved on his knees.
He circumambulated the Fó a hundred times,
came before the Fó,
and with several verses
after praising the Fó,
he took the Fó's two feet and placed them respectfully on his head.
Thus he did three times,
and with palms joined in attendance to the Fó,
he said:
"Now is the last time
I shall see the Shìzūn."
With hands clasped in solemn respect, he withdrew and departed.
Taking the Shāmí Jūntí,
he went to Luóyuèqí,
reaching his birthplace.
Upon arriving, he instructed the Shāmí Jūntí:
"Go into the city
and to the villages,
telling the king, ministers, old friends, acquaintances, and all the Tányuè:
'Come together to bid farewell.'"
At that time, Jūntí, after bowing at his master's feet,
went everywhere and announced:
"My Héshang Shèlìfú
is here now
wishing to enter Bānnièpán.
All who wish to see him should go at once."
At that time, King Āshéshì
and the nation's prominent and worthy people, along with the four groups of Tányuè,
hearing Jūntí's words,
were all filled with tragic mourning, and with one voice
they said:
"Venerable Shèlìfú!
The great general of the Fǎ,
whom all kinds of sentient beings look up to and rely upon.
He is now entering Bānnièpán—
why is it so soon?"
Each of them hurried
to where he was,
bowed,
and after inquiring after him,
they all said:
"We have heard that the Venerable one
wishes to abandon his life and reach Nièpán;
people such as we
will lose our reliance and protection."
At that time, Shèlìfú
said to the crowd:
"All things are impermanent;
those who are born must all end.
The three realms are all suffering;
who can find peace?
You have the blessing from past lives
to be born at the time of the Fó's appearance in the world.
The Jīng and Fǎ are difficult to hear,
and a human body is difficult to obtain.
Be mindful to diligently practice meritorious deeds
and seek delivery from birth and death."
In various ways such as these,
through many skillful means,
he spoke extensively to everyone,
administering medicine according to their illnesses.
At that time, the assembly,
hearing what he said—
some attained the first fruit up to the third fruit,
or some left home and became Āluóhàn,
while others made vows to seek the path of the Fó.
Having heard the Fǎ,
they bowed and departed.
At that time, Shèlìfú,
in the latter part of the night,
with his body upright and his mind focused,
fixed his mind before him and entered the first chán.
Arising from the first chán, he entered the second chán.
Arising from the second chán,
he entered the third chán.
Arising from the third chán,
he entered the fourth chán.
Arising from the fourth dhyāna,
he entered the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
Arising from the sphere of infinite space,
he entered the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Arising from the sphere of infinite consciousness,
he entered the sphere of nothingness.
Arising from the sphere of nothingness,
he entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
he entered the concentration of cessation.
Arising from the concentration of cessation,
he then entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Tiāndì Shì,
knowing that Shèlìfú had already attained extinction,
together with many heavenly hosts and hundreds of thousands of followers,
each carrying flowers, incense, and items for making offerings, came to where he was.
They filled the void,
and everyone cried out in grief,
their tears falling like heavy rain.
They scattered various flowers everywhere,
which piled up as high as the knees.
Furthermore, each said:
"The wisdom of the Venerable One
is as deep as a great ocean.
His quick eloquence responds to every occasion,
and his voice is like a gushing spring.
Perfected in precepts, concentration, and wisdom, he is the Great General of the Law.
He should have followed the Rúlái in turning the Great Dharma Wheel extensively.
That he has taken nirvāṇa—
how rapid it was!"
Inside and outside the city,
upon hearing that Shèlìfú had already attained extinction,
everyone brought clarified butter, oil, incense, flowers, and items for making offerings,
and they all hurried to gather there.
Their grief and sorrowful attachment were unbearable.
Each held incense and flowers
to use as offerings.
Then Tiāndì Shì
commanded Píshǒujiémó
to collect various treasures
and adorn a high carriage.
They placed Shèlìfú upon the high carriage.
All the devas, dragons, and ghosts,
the kings, ministers, and common people,
followed and escorted him, wailing and crying,
until they reached a flat and broad ground.
Then Tiāndì Shì
commanded various Yèchā:
"Go to the shore of the great ocean
and fetch ox-head sandalwood."
The Yèchā received the instruction
and immediately went to fetch it and returned.
They piled it into a large pyre,
placed the body upon it,
poured clarified butter and oil over it,
and set it on fire for the Yéxún.
They bowed in worship and made offerings,
and then each departed and returned.
After the fire was extinguished,
the Shāmí Jūntí
collected his master's relics
and placed them in a bowl.
He gathered the master's three robes
and carried them to where the Buddha was.
He bowed to the Buddha
and kneeling on both knees, said to the Buddha:
"My preceptor Shèlìfú
has already entered parinirvāṇa.
These are his relics, and these are his robes and bowl."
At that time, the Venerable Ānán,
hearing these words,
was filled with grief and distress,
his feelings of sorrow increasing.
He said to the Buddha:
"Now this Venerable One,
the Great General of the Law,
has already taken nirvāṇa.
Upon whom shall I rely?"
The Buddha told him:
"Although Shèlìfú
has attained extinction,
his precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation—
this Dharma-body
also does not perish.
Furthermore, Ānán!
Not only today
could Shèlìfú not bear to see me enter parinirvāṇa
and thus entered extinction first;
in past lives,
he also could not endure seeing me die
and died before me."
The Venerable Ānán
joined his palms and said to the Buddha:
"I am not certain,
World-Honored One!
In the past, concerning his dying beforehand,
what was that matter like?
I pray that you will explain it for us."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In the distant past,
incalculable, countless, and inconceivable asamkhyeya kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Zhāntuópóluópí
(which in the language of Jìn means Yuèguāng).
He ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms in Yánfútí,
sixty thousand mountains and rivers,
and eight billion villages.
The king had twenty thousand consorts and court ladies.
His first consort
was named Xūmótán
(which in the language of Jìn means Huāshī).
There were ten thousand great ministers,
the first of whom
was named Mózhāntuó
(which in the language of Jìn means Dàyuè).
The king had five hundred princes,
the eldest of whom
was named Shīluóbátuó
(which in the language of Jìn means Jièxián).
The city where the king resided
was named Bátuóqípó
(which in the language of Jìn means Xiánshòu).
The city was
four hundred yojanas in length and breadth,
and was made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On the four sides, there were a total of one hundred and twenty gates.
The streets and lanes
were orderly and well-arranged.
Furthermore, within that country,
there were four rows of trees,
also made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Some had golden branches and silver leaves,
some had silver branches and golden leaves,
some had lapis lazuli branches and crystal leaves,
and some had crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves.
There were various precious ponds,
also made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The sand at the bottom of the ponds
was also made of these four treasures.
The king's inner palace
was forty lǐ in circumference
and was made entirely of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The country was abundant and fertile,
the people were happy,
and the rare and wondrous treasures
were beyond count.
At that time, the king,
while sitting in the main hall,
suddenly had this thought:
'When a person is in the world,
enjoying honor and nobility,
respected and looked up to by all under heaven,
with their words never disobeyed,
and the wondrous five desires
coming as they wish—
this retribution
is all caused by the accumulation of virtue and the cultivation of merit.
It is like a farmer: by planting extensively in the spring, he has a bountiful harvest in autumn and summer.
When the spring season returns,
if he does not diligently plant,
what hope has he for autumn and summer?
I am now in this state because of my prior cultivation of merit,
and so I now obtain this wondrous fruit.
If I do not plant again now,
I will have no hope for the future.'
After having this thought,
he told his ministers:
'Now I wish to bring out my treasury of wondrous treasures and place them at all the city gates,
as well as in the markets,
and establish a great dāna.
Whatever sentient beings require,
I will provide all of it to them.'
He also announced this to the eighty-four thousand small kingdoms below:
'All of you shall open your treasuries and give to everyone.'
The ministers said:
'Excellent!
We respectfully obey the king's command.'
They then set up golden banners,
struck golden drums,
and spread the announcement far and wide,
proclaiming the king's compassionate decree,
so that everyone near and far, inside and outside,
would hear and know of it.
At that time, in the country,
Shāmén and Póluómén,
the poor, the lonely, and the aged,
and those who were in want,
supporting one another, both the strong and the weak,
gathered like clouds and rain.
To those who needed clothes, clothes were given;
to those who needed food, food was given.
Gold, silver, precious items,
and medicine according to their illnesses—
everything that was required
was given as they desired.
All the ministers and people within Yánfútí
received the king's kindness and grace.
Happiness was infinite,
and songs of praise
filled the streets and roads.
His good name was proclaimed afar,
spreading to the four quarters.
There was none who did not look up to him with reverence
and yearn for the King’s benevolent influence.
"At that time, on the frontier,
there was a small kingdom
whose king was named Pímó Sīnuà.
When he heard of the lofty and great reputation of Yuèguāng Wáng,
his heart harbored jealousy,
and he could not rest peacefully in his bed.
He then thought to himself:
'If Yuèguāng is not removed,
my own name will not be known.
I must devise a means to invite various Dàoshì
and seek out people
to accomplish this matter.'
Having finished this thought,
he immediately issued a command to invite the Fànzhì within his kingdom.
He prepared a feast of a hundred flavors
and served them with reverence,
never failing to satisfy their wishes.
After three months had passed,
he told the Fànzhì:
'I now have a sorrow
that entangles my heart,
causing me to toss and turn morning and night.
By what means can it be released?
You Dàoshì
are those whom I serve;
you must think of a way to assist me in removing this grievance.'
The Póluómén spoke together to the King, saying:
'What sorrow does the King have?
You must show it to us and tell us.'
The King then said:
'That Yuèguāng Wáng’s
reputation and virtue are established afar,
and the four distances follow his influence.
But I alone am low and vulgar,
lacking such a beautiful reputation.
The wish of my heart
is to desire to remove him.
What means can be used to accomplish this matter?'
When the Póluómén heard these words,
they each said:
'That Yuèguāng Wáng’s
compassion, grace, and benevolence
nourish all things,
and he compassionately rescues the poor and distressed
like a parent to the people.
With what heart could we follow such an evil plot?
We would rather kill ourselves
than do this.'
They immediately dispersed,
disregarding the offerings.
At that time, Pímó Sīnuà's distress and confusion increased even more.
He then went out and issued a widespread recruitment, proclaiming everywhere:
'Whoever can obtain the head of Yuèguāng Wáng for me
shall share in governing half the kingdom,
and I will give my daughter to him as a wife.'
At that time, on a mountain slope, there was a Póluómén
named Láodùchā,
who heard the King's proclamation and came to answer the recruitment.
The King was very joyful
and spoke to him again, saying:
'If you can truly accomplish this,
I will not go back on my solemn oath.
If you are able to go,
on what day will it be?'
The Póluómén said:
'Prepare the food and provisions I need for the journey,
and in seven days I shall set out.'
Then the Póluómén performed incantations for his own protection.
When the seven days were completed,
he came to take leave of the King.
The King provided what was needed,
and he set out on his way.
"At that time, in the kingdom of Yuèguāng Wáng, various strange omens appeared in advance:
the earth cracked in various places, lightning trailed, and stars fell;
dark mists clouded the day, and there were crashes of thunder and lightning.
Various birds in the empty sky
wailed with piercing sorrow and plucked out their own feathers.
Tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, and other animals
threw themselves down, leapt about, and cried out.
Eighty-four thousand minor kings
all dreamed that the Great King’s golden banner suddenly snapped
and his golden drum suddenly cracked.
The minister Dàyuè
dreamed that a ghost snatched the King's golden crown.
Each harbored sorrow and worry
and could not find peace.
At that time, the spirit of the city gate,
knowing that the Póluómén wanted to beg for the King's head,
was also troubled and blocked him, not allowing him to enter.
Then the Póluómén
went around the city gate several times but could not proceed forward.
A deity from the Shǔtuóhuì Tiān, knowing that Yuèguāng Wáng
would give this head
to complete the perfection of giving,
then spoke to the King in a dream, saying:
'You have vowed to practice giving
and not go against the hearts of the people,
but a beggar is at the gate
and has no way to come forward.
If you wish to be a donor,
it is not meant to be so.'
The King woke up in astonishment
and immediately commanded the minister Dàyuè:
'You go to the various gates
and command that no one be blocked.'
The minister Dàyuè went to the city gate.
Then the spirit of the city gate
manifested his form and told Dàyuè:
'There is a Póluómén who has come from another kingdom
harboring an evil heart, wishing to beg for the King’s head;
that is why I did not allow him in.'
The minister replied:
'If there is such a thing,
it is a great disaster.
However, the King has issued a command,
and in principle, it cannot be disobeyed.
What can be done?'
Then the spirit of the city gate
ceased and no longer blocked him.
The minister Dàyuè then thought to himself:
'If this Póluómén
must beg for the King's head,
I should make heads out of the seven treasures,
five hundred of each,
to trade for it.'
He immediately ordered them to be made.
Then the Póluómén went straight to the front of the palace
and called out in a loud voice:
'I am from a distant land
and have heard of the King's merit,
that he gives everything
and does not go against people's wishes.
Therefore, I have traveled from afar,
wishing to obtain something.'
The King was joyful upon hearing this,
welcomed him, paid respects, and asked:
'Were you not exhausted by the journey?
Whatever you wish—
the kingdom, the city, my wife and children,
precious jewels, carriages,
palanquins, elephants, and horses,
slaves and servants of the seven treasures—
all that you desire shall be given to you.'
The Póluómén said:
'All external objects,
though given in charity,
bring a reward of merit
that is not yet vast and great.
The giving of one's own flesh and body
brings the most wonderful merit.
I have come from afar
specifically to obtain the King's head.
If you do not fail or refuse me,
you should grant it to me.'
When the King heard these words,
his joy was boundless.
The Póluómén said:
'If you are to give me your head,
when will you give it?'
The King said, 'In seven days I shall give you my head.'
At that time, the minister Dàyuè
carried the heads made of the seven treasures
to persuade and thank him.
He beat his breast before him
and said to the Póluómén:
'This King's head
is a combination of bone, flesh, and blood,
an impure thing.
Why seek this?
I now bring these heads of the seven treasures
to trade for it.
You may take them;
by trading them, you will surely obtain lifelong wealth.'
The Póluómén said:
'I have no use for these.
I wish to have the King's head;
that alone matches my intent.'
At that time, the minister Dàyuè
used all kinds of persuasion, but the man would never turn back.
Filled with grief and indignation,
his heart split into seven pieces,
and he died before the King.
"At that time, the King
commanded his ministers
to ride elephants that could travel eight thousand lǐ
and announce to all the kingdoms:
'In seven days, Yuèguāng Wáng
shall give his head to a Póluómén.
If you wish to come,
hasten there quickly.'"
At that time, the eighty-four thousand kings,
arriving one after another,
all saw the Great King
and fell prostrate before him,
saying, "The people of Yánfútí
rely on the King’s grace and kindness,
and each has attained abundance and joy,
living in happiness without affliction.
Why would you, for the sake of one person,
forever abandon the masses
and no longer show pity or concern?
We only wish that you would show compassion!
Do not give your head as an offering."
Ten thousand ministers
all threw themselves upon the ground
and fell prostrate before the King, saying,
"Only have pity and compassion for us;
do not give your head as an offering
and abandon us forever."
Twenty thousand ladies also threw themselves upon the ground
and looked up to speak to the King:
"Do not forget and abandon us;
only grant us your protection.
If you give your head as an offering,
upon whom shall we depend?"
Five hundred princes
wept before the King:
"We are young and orphaned;
where shall we return?
We wish that you would have pity and concern for us,
and not give your head as an offering,
but raise us
until we reach maturity."
Thereupon the Great King
told the kings, ministers, people, ladies, and princes:
"I calculate that since I first received a body,
I have traveled through birth and death for a very long time.
If I was in the hells,
within a single day,
I would be born and then immediately die,
discarding my body countless times,
passing through Huīhé,
Tiěchuáng,
Fèishǐ,
Huǒchē,
Tànkēng, and other hells.
Bodies such as these
were burned, pierced, boiled, and roasted;
discarded again and again,
with never any karmic reward.
If I was among the animals,
eating one another,
or being killed by humans,
my body providing for the mouths of the masses,
destroyed and rotted away
also countless times;
discarding this body in vain,
also without karmic reward.
Or if I fell among the hungry ghosts,
with fire emerging from the body,
or as a flying wheel
coming to sever my head,
which was cut and then regrown,
in such a way countless times;
killing the body like this
was also without karmic reward.
If I was born among humans,
contending over wealth and beauty,
with eyes wide in intense anger,
killing and harming one another,
or raising armies to face each other in battle,
hacking and severing one another—
killing the body like this
was also countless times.
Because of greed, hatred, and ignorance,
I have constantly killed many bodies,
yet never for the sake of merit have I given up this life.
Now this body of mine
is filled with various impurities;
it will surely be discarded,
as it cannot last for long.
Giving up this fragile, filthy, and evil head
to trade for a great benefit—
how could I not give it?
I take this head
and give it to the Póluómén;
taking this merit,
I vow to seek the path of the Buddha.
If I achieve the path of the Buddha and my merit is perfected,
I shall use skillful means to save you all from suffering.
Now my intent to give
is about to be fulfilled;
be careful not to obstruct my resolve for the Unsurpassed Path."
All the kings, ministers, people, ladies, and princes,
having heard the King’s words,
were silent and said nothing.
"At that time, the Great King
said to the Póluómén:
'You who wish to take my head,
now is the right time.'
The Póluómén said:
'Now the King is surrounded by a great multitude of ministers and people,
while I am but one person,
my strength and power are solitary and weak;
I cannot cut off the King’s head here.
If you wish to give it to me,
you should go to the back garden.'
At that time, the Great King
told the minor kings, princes, ministers, and people:
'If you indeed love and respect me,
be careful not to harm this Póluómén.'
Having spoken these words,
he entered the back garden together with the Póluómén.
Then the Póluómén again said to the King:
'Your body is vigorous and has the strength of a wrestler;
if you encounter the pain of the cutting,
perhaps you might then regret it.
Take your hair
and tie it firmly to a tree;
only then after that
can I cut it off.'
Then the King followed his words
and sought out a strong tree
with lush branches and leaves.
Intending to tie himself firmly,
he knelt before the tree
and tied his hair to the tree,
saying to the Póluómén:
'Cut off my head
so that it falls into my hands,
and then take it away from my hands.
Now I give my head to you;
taking this merit,
I do not seek the pleasures of the Mó, Fàn, Tiāndìshì, Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng, or the Sānjiè,
but use it to seek the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path,
vowing to save all living beings
and bring them to the joy of Nièpán.'
Then the Póluómén
raised his hand, wishing to strike.
The Shùshén saw this
and was greatly distressed:
'Such a person as this—
how could one wish to kill him?'
He immediately struck the Póluómén's ear with his hand;
his neck was twisted backward,
his hands and feet were contorted,
he dropped his knife on the ground,
and he could not move.
At that time, the Great King spoke to the Shùshén:
'In the past,
beneath this tree,
I have already given nine hundred and ninety-nine heads
as offerings.
Now giving this head
will make it a full thousand.
Once I have given this head,
the Tán will be perfected.
Do not obstruct my mind for the Unsurpassed Path.'
At that time, the Shùshén, hearing these words from the King,
restored the Póluómén to his former state.
Then the Póluómén
rose from the ground,
took up the knife again,
and cut off the King’s head,
which fell into his hands.
At that time, heaven and earth
shook in six ways.
The palaces of the devas
shook and were unstable.
Each inhabitant felt terror
and wondered at the cause.
They quickly saw the Púsà
who, for the sake of all,
had given his head as an offering.
They all descended,
moved by his extraordinary act,
their tears of sorrow falling like rain,
and they praised him together, saying:
'The Great King Yuèguāng
has given his head as an offering,
and in the Tán-bōluómì,
he has now attained perfection.'
At that time, the sound
spread throughout the world.
That King Pímóxiàn heard these words;
he was filled with joyful shock and alarm,
and his heart split open and he died.
Then the Póluómén
carried the King’s head away.
The kings, ministers, people, ladies, and princes,
having seen the King’s head, threw themselves upon the ground,
crying out in sorrow together,
fainting and then reviving.
Some died from their grief, vomiting blood;
some stood in shock, losing consciousness;
some tore out their own hair;
some ripped their own clothing;
