some scratched and damaged their faces with both hands,
weeping in all directions
and rolling on the ground.
At that time, the Pó luó mén,
finding the King’s head to be foul-smelling,
immediately threw it on the ground
and trod upon it with his feet as he left.
Some other people
said to the Pó luó mén:
“Your cruelty
is as extreme as this!
Since it is of no use,
why did you seek it?”
At that time, the Pó luó mén
proceeded along the road to leave,
but when people saw him, they scolded him,
and none gave him food.
He became emaciated from hunger
and suffered to the utmost degree.
On the road there was a person
who asked for news
and learned that King Pí mó xiàn
had already passed away.
Having lost his hope,
he was filled with anguish and confusion;
his heart split into seven pieces,
and he vomited blood and died.
King Pí mó xiàn and Láo dù chà,
after their lives ended, both fell into Ā bí ní lí.
The rest of the ministers and people,
out of remembrance of the King’s kindness,
were so deeply moved that those who died
all attained rebirth in the heavens.
“In this way, Ā nán!
If you wish to know who King Yuè guāng of that time was,
he is my current self.
King Pí mó xiàn
is now Bō xún.
The Pó luó mén Láo dù chà of that time
is now Diào dá.
The Tree Spirit of that time
is now Mù lián.
The Great Minister Dà yuè of that time
is now Shè lì fú.
At that time,
they could not bear to see me die
and so died before me;
even to this day,
they cannot bear to see me enter Niè pán
and so have passed into extinction first.”
After the Buddha had said this,
the Worthy Ā nán
and all the disciples,
having heard what the Buddha said,
felt a mixture of sorrow and joy.
With different mouths but one voice,
they all sighed in admiration
at the extraordinary conduct of the Rú lái’s merit.
They all practiced with focus;
some attained the fruits of the four paths,
and some developed the aspiration for the unsurpassed, correct, and true path.
Everyone was greatly rejoiced,
and they respectfully upheld and practiced it.
*Xián yú jīng*, Volume Six.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the country of Shèwèiguó, in the Jǐshù Gěigūdú Yuán.
At that time, the Shìzūn
was surrounded by a great assembly,
and was preaching the Dharma for them.
The people in the city
who delighted in hearing the Dharma
went to where the Buddha was,
one after another in succession.
At that time, in the city, there was a blind Póluómén
sitting by the side of the road.
Hearing the many people walking quickly,
he then asked the passersby:
"This great crowd of people,
where do they wish to go?"
A passerby answered:
"Do you not know?
A Rúlái has appeared in the world;
this is difficult to encounter.
He is now in this country,
expounding on the Way and its transformation.
We wish to go and listen to his preaching of the Dharma."
This Póluómén
possessed an art:
among sentient beings,
there are eight kinds of voices,
all of which he could distinguish and recognize,
knowing their signs and fortunes.
What are the eight kinds?
The first is called the crow voice,
the second is called the three-foot crow voice,
the third is called the broken voice,
the fourth is called the goose voice,
the fifth is called the drum voice,
the sixth is called the thunder voice,
the seventh is called the golden bell voice,
and the eighth is called the Fàn voice.
As for the crow voice:
the nature of such a person
is to not recognize kindness or care,
and their intentions are not honest or pure.
As for the three-foot crow voice:
their nature is fierce and violent,
they delight in causing harm,
and they lack compassion and compliance.
As for the broken voice:
a man makes a woman's voice,
or a woman makes a man's voice;
such a person has meager virtue, is poor, and is lowly.
As for the goose voice:
their nature and intent are swift and clear,
they have many friends and relatives,
and they treat those from all four directions well.
As for the drum voice:
their words and speech are eloquent and quick,
they explain principles and truths,
and they are certain to become a Guóshī.
As for the thunder voice:
their wisdom is deep and far-reaching,
they analyze the Fǎxìng,
and they are fit to transform the world.
As for the golden bell voice:
they are immensely wealthy with abundant riches;
such a person will surely accumulate a hundred billion taels of gold.
As for the Fàn voice:
their blessings and virtues are exceedingly high;
if they remain in the household life,
they will become a Zhuànlún Shèngwáng;
if they leave the household life to study the Way,
they will certainly achieve Buddhahood.
At that time, the Póluómén
said to the passersby:
"I can distinguish the voices of people's speech.
If he is truly a Buddha,
he must have the Fàn voice.
You may take me to where he is;
I should try to listen to it
to examine whether he is a Buddha or not."
Then the passersby
consequently led him there,
gradually approaching the Buddha's place.
Hearing the Buddha preaching the Dharma,
the Fàn voice was fully present,
deep, far-reaching, and smooth.
He rejoiced with great exuberance,
both his eyes were opened,
and he then saw the Buddha—
the color of purple-burnished gold,
with the thirty-two marks,
bright and clear like the sun.
He immediately prostrated to the Buddha,
with immeasurable joy and celebration.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him;
he listened and received it with a sincere mind.
He immediately broke through twenty billion evils,
attained the fruit of Xūtuóhuán,
and having already attained the eye of wisdom,
he then requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome!"
and he then became a Shāmén.
The Buddha again used skillful means
to extensively preach the Dharma for him,
and he then subsequently attained the fruit of Āluóhàn.
All the members of the assembly
were all amazed.
The Worthy Ānán
rose from his seat,
knelt with palms together,
and said to the Buddha:
"The Shìzūn's appearance in the world
truly brings much benefit,
rescuing those who are blind and in darkness;
such kindness is difficult to fully describe.
This Póluómén,
in a single moment,
had his physical eyes opened
and his wisdom eye purified.
For the Buddha to this person,
how could such kindness be so profound?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"My giving him eyes
is not only on this day;
in past lives,
I also gave him eyes."
Ānán again said:
"I do not know,
Shìzūn!
Concerning the giving of eyes in the past,
how did that matter occur?
I only wish you would show compassion
and fully explain it for us."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In the distant past,
for immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable Āsēngqí kalpas,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great city
named Fùjiāluóbá.
At that time there was a king
named Xūtíluó
(which means Kuàimù).
The reason he was named Kuàimù
was that his eyes were bright and clear,
pure and wonderful beyond compare.
He could see through walls
and see for forty lǐ.
For this reason, he was given the title Kuàimù.
He governed eighty-four thousand kingdoms in Yánfútí,
sixty thousand mountains and rivers,
and eight billion villages.
The king had twenty thousand consorts and ladies-in-waiting,
ten thousand great ministers,
and five hundred princes.
His first prince
was named Shīluóbátuótí
(which means Jièxián).
The king possessed compassion
and felt pity for all;
he nurtured the people and all things
just like a kind father.
He guided them with goodness,
and the people followed his ways.
The winds were timely and the rains were favorable,
the four seasons were harmonious and suitable,
the country was prosperous and joyful,
and all living beings received his care.
At that time, the king
withdrew and reflected to himself:
'Because of my past merit,
I am now the lord of men.
With wealth, treasures, and the five desires,
I am as rich as the four seas.
My words transform those below me
like the wind bending the grass.
If I only use them in this life
without continuing them further,
I fear that in my future lives,
poverty and suffering will be my lot.
It is like a farmer
who plants many seeds on a spring day;
when he harvests in autumn and summer,
what he obtains will surely be vast.
When encountering the spring season again,
if he should be lazy,
what hope would he have for grain in the coming autumn?
Therefore, I should now, in the fields of merit,
sow widely and in a timely manner,
and I should not be negligent.'
He immediately told his ministers:
'Take out the gold, silver, precious jewels, clothing, food, and drink from my storehouses, and all necessary items;
place them at all the city gates
and pile them in the marketplaces.
Proclaim the decree everywhere:
"All people,
whoever lacks anything,
should all come and take it."'
And he also informed the eighty-four thousand kingdoms below,
ordering them as well to open their storehouses and give to all.
Then all the ministers,
having received the king's command,
Immediately golden banners were erected,
and large golden drums were struck,
the King's benevolent teachings were disseminated,
spreading throughout Yánfútí.
The people of Yánfútí,
whether Shāmén or Póluómén,
the solitary, the poor, and those in hardship and distress,
the elderly or the ill,
whatever they desired to obtain,
it was given to them according to their wishes.
All people's hearts
relied on the King's benevolent favor;
they were peaceful and happy, amusing themselves,
no longer having worries or anxieties.
They sang songs of praise and admiration,
all commending the King's virtue.
"At that time on the borders,
there was a small kingdom.
Its king was named Bōluótuóbámí.
Relying on his distance, he was arrogant and haughty,
not submitting to the King’s civilizing influence.
Furthermore, in his governance,
five matters were without moderation:
his nature was hasty,
he was lacking in reflection,
he was addicted to and dissolute in sensual desires,
he did not manage state affairs,
and although the state had loyal and worthy men,
he did not go to consult them.
In the border lands,
labor and service were doubled in their burden.
When merchants arrived in the kingdom,
taxes and seizures exceeded the norm.
That king had a minister
named Láotuódá,
who was intelligent and possessed strategic wisdom,
clearly understanding principles.
Observing the King’s transgressions of moderation,
he stepped forward to remonstrate with the King, saying:
'Your Majesty, there are five matters
that make it impossible to stabilize the state;
they will surely bring about disaster and misfortune,
and I fear it will not be long.
If you are not averse to hearing it,
please listen to your servant speak of them.'
The King said:
'Speak then.'
He immediately knelt for a long time and addressed the King:
'Your nature is hasty,
and you are lacking in reflection;
when major matters are handled improperly,
regret will surely follow.
Your Majesty is addicted to and dissolute in sensual desires
and does not manage state affairs, so that outside there are grievances and stagnations,
with no place to voice one's reasoning or feelings.
The state has loyal and worthy men,
but you do not go to consult them;
thus you do not guard against or consider matters before they occur.
For the people of the border lands,
labor and taxation are burdensome and severe;
they then think of rebelling and submitting to other kingdoms.
Taxes and seizures from merchants
violate the normal standards;
they will dread coming and going,
and precious goods will become extremely expensive.
These five matters are omens of a kingdom’s downfall.
I wish Your Majesty would change your conduct
and start anew with the people.
King Xūtídéluó
has widespread and universal kindness and benevolence;
the people of Yánfútí
all receive his wise favor.
Our kingdom alone
is not respectful or submissive,
and the people of these remote regions
do not receive his enrichment.
I wish Your Majesty would lower your pride
and return to serving him;
then your descendants may enjoy their emoluments for a long time.'
Bōluótuóbámí,
hearing these words from the minister,
became angry in his heart and showed it on his face,
not following his advice.
The minister Láotuódá
grew increasingly indignant and agitated.
He thought to himself:
'I see the King's governance
and reform are incomplete.
I presented my loyalty and sincerity,
hoping to support and assist him,
but instead his anger flared up,
and he did not follow my words.
Since my words are not used,
perhaps I will be killed;
I should just remove him
to eliminate the affliction for the people.'
Before the plot could be completed,
the matter was already revealed.
The King gathered his troops
intending to execute him.
At that time, Láotuódá
knew the King wanted to arrest him,
so he immediately mounted a swift horse
and fled away.
The troops pursued him.
That Láotuódá
was naturally skilled in archery,
and he also knew that there are eighteen places on the human body where being shot leads to certain death.
Although the troops caught up,
they did not dare to get close.
He managed to reach the kingdom of Fùjiāluóbá.
He saw King Kuàimù.
After bowing and paying his respects,
he spoke with the King.
Every matter he spoke of was reasonable,
and the King found him excellent,
appointing him as a high minister.
Gradually gaining closeness,
he fully related past events
and reported them.
After the King heard this,
he asked his ministers, saying:
'Does that land
not belong to me?'
The ministers replied:
'It all belongs to the Great King,
but relying on its great distance,
they have not come to submit.'
Láotuódá said:
'That Bōluótuóbámí
is stubborn, ignorant, cruel, and dim-witted.
He is indulgent, dissolute, and confused.
He does not know rites or standards,
relies on distance to persist in error,
and does not follow the King's commands.
His people loathe him
and look upon him as an enemy.
Give me troops and horses,
and I will go personally to subdue him.'
The King heard his words
and immediately approved.
He issued an order to various states
to select troops,
to assemble on a fixed day,
and go to the kingdom of King Bōluótuóbámí.
"At that time, a king of a neighboring country to Bōluótuóbámí
sent someone to tell him:
'Within Yánfútí,
troops have been ordered to mobilize from all over,
and they will assemble at your kingdom.
How can you sit there so peacefully and at ease?'
When Bōluótuóbámí heard this news,
he was distressed and confused,
not knowing where to go.
He put on dirty black clothes
and sat in a dark place.
There was a prime minister who was a Póluómén
who came to his place
and asked the reason for his state:
'What worry does the King have?
Please tell me.'
King Bōluótuóbámí said:
'Have you not heard?
Previously, Láotuódá
fled to King Kuàimù,
and because of their instigation,
King Kuàimù has mobilized troops from eighty-four thousand countries
to come and attack me.
If they come,
they will destroy my kingdom.'
The prime minister said:
'Let the ministers try to discuss it together.'
They immediately assembled for discussion,
each having different plans.
Together they said to the prime minister:
'We hear that King Kuàimù
has vowed to practice charity;
only his parents
he does not give away,
but as for everything else,
he does not go against the wishes of those who come.
Now in this kingdom,
there is a blind Póluómén.
We should encourage him to go and beg for the King's eyes.
If he can obtain them,
the army will surely retreat.'
The King heard these words
and immediately approved.
He soon sent the prime minister
to go and explain this to him.
The prime minister immediately
sent someone to call him,
and when he arrived, he told him:
'Now there is a national matter
for which we wish to trouble you.
Please pay attention
and assist us in accomplishing it.'
The Póluómén said:
'I am now blind and in darkness,
"After all, what can he do to assist in this matter?"
The minister said again:
"King Xūtíluó
desires to gather his troops to invade our country.
If he should come,
we who are strong,
though we might be able to escape and hide,
still fear being slaughtered;
how much more so for you who have no eyes—
would you be able to escape?
That king has made a vow:
'In all charity,
I follow what people need
and do not go against their wishes.'
Go and beg for his eyes;
you will surely obtain them.
If you obtain his eyes,
the military campaign can be stopped.
If this matter is indeed accomplished,
I shall reward you handsomely."
The Póluómén said:
"Now I have no sight;
how can this matter be done?"
The king repeatedly encouraged him:
"I shall send someone to guide and protect you on your way."
He then provided the provisions and necessities for the journey
and led him on the path to depart.
At that time, in the kingdom of King Kuàimù,
various disasters and strange occurrences all began to appear.
There were sounds of collapsing in the sky,
flashing lightning and falling stars,
dark mists and thunderclaps,
and the earth cracked in many places.
The various types of flying birds
wailed sorrowfully and piercingly,
contorting their bodies
and plucking out their own feathers and wings.
Tigers, wolves, lions, and other four-legged beasts
roared and howled among the people,
rolling and writhing on the ground.
The king, ministers, and subjects
wondered at the reason for this.
At that time, the Póluómén
gradually reached the great city
and went straight to the front of the palace hall,
crying out in a loud voice:
"I am from another country;
having heard of the king's reputation and virtue,
that he gives everything in charity
and does not go against people's wishes,
I have therefore traveled a long way,
wishing to beg."
The king, hearing these words,
immediately descended to inquire:
"Having traveled such a long way on foot,
are you not exhausted?
Whatever you wish to obtain,
all that you need—
territory or precious treasures,
carriages, horses, or sedan chairs,
clothing, bedding, food, or drink,
medicine according to your illness—
all that you need
shall be given to you."
The Póluómén said:
"Charity of external things
brings no wondrous merit;
charity of the inner body
brings the greatest reward.
I lost my eyes long ago
and have dwelt in darkness through the long night;
having heard of the Great King,
I have thus set my mind to come,
wishing to beg for the king's eyes."
The king, hearing this, was joyful
and said to the Póluómén:
"If you wish to have eyes,
I shall give them to you."
The Póluómén said:
"If you wish to give them to me,
when can you give them?"
The king said to him:
"Seven days from now,
I shall give them to you."
The king then issued a proclamation to the eighty-four thousand small kingdoms:
"King Xūtíluó,
seven days from now,
shall gouge out his eyes to give in charity to a Póluómén.
All those who wish to come
should all gather at that time."
When the various kings and people heard this command,
they all came running to the Great King's place.
The eighty-four thousand kings, ministers, and subjects
threw themselves onto the ground,
prostrating before the king,
with tears streaming down,
and said to the king:
"We and our kind,
the people of Yánfútí,
rely on the Great King
for protection and shelter.
If you gouge out your eyes to give to a Póluómén,
what will all the people
have to rely on?
We only wish you would change your mind
and not abandon everyone for the sake of one person."
Ten thousand ministers also threw themselves on the ground
and looking up, said to the king:
"Why do you not have pity and compassion for us?
For the sake of one person's wish,
you abandon us.
We only wish you would change your mind
and not give him your eyes."
Twenty thousand consorts
struck their heads against the ground
and prostrating before the king,
also pleaded:
"We only wish, Great King,
that you would change your mind and alter your will;
do not give your eyes in charity,
and comfort us."
Five hundred princes
wept before the king:
"We only wish, Heavenly Father,
that you would show compassion and not give your eyes in charity,
but instead nurture us."
At that time, Crown Prince Jièxián
again said to the king:
"I wish for you to gouge out my eyes
to replace those of my Father King.
Why is this?
Although I might die,
there would be no loss or benefit to the country;
but if the Great King has no eyes,
all within the seas will have no one to rely on."
At that time, King Kuàimù
said to the various kings, ministers, consorts, and princes:
"Since I first received a body,
through the long duration of births and deaths,
if my bones were piled up,
they would be higher than Mount Xūmí;
the blood from my being cut and stabbed
would be double the volume of the four seas;
and the mother's milk I have drunk
exceeds the four great rivers;
the tears of sorrow from separations
are more than the four seas.
In the hells,
my body was broken and destroyed,
burned, boiled, hacked, and stabbed,
and I have discarded countless eyes.
Among the Èguǐ,
I received various forms,
with fire emerging from my body,
which was then scorched by it;
being destroyed in this way,
my eyes were also countless.
Among the Chùshēng,
eating one another,
with various deaths and injuries
that are also beyond calculation.
Receiving a body in the human realm,
many lives were cut short;
or fighting over lust and desire,
plotting against each other
and killing one another,
death occurred in many ways.
Being scattered and destroyed in this manner,
I lost infinite numbers of eyes;
and even if I were born in the Tiān,
my life would not be long.
Considering from the beginning,
I have also received many forms;
in this Sānjiè,
cycling through the Wǔdào,
because of Tān, Huì, and Chī,
my body has been broken into pieces as numerous as dust,
yet I have never given them in charity to seek the Fódào.
These foul eyes,
these fragile things,
after not too long a time,
will naturally rot and decay;
now that I can use them for charity,
I should not fail to give them.
Now I take these eyes
and use them in charity to seek the Buddha's unsurpassed eye of all-knowledge.
If my vow is fulfilled,
I shall give all of you
the pure eye of wisdom.
Do not obstruct my mind set on the unsurpassed way."
Those present in the assembly
were silent and without words.
The King then spoke to his attendants:
"You may gouge out my eyes."
The various ministers and attendants
all said:
"We would rather have our own bodies broken
into pieces as small as mustard seeds
than raise a hand toward the Great King's eyes."
The King said to the ministers:
"Search for one whose eyes are pure black and who looks downward with focus;
then summon him here."
The ministers sought and found such a person,
and brought him before the King.
The King immediately handed him a knife
and commanded him to gouge them out.
He gouged out one eye
and placed it in the King's palm.
The King then made a vow:
"I take this eye
to give in charity,
and vow to seek the path of the Buddha.
If it is certain that I shall attain the path of the Buddha,
may this Pó-luó-mén,
upon receiving this eye of mine,
immediately be able to use it to see."
Having made this vow,
the King then took the eye,
placed it within the Pó-luó-mén’s eye socket,
and immediately he was able to use it to see.
Being able to see the King's body and the rest of the assembly,
he was overjoyed and leaped for joy,
unable to contain himself.
He then addressed the King, saying:
"Having received one of the King's eyes,
it is sufficient for me to see.
I pray that you keep the other eye
for the King's own use to see."
The King replied again, saying:
"My word is already determined;
I promised to give both eyes,
and I must not go back on my word."
He then gouged out the other eye,
placed it again in his palm,
and repeated the vow:
"I hold this eye to give
to seek the path of the Buddha.
If I am truly able to become a Buddha,
with utmost sincerity and no falsehood,
let this Pó-luó-mén,
upon receiving my eye,
then be able to use it to see."
He placed the other eye in,
and immediately he was able to use it to see.
At that time,
the heaven and earth shook,
and the palaces of the various heavens
all trembled as well.
Then the various heavenly beings
were astonished and filled with fear.
They then saw the Pú-sà gouging out his eyes in charity,
and they all flew down,
filling the void of space,
scattering various flowers and incense as an offering,
and praising him, saying:
"Excellent!
What the Great King has done
is most marvelous and extraordinary!"
Tiān-dì came forward and asked:
"It is truly extraordinary!
Being able to do such a thing,
what reward do you seek?"
The King replied, saying:
"I do not seek the pleasures of Mó, Fàn, the Sì Wáng, Dì-shì, a Zhuǎn-lún Shèng-wáng, or the Sān Jiè.
With this merit,
I vow to seek the path of the Buddha,
to deliver and liberate all sentient beings
to the bliss of Niè-pán."
Tiān-dì asked again:
"You have now gouged out your eyes,
and the pain is like this;
do you perhaps have any regret, retreat, or anger?"
The King said he did not regret it,
nor did he feel anger or resentment.
Tiān-dì spoke again:
"I see you now,
blood flowing and scattering,
your body trembling and shaking;
to say you have no regret or resentment
is hard to believe."
The King then made a vow himself:
"In gouging out my eyes to give,
I have no thought of regret or resentment,
and I use this to seek the path of the Buddha,
which I shall surely attain.
If this is truly not false,
let my two eyes be restored as they were before."
After the King finished his vow,
both eyes were restored and whole,
seeing clearly and purely,
twice as well as before.
The various heavenly beings and people,
and the entire great assembly,
cheered and leaped with joy,
unable to contain himself.
The King spoke to the Pó-luó-mén:
"I have now given you eyes
to enable you to see.
Later, when I attain Buddhahood,
I shall also enable you to see with the Eye of Wisdom."
He led the Pó-luó-mén
into the treasury,
allowed him to take a full load as he pleased,
and sent him away.
Returning to his own country,
Bō-luó-tuó-bá-mí
came out in person to welcome him.
Upon seeing him, he first asked:
"Did you get the eyes or not?"
He answered:
"I have the eyes,
and I can now use them to see."
He asked again:
"That King now,
is he alive or dead?"
He answered:
"The various heavenly beings came down,
and he immediately made a vow;
his eyes were restored,
and his eyes are better than before."
Bō-luó-tuó-bá-mí,
upon hearing these words,
was filled with distress and pent-up fury;
his heart burst and he died."
The Buddha told Ā-nán:
"If you wish to know who King Xū-tí-luó was at that time,
it was I.
Bō-luó-tuó-bá-mí
is now Diào-dá.
The Pó-luó-mén who begged for my eyes at that time
is, within this assembly,
the blind Pó-luó-mén who has attained the Way.
In a previous life,
I gave him my eyes,
and even until today,
because he has seen me,
he has obtained both the physical eye
and the Eye of Wisdom.
For your sake,
I have practiced asceticism life after life,
accumulating merit and virtue,
until today I have attained Buddhahood.
You all should diligently seek the essentials of liberation."
When the Buddha spoke these words,
those in the assembly
were moved by the Buddha's kindness
and exerted themselves inwardly.
Some attained the stages of Xū-tuó-huán,
Sī-tuó-hán,
Ā-nà-hán,
or Ā-luó-hàn.
Some gave rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way.
The Worthy Ā-nán,
and all those in the assembly,
having heard what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was staying in Shèwèi Guó at the Qí Shù Jǐ Gū Dú Yuán.
At that time, in the kingdom of Píshèlí,
there were five hundred blind people
who lived by begging.
They heard people say:
“The Rúlái has appeared in the world;
he is most rare and extraordinary.
Any sentient beings who see him,
though they have infirmities and a hundred diseases,
will all receive healing.
The blind will see and the deaf will hear;
the mute will speak and the hunchbacked will straighten;
crippled hands and feet will be restored;
the insane will regain their minds;
the poor will be given clothing and food;
and all worries, sorrows, sufferings, and hardships
will be fully liberated and removed.”
When the blind people heard these words,
they discussed among themselves, saying:
“Our sins have accumulated
and our suffering is particularly intense.
If we should encounter the Fó,
we will surely be saved.”
They then asked someone:
“Where is the Shìzūn now?
In which kingdom is he?”
The person replied to them:
“He is in Shèwèi Guó.”
Having heard this,
they stood together by the roadside
and spoke humbly, pleading for mercy:
“Who has compassion
and pities us?
We wish for someone to lead us
to Shèwèi Guó,
to where the Fó is!”
They called out and requested help for a long time,
but no one responded.
Then the five hundred people
discussed it again, saying:
“If we request help with empty hands,
no one will respond.
Now let us go begging together,
so that each person obtains one gold coin
to use for hiring someone;
that should be enough to reach there.”
Each of them went begging,
and after some time,
each person had obtained one coin.
Altogether there were five hundred.
Once the money was collected,
they called out to those around them:
“Who will take us
to Shèwèi?
We have five hundred gold coins
to pay for the labor and hardship.”
At that time, there was a man
who came and agreed to do it.
After the agreement was made,
they gave him the money.
He instructed the blind people
to hold on to one another in succession.
He himself led the way in front,
but he took them to Mójié Guó,
abandoned the blind people,
and left them in a marsh.
At that time, the blind people
did not know where they were
or which kingdom it was.
Holding each other's hands,
they wandered through another's fields,
damaging the sprouts and grain.
At that time, there was an elder
who happened to come to inspect the fields.
He saw the five hundred people
treading upon the crops,
causing much damage.
Filled with intense anger,
he ordered them to be severely beaten.
The beggars pleaded for mercy
and fully explained the matter mentioned above.
The elder pitied them
and ordered a servant to lead them to Shèwèi.
Just as they reached that kingdom,
they heard that the Shìzūn
had already set out again toward
Mójiétí Guó.
At this time, the servant
again led them back toward Mójié Guó.
At that time, all the blind people
admired and longed for the Fó,
focusing their minds on wanting to see him.
Though their physical eyes were closed,
their mind's eye had already seen him.
Joy arose from within them,
and they did not feel fatigued.
Having arrived at Mójié,
they again heard that the Shìzūn
had already returned to Shèwèi.
In this way, they pursued him
for a total of seven round trips.
At that time, the Rúlái observed that the blind people’s
roots of goodness had matured
and their respectful faith was pure and firm.
In Shèwèi Guó,
he then stayed and waited for them.
The servant led the blind people,
and they gradually arrived at where the Fó was.
The Fó's light touched their bodies,
and they were immeasurably surprised and joyful.
Immediately, both eyes
were opened and became clear.
They then saw the Rúlái,
surrounded by the fourfold assembly,
his body's color dazzling and brilliant,
like a mountain of purple gold.
Feeling deeply grateful for his extraordinary grace,
their joy was overwhelming.
They went forward to where the Fó was,
prostrated themselves with five limbs to the ground,
and paid homage to the Fó.
After completing their homage,
with different mouths but one voice,
they together said to the Fó:
“We only wish that you would show compassion
and allow us to join the ranks of the Path.”
Then the Fó declared to them:
“Welcome, Bǐqiū!”
Their hair and beards fell off naturally,
and Dharma robes were upon their bodies.
He preached the Dharma to them again,
and they attained the state of Āluóhàn.
At that time, Ānán,
seeing that all the blind people’s
physical eyes were bright and clear,
and that they had also ended all outflows
to become Āluóhàn,
knelt down with palms joined
and went forward to say to the Fó:
“The Shìzūn's appearance in the world
is truly extraordinary.
The good deeds he performs
are inconceivable.
Moreover, these blind people
have especially received extraordinary grace;
their physical eyes are now clear,
and they have also obtained the eye of wisdom.
The Shìzūn's appearance in the world
is precisely for people like these.”
The Fó said to Ānán:
“Not only today
have I removed their darkness;
in the distant past,
an immeasurable number of kalpas ago,
I also removed great darkness for them.”
Ānán said to the Fó:
“I do not know,
Shìzūn!
In a past life,
how did you remove their darkness?
What was the matter like?”
The Fó said to Ānán:
“In the distant past,
immeasurable and innumerable Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí,
five hundred merchants
were traveling together through a wilderness.
They passed through a treacherous path
in a great mountain valley,
which was extremely dark.
At that time, all the merchants
were lost, distressed, and worried,
fearing they would lose their property.
As there were many bandits there,
they were also terrified.
With one mind, they all
turned toward the heaven and earth, sun and moon, mountains and seas, and all the gods,
weeping and pleading for mercy.
At that time, the Sàbó leader,
pitying the merchants' suffering of being lost and distressed,
then said:
‘Do not be afraid!
Put your minds at ease.
I shall provide great illumination for you.’
At that time, the Sàbó
then used white cotton cloth
to wrap his own two arms,
poured clarified butter over them,
and set them on fire to serve as torches.
Leading the merchants,
after seven days,
they finally passed through the darkness.
At that time, all the merchants were grateful for his kindness.
Their compassion and respect were immeasurable.
Each attained safety
and joy beyond measure.”
The Fó said to Ānán:
“The Sàbó of that time,
could he be anyone else?”
It was my own body.
From the distant past,
kingdoms, cities, wives, and children,
as well as flesh and blood,
I have constantly given as charity to sentient beings.
Because of this,
I have now attained this supreme honor.
Those five hundred merchants of that time,
who else could they be?
They are these five hundred Bǐqiū.
In past lives,
through the power of birth and death,
I bestowed light upon them;
now that I have attained the state of a Fó,
I also bestow the untainted eye of wisdom."
At that time, the great assembly,
hearing what the Fó had spoken,
some attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
some planted the roots of goodness of a Pìzhīfó;
and many were those who resolved to seek the unsurpassed path to deliverance.
Huìmìng Ānán
and the entire assembly,
hearing what the Fó had spoken,
rejoiced and practiced it faithfully.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi, in the Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Garden.
At that time, in the country of Fàngbō,
there was an elder
named Tánmóxiàn
(this means Dharma Army),
who, in that country,
was the wealthiest of all.
At that time, the elder's wife
gave birth to a son.
It happened when the army had gone out to conquer other countries,
so he named the son
Xiànnà
(this means Army);
later she gave birth to another son,
which happened when the King had led the army out on a campaign and gained victory,
so he again named the son Bǐqítuóxiànnà
(this means Victorious Army).
The two sons grew up,
and each took a wife.
At that time, the elder
fell seriously ill,
and frequently summoned various physicians
to attend to and care for his illness.
While looking after the physicians,
he provided them with every sweet food and offering.
The physicians were greedy for the benefits and offerings,
and wishing to prolong the remaining illness,
they harbored deceit and fraud,
and gave him different medicines
to ensure the illness would not be cured.
At that time there was a servant girl
who served the elder
with food, drink, and medicinal decoctions,
always knowing the proper timing.
She said to the elder:
"From now on,
these various physicians
are not worth calling anymore.
They are deceiving you with ill intent,
so the illness will never be cured.
Now I shall personally,
according to the previous methods
and as the illness requires,
provide what is needed; do not call the physicians again."
The servant girl then looked after him,
and the elder was cured.
Thereupon, the servant girl
said to the elder:
"Master!
I have looked after you, Master,
attending to and serving you
until the illness was removed and cured;
I only ask that you have compassion and grant me one wish."
The elder replied:
"What do you seek?"
The servant girl then said:
"I wish for you, Master, to have a union with me;
if you do not refuse, my desire will be fulfilled."
The elder did not refuse
and immediately fulfilled her wish.
After they had finished the union,
she realized she was pregnant.
When the servant girl was pregnant
and ten months were complete,
she gave birth to a son.
Since her wish was fulfilled,
they named the son
Fùnàqí
(this means Fulfilled Wish).
He was upright and possessed merit,
was well-suited for acquiring wealth,
was skilled at trade and commerce,
and in various ways of making a living,
he obtained double profits.
Wherever he went,
there was nothing that was not auspicious.
Although he received his physical form from the elder,
his talents, skills, wisdom, and capacity
surpassed those of ordinary people.
However, because he was born of a lowly servant girl,
he did not rank among the legitimate sons,
and his name was listed among the slaves.
At that time, the elder
again suffered from a chronic illness,
becoming bedridden and seriously ill.
Soon to die,
he gave earnest last instructions
to his two sons:
"If I should pass away,
be careful not to live separately."
The elder was stricken with illness,
and although he took medicines,
they could not save him,
and he suddenly reached the end of his life.
At that time, the two sons,
following their father's instructions,
lived together in one place
for many years.
It happened that there was an opportunity
as they wished to go to another country to engage in trade and business.
They each took their wives and children at home
and entrusted them to Fùnàqí:
"Look after these for me, both great and small,
and the other affairs of the house."
Having burdened him with everything,
they then departed.
Then Fùnàqí
immediately accepted their instructions
and managed the household affairs.
At that time, the sons of the two elder brothers
frequently went to him
to ask for food, drink, and other necessities.
At those times, Fùnàqí
satisfied their wishes,
and according to what they sought,
he bought and provided it for them.
It happened one day that he had no money on hand.
Shèngjūn's son said to Fùnàqí:
"I am now hungry and thirsty,
give me food and drink."
With no money in hand,
seeking food was impossible.
The boy grew angry
and went to tell his mother:
"Now Fùnàqí
is not impartial in his heart;
when he sees my older uncle's sons,
he gives them everything they want,
but when I ask for food,
he alone does not give it to me."
When the mother heard her son's words, resentment arose in her heart,
thinking that this son of a servant girl
dared to harbor partiality.
When Shèngjūn returned home,
his wife and son's anger had not subsided,
and detailing the aforementioned matters,
they spoke to Shèngjūn.
Hearing this, Shèngjūn felt doubly enraged:
"This slave son of a servant girl
dares to disobey my instructions
and treats my son with contempt!
I shall kill him!"
Having made up his mind,
he asked his elder brother to live separately.
The elder brother respected his father's decree
and at first would not agree.
Shèngjūn was frustrated
and requested it repeatedly without stopping.
The elder brother saw his intent was strong
and observing his scheme,
he knew his younger brother harbored anger.
His mind having no other choice,
he then agreed to his words:
"I grant that we each live separately.
I, the younger brother, will take the family wealth,
and everything we own,
the gardens and house for our livelihood,
to serve as one portion,
and take Fùnàqí
to serve as another portion;
of these two portions,
I leave it to you, elder brother, to choose."
He thought his elder brother would take the wealth,
planning for himself to take Fùnàqí
so that he could kill him.
The elder brother knew Shèngjūn's heart intended to harm Fùnàqí,
and out of a compassionate heart of pity,
he chose Fùnàqí.
Taking only his wife and children,
he came out empty-handed
and stayed at another house.
Then Fùnàqí
asked his sister-in-law:
"Give me a little money;
I wish to use it to buy firewood."
The sister-in-law replied:
"I only have five coins."
She immediately untied them and gave them to him to use.
Then Fùnàqí,
taking these five coins,
went to the market to buy firewood.
He saw a bundle of firewood being sold for five coins.
Then Fùnàqí
immediately bought the firewood,
paying the five coins for it.
Soon he saw a piece of Ox-head Candana sandalwood within the bundle of firewood.
In his heart he was very joyful.
He carried the firewood back home,
took this fragrant wood,
and divided it into ten pieces.
It happened that the King's wife was suffering from extreme fever.
She required Ox-head Candana sandalwood
to be ground and applied to her body to remove her illness.
Throughout the whole country they searched for it but could not find any.
A command was then issued within the country:
"Whoever has one tael of the fragrant wood
shall be given a thousand taels of gold."
Then Fùnàqí
went to respond to the King's recruitment,
Carrying a small piece,
he offered it to the King’s household;
as the King had originally ordered,
he paid a thousand taels of gold.
In this manner, repeatedly,
all ten pieces of fragrant wood
were completely sold,
and ten thousand pieces of gold were obtained.
Because of this, his standard of living,
gardens, fields, and houses,
elephants, horses, and carriages,
servants and livestock,
and thus his family estate,
became rich and abundant,
far exceeding the past,
several times greater than before.
At that time, there were another five hundred merchants
who made a pact with one another,
wishing to enter the great sea;
they called for Fùnàqí
to be their companion.
Fùnà said to his elder brother:
“I seek to go and gather treasures.”
The elder brother then granted it
and provided what he needed.
When he arrived at the great sea with the companions,
they took treasures as they wished
and returned heavily laden.
Coming to a treacherous place midway,
the people all saw three suns appearing in Yánfútí.
In astonishment, they asked the guide:
“Now that three suns have appeared,
what kind of omen is this?”
The guide answered:
“You all should know!
One is the true sun,
and two are the eyes of a fish.”
The white part between them,
“this is the fish's teeth;
where the water now flows
into the dark place
is the fish's mouth,
which is most fearsome.
We now
have no way to survive;
reaching the fish's mouth,
we are certainly on the brink of death.”
There was a virtuous man
who reverently believed in the Buddha’s Way;
he told the merchants:
“You must only sincerely recite ‘Nāmó Fó.’
The virtue of the Three Realms is great;
none are greater than the Buddha,
who rescues from distress and responds to emergencies,
showing compassion to all;
he is best able to protect sentient beings in suffering and hardship.
Only the Buddha is divine and holy!
We pray he will save us from danger
and rescue these people's
lives, which hang by a thread.”
At that time, the Mójé fish,
hearing the name of the Buddha being recited,
immediately closed its mouth
and submerged to the bottom of the sea;
the merchants then
returned safely to their country.
At that time, Fùnàqí
took a large golden tray,
and with various wondrous treasures and Móní pearls and such,
he piled and filled it,
and offered it to his elder brother Xiànnà.
Kneeling long and looking up,
he spoke to his elder brother, saying:
“I have already for my brother
accumulated treasures;
the houses and all possessions are sufficient,
and for seven generations of descendants,
food and use will not be exhausted.
I only hope, elder brother!
allow me to leave home.”
Xiànnà replied:
“I will not oppose you,
but you are young
and have not yet mastered human relations;
the Buddha’s Law is essential and weighty,
and maintaining it is very difficult.
After a few more years,
you may then fulfill your wish.”
Fùnàqí said:
“Elder brother should know!
Human life is impermanent
and difficult to preserve for even a moment.
Previously at the great sea,
we encountered a Mójé fish;
it drew the ship toward its mouth,
and life was on the brink of death.
Receiving the Buddha's divine grace,
I was able to save my remaining life.
I only hope you will grant permission
and let me join the ranks of the Way.”
The elder brother then granted it.
Then Fùnàqí,
with his company of five hundred treasure-gatherers,
all with a heart of faith, went to Shèwèiguó.
Reaching the Buddha's place,
they paid respects and inquired after him.
He then fully informed the Buddha,
seeking to leave home.
The Buddha then permitted it
and let them enter the Way.
He praised them, saying:
“Welcome!”
and they became Shāmén.
For them the Buddha preached various
earnest teachings on the Dharma of suffering.
The five hundred Bǐqiū
had their minds opened and awakened,
ended the boundaries of all suffering,
and became Āluóhàn.
Only Fùnàqí
had deep and heavy afflictions;
though the Buddha preached the Dharma for him,
he could not yet fully grasp it.
With intense sincerity and effort,
he finally entered the first stage of realization.
He practiced with diligence and focus,
without any rest or laziness.
At that time, as the day for the summer retreat drew near for the Bǐqiū,
the Buddha allowed each to spend the retreat as they pleased.
Then Fùnàqí
went and spoke to the Buddha, saying:
“Your disciple wishes to go to Fàngbōguó for the three-month retreat;
I only hope you will grant permission.”
At that time, the Shìzūn
told Fùnàqí:
“The people of that country are wicked
and believe in heterodox and inverted views.
You are now a beginner
in the Buddha's Law and
have not yet perfected the holy practices of the Buddha's Law.
If you are insulted or humiliated by those people,
what will you do?”
Fùnàqí said:
“Even if I am insulted and humiliated to the extreme,
as long as they do not harm me.”
The Shìzūn further said:
“Those people are extremely wicked;
if you are harmed,
what will you do then?”
Fùnàqí said:
“The Shìzūn should know!
Even if those people insult and harm me,
as long as they do not end my life,
I will still harbor gratitude for them.”
The Buddha further said:
“If you go there,
and suddenly encounter wicked people
who brutally end your life,
which would be of no benefit to you,
what will you do?”
Fùnàqí said:
“The Shìzūn should know!
All ten thousand things
that have form return to nothingness.
If they kill me,
I will simply accept that death.”
At that time, the Shìzūn told Fùnàqí:
“If those wicked people
insult and harm you,
or even before they end your life,
will you feel anger?”
Fùnàqí said:
“No,
Shìzūn!
Even if those people slander me without cause,
or insult me with the most worldly and lawless matters,
or even use knives and staves
to beat, harm, or even kill me,
and before they have finished the slaughter
when my life is about to end,
I will never for a single moment give rise to a heart of anger.”
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
Such practice by a disciple
is truly delightful.”
Then Fùnàqí
gathered his robes and bowl,
paid respects to the Buddha and took his leave,
and went to Fàngbōguó.
Early the next morning,
he entered the city to beg for food
and came to the house of a very wealthy Póluómén.
At that time, the Póluómén,
seeing this Bǐqiū,
immediately harbored a wicked heart
and came out to curse and chase him away.
The Bǐqiū then went to another house to beg for food.
From the next day,
He continued his rounds to beg for food at that house.
At that time, the Póluómén,
again struck him with great force.
The Bǐqiū was joyful,
and his facial expression did not change.
At that time, the Póluómén,
observing this Bǐqiū,
saw him slandered and harmed,
suffering and on the verge of death,
yet without a look of resentment,
and without giving rise to anger or hatred.
He then felt regret and reproached himself,
repenting for his past transgressions.
At that time, Fùnàqí,
within that kingdom,
practiced diligently without laziness.
Having exhausted all afflictions,
his mind suddenly opened in realization,
and he obtained the state of no-outflows.
When the summer retreat was completed,
he took leave of the Dányuè,
and exhorted his elder brother:
"Be careful not to enter the sea.
The dangers within the great sea are extremely numerous and beyond count.
Brother, your wealth and treasures
are sufficient to last for seven lifetimes."
Having finished his exhortation,
he returned to where the Fó was.
He bowed his head in greeting,
and after the greeting was completed,
he stayed there as he pleased.
At that time, the elder brother Xiànnà
did not heed his instructions.
There were various merchants
who came to Xiànnà,
using all sorts of persuasion
to enter the great sea together.
Xiànnà did not refuse them
and went along immediately.
Upon reaching an island in the sea,
everyone took what they could according to their own capacity.
Only Xiànnà
took a great amount of Niútóu Zhāntán incense wood,
filling the ship to return.
The Lóng, being stingy by nature,
begrudged him the incense wood.
Thus, while on the way,
it seized the ship.
Though they raised the sails and gathered the wind,
they could not pass.
All the passengers
were certain they would die of fear.
Xiànnà, with a focused mind,
called upon Fùnàqí:
"Now that I have encountered suffering and distress,
I pray that you will come to rescue me."
At that time, Fùnàqí
was at the Qíhuán Jīngshè in Shèwèiguó,
sitting in meditation and contemplation.
From afar, with his divine ear,
he heard his brother Xiànnà
in a dangerous situation,
sincerely stating his plight
with a sorrowful and focused mind,
calling upon Fùnàqí.
Fùnàqí immediately used his Luóhàn spiritual powers;
in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm,
he transformed his body into a Jīnchì Niǎowáng
and went to the great sea
to intimidate and constrain the Lóng.
When the Lóng saw the form of the bird,
it fearfully dove to the bottom of the sea.
Thus, the merchants returned home safely.
Then Fùnàqí
taught and transformed his brother,
telling him to build a small hall for the Shìzūn.
The timber for the hall's roof was entirely made of Zhāntán.
Once the hall was completed,
he taught his brother to invite the Fó.
Xiànnà replied:
"Regarding the propriety of inviting the Fó,
with what sort of things can one move the Shìzūn to come?"
At that time, Fùnàqí,
together with his brother,
prepared sufficient offerings.
Each holding an incense burner,
they ascended a high tower together.
Facing Qíhuán from afar,
they burned incense and took refuge in the Fó and the Shèngsēng:
"We only pray that tomorrow,
you will grace our humble kingdom with your presence,
to awaken and enlighten the foolish, ignorant, and blinded sentient beings."
After making the vow,
the incense smoke, following their intent,
mounted the void and reached the top of the Shìzūn’s head,
gathering together to form a canopy of smoke.
Later, from afar, he used water
to wash the Shìzūn’s feet;
the water also traveled through the void,
like the prongs of a hairpin,
and reached the Shìzūn’s feet directly as intended.
At that time, Ānán,
seeing these things,
wondered and asked the Fó:
"Who sent this smoke and water?"
The Fó told Ānán:
"It is the Luóhàn Bǐqiū Fùnàqí
in the Fàngbōguó,
who encouraged his brother Xiànnà
to invite the Fó and the Sēng.
Therefore, he sent the smoke and water
to serve as a token of the invitation."
He then commanded Ānán:
"Go among the Sēng
and distribute the counting sticks to inform the Bǐqiū with spiritual powers:
'Tomorrow you shall all come
to respond to Xiànnà's invitation
and display transformations
while traveling to that kingdom.'"
Ānán followed the command,
assembled the Sēng, and distributed the counting sticks.
Those with spiritual powers
should accept the invitation for tomorrow.
At that time, the Bǐqiū
each accepted a counting stick.
At dawn the next day,
the man who prepared food for the Sēng,
named Qíqiánzhíqí
(which means "Continuous Birth"),
had already attained the path of the Ānàhán.
He constantly provided for all the Sēng.
Sitting in the lotus position,
his body emitted light
that shone in all directions.
He led the cooking utensils,
such as ladles, spoons, and strong supports,
and large cauldrons holding a hundred Hú,
which followed behind him.
Flying through the void,
he headed toward that kingdom.
Xiànnà asked:
"Is this your teacher?"
He answered:
"No.
Among the Bǐqiū,
he is the person who prepares the food,
so he has come beforehand to assist
in preparing the food and drink."
Thereupon Xiànnà
immediately offered flowers, incense, and music.
After the offering was finished,
he then passed by.
Next, there were sixteen Shāmí such as Jūntí and others.
Each used spiritual powers
to transform into a forest,
gathering flowers and fruits.
With various transformations,
they displayed bodily light
that shone through heaven and earth.
Ascending the void in succession,
they arrived one after another.
Xiànnà asked again:
"Is this your teacher?"
He answered:
"No.
These people
who arrived earlier
are disciples of the same teacher as us.
They are only seven years old,
yet they have attained the path of the Luóhàn.
All outflows are forever exhausted,
and their spiritual powers are fully perfected.
They have come ahead now to gather flowers and prepare fruit."
He then used flowers and incense
to make full offerings.
After the offerings were finished,
each of them passed by.
Next came the elder Great Āluóhàn,
who transformed into a thousand Lóng.
Their bodies were entwined to form a throne,
with their heads protruding in all four directions,
their thunderous roars shaking the heavens.
From the mouths of all these Lóng,
there rained down the seven treasures.
Furthermore, upon them,
they set a great jeweled throne.
Flying up into the void,
their bodies emitted light
illuminating the world,
and they arrived at the kingdom.
Xiànnà asked again:
"Is this your teacher?"
He answered:
"No.
This is a disciple of the teacher,
named Jiāochénrú.
When the Fó first attained the Way,
at Lùyěyuàn,
he first turned the Wheel of the Dhárma
to liberate sentient beings extensively.
"These five people,
were the first to be converted;
among the disciples,
they are the primary leaders,
fully possessing supernatural powers
without any hindrance."
When Xiànnà heard this,
his respect increased twofold;
with incense, flowers, and musicians,
he made offerings to them all.
When the offerings were finished,
they then passed on.
Subsequently, there was Móhē Jiāyè,
who manifested a lecture hall of the seven treasures,
adorned with the seven treasures.
His body emitted light
that shone and spread in all directions
as he went to that kingdom.
Xiànnà saw him
and asked Fùnàqí:
"Is this your teacher?"
He answered:
"No.
This is the teacher's disciple,
Móhē Jiāyè,
who is pure, frugal, and content,
always practicing the dhūta austerities,
pitying the lowly,
and relieving the poor and destitute."
Xiànnà immediately used incense, flowers, and musicians
to complete the offerings,
and he then immediately passed on.
Then Shèlìfú
followed, riding a thousand lions
with their coiled bodies serving as a seat,
their heads all facing the four directions,
their mouths raining the seven treasures,
roaring like thunder
and shaking heaven and earth.
Furthermore, upon them,
he spread a great jeweled bed
magnificently adorned,
and he sat upon it.
His body emitted light
that shone throughout the four regions,
soaring through the void
and hovering as he arrived.
Xiànnà asked:
"Is this your teacher?"
He answered:
"No.
The one who comes riding now
is the teacher's great disciple
of vast and great wisdom,
named Shèlìfú."
After Xiànnà heard this,
his joy increased twofold;
he immediately made offerings of flowers, incense, and musicians.
When the offerings were finished,
he then passed on.
Then Dà Mùlián
set out soon after,
manifesting a thousand elephants
with their heads arranged in the four directions.
In the mouths of those elephants,
each had six tusks;
at the tip of each tusk,
there were seven bathing pools of water.
In each and every pool,
there were seven lotus flowers;
on each flower,
there were seven jade maidens
performing various transformations,
infinite in number.
Emitting great light
that moved the surrounding neighbors,
furthermore, upon them,
he placed a jeweled throne
and sat upon it himself,
arriving directly through the void.
Xiànnà asked:
"Is this your teacher?"
He replied:
"No.
This is the teacher's disciple,
named Dà Mùlián,
foremost in supernatural powers,
and of pure and complete virtuous conduct."
When Xiànnà heard this,
he rejoiced and looked up with respect;
with incense, flowers, and musicians,
he made offerings.
After making offerings,
he then passed on.
Next, there was Ānàlǜtí,
who manifested a bathing pool of the seven treasures.
In the bathing pool, golden lotus flowers grew;
the stems of the lotuses were all composed of the seven treasures.
Staying upon the flower,
he sat cross-legged,
with a halo of sunlight around his neck
that shone upon all under heaven.
Wherever the light shone,
everything became golden
as he arrived at the kingdom through the void.
Xiànnà asked again:
"Is this your teacher?"
He replied:
"No.
This is the teacher's disciple,
Ānàlǜtí,
who among this great assembly
is foremost in divine vision."
When Xiànnà heard this,
he rejoiced with respect
and made offerings of flowers and incense,
and he then passed on.
Next, there was the Buddha's brother Nántuó,
who manifested a thousand horses
pulling a chariot of the seven treasures.
Upon the chariot was a great canopy of the seven treasures,
emitting and spreading light
that shone in the four directions
as he galloped through the void to arrive
at the Fàngbō Kingdom.
Xiànnà saw him
and asked Fùnàqí:
"Is this your teacher?"
He replied:
"No.
This is the World-Honored One's brother,
named Nántuó,
complete with all marks
and of pure and complete virtuous conduct."
Xiànnà immediately used incense, flowers, and musicians
to complete the offerings,
and he then passed on.
Then Xūpútí followed,
creating a mountain of the seven treasures.
Sitting in a lapis lazuli cave,
his body emitted various multi-colored lights
that shone upon heaven and earth
as he arrived at that kingdom.
Xiànnà asked:
"Is this your teacher?"
He replied:
"No.
This is the teacher's disciple,
named Xūpútí,
of broad wisdom and great learning,
and foremost in understanding emptiness."
He immediately used flowers and incense
to complete the offerings,
and he then passed on.
Next was Fēnnòuwéntuónízǐ,
who manifested a thousand Jiālóuluó Wáng
with their bodies joined to form a seat,
their heads arranged in four directions.
They held various treasures in their mouths
and emitted sorrowful and harmonious sounds.
Furthermore, upon them,
he set a great jeweled throne
and sat upon it
as he arrived through the void.
Xiànnà asked:
"Is this your teacher?"
He replied:
"No.
He shares the same teacher with me,
and is named Fēnnòuwéntuónízǐ.
His eloquence is suitable,
and he is the foremost."
He immediately used flowers and incense;
having finished the offerings,
he then passed on.
Next was the disciple
named Yōubōlí,
who manifested a thousand geese with their bodies joined together,
their heads and mouths making sounds,
crying out harmoniously.
They held various treasures in their mouths
and soared through the void.
Upon their bodies,
he spread a throne of various treasures,
emitting great light
that shone near and far.
He sat upon it
and came rushing.
Xiànnà asked:
"Is this your teacher?"
He replied:
"No.
This is the teacher's disciple,
named Yōubōlí,
who among the assembly of bhikṣus
is foremost in upholding the Vinaya."
When Xiànnà heard this,
he immediately held flowers and incense
to complete the offerings,
and he then passed on.
Next, there was the Shàmén Èrshíyì.
He transformed rows of trees in the void.
Using dark blue lapis lazuli,
he created a path for walking.
Furthermore, using the seven treasures,
he lined both sides of the trees.
Various wonderful jewels
bordered the path.
He walked within it
and gradually reached that country.
Xiànnà asked,
“Is this your teacher?”
The reply was,
“No.
This is a disciple of the Buddha,
named Shàmén Èrshíyì.
Among the Bhiksus,
he is foremost in diligence.”
After offering flowers, incense, and music
and completing the worship,
he then passed by.
Next, there was Dà Jiébīnníng.
He transformed trees of the seven treasures.
Upon the trees were various flowers and fruits.
Beneath the trees were high seats of the seven treasures.
Sitting upon a seat,
he emitted great light
and came through the void.
Xiànnà asked,
“Is this your teacher?”
The reply was,
“No.
This is a disciple of the Buddha,
named Jiébīnníng.
He is exceptionally valiant and
foremost in dignity.”
Having heard this, Xiànnà
joyfully offered flowers, incense, and music.
After the offering was finished,
he then passed by.
Next was a disciple named Bīntóulú Duòshé.
Sitting upon a precious lotus flower,
with a halo like the sun around his neck,
emitting a thousand beams of light,
illuminating heaven and earth,
he flew through the void
and came to that country.
Xiànnà asked,
“Is this your teacher?”
The reply was,
“No.
This is a disciple of the teacher,
named Bīntóulú Duòshé.
He is skilled at entering samādhi
and is foremost in meditation.”
Xiànnà then used incense and flowers
to complete the offering,
and he then passed by.
Next was Luóhóuluó,
who followed afterward.
He transformed his own body
to become a Wheel-turning King.
With a thousand sons and the seven treasures,
all fully present,
leading and following before and after,
he came to that country.
Xiànnà asked,
“Is this your teacher?”
The reply was,
“No.
This is the son of the Buddha,
named Luóhóuluó.
Had he remained in the household life,
he would have ruled the four worlds.
The seven treasures would have come to him naturally,
and without using weapons,
all would have naturally submitted.
He has now renounced this position,
left the household life to study the Way,
and attained the state of Āluóhàn.
His six supernormal powers are clear and thorough
without any obstruction.
He has now transformed his body
into this form and rank.”
Having heard this, Xiànnà
offered incense and flowers,
and he then passed by.
Five hundred disciples with supernormal powers
each displayed transformations
beyond calculation.
At that time, the Shìzūn
knew that all the disciples had arrived at that country.
He emitted great light,
illuminating heaven and earth
until all was golden.
Then Fùnàqí
said to his elder brother,
“Now the Shìzūn
has just intended to come here;
therefore, he first emits light
as this auspicious sign.”
At that time, the Shìzūn
began to leave his seat
and stepped upon the ground.
Immediately, heaven and earth
shook in six ways.
Then Fùnàqí
said to his elder brother,
“Now the Shìzūn
has just left his seat
and stepped upon the ground.
For this reason,
heaven and earth shake greatly.”
At that time, the Shìzūn
first emerged from the vihara
and stood outside.
Eight Jīngāng Shén stood on eight sides.
The Sì Tiānwáng led the way.
Tiāndìshì,
along with hundreds of thousands of multitudes of sons of the heavens of the Desire Realm,
guarded the left side.
Dàfàntiānwáng,
with countless multitudes of the various heavens of the Form Realm,
stood on the right side.
The disciple Ānán
stood behind the Buddha.
Surrounded by the great assembly,
he emitted radiant light,
illuminating heaven and earth.
Flying through the void,
he proceeded to the country of Fàngbō.
On the way,
he met five hundred laborers
with a thousand teams of oxen and plows,
tilling the fields.
When the oxen saw the Buddha passing through the air,
his body emitting golden light that illuminated the world,
the oxen, with sincere hearts,
looked up at the Shìzūn
with deep respect in their minds
and stood in the furrows without moving.
The laborers saw the oxen looking up and gazing,
and were surprised by the reason.
They also looked and saw the Buddha,
and each knelt and said,
“We all take refuge with sincerity.
We only wish the Rúlái
would take pity on us and briefly descend to liberate us,
causing us to leave birth and death.”
The Buddha, with a heart of compassion,
knew they could be saved.
He immediately descended to speak various wonderful dharmas for them.
The five hundred laborers
were enlightened in their minds.
They cut off twenty billion blazing evils
and became Sūduóhuán.
Then the oxen’s lives ended,
and they were all born in the heavens,
everyone being filled with joy.
At that time, the Rúlái
set off once again.
Before long,
there were five hundred young girls
playing together in the wilderness.
Seeing the ground turn golden,
they looked up at the transformation
and saw him traveling through the void.
They were all filled with joy,
joined their palms, and said,
“We only wish the Tiānzūn
would lower his heart in pity and briefly grant us salvation.”
The Buddha knew that their past actions made them ready for conversion.
He granted their wish
and went to where they were.
According to their capacity,
he spoke the various dharmas for them.
They received them with faith and were enlightened,
becoming Sūduóhuán.
After the transformation and conversion were completed,
he then proceeded on foot.
There were also five hundred immortals
dwelling in the forests and marshes.
They saw the light illuminating the ground, making it all golden.
Looking up, they saw the Rúlái and the great assembly traveling through the void.
Their hearts leaped with joy,
and their respect doubled.
Looking up, they entreated the Buddha, saying,
“We only wish the Dàshèng
would briefly trouble his divine form
to see and deliver us,
allowing us to follow in the order of the Way.”
The Buddha observed their fundamental causes
and knew they should be saved.
He immediately descended before them.
They requested to become Shàmén.
The Buddha then permitted them, saying,
“Welcome, Bhiksus!”
They then became Shàmén.
Because he spoke the dharma for them,
their minds were purified and enlightened.
All defilements were forever exhausted,
and he became an Āluóhàn;
following behind the Buddha,
he arrived by traveling through the air.
At that time, Fùnàqí
saw from afar the Buddha coming,
His light illuminating heaven and earth,
and the great assembly moving through the air.
He said to his older brother Xiànnà:
“The World-Honored One and the assembly
are just now arriving.”
When the Buddha reached that kingdom,
Xiànnà was filled with joy.
He immediately took incense, flowers, and various forms of music,
and after completing the offerings,
they went together to the meeting place.
The Buddha went to his house
and took His seat according to the Dharma.
Xiànnà’s entire household
prepared and provided sweet delicacies;
he personally brought water for washing,
and respectfully offered the food.
The Buddha performed the dākṣiṇā for them.
After finishing the meal and rinsing His mouth,
for the sake of the entire kingdom and the household, both old and young,
He expounded the subtle Dharma.
Every member of the family
attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán.
Some attained the second, third, or fourth fruits of the path;
some resolved their minds toward the Dàchéng;
and some firmly dwelled in the stage of non-retrogression.
When the Buddha finished preaching the Dharma,
among the men and women of the entire kingdom,
the number of those who attained liberation was great,
beyond calculation.
Ānán knelt on both knees,
pressed his palms together,
and stepped forward to say to the Buddha:
“I am unsure,
World-Honored One!
In past lives,
what evil deeds did this Fùnàqí
commit
to be born of low and humble status
and belong to another as a slave?
Furthermore, what merit does he have
to meet the Buddha and attain liberation?”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“If you wish to know this,
listen clearly and contemplate well!
I shall explain it for you.”
He replied:
“Yes indeed,
I wish for a full explanation.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“Long ago, in the time of Jiāyè Buddha,
there was an elder
with countless wealth.
For the Buddha and the assembly of monks, he established a sēngjiālán,
and provided the four necessities of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine,
supplying everything without any deficiency.
At that time, the elder fell ill and died.
Afterwards, one of his sons left the household to study the Way.
After the father’s death, the offerings for the monastery
all gradually decreased;
the monks dispersed,
and the temple fell into ruin,
with no one living there.
That son, a Bǐqiū,
worked diligently to gather patrons and acquaintances,
accumulating wealth
to repair what was broken and missing.
He reassembled the monks
and resumed the offerings.
At that time, a great number of people
lived in that temple,
diligently and single-mindedly practicing.
Among those who possessed the various paths,
at that time, that practitioner
acted as the administrator of the monks.
There was then an Āluóhàn practitioner
whose turn it was to be on duty;
he swept the grass and dirt
and piled it in the courtyard,
but did not remove it in time.
At that time, the Bǐqiū administrator
scolded him with a malicious mind:
‘This Bǐqiū now
is no different from a slave.
Although he knows how to sweep the ground,
he cannot remove the refuse.’
Ānán, you should know!
The Bǐqiū of that time,
the great administrator,
was this very Bǐqiū Fùnàqí.
Because of his malicious mind in scolding a practitioner who had attained the Way and comparing him to a slave,
because of those words,
throughout five hundred lifetimes,
he was always born as a slave.
Furthermore, because he established the temple and encouraged many people to provide offerings to the monks,
now that he has finished paying for his offense,
he has again encountered my era
and received liberation.
In this kingdom today,
the people who receive conversion
are all those who were encouraged and assisted by him in the past.
Due to these causes and retributions,
they have all attained liberation.”
Ānán and the others,
as well as the great assembly,
having heard what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and carried it out.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in Shè-wèi-guó at the Qǐ-shù Jǐ-gū-dú-yuán.
At that time, in the city of Shè-wèi-chéng,
the population was numerous,
the dwellings were cramped and narrow,
and latrines were few.
When needing to relieve themselves,
many people went outside the city.
There were some who were wealthy and noble
but unable to go,
so they relieved themselves in vessels
and hired someone to remove it.
At that time there was a man
named Ní-tí,
who was extremely poor and of the lowest caste.
Having no place to turn,
he relied on being a hired laborer to remove night soil
to earn wages to support himself.
At that time the Shì-zūn,
knowing he was ready for deliverance,
took only Ā-nán
and entered the city,
wishing to rescue and deliver him.
Arriving at the entrance of a lane,
he happened upon Ní-tí,
who was carrying an earthenware vessel
filled with impurities,
intending to go and discard it.
Seeing the Shì-zūn from afar,
he felt extreme shame and humbleness.
He retreated by a different path,
wishing to hide away and leave.
Just as he was about to exit the lane,
he saw the Shì-zūn again.
Feeling doubly ashamed and humiliated,
he turned toward another path
and again wished to avoid him and leave.
In his haste and confusion,
he struck the jar against a wall.
The jar immediately broke,
and excrement and urine drenched his body.
Feeling deep shame and remorse,
he could not bear to see the Fó.
At this time, the Shì-zūn
approached his location
and said to Ní-tí:
"Do you wish to leave the household life?"
Ní-tí replied:
"The Rú-lái is honorable and respected,
of the Jīn-lún-wáng lineage.
His attendant disciples
are all noble people.
I am of the lowest class and extremely vile;
how could I be like them and be able to leave the household life?"
The Shì-zūn told him:
"My Dharma is pure and subtle,
just like clean water,
which can wash away all filth and impurity.
It is also like a great fire that can burn all things;
whether large or small, good or bad,
all can be burned by it.
My Dharma is also like this;
it is vast and boundless.
Whether poor or rich, noble or base,
men or women,
those who are able to cultivate
will all exhaust all desires."
At this time, Ní-tí,
hearing what the Fó had said,
immediately gave rise to faith
and wished to leave the household life.
The Fó had Ā-nán take him outside the city
to the bank of a great river
to bathe his body.
Once he was clean and pure,
he was taken to Qǐ-huán
to have the sutra Dharma explained to him,
regarding the principles of suffering,
how birth and death are to be feared,
and how Niè-pán is eternal peace.
Suddenly his mind was liberated,
and he attained the realization of the first fruit.
Joining his palms toward the Fó,
he requested to become a Shā-mén.
The Fó then told him:
"Welcome, Bǐ-qiū!"
His beard and hair fell off naturally,
and Dharma robes appeared on his body.
The Fó again explained the essential Dharma of the Sì-dì,
and all his outflows were exhausted.
He became an Ā-luó-hàn,
and the Three Clarities and Six Supernormal Powers
were all fully complete.
At that time, the people of the country,
hearing that Ní-tí had left the household life,
all harbored resentment in their hearts
and said this:
"How can the Shì-zūn
allow this lowly person to leave the household life to study the Way?
How can we
bow to him?
If we prepare offerings
and invite the Fó and the Sēng,
if this person comes,
he will defile our couches and mats."
This was passed from person to person
until it was heard by the Wáng.
The Wáng, hearing this, was also resentful
and felt restless.
He immediately rode in his chariot with feathered canopies
with various attendants
to go to Qǐ-huán,
wishing to ask the Rú-lái about the matter of his doubt.
Once he arrived before the gate,
he paused for a short rest.
Outside the gate of Qǐ-huán,
there was a large stone.
Bǐ-qiū Ní-tí
was sitting on the rocky ledge,
mending old clothes.
There were seven hundred celestial beings,
each holding flowers and incense,
making offerings to him
and circling him to the right in respectful salutation.
At that time, the Wáng saw this
and was deeply joyful.
He went to the Bǐ-qiū's location
and said to him:
"I wish to see the Fó;
I hope you will announce me."
The Bǐ-qiū immediately
submerged his body into the stone
and emerged within the grounds.
He said to the Shì-zūn:
"Bō-sī-nì-wáng
is now outside
wishing to come in to pay respects and inquire."
The Fó told Ní-tí:
"Return by your original path
and tell him to come forward."
Ní-tí then
returned and emerged from the stone
as if emerging from water,
without any hindrance.
He then said to the Wáng:
"I have finished informing the Fó;
the Wáng may proceed forward."
The Wáng thought this:
"The matter I doubted earlier
should be set aside for now.
First I should ask
who this Bǐ-qiū is
and what meritorious deeds he performed
to have such spiritual power."
The Wáng entered and saw the Fó,
bowed his head to the Fó's feet,
circled three times to the right,
and then sat to one side.
He said to the Shì-zūn:
"The Bǐ-qiū from just now
has incomparable spiritual power,
entering stone like water
and emerging from stone without leaving a hole.
What is his family name and given name?
I hope you will tell me."
The Shì-zūn told him:
"He was, in the Wáng's country,
the lowest of persons.
I have transformed and delivered him,
and he has attained the state of Ā-luó-hàn.
The Great Wáng came precisely
because he wished to ask about this matter."
When the Wáng heard the Fó's words,
his pride was immediately removed,
and he was boundlessly joyful.
The Fó then told the Wáng:
"When people live in the world,
whether noble or base, high or low,
poor or rich, suffering or happy,
all are due to past actions
which lead to these results. Those who are kind, compassionate, humble, and submissive,
respecting the elderly and loving the young,
will become noble people.
Those who are fierce, cruel, and overbearing,
arrogant, willful, and self-important,
will become lowly people."
Bō-sī-nì-wáng said to the Shì-zūn:
"The Dà-shèng appears in the world
to benefit and deliver many,
taking such an ordinary, ugly, and lowly person,
rescuing him from his bitter misery
and causing him to be always peaceful and happy.
As for this Ní-tí,
what were the causes and conditions
for him to be born in a lowly place?
And what virtues did he plant
to meet the Shèng-zūn
and receive this immortal transformation?"
"...soon become an Yìngzhēn?
I only wish, Shìzūn!
that you would elaborate and explain."
Fó told the Wáng:
"Listen carefully and hold this well!
I shall explain to make you awaken.
In the distant past,
Jiāyè Rúlái
appeared in the world.
After his parinirvana,
there was a Bǐqiū Sangha numbering one hundred thousand.
Among them was a Shāmén
who acted as an administrator of the Sangha.
His body having an illness, he took medicine to purge himself.
Arrogant and relying on his influence,
he did not go out to relieve himself.
Using a washbasin of gold and silver,
he held his urine within it,
and ordered a disciple to carry it and discard it.
However, that disciple
was a Sūtuóhuán.
Because in that previous life,
he could not be humble and compliant,
relying on his great wealth
while managing the affairs of the Sangha,
and having a slight ailment for a short time,
he was too lazy to get up himself
and drove a sage into service,
ordering him to remove filth and excrement.
Because of these causes and conditions,
he wandered through birth and death,
always being of lowly status.
For five hundred lifetimes,
he cleared away excrement for others,
even until now.
Because of his leaving the home life
and the merit of upholding the precepts,
he has now encountered my age,
heard the Fǎ and attained the Dào."
Fó told the Dàwáng:
"If you wish to know who the Sangha administrator was at that time,
it is the current Bǐqiū Nítí."
Bōsīnuì Wáng said to the Shìzūn:
"The Rúlái's appearance in the world
is truly extraordinary,
benefiting immeasurable suffering sentient beings."
Fó told the Dàwáng:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is as you say."
Fó further told him:
"In the rotation of the Sānjiè,
there are no fixed ranks.
Accumulating goodness, benevolence, and harmony,
one is born into nobility and honor;
practicing evil and indulgence,
one is then born into lowliness."
The Wáng was greatly delighted
and had no pride.
He immediately rose and knelt on both knees,
took hold of Nítí’s feet,
and performed a prostration,
repenting and apologizing
in the hope of removing his offenses and faults.
The Shìzūn then,
for his sake, extensively spoke on the subtle meanings of the Fǎ:
the so-called discourses,
the discourse on giving and the discourse on precepts,
the discourse on birth in the heavens,
the contemplation of the impurity of desire,
and the bliss of the path of liberation.
At that time, the Great Assembly,
hearing what the Fó had said,
each attained the realization of the Dào
and faithfully accepted and practiced it.
Xiányú Jīng, Juàn Dì Qī
Translated by the Shāmén Huìjué and others of Liángzhōu in Gāochāng Qùn during the Yuán Wèi.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, at the Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, there was a king named Bōsīnuì.
At this time, in the south, there was a country
called Jīndì,
and its king was named Jiébīnníng.
The king had a crown prince
