named Móhē Jiébīnníng.
When his father passed away,
the crown prince succeeded to the throne.
By nature, he was intelligent,
possessed great strength, and was brave and vigorous.
The lands he governed
numbered thirty-six thousand.
His military forces were vast and flourishing,
such that no one could rival him.
His majestic reputation spread far and wide,
and there was none who did not submit to him.
However, with the Zhōngguó,
he had no communication.
Later, there were merchants
who traveled to Jīndì,
bringing four pieces of fine woolen cloth
to offer to the king.
After the king had accepted them,
he asked the merchants:
"These items are very fine;
from where do they originate?"
The merchants replied:
"They originate from the Zhōngguó."
The king asked again:
"As for this Zhōngguó,
what are its names?"
The merchants informed him:
"It is named Luóyuèqí,
and also named Shèwèi;
its territories are so numerous
that I cannot describe them all in detail."
The king asked again:
"For what reason do the various kings of the Zhōngguó
not come to offer tribute to me?"
The merchants informed him:
"Each rules their own territory,
and their power and fame are equal to one another.
For this reason,
they do not come to pay homage."
The king thought to himself:
"With my current power and influence,
I am able to command and subdue all under heaven.
Why should these kings not come to bring tribute?
Now I shall exert my authority to make them submit."
He then asked the merchants:
"Among the various kings of the Zhōngguó,
who is the greatest?"
The head merchant said:
"The King of the Kingdom of Shèwèi
is the foremost and greatest."
At that time, the King of Jīndì
immediately dispatched an envoy
to the Kingdom of Shèwèi,
bearing a letter of instruction
whose details were thorough and complete,
to address King Bōsīnuì, saying:
"My majestic influence
pervades all of Yánfútí.
What is it that you rely upon
to have severed all diplomatic missions?
Now I have sent an envoy to communicate with you.
If you are lying down
when you hear my voice,
you should immediately rise and sit up;
if you are sitting when you hear it,
you should immediately stand;
if you are eating when you hear the sound,
you should immediately spit out the food;
if you are bathing when you hear the sound,
you should immediately grasp your hair;
if you are standing when you hear it,
you should immediately set out towards me.
Within seven days,
you must meet with me;
if it is not so,
I shall raise an army to destroy your borders."
When Bōsīnuì heard this, he was deeply terrified.
He immediately went to the Buddha
and reported this matter in detail.
The Buddha told the king:
"The King should return and tell the envoy:
'I am not great;
there is an even greater king.'"
The king followed the Buddha's teaching
and told the envoy:
"There is a Sagely King in the world,
nearby in this very place.
You may go there
to deliver your king's command."
The envoy immediately went to Jǐhuán.
At that time, the Shìzūn transformed his own body
into a Zhuǎn lún wáng.
He made Mùlián the minister of war,
and the seven treasures and attendants
were all fully present.
He also transformed Jǐhuán
into a city of jewels.
Surrounding the four sides of the city
were seven layers of moats.
Between them were rows of trees made of the seven treasures and multi-colored lotuses
beyond counting,
with a brilliant light
shining brightly and magnificently.
The palaces within the city
were also made of various jewels.
The king was upon the palace,
solemn and awe-inspiring.
Thereupon, the envoy
entered the transformed city.
Having seen the Great King,
his heart was greatly alarmed,
and he thought to himself: "My own ruler
has pointlessly invited calamity."
However, since he had no choice,
he presented the letter.
The Transformed King received the letter,
trampled it under his feet,
and told the envoy:
"I am the Great King,
ruling over the four realms.
Your king is stubborn and deluded
to dare to show defiance.
Return quickly to your country
and proclaim my instruction.
On the day the message arrives,
gallop here to see me.
If lying down when hearing it, he must rise;
if sitting when hearing it, he must stand;
if standing when hearing my command, he should immediately take to the road.
The deadline is seven days,
and there must be no delay.
If he dares to violate this decree,
the guilt will be his for not having sought pardon."
After the envoy received the instruction,
he returned to his home country
and reported everything he had seen and heard
to the King of Jīndì.
Upon hearing this, the King
deeply blamed and reproached himself.
He assembled the various lesser kings under his command,
prepared chariots and horses,
and wished to pay court to the Great King.
However, he still had some doubts
and did not set out on the road immediately.
He first sent an envoy to inform the Great King:
"The kings governed by your servant
number thirty-six thousand.
Should they all come with me,
or should I bring half?"
The Great King sent back a reply:
"Let half remain,
and just bring half with you."
Then the King of Jīndì brought eighteen thousand lesser kings
and they arrived all at once.
Having seen the Transformed King
and finished his ceremonial bows,
he thought to himself:
"Although the Great King's appearance
is superior to mine,
his strength surely cannot match mine."
At that time, the Transformed King
ordered the minister of war
to give him a bow.
The King of the Kingdom of Jīndì
could not even lift it with his hands.
The Transformed King took it back,
drew the bow with his finger,
and then held it out to him again,
ordering him to pull and draw it.
The King of the Kingdom of Jīndì was completely unable to draw it.
The Transformed King took it back again
and plucked it;
the Three Thousandfold World
all vibrated from the sound.
Next, he took an arrow,
drew the bow and shot.
After it left his hand,
it transformed into five shafts.
Each of the arrowheads
emitted countless rays of light.
At the head of each ray of light,
there was a lotus flower
as large as a wagon wheel.
Upon each and every flower,
there was a Zhuǎn lún wáng,
fully endowed with the seven treasures,
radiating light
that illuminated the Three Thousand Great Thousandfold Worlds.
Of the sentient beings in the five realms,
none did not receive its benefit.
In the realms of the various heavens,
they saw the light
and heard the preaching of the Dharma.
Their bodies and minds became pure;
there were those who attained the second and third fruits of the path,
there were those who gave rise to the aspiration for the unexcelled, correct, and true path,
and there were also those who attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Sentient beings of the human realm,
upon seeing the Buddha's light
and hearing what was spoken,
leaped with joy in their hearts;
among them, there were those who attained the first path, the second path, or the third path;
those who left the home-life to enter the essentials and attained the status of Yìngzhēn;
those who gave rise to the aspiration for the unexcelled, correct, and true path;
and those who attained the stage of non-retrogression,
beyond calculation.
Those among the hungry ghosts, seeing the Buddha's light
and hearing what was spoken,
all became full and satisfied,
their bodies and minds pure,
free from all feverish afflictions;
they all gave rise to compassionate hearts,
revering the Buddha,
and immediately attained liberation,
being born among humans or devas.
Those among the animals,
seeing the Buddha's light,
their greed, desire, and the poison of anger
were all eliminated;
their deluded and darkened minds
immediately attained awakening;
they were all joyful
and faithfully revered the Buddha,
immediately attaining liberation
and being born among humans or devas.
Those in the hells,
seeing the Buddha's light—
where it was cold, it became warm;
where it was hot, it became cool and refreshing;
where there was suffering and pain,
they immediately found relief;
their bodies and minds leaped with joy,
and compassionately revering the Buddha,
they immediately attained liberation
and were born among humans or devas.
At that time, King Móhē Jiébīnníng
and the various kings of Jīndì,
having seen these transformations,
their hearts were filled with faith and submission;
distancing themselves from dust and leaving behind defilement, they attained the purity of the Dharma Eye,
and the eighteen thousand kings
all did so simultaneously.
In a brief moment,
the Buddha withdrew his spiritual power
and returned to his original form,
with the community of bhiksus
surrounding him before and behind.
The assembly of the kings of Jīndì
requested to leave the home-life,
and the Buddha immediately granted permission;
their beards and hair fell away on their own,
kasaya robes appeared on their bodies,
and as they contemplated the wonderful Dharma,
all attained the fruit of Āluóhàn.
Ānán said to the Buddha:
"This King of Jīndì,
what merit did he plant in the past
to be born into such noble prominence,
with majestic merit,
encountering the era of a Buddha,
and attaining the state of no-outflows?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Sentient beings receive their retributions based on their actions.
Long ago in the past,
there was the Buddha Jiāshè.
After his parinirvana,
there was an elder
who built a pagoda and shrine for him,
constructing halls and towers,
and providing the four kinds of offerings.
As time passed,
the pagoda crumbled,
and the bedding, clothing, and food
were also cut off.
The master of that house, the elder,
had a son who was a bhiksu,
who then went out to encourage and transform the people,
telling each of them to give a portion of their resources to repair the pagoda,
and he also prepared food, drink, and bedding.
The people were of one mind,
all making offerings together,
and they then made a vow:
'In future lives,
may we be wealthy, noble, and long-lived,
encounter a Buddha's appearance in the world,
hear the Dharma and attain realization,
with our deeds and rewards being fully fulfilled,
and causing all fruits to be perfected.'"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"The bhiksu who was the elder's son at that time
is now the King of Jīndì, Móhē Jiébīnníng.
Those people who received his teaching and transformation
are now these eighteen thousand kings."
When the Buddha preached this Dharma,
those in the great assembly who heard it
attained realization of the path;
they gave rise to the mind of non-retrogression,
accepted and upheld the ultimate teaching,
and joyfully put it into practice.
Thus have I heard:
at one time, the Fó was in the kingdom of Shèwèiguó, in the Jǐshù Jǐgūdúyuán.
At that time, King Bōsīnuì
had a high minister
named Líqímí.
His household was very wealthy,
and he had sired seven sons.
He sought wives for them,
and had already done so for six;
only the seventh son remained,
for whom he was about to seek a wife.
He thought to himself:
"I am old and frail,
with only one son left.
In taking a wife for him,
it is essential that she be exceptional."
At that time, this elder
had a close friend who was a Póluómén,
who came to visit him.
Consequently, Líqímí consulted him, saying:
"Now I wish to seek a marriage for my youngest son,
but I do not yet know where to look.
Since you have long
traveled through many kingdoms,
I now wish to trouble you
to search on my behalf.
If you see a girl who is upright, virtuous, and wise,
with a compatible temperament and lifespan,
and who would suit my son's wishes,
then we should seek her."
At that time, the Póluómén
immediately agreed.
He traveled everywhere looking for her,
and arrived at the kingdom of Tèchāshīlìguó,
where he saw five hundred young maidens
playing together in a group,
picking beautiful flowers
to use as adornments.
This Póluómén
followed and observed them.
Proceeding further,
they had to cross some shallow water.
All the girls
took off their leather sandals,
but among them was one girl
who alone did not take them off,
entering the water with her sandals on.
Proceeding further,
they subsequently came to a river.
The girls lifted their robes and then entered the water,
but only this one girl
alone entered with her robes down.
Walking forward into a forest,
the girls each climbed the trees to pick flowers.
At that time, this one girl
did not climb the trees herself,
but asked others for them,
and obtained a great many flowers.
At that time, the Póluómén
asked this girl, saying:
"I have a few doubts
and wish to ask you about them."
The girl replied:
"If you have doubts, then ask."
The Póluómén said:
"Earlier, when the girls
were about to enter the water,
they all took off their leather sandals,
but you alone did not.
For what reason was this?"
At that time, the girl answered:
"How very foolish you are!
The reason sandals are made
is precisely to protect the feet.
On land,
where the eyes can see,
thorns, shards, and stones
can be avoided.
But things are hidden beneath the water,
where the eyes cannot see;
should there be thorns or various venomous insects
that might harm one's feet,
that is why I did not take them off."
At that time, the Póluómén
asked again, saying:
"For what reason
did you enter the water with your robes down?"
At that time, the girl answered:
"A woman's body
has features that are either good or bad.
If one lifts one's robes to enter the water
and is seen by others,
if the features are good, it is fine,
but if they are not good, people will laugh.
For this reason,
I did not lift them."
At that time, the Póluómén
asked again, saying:
"For what cause
did you alone not climb the trees?"
The girl then answered:
"If I were to climb a tree,
should a branch break,
it would endanger one's body.
For this reason,
I simply did not climb."
This girl was the daughter of King Bōsīnuì's younger brother, Tánmóhēxiàn.
Tánmóhēxiàn had formerly fled to that kingdom because of a crime;
there in that land,
he had settled down and taken a wife,
and sired this daughter,
named Píshèlì.
At that time, the Póluómén,
hearing what the girl said,
knew she must be virtuous and capable,
so he asked the girl, saying:
"Are your parents still living?"
The girl replied:
"They are."
He then followed her to their gate
and asked to see them.
The girl went inside and told her father:
"There is a Póluómén outside
who wishes to see you, Father."
At that time, Tánmóhēxiàn came out to see him.
After the greetings were finished,
he spoke to him, saying:
"That girl from before—
is she your daughter?"
He replied:
"She is."
"Is she betrothed yet?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
The Póluómén said:
"In the kingdom of Shèwèiguó,
there is a high minister
named Líqímí.
Do you know him?"
He replied:
"He is an old acquaintance."
The Póluómén said:
"This Líqímí's
youngest son is upright and intelligent.
He wishes to seek your daughter for marriage.
May this be so?"
Tánmóhēxiàn said:
"His is a noble family,
originally a match for ours.
If he truly desires her,
I have no intention to refuse."
Having received permission,
they set a date together.
At that time, there was a traveling party
going to Shèwèiguó.
At that time, the Póluómén
immediately wrote a letter to Líqímí
explaining the circumstances.
After the elder heard this,
he prepared the betrothal gifts, carriages, and horses,
and went to the kingdom of Tèchāshīlìguó.
When he was nearing his arrival,
he first sent a messenger ahead.
At that time, Tánmóhēxiàn received them with great respect and hospitality,
promptly hosting a banquet
to betroth his daughter to him.
After all the matters were concluded,
they were to return to Shèwèiguó.
At that time, this girl's mother,
in front of everyone,
instructed her daughter, saying:
"From this day forward,
always wear fine clothes,
constantly eat delicious food,
and gaze into the mirror every day;
do not let these practices cease."
The girl then knelt long
and respectfully accepted the instructions.
When Líqímí heard this,
he secretly felt resentful.
"In a person's life,
suffering and joy are not fixed.
How can fine clothes and delicious food
be constant?
To constantly gaze into a mirror
is also unreasonable."
Although he had these thoughts,
it was difficult to ask about it.
The guests and hosts took their leave of each other,
and then they departed.
The entire company, great and small,
set out on the road to return to their kingdom.
While on the way,
there was an inn
with eaves hanging on all four sides,
which was extremely cool and pleasant.
Those who arrived first rested beneath it,
and when the daughter-in-law arrived later,
She spoke to her father-in-law:
"We cannot stay here;
go outside quickly."
Her father-in-law did not disobey her
and went out into the open.
Several people nearby
refused to leave.
At that time, there were elephants and horses;
their bodies were itchy, so they rubbed themselves against the pillars.
The house then collapsed
and crushed the servants underneath.
Then Lí Qí Mí
thought to himself:
"That I have now escaped death
is due to this daughter-in-law."
His feeling of respect
became even more profound.
He then prepared the carriage
and proceeded on the road to return home.
They reached a large ravine
where the grass was lush and the water beautiful.
Everyone rested the carriage
and stayed by the ravine.
The daughter-in-law arrived later
and said to them:
"Staying here is not pleasant;
quickly go up to the bank."
They followed her words
and rested far from the ravine.
In a short while,
clouds arose,
thunder roared and rain fell,
pouring down in torrents
and flooding the ravine.
Then Lí Qí Mí
thought again:
"Today we
have escaped death for a second time;
because of this daughter-in-law,
we have saved our lives."
He again ordered the carriage prepared
and advanced along the road.
Having reached their home country,
relatives and neighbors
all came to congratulate and inquire.
The Elder was joyful
and set out provisions
for mutual entertainment.
After the whole day,
the guests departed.
At this time, the Elder
summoned all his daughters-in-law
and told them:
"I am now old in years
and weary of many affairs.
Regarding the household items and vessels,
I wish to entrust them.
Among you all,
who can manage the storehouse and hold the keys for me?"
The six eldest daughters-in-law all declined, saying they were not capable.
The seventh one said she could take the responsibility.
Then the Elder
took all the storehouse keys
and entrusted them to her.
Having received the order,
she was diligent and cautious without slackness.
Every morning she rose early,
swept the halls and rooms,
and once the cooking was finished,
she first fed her father-in-law and mother-in-law and the various children,
and then fed the slaves and servants.
She assigned tasks to the workers,
and then ate herself;
this became her routine.
Her father-in-law saw her loyalty and respect were unlike common people,
and wondered why she did not follow her mother's previous instructions,
so he asked her:
"When you came before,
you were instructed by your mother:
'Wear good clothes and eat good food,
and let the sun shine on the bright mirror.'
What is the meaning of those things?
You may speak of it."
The daughter-in-law knelt
and answered in detail:
"Regarding what my mother enjoined,
as for wearing 'good clothes,'
she meant the large garments on the body,
teaching me to care for them
and always keep them clean,
so that during gatherings with guests,
they would look fresh and wonderful.
As for the 'good food' she ordered,
it did not mean sweet or fatty food;
she taught me to eat late when hungry,
for then coarse or fine food would all be delicious.
As for the 'bright mirror,'
it is not a mirror of bronze or iron;
she taught me to rise early to sweep inside and out
and to straighten the beds and mats,
making sure they are clean.
These are the matters my mother entrusted to me;
it is as such."
When the father-in-law heard this,
he knew she had wonderful talent.
His feelings of respect for her
were even more than before.
He entrusted all the household items
to her
and was joyful and at ease,
with no more worries.
At that time, a flock of wild geese
flew to an island in the sea to eat non-glutinous rice.
Having eaten their fill,
they flew while carrying stalks in their beaks, passing over the king's palace and dropping them in front of the hall.
People saw them,
took them, and offered them to the King.
The King saw they were rare and fine
and surely suitable for medicine.
He ordered the seeds to be kept and not discarded,
and distributed them to his ministers, ordering each to cultivate them.
Lí Qí Mí also received a small amount and took it home,
ordering it to be planted.
The daughter-in-law received it,
led the servants
to prepare the fields,
and sowed the seeds;
they grew abundantly and yielded a great harvest of grain.
As for the others who planted them,
they missed the proper timing and none grew.
Then the King's wife
suddenly became seriously ill.
He summoned the physicians to ask for the cause and treatment.
Among them, a physician said:
"One must use the non-glutinous rice from the sea island to make food;
only by eating it can she recover."
The King remembered:
"Previously I obtained the seeds
and gave them to people to cultivate;
now I should check if there are any."
He summoned the ministers
and asked them:
"The rice I ordered to be planted before,
did it ripen?
Today it is urgently needed to treat a serious illness."
The ministers each explained what happened;
some said it didn't grow,
others said mice ate it.
Lí Qí Mí returned home and asked:
"The rice planted before,
did it yield fruit?
I want to give it to the King to treat the Queen's illness."
The daughter-in-law replied:
"Our house has plenty;
if used for medicine, it is enough for the whole country,
not just for one person."
Then Lí Qí Mí
sent it to the King.
It was immediately used to make food
for the Queen.
After the Queen ate it,
her illness was cured.
The King was very happy
and gave great rewards.
At that time, the two kingdoms of Tèchāshīlì and Shèwèi
had a grudge against each other
and were often not in harmony.
Then the King of Tèchāshīlì
wished to test if Shèwèi had sagacious wisdom.
He sent an envoy to the kingdom of Shèwèi,
bringing two horses.
These were a mother and child,
but their shape and coat color
were identical without difference.
To be able to distinguish them would be truly excellent.
The King and his ministers
could not distinguish them.
Lí Qí Mí
returned home from the palace,
and the daughter-in-law asked:
"Is there any news?"
Her father-in-law answered according to what he had seen.
The daughter-in-law said:
"This is easy to know,
why worry?
Just take good grass
and offer it to them together.
The one that is the mother
will push the grass toward the other;
the one that is the child
will snatch and eat it."
Lí Qí Mí immediately went to tell the King.
The King did as she said
and tested them with grass.
It happened just as she planned,
and the mother and child were distinguished.
He then said to the envoy:
"This is the mother horse,
and that is her foal."
The envoy replied:
"Indeed, the words just brought
are without error."
The King was greatly delighted
and doubled his titles and rewards.
At that time, the messenger who had come
returned to his own country
and reported all the matters in detail.
Then King Tèchāshīlì
sent another messenger
to deliver two snakes,
identical in girth and length.
"If you can distinguish the male from the female,
that would also be excellent."
King Bōsīni
and his ministers
were unable to identify them.
Then Líqímí
returned home and asked his daughter-in-law:
"What about this?"
The daughter-in-law replied:
"Take a piece of fine felt
and spread it on the ground.
Take these two snakes
and place them on the felt.
If it is the female,
she will remain quiet and not move.
If it is the male,
he will be restless and unsettled.
How is this known?
The nature of a female
is to love fine and smooth things;
upon finding softness, she becomes attached
and does not wish to move.
The nature of a male is stiff;
he will toss and turn without peace.
Deducing by this,
it can be sufficiently known."
After the Elder heard this,
he immediately went to tell the King.
The King followed the plan
and tested it at once.
It was indeed as she had said,
and he clearly identified them.
He said to the messenger:
"This is the male and this is the female."
The messenger immediately replied:
"It is indeed so, not false."
The King was very joyful
and bestowed great treasures.
Then that King
sent a piece of wood,
exactly ten feet long,
with the root and tip being identical.
There were no knots or marks of knife or axe.
He said to him:
"If you can distinguish the top and bottom of this wood,
it would also be a great delight
beyond measure."
The King and his ministers
were unable to identify it.
Then Líqímí
again asked his daughter-in-law.
The daughter-in-law replied:
"This matter is easy.
Simply take the wood
and place it in water.
The root will naturally sink,
and the tip will float on top."
After the Elder heard this,
he again went to tell the King.
The King used her words
and tested it.
It was indeed as she planned;
the sinking and floating ends were distinct.
He said to the messenger:
"The floating part is the top,
and the sinking part is the root."
The messenger replied:
"Truly it is as you have reasoned."
The King was increasingly happy
and gave rewards once again.
The messenger returned to his country
and reported all the circumstances.
When that King heard it,
his heart was convinced.
He sent another mission
along with precious treasures,
and further said:
"In the Great King's country,
there are indeed wise and enlightened people.
From now on,
we shall cultivate righteousness and friendship."
King Bōsīni's
feelings were doubly elated.
He summoned Líqímí
and asked him:
"Regarding all these recent matters,
how did you know the answers?"
Líqímí said:
"It was not my own understanding;
it was but the wisdom and discernment of my daughter-in-law."
After the King heard this,
he deeply increased his respect and joy.
He honored the daughter-in-law
by appointing her as the King's sister.
After a short time,
the daughter-in-law became pregnant.
When her days were full,
she gave birth to thirty-two eggs.
From each egg
a boy was born.
Their physical forms and countenances
were dignified and extraordinary.
As they grew up,
they were matchless in bravery and strength.
The strength of one man
could rival a thousand.
Their parents loved them,
and the entire country respected and feared them.
Later, marriages were arranged for them,
and all were fully completed.
They were all daughters of the noble and worthy within the kingdom.
At that time, Píshèlí's
faith was awakened and enlightened.
She invited the Buddha and the Sangha to her home for offerings.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them,
and all the family members
attained the stage of Sūtuóhuán,
except for the youngest son,
who had not yet attained the fruit of the path.
Once, riding a white elephant,
he wanted to go out for recreation.
Outside the gate was a moat,
both deep and wide.
Over the moat
was a large wooden bridge.
At that time, this young man
had just reached the bridgehead.
At that moment, the son of a minister arrived from outside in a carriage.
They met in the middle of the bridge.
Each, relying on his noble lineage,
would not yield to the other.
Píshèlí's son
then harbored anger.
From atop the elephant,
he leaned down,
seized the minister's son and his carriage,
and threw them into the moat.
His body was wounded and broken,
and all his joints were in pain.
He returned home weeping
and told his father:
"Píshèlí's son
has wantonly insulted me,
injured my body,
and the pain is like this."
When the father heard this,
he was greatly distressed.
He consoled his son, saying:
"That man's strength is robust,
and he is a relative of the kingdom.
It is difficult to contend with him.
We must think of a secret plan to avenge this grievance."
He then took the seven treasures
and made thirty-two horsewhips.
Using fine, pure steel,
he fashioned blades and placed them inside.
To each of the thirty-two men,
he presented one,
and said to them:
"You are all young
and by nature enjoy sport.
Therefore I have made these whips
to give to you.
I hope you will accept them
and always keep them in your hands."
All the men were joyful
and accepted them.
At that time, the law of the kingdom was that
when meeting the King,
etiquette forbade carrying a blade.
Thereupon the minister,
having seen that they had accepted and always held them,
went to the King
and slandered them deeply,
saying:
"Píshèlí's thirty-two sons
are in their prime and strong;
one man can rival a thousand.
They now harbor rebellious designs
and are plotting to harm the King."
Although the King heard this,
he still did not believe it.
The minister again told the King:
"The matter is truly not false;
there is proof.
They have each made sharp blades
and placed them inside their horsewhips.
Deducing from this,"
"The matter is clear enough."
The King immediately asked to see it,
and it was indeed as had been said.
The King's mind then believed it
and thought it must be so.
He selected strong men
and stationed them inside the palace;
he summoned the sons one by one
and killed them inside.
Taking the thirty-two heads,
he placed them in a box,
tied it up and sealed it,
and sent it to his sister.
On that very day,
Píshèlí
had invited Fó and the Sēng to her home to provide offerings.
Seeing the King send a box,
she thought he was sending offerings to assist with the preparations
and wanted to open it to look.
Shìzūn told her,
"Wait a moment and do not open it;
you must wait until the meal is finished."
After they had eaten their fill,
he then commanded her to sit
and spoke the Dharma for her:
"This body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.
Life is full of danger and fear
and cannot last long.
It is bound by many afflictions
and its bitterness and pain are hard to calculate.
Attachment and love lead to separation and mutual grieving,
which vainly exhausts the body and consciousness
and is of no benefit to the Path.
Only the wise
can liberate themselves from this evil."
At that time, Píshèlí
suddenly awakened in spirit
and attained the Ānàhán Path.
She joyfully joined her palms
and said to Shìzūn,
"I only pray for your compassion!
Grant me four wishes:
First, for all sick Bǐqiū,
provide sufficient medicine, soup, and food according to their illness.
Second, for the Bǐqiū who care for the sick, also provide them with food.
Third, for Bǐqiū arriving from afar,
provide offerings to them first.
Fourth, for Bǐqiū going on long journeys,
provide them with provisions.
Why is this?
For sick Bǐqiū,
because they lack medicine, soup, and good food,
their illnesses are difficult to cure
or they may even lose their lives.
For Bǐqiū attending the sick,
because they lack food,
they must leave to beg for food
at irregular times.
What the patient needs might be neglected or mistaken,
leading to frustration and anger
and making the illness hard to heal.
For this reason,
food should be provided to them.
All Bǐqiū arriving from distant lands
arrive in a strange territory for the first time
and have no acquaintances.
If they go to beg for food,
they might encounter vicious dogs
or meet wicked people
who might become angry
and cause them harm or humiliation.
For this reason,
they should be given food first.
For Bǐqiū departing for afar,
they need companions;
because they lack provisions,
they might not keep up with their companions.
The roads are long and dangerous
and full of many poisonous beasts;
if they must travel alone, they may face danger.
For this reason,
I should provide for them."
At that time, Shìzūn, hearing Píshèlí request these four wishes,
praised her, saying,
"Excellent, excellent!
According to your wishes,
the merit is vast and great,
no different from making offerings to Fó."
He then, with the assembly of Sēng,
returned to Qǐhuán.
After Shìzūn had left,
she opened the box and looked at it.
The thirty-two heads
were all inside the box.
Because her attachments had been severed,
she did not give rise to distress,
but only spoke these words:
"How painful, how sad!
In human life there is death,
and it does not last long.
Driven through the five realms,
why must the suffering be like this?"
The thirty-two sons'
families and kinsmen on their wives' side,
hearing of this matter,
were filled with extreme anger.
They all shouted together,
"The Great King is unprincipled
and has unjustly killed good people!"
They gathered soldiers and horses,
wishing to take revenge.
The troops gathered like clouds
and surrounded the royal palace.
At that time, the King was terrified
and retreated to Fó's place.
When the people heard of this,
they immediately led the troops and horses
to surround Qǐhuán.
At that time, Ānán,
hearing that Bōsīnì wáng
had killed Píshèlí's thirty-two sons
and that the wives' clans wished to take revenge,
knelt for a long time with palms together
and said to Shìzūn,
"What was the cause and condition
for the thirty-two sons
to be killed by the King?"
Shìzūn told him,
"Píshèlí's thirty-two sons
were not killed by the King only today;
the thirty-two of them once died all at once.
Now listen well
and keep it in your heart;
I shall tell it to you."
Ānán said,
"Yes."
Fó told Ānán,
"In the distant past, long ago,
these thirty-two people
were close friends with one another.
They discussed together
and stole someone else's cow.
At that time in the kingdom,
there was an old mother
who had no children
and was solitary and poor.
Then the thieves
went to her house
wishing to kill the cow together.
The old mother was delighted
and prepared the firewood, water, and boiling tools.
When the knife was about to fall, the cow knelt and begged for its life.
The men's intent was fierce,
and they insisted on killing it.
The cow then made a vow:
'You kill me now,
but in future lifetimes,
I will not let you go.
Even if you attain the Path,
I still will not release you.'
Having finished the vow,
it was then killed.
The men roasted and boiled it
and competed to eat it.
Because of her turn, the old mother
also ate her fill
and said joyfully,
'I have always hosted guests,
but today is the best.' "
Fó told Ānán,
"The cow at that time
is now Bōsīnì wáng.
The cow thieves at that time
are now Píshèlí's thirty-two sons.
The old mother at that time
is now Píshèlí.
Due to this retribution,
for five hundred lifetimes,
they have always been killed by him,
even until now.
That old mother,
because of her shared joy,
for five hundred lifetimes,
has always served as their mother
and harbored extreme distress.
Now that she has met me,
she has finally attained realization of the Path."
Ānán joined his palms
and spoke to Fó again,
"What merit did they further cultivate
to be so wealthy, powerful, and strong?"
Fó told Ānán,
"In the past, during the time of Jiāyè Fó,
there was an old mother
who believed in and respected the Sānbǎo.
Her family was very wealthy.
She collected various fragrances,
mixed them with oil,
and wished to go and coat a stūpa.
On her way there,"
[She] met thirty-two people,
and consequently encouraged them:
“I wish to coat the pagoda with oil;
you may assist me.
You shall obtain blessings and merit;
in every lifetime you are born,
you will be upright and strong.”
At that time, the thirty-two people
happily went together.
After the coating of the pagoda was finished,
each spoke these words:
“Because of this elderly mother,
we have been able to plant the seeds of merit.
We vow that wherever we are born,
we shall be honored and wealthy,
she shall always be our mother,
and we shall be her sons,
never to be separated.
May we see the Buddha and hear the Dharma,
and swiftly attain the fruits of the path.”
The elderly mother was delighted
and consented to this.
From then on,
for five hundred lifetimes,
they were always born into honor and wealth.
That elderly mother of that time
is now Píshèlì.
Those thirty-two people of that time
are now the thirty-two sons.”
At that time, the entire army,
hearing what the Buddha said,
had their hearts of anger cease,
and they spoke these words:
“What the Great King executed
was not done without cause;
these people planted the seeds themselves
and now receive their retribution.
For the killing of a single cow,
it is still like this.
Bōsīniwáng
is our master;
how could we harbor malice
and wish to harm him?”
They immediately cast aside their weapons,
threw themselves before the king,
and begged for mercy and repented their faults.
The king was also relieved
and did not investigate their crimes.
At that time, the Shìzūn
consequently spoke the various teachings extensively for the fourfold assembly:
that good karma should be cultivated
and evil actions should be abandoned,
expounding and differentiating the wonderful Dharma of the Sìdì.
Those in the assembly who heard it all attained the realization of the path,
accepted and upheld the Buddha’s teaching,
and joyfully practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Fó was in the Zhúyuán of Luóyuèqí.
At that time, the Worthy Ānán
rose from his seat,
adjusted his robes, knelt down, and joined his palms,
then came forward to address the Fó, saying:
“Āruò Jiāochénrú
and his four companions—
what blessings did they have in the past,
and by what causes and conditions
when the Rúlái appeared in the world,
were they the only ones to first hear the initial beating of the Dharma drum,
and the first specifically to taste the Dharma flavor of ambrosia?
I only wish you would show compassion
and explain this fully.”
Then the Shìzūn
told Ānán:
“These five people,
in a former life,
were the first to eat my flesh,
which led them to find peace;
for this reason today,
they are the first to receive the food of the Dharma,
by which they have attained liberation.”
Then Ānán addressed the Fó again:
“Eating flesh in a former life—
what were the causes and conditions for this?
I wish for you to fully reveal and show them.”
The Fó told him:
“In the distant past,
immeasurable and innumerable Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Shètóuluójiànníng.
He ruled over Yánfútí,
with its eighty-four thousand kingdoms,
sixty thousand mountains and rivers,
eight billion villages,
and twenty thousand wives and ladies-in-waiting.
The king possessed compassion
and cared for all;
among all types of people,
none failed to receive his support.
At that time in the kingdom,
the star Huǒxīng appeared.
A physiognomist soon saw it
and told the king:
‘If Huǒxīng appears,
there will be a drought without rain for twelve years.
Now that there is this omen,
what should be done?’
When the king heard these words,
he was greatly worried:
‘If there is such a disaster,
what will become of the people and things?
If the people’s lives are not saved,
the kingdom will no longer exist.’
He immediately gathered his ministers
to deliberate together.
The ministers all said:
‘We should go to all the kingdoms to count the current population,
and also calculate the grain currently in the granaries,
to determine the exact measures
and how much each person can receive over twelve years.’
The king followed their advice
and immediately issued an order,
urgently commanding the calculation.
When the total calculation was finished,
for all the people,
each would receive one shēng per day,
which was still insufficient.
From then on,
the people were hungry,
and those who died were many.
The king thought to himself:
‘What plan should I devise to save the people?’
Thereupon, with his wives and ladies-in-waiting,
he went out to travel through the gardens and parks,
arriving at each to rest.
The king waited until everyone was asleep,
then rose from his seat,
bowed toward the four directions,
and made a vow:
‘Now the people of this kingdom
are famished and without food.
I shall give up this body
and wish to become a great fish,
so that with the flesh of my body,
I may satisfy and save everyone.’
He then climbed to the top of a tree
and threw himself to the ground.
He died immediately
and, in a great river,
was reborn as a transformed fish.
Its body was long and large,
five hundred yóuxún in length.
At that time in the kingdom,
there were five woodworkers
who each took an axe
and went to the riverbank
to cut timber.
That fish saw them
and immediately spoke in human language, telling them:
‘If you are hungry
and need food,
come and take my flesh;
if you eat your fill,
you may also carry some away.
You now first eat my flesh
and are filled,
and later when I become a Fó,
I shall save and liberate you with the food of the Dharma.
You should also tell everyone in the kingdom, great and small,
that those who need food
should all come to take it.’
The five people were joyful
and immediately each cut and took some,
ate their fill and carried some home,
and then told the people of the kingdom about it in detail.
Thereupon the people
told one another,
and throughout Yánfútí,
they all gathered together
to eat its flesh.
When the flesh on one side was exhausted,
it immediately turned its body,
and they took from the other side.
When that too was eaten up,
the flesh grew back in the original place,
and it turned its body again to give to them.
Turning over and over like this,
it constantly used its body’s flesh
to provide for and save everyone
for twelve years.
All those sentient beings
who ate its flesh
developed a mind of compassion,
and after they died,
they were reborn in the heavens.
Ānán!
If you wish to know who King Shètóuluójiànníng was then,
it was my own self.
The five woodworkers of that time
who were the first to eat my flesh
are the five Bǐqiū including Jiāochénrú now.
Those many people who ate the flesh later
are the eighty thousand devas
and the various disciples who have attained deliverance.
At that time,
I first used my body’s flesh
to satisfy those five people
so they could be saved and survive;
for this reason today I first spoke the Dharma
to deliver those five people,
using a small portion of the flesh of my Dharma-body
to remove their suffering of the hunger and exhaustion of the three poisons.”
The Worthy Ānán and all those in the assembly,
hearing what the Fó said,
were both sorrowful and joyful,
and they received and practiced it with reverence.
Xiányú Jīng, Scroll Seven
Xiányú Jīng, Scroll Eight
Translated by the Shāmén Huìjué and others of Liángzhōu during the Yuán Wèi dynasty in Gāochāng Jùn.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in Luóyuèqí at the Zhúlín Jīngshè.
The Huìmìng Ānán,
sitting within the Bamboo Grove,
reflected within his mind:
“The appearance of the Rúlái in the world
is most extraordinary and unique!
Now all the disciples,
having received the Buddha’s grace,
regarding the four offerings,
are lacking in nothing.
Each has attained tranquility
and reached the end of suffering;
all the world,
its kings, ministers, and people,
have also gained great benefit.
Encountering the Sānbǎo,
the people are at peace and happy,
all thinking this is due to the majesty and power of the Shìzūn.”
Having had this thought,
he rose from his seat
and went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Shìzūn
was for the fourfold assembly
extensively preaching the wondrous Dharma.
The Huìmìng Ānán
stepped forward and adjusted his robes,
bared his right shoulder,
placed his right knee on the ground,
and knelt with palms joined,
speaking to the Buddha of the thoughts he had while in the grove.
The Buddha told Ānán:
“It is as you say.
The appearance of the Rúlái in the world
is truly extraordinary!
It causes all sentient beings to gain benefit.
Furthermore, Ānán!
The Rúlái, the Perfectly Awakened One,
has not only blessed and benefited sentient beings today;
in past lives
he also brought benefit.”
Ānán said to the Buddha:
“I do not know,
Shìzūn!
In past lives,
regarding the benefit of sentient beings,
how was it then?”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“In the distant past, immeasurable Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí, there were four rivers
and two great kings.
One king was named Póluótípó,
which in Jìn means Fàntiān.
He alone controlled three rivers,
and his people were numerous
yet weak.
The other king was named Fáshédátí,
which in Jìn means Jīngāngjù.
He possessed only one river,
and his people were few,
yet the people of that country were all brave and strong.
At that time, Jīngāngjù,
while in the main hall,
sat alone and reflected:
‘As for me now,
my troops are brave and fierce,
yet the water I have is little.
That country is weak but dominates three rivers.
I should now send an envoy to peacefully request one river.
If he gives it to me,
we shall be close and friendly;
if our countries have good things,
we will exchange them as gifts;
if there are hardships,
we will come to each other’s rescue.
If he will not give it,
then I shall use force to seize it.’
Having had this thought,
he summoned his ministers to discuss the matter.
The ministers all said:
‘Now is exactly the time.’
They immediately sent an envoy
to the kingdom of Fàntiān,
and with the king's full intent
proclaimed it to Fànwáng.
When Fànwáng heard this,
he also reflected:
‘My country is prosperous and substantial,
and the people are numerous.
Moreover, these borders
were possessed by my father the king
who passed them down to me.
As for a contest of strength,
I am not inferior to him.’
Having had this thought,
he replied to the envoy:
‘This land today
was not acquired by me,
but it was my father the king
who passed it down to me.
As for me now,
my strength is not less than yours.
If you wish for a decision by force,
I am not afraid.’
The envoy returned to his own country
and reported fully to the king.
The king immediately assembled his army
and attacked the kingdom of Fàntiān.
They fought one engagement,
and Fàntiān’s army was broken.
Pursuing them from behind,
they reached the edge of the city.
The people were terrified and withdrew;
they dared not come out again.
The ministers together
all gathered
and went to the place of Fànwáng,
all of one mind,
and said to the Great King:
‘The other country’s troops are strong,
and our country’s are weak.
By begrudging one river,
we have now brought about this defeat.
If it continues like this,
we fear we will lose the kingdom.
We only wish you would be open-minded
and give them one river
to become close and friendly;
that will be enough to ensure safety.’
The king’s mind then opened,
and he agreed to the ministers’ wish.
He immediately sent an envoy
to the enemy’s army
to say to their king:
‘Our neighboring countries,
why should we commit evil?
The river you requested,
I now give to you.
I shall also give my daughter to be your lady;
if our countries have special items,
we will exchange them as gifts;
in times of urgent difficulty or danger,
we will come to each other’s rescue.’
At that time, Jīngāngjù
followed the proposal,
immediately welcomed the daughter,
and appointed her as his lady.
Each reconciled,
and he turned his army back to his own country.
“After some time,
the king’s lady
realized she was pregnant.
After conceiving,
there was always a natural great canopy of the seven treasures
constantly above her body;
whether sitting, lying, walking, or standing, it never left her.
When ten months were complete,
she gave birth to a boy,
whose body was purple-gold in color,
with hair of deep blue-black,
and radiant features that were bright and prominent,
having few equals in the world.
Once the child had left the womb,
the canopy remained above him.
They summoned many physiognomists
to examine the child.
The physiognomists looked closely,
raised their hands, and exclaimed:
‘Excellent, excellent!’
With different mouths but one voice, they said to the Great King:
‘Looking now at the prince,
his virtue and power are incomparable,
his human features are complete and perfect,
and he is rare in the world.’
The king and his ministers
were overcome with joy.
They immediately told the physiognomists
to establish a name for him.
According to the laws of the country at that time,
names were given based on two matters
for the creation of names:
first, auspicious omens;
second, the constellations.
The physiognomists said to the king:
‘Regarding this prince,
since he entered the womb,
what kind of omens have there been?’
The king answered them, saying:
‘There has been a canopy of the seven treasures
constantly above him.’
They then gave him the name Chàluójiālì,
which in Jìn means Gàishì,
and with various wonderful offerings
they served and attended him at all times.
When he reached adulthood,
his father’s life came to an end.
After the funeral was completed,
the various lesser kings and ministers
together established Gàishì
as the Great King.
Having governed for several years,
he went out to travel and observe.
Seeing all the people toiling and suffering at plowing and planting,
he asked his attendants, saying:
“The people of my country are numerous;
why are they made to do such various kinds of labor?”
A minister replied to the king, saying:
“The state takes the people as its foundation,
and the people take grain as their life.
If it were not so,
the people's lives would not be sustained;
if the people's lives are not sustained,
the state will then perish.”
The king then spoke, saying:
“If my merit corresponds to being a king,
let my people obtain spontaneous grain,
and never again perform this work.”
Once he had finished speaking,
for all the people,
the granaries and storehouses filled themselves,
and all kinds of miscellaneous grains
were completely available as they desired.
After some more time had passed,
he again went out to travel,
and saw the people of the country
gathering firewood, drawing water,
and performing the labor of pounding and grinding.
He again asked his ministers, saying:
“Now all these people
are still toiling and suffering?
Why is this so?”
A minister said to the king:
“By the grace of the king,
they have obtained spontaneous grain,
but grain cannot be eaten raw;
it must be prepared and cooked.
Therefore, the common people
prepare and make food provisions.”
The king spoke again, saying:
“If my merit and virtue
should make me a king,
let all the people in my country,
whenever they wish to eat,
have spontaneous food
constantly appear before them.”
Once he had finished speaking,
the entire territory obtained spontaneous food.
After more time had passed,
the king again went out to travel and observe.
He saw everyone busily engaged in their duties,
spinning, weaving, cutting, and sewing,
to prepare and make clothing provisions.
The king asked the ministers, saying:
“All these people!
For what reason
are they toiling and working so hard?”
A minister said to the king:
“By the grace of the Great King,
they have obtained spontaneous food,
but now they are laboring
to prepare and make clothing.”
The king spoke again, saying:
“If my merit and virtue
should make me a king,
make all the trees in my country produce spontaneous clothing.”
As soon as these words were spoken,
the various trees in the country
all produced marvelous clothing,
extremely fine and soft,
in blue, yellow, red, and white,
according to each person's preference.
After some more time had passed,
the king again went out traveling,
and saw the people each competing to make various musical instruments.
The king again asked the ministers:
“The people of my country,
for what reason
are they toiling and busily working?”
A minister said to the king:
“All these people,
by the grace of the Great King,
have clothing and food spontaneously,
and each has obtained peace and stability.
They now require music
to amuse and enjoy themselves,
and that is why they are now crafting musical instruments.”
The king then spoke, saying:
“If I have merit
and should be a king,
let all the trees in my country
have all kinds of musical instruments—
drums, zithers, and harps,
pipas and konghous—
everything that is needed,
all according to their wishes.”
After some more time had passed,
the various kings, ministers, and people
all came to pay their respects and offer congratulations,
occurring just as it was time for the king to eat.
At that time, the king immediately invited them
to stay and share food and drink.
At that time, the various ministers,
having received the king's food,
complete with a hundred flavors,
all spoke together, saying:
“The food in our homes
is thin and lacking in flavor,
but now that we have received the king's food,
its delicious taste is extraordinary.”
The king told them:
“You, my ministers and people,
if you wish to always have food like mine,
by using the time of my meal,
all who eat shall obtain such food.”
He immediately commanded the officials:
“When the time for my meal arrives,
always strike a large drum
to let all the people hear and know,
so that by eating at the time of my meal,
they shall obtain an offering of a hundred flavors of superior excellence.”
From then onward,
drums were struck whenever it was time to eat,
and all the people,
hearing the sound and thinking of food,
had superior delicacies of a hundred flavors
spontaneously appear before them.
The happiness and joy of the people
cannot be fully described.
At that time, King Fàntiān
sent an envoy to the kingdom of King Gàishì,
saying to Gàishì:
“When your father was alive,
I took the river water
and gave it to your father.
Now that your father has passed away,
it should be returned to me.”
Then King Gàishì
replied to the envoy, saying:
“My territory now
as well as the river water
were not by my power
nor forcibly obtained from you.
However, as I am king,
I do not burden my people or their property.
This is but a small matter;
it should be put aside for later,
until I must meet your king face to face,
and then the essentials of the territory shall be fully explained.”
The envoy returned to the kingdom,
and reported everything to the king.
The king agreed with his intention,
and they set a date to meet.
When the appointed day arrived,
the two kings both advanced,
surrounded by their armies,
great in number and beyond count.
Each established a large camp
on one side of the river.
The two kings boarded a boat
to meet in the middle of the river.
When King Fàntiān
first saw Gàishì,
his body's complexion was dazzling,
like a mountain of purple gold.
His hair was glossy and shining,
like dark blue lapis lazuli.
His eyes were broad and long,
rarely found among men.
Respect arose from within him,
and he thought he was Fàntiān.
Having exchanged greetings,
they sat together in one place,
discussing their two territories
and debating the matter of the water.
Gàishì replied:
“The people of my country,
what they desire is spontaneous,
and they have neither the toil of paying taxes nor royal labor.”
Before he had finished speaking,
the time for the meal had arrived;
in King Gàishì's army,
the drums were struck to eat.
At that time, King Fàntiān
became very terrified,
thinking they intended to seize and take him to be killed.
In his restless fear, he stood up to apologize for his faults,
with his limbs spread out
and his belly striking the ground in front of him.
Gàishì stood up himself
to console him and make him sit down again.
He then said to him:
“Great King!
Why are you terrified like this?
When it is time for my army to eat,
the drums are always struck.
The reason for this
is that this is the time I eat,
and by using the time of my meal,
all receive an offering of superior delicacies of a hundred flavors.”
Then King Fàntiān again rose and joined his palms,
Bái Gài Shì said:
“I only wish, Great King!
That you would universally oversee and protect me and my countrymen,
wishing that all would submit,
and let all the common people receive your grace.”
Thereupon Gài Shì,
ruling over Yánfútí
and all the people,
all attained peace and happiness.
“After ascending the throne,
while residing in the main hall,
the various ministers and officials
and the imperial guards stood in attendance.
When the sun first rose,
a Golden Wheel Treasure came from the East.
The King saw it from afar,
and immediately descended from his throne,
placed his right knee on the ground,
and facing the location of the wheel,
beckoned three times with his hand.
The wheel then arrived;
its thousand spokes were complete,
and its light and color were brilliant.
The King told it:
‘If I am to be a Wheel-Turning King,
then abide in the place that accords with the Dharma,
and stay within it.’
Thereupon the Wheel Treasure
stayed in the air before the King,
the wheel being seven Duōluó trees from the ground;
the Elephant Treasure,
the Divine Pearl,
the Jade Woman,
the Minister of War,
and the Minister of the Treasury Treasure
arrived in succession.
At that time, King Gài Shì was complete in the Seven Treasures,
governing the Four Under-Heavens,
and all sentient beings
received the King’s favor and virtue,
doing as they pleased.
The King taught them all to practice the Ten Good Deeds,
and after their lives ended,
they all attained birth in the heavens.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“At that time, was King Chàluójiālì
some other person?
He was my own self.
The father king at that time, Fázhédǎtí,
is now my father, King Jìngfàn.
The mother at that time
is now my mother, Móhēmóyé.
Because I had compassion for sentient beings in the past
and always used wealth and the Dharma to gather them,
through these causes and conditions,
I naturally achieved Buddhahood,
the uniquely honored of the Three Realms,
with none equal to me.
For this reason,
all sentient beings
should all practice great compassion and bring benefit to others.”
At that time, Ānán again said to the Buddha:
“I am uncertain,
World-Honored One!
In past ages,
King Chàluójiālì, the Wheel-Turning Holy King,
by what causes and conditions did he obtain such immeasurable merit,
and when he first entered his mother’s womb, a jeweled canopy followed to cover him?”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“In the distant past,
immeasurable Āsēngqí Jié ago,
in this Yánfútí,
in the kingdom of Bōluónài,
on Xiānrén Shān,
there was a Pìzhīfó
who always stayed and lived on the mountain.
At one time, the Pìzhīfó,
suffering from physical disharmony,
went to ask a physician.
The physician said:
‘You have a wind-related illness;
you should consume milk.’
At that time in that kingdom,
there was a Sàbó
named Ālìyēmìluó,
which in the Jìn language is Shèngyǒu.
At that time, the Pìzhīfó
went to his house,
explained the cause of his illness,
and begged milk from him.
The Sàbó was joyful
and invited him to receive offerings,
providing him with milk daily
for three months.
After the three months were finished,
the physical illness was cured.
Moved by his good intentions
and wishing to let the host obtain great benefits,
he leaped into the air,
sitting, lying, walking, and standing,
his body emitting water and fire,
sometimes manifesting a large body filling the air,
and again manifesting a small one entering the space within an autumn hair;
in such various ways,
he manifested the eighteen transformations.
Thereupon Shèngyǒu
was extremely joyful.
The Pìzhīfó descended from the air
and received his offerings once more,
and after some time
entered Nièpán.
The Sàbó was grieved and mourned,
with immeasurable recollection;
he performed Zhévéi on the body,
collected the Shèlì,
placed them in a precious vase,
and built a Tōupó,
with incense, flowers, and music,
and various wonderful items,
he made offerings.
The large canopy he held,
he placed upon it,
and for the rest of his life,
he made offerings to this stupa.
Due to his offering to one Pìzhīfó
with the four types of offerings,
because of this karmic reward,
through immeasurable lifetimes,
he was either born in the heavens
or dwelt among humans,
honored and distinguished,
with few equals in the world.”
He further told Ānán:
“All sentient beings,
those at home and those who have left home,
should all cultivate merit,
so that in birth after birth,
they may obtain such benefits.”
At that time, Ānán
and the whole assembly,
hearing what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the city of Luóyuèqí, on the mount Qíshéjué,
together with a group of one thousand two hundred and fifty venerable disciples.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
thinking of the need for an attendant,
the venerable disciples such as Jiāochénrú and others,
each observed together,
knowing what the Buddha was thinking.
Then Jiāochénrú rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder,
joined his palms, knelt, and addressed the Buddha:
"I long to be near you as your attendant, to hold your robes and carry your bowl.
I only pray that you look upon me with pity!
Grant me your instruction and allow this."
The Buddha told him:
"You are advanced in years,
and you yourself need someone to serve you;
how could I bear to have you serve and attend to me again?"
Then Jiāochénrú knew that the Buddha would not permit it,
so he paid his respects and returned to his seat.
Móhē Jiāyè,
Shèlìfú,
Mùjiánlián,
and five hundred other disciples,
one after another addressed the Buddha,
all seeking to serve as his attendant,
but the Buddha would not permit any of them.
Then Ānàlǜ examined the Buddha's intent
and saw where the Buddha's mind was directed:
his heart was set on Ānán.
Just as when the sun is in the east, it shines upon a house,
its light passing from the eastern window directly to the western wall,
the World-Honored One's intent was just like this.
The great disciples
all also observed and knew this.
Then Shèlìfú and Mùjiánlián
rose from their seats
and went before Ānán,
saying to Ānán:
"The World-Honored One's intent
is to have you, virtuous one, as his attendant.
You, virtuous one, have gained a great benefit,
being uniquely favored.
You should quickly go and request to be the Buddha's attendant."
Then the worthy Ānán,
seeing the elders coming before him
and hearing their words,
immediately rose, joined his palms,
and addressed the elders, saying:
"The World-Honored One's virtue is heavy,
and his wisdom is deep and far-reaching.
If I were to constantly be near him to serve and attend him,
I fear I would incur faults and blame,
bringing misfortune upon myself."
Shèlìfú and the others again said to him:
"Now we observe that the World-Honored One,
focusing his attention,
wishing to have you, virtuous one, as his attendant.
Just as when the sun first rises and shines upon a house,
its light from the eastern window shines directly on the western wall,
the World-Honored One's focused heart is just like this.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One
understands human nature and knows you are capable of this responsibility;
therefore, he has set his mind on you.
You should quickly go and request to be his attendant."
The worthy Ānán, hearing these words again
and contemplating the matter,
did not know what to do.
He again joined his palms
and addressed the elders:
"If the World-Honored One now grants me three wishes,
then I can undertake the duty of being the Buddha's attendant.
What are the three?
The World-Honored One's old robes,
do not let me wear them.
The World-Honored One's leftover food,
do not make me eat it.
The timing for visitors to enter,
let it be at my discretion.
If these three wishes are granted,
only then can I serve the Buddha."
After Shèlìfú and the others heard these words,
they took the matter in full
and went to inform the World-Honored One.
When the Buddha heard this,
he told Shèlìfú:
"Disciples!
The reason Ānán asks not to wear my old robes
is that he is thinking long-term and fears that other disciples might harbor jealousy,
giving rise to such thoughts as:
'Kings, officials, and the common people,
and various Tányuè,
offer the Buddha expensive and fine soft robes;
Ānán covets these,
which is why he sought to serve him.'
Furthermore, as for asking not to eat my leftover food,
he fears other disciples would again have this thought:
'In the Rúlái's bowl,
the leftovers of what he ate
are of a hundred delicious flavors,
such food as does not exist in the world;
Ānán is gluttonous,
which is why he stays close.'
The reason Ānán asks for the timing of visitors to be at his own discretion
is that he fears other disciples and followers of external paths might come seeking an audience,
bringing difficult questions,
and not knowing the proper timing,
they might cause disturbance or annoyance.
Also, as an attendant,
he must wait for the proper time,
for what is appropriate in food and drink,
what benefits the body and is good for health;
every single arrangement,
he fears he might overlook.
Therefore, he has requested these three wishes in advance.
Furthermore, Ānán
did not only today request to know the proper timing himself;
in past lives,
when he served me,
he already well knew the appropriate timing."
Then Shèlìfú addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"We do not know of his serving the Buddha in the past
and well knowing the appropriate timing.
What was that matter?"
The Buddha told Shèlìfú:
"If you wish to hear it,
listen attentively and take it to heart!
I shall speak for you."
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
We shall listen well."
The Buddha told Shèlìfú:
"In the past, countless and immeasurable Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
there was a great king
who ruled over the eighty-four thousand small kingdoms and
eighty billion villages of Yánfútí.
The city where the king resided
was named Pólóushīshè.
In this city,
there was a Póluómén
named Níjūlóutuó,
who was intelligent and widely learned,
with extraordinary natural talent.
The king greatly honored and respected him,
taking him as a teacher and serving him.
The eighty-four thousand small kings
all respected and admired him from afar,
looking up to wherever he was.
From all four directions, they sent contributions
and dispatched envoys to consult and receive him,
to put it briefly,
just as they would serve the Great King.
This Póluómén
had wealth that rivaled the royal family,
but he had no son to be his successor.
Whether going out or coming in, sitting or lying down,
he always harbored this sorrow,
not knowing by what means he might obtain a son.
He then prayed and offered sacrifices to Fàntiān,
Tiāndì, the Sìwáng,
Móxībáluó,
and other various heavens, the sun, the moon, and the stars,
the mountains, rivers, and tree spirits,
making all kinds of prayers and sacrifices,
leaving no place unvisited.
After twelve years of sincere accumulation of merit,
his chief lady realized she was pregnant.
Being an intelligent woman,
she was able to know this;
she knew by herself that what she carried
must be a boy.
She immediately informed the Póluómén of the situation.
The Póluómén was delighted,
and his joy redoubled.
He immediately ordered the ladies and attendants of the household
to come and together protect the lady's movements,
providing food, bedding, and mats
that were extremely fine and soft.
Everything was arranged and supplied to be comfortable and suitable,
never going against her wishes.
When the ten months were complete,
she gave birth to a boy.
His body was of a purple-gold color,
his hair was dark blue,
he was extraordinarily upright and handsome,
with human features that are rare to find.
When the Póluómén saw him,
his joy was uncontrollable.
He immediately summoned physiognomists
to come and examine him.
The physiognomists examined him
and marveled that such a thing had never happened before.
This child's auspicious features and marks
showed a grand and vast merit and virtue,
such that the whole world would look up to him,
just as a child relies on its mother.
His father was delighted
and ordered that a name be established for him.
When giving names in Tiānzhú,
it is done according to two methods:
Some rely on the stars,
and some rely on omens.
The physiognomist then asked:
“Since she became pregnant,
what omens have there been?”
The father replied:
“This child’s mother
was usually adverse to others,
lacking in compassion and obedience,
and did not practice kind wisdom.
Since she became pregnant,
her nature has changed;
she pities those in suffering and distress
as a mother loves her child,
she delights in giving,
and has no greed or stinginess.”
When the physiognomist heard this,
he rejoiced and said:
“This is the child’s will
that has caused it to be so.
He should be given the name Móhē Shéjiāfán,
which in the Jìn language means Dà Shī.
As the child grew older,
his father loved and cared for him deeply,
building him a separate palace
and establishing three seasonal halls:
warm in winter and cool in summer,
and a moderate one for spring and autumn.
He placed many musicians and attendants there
to entertain him.
The child was intelligent
and delighted in learning.
He recited and held the secular classics
and the eighteen categories of books.
He became fluent and skilled in the texts
and also mastered their meanings.
He studied various arts and skills,
and there was none he did not master.
Later, Dà Shī said to his father:
“I have been in the deep palace for a long time
and wish to go out for an excursion.”
When the father heard these words,
he immediately ordered the officials:
“My son Dà Shī
wishes to go out on an excursion.
Sweep and wash the streets,
remove all impurities,
set up banners and pennants,
scatter flowers and burn incense,
and adorn the roads
to make them extremely clean.”
When the preparations were complete,
Dà Shī then rode a great white elephant
adorned with the seven treasures.
Striking bells and beating drums,
with music and entertainment,
a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen
led and followed him.
They traveled along the Great Royal Road
toward the city gate.
At that time, the people of the kingdom
were atop the towers and pavilions
and on both sides of the road,
competing to watch him
without ever tiring.
They all said:
“How extraordinary and wonderful!
To behold his majestic appearance
is like seeing Fàntiān.”
Moving further forward,
he saw many beggars
wearing tattered and ruined clothes,
holding broken vessels,
and pleading in humble voices:
“Give me a little something.”
When Dà Shī saw them,
he asked:
“Why are you suffering so much?”
Some replied:
“I have no parents, brothers, wife, or children;
I am poor, orphaned, and alone,
with no one to rely on.”
Some replied:
“I have a chronic illness
and cannot work;
I have no way to support myself.”
Some replied:
“By my misfortune,
I have repeatedly met with ruin
and am burdened with debts;
pressed by the needs of my body and mouth,
I have no way to save myself,
and thus I go begging
to sustain my remaining life.”
Having heard this, Dà Shī
sighed in sorrow and moved on.
Next, moving forward again,
he saw butchers
skinning and flaying animals,
cutting and carving them to weigh and sell.
Dà Shī saw them and asked:
“Hey, what are you doing?”
They each said:
“Since the time of our grandfathers,
slaughtering has been our trade;
if we abandon this work,
we will have no way to support ourselves.”
Dà Shī sighed
and left them.
Next, he saw plowmen
tilling the earth with plows;
insects came out from the soil,
and frogs picked them up and swallowed them;
then a snake came
and swallowed the frog;
a peacock flew down
and pecked at and ate the snake.
Dà Shī asked:
“What is being done here?”
They replied:
“We till the land and sow seeds in it;
later we will get grain to support ourselves
and also to pay taxes to the royal house.”
Having heard this,
Dà Shī sighed deeply and moved on.
Next, moving forward again,
he saw hunters
spreading nets and setting traps
to catch birds and beasts;
he saw the birds and beasts
falling into the traps and nets,
pulling and struggling by themselves
but unable to escape,
crying out in sorrow to one another,
each filled with fear.
Dà Shī saw this
and asked, “Why do you do this?”
They all replied:
“We rely solely on hunting and killing as our trade;
if we do not do this,
we have no way to survive.”
Having heard their words,
he went away in sorrow.
Next, moving forward again,
he saw fishermen
spreading out their nets;
what they caught was very much,
piled upon the dry land,
still struggling and moving.
Again, he asked the reason:
“Hey, why is it like this?”
They each came forward and replied:
“Since the time of our grandfathers,
we have had no other livelihood;
we rely solely on catching fish
to sell for food and clothing.”
When Dà Shī saw this,
he felt great pity and grief
and thought to himself:
“All these sentient beings,
because of poverty and lack of food and clothing,
commit these evil deeds,
killing and harming sentient beings,
doing so with delight and to their heart’s content;
after their lives end,
they will fall into the Sāntú,
passing from darkness into darkness.
How strange and tragic!”
Having had these thoughts,
he turned his carriage and returned to the palace;
he brooded on these matters,
sorrowful and unhappy.
He went to see his father
and asked for one wish.
The father said to Dà Shī:
“Whatever you ask for,
I shall never go against you.”
He then said:
“The other day I went out on an excursion
and saw the people
seeking food and clothing,
exhausting their bodies and overworking their minds,
killing, harming, and deceiving,
performing all kinds of evil deeds.
My heart pities them greatly,
and I wish to provide for them.
I only hope you will grant me your favor
and give me the great treasury,
allowing me to give freely to relieve the people’s needs.”
The father told him:
“I have gathered wealth and treasures
entirely for your sake;
since this is your wish,
how could I go against you?”
Having received his father’s permission,
the son then ordered a proclamation to all the people:
“Móhē Shéjiāfán wishes to perform a great charity;
those who have needs,
all should come and take.”
The proclamation was concluded.
Shāmén, Póluómén,
the poor and those in debt,
the lonely, suffering, and diseased
came and went from various cities and roads.
All these people,
some coming from a hundred, two hundred, three hundred, five hundred, or a thousand lǐ,
and others coming from three thousand or five thousand lǐ,
all supported the strong and weak among them.
They gathered from the four directions like clouds,
and all were provided for,
fulfilling their wishes.
Those needing clothes were given clothes;
those needing food were supplied food.
Gold, silver, the seven treasures,
carriages, horses, litters, and sedan chairs,
gardens, fields, and the six kinds of livestock
were given as they desired.
In this way, charity continued.
After some time,
of the items in the storehouses,
two-thirds were gone.
At that time, the official in charge of the treasury
went to inform his father:
“Móhéshéjiāfán,
since the charity began,
of the three parts of the treasury’s goods,
two have already been given away.
Envoys from various kings
will be coming and going;
please reflect deeply on this,
lest you blame me later.”
The father heard the official’s words
and thought to himself:
“I love this son
and cannot oppose him.
I would rather the treasury be empty;
how could I interrupt such charity?”
After more time passed,
of the remaining treasury goods used,
another two-thirds were gone.
The official reported again:
“Of the previously remaining goods,
two of the three parts have been used again.
Envoys from various kings
must be notified of matters;
now the treasury is nearly empty.
I hope you will reconsider.”
At that time, the Póluómén said to the official:
“I love this son;
my love is deep and thick, and I have never gone against him
or rebuked his intentions to his face.
You should find a way
to create a pretext.
When he comes seeking items, pretend you are not there for a time,
to let the remaining items last for more days and months.”
The official, having received these words,
immediately closed the treasury door
and briefly went elsewhere.
Beggars gathered
at the place of the Dàshī.
Dàshī brought them to the official to seek items,
but the official was not there.
He searched for him
through many seasons
and finally found him after much effort.
Although he obtained the items,
it did not meet the immediate needs.
Dàshī thought to himself:
“How would this low official dare to not obey me by his own strength?
This must be my father’s intention, which is why it is so.
Furthermore, by the law of a son,
it is not right to empty his parents’ treasury until it is exhausted.
In this treasury,
very little remains.”
After having this thought,
“How can I obtain many treasures
to fulfill my wishes
and provide for all living beings?”
He then asked various people:
“In this world today,
what enterprise
can yield much wealth that is difficult to exhaust?”
Some said:
“Planting many of the five grains
and cultivating gardens
can yield much wealth.”
Some said:
“Raising many of the six kinds of livestock
and letting them multiply in season
can yield much wealth.”
Some said:
“Not avoiding great hardships
and traveling far to trade
yields the most wealth.”
Some said:
“Only by going into the sea
to collect precious treasures
yields the most wealth.”
Dàshī heard this
and said to himself:
“Farming, raising livestock,
and traveling far to trade
are not suitable for me
and yield little profit.
Only going into the sea
is a plan that can be followed.
I must exert myself
to accomplish this task.”
After thinking this,
he went to inform his parents:
“I now wish to go into the sea
to seek many precious treasures,
to use them for charity
and relieve the needs of the people.
I only wish you would grant me permission
so that my goal can be achieved.”
His parents heard these words,
and asked in alarm:
“People of the world who enter the sea
are the poor and desperate
who cast aside their lives
and have no attachments.
What business have you
wanting to practice this?
If you wish to give charity,
all that our family owns,
all the various items,
and what remains in the treasury,
are all for you to use.
Do not enter the great sea.
Furthermore, in the sea
there are many dangers:
swirling waves,
the great Mójié fish,
evil dragons and Luóchà,
and water-colored mountains.
Such perils
are hard to pass.
What emergency do you have
that you would throw yourself into such danger?
As long as we are alive,
we will never permit it.
You should cease this intention
and speak no more of it.”
Dàshī heard this,
and since his wish was not granted,
he felt very melancholy
and thought to himself:
“What I desire now
is to accomplish a great deed.
If I cherish my life too much,
how can the task be completed?”
He threw himself on the ground,
prostrating before his parents,
and said:
“If you insist on keeping me back
and go against my vow,
I will lie here on the ground
and never rise again.”
His parents heard this
and their hearts burned with anxiety.
Together with the inner court officials,
they came forward to advise and illustrate:
“The sea route is distant,
and there are many dangers.
Many go,
but few return.
I remember seeking a son,
praying and sacrificing to the Tiān,
with such sincerity and piteousness,
there was nowhere I did not go.
After twelve years,
my wish was finally granted with difficulty.
Just as you have grown up,
you want to abandon me?
Think on abandoning this intention,
and get up to eat and drink.”
From one day, two days, until the sixth day,
in various such ways,
they advised and tried to enlighten him;
but his words remained as they were at first,
holding to his resolve without turning back.
The parents were afraid
and discussed it together:
“Whenever this child
wants to do something,
he insists on completing it
and never retreats halfway.
Even if we let him enter the sea,
there is still hope for his return.
If we continue to refuse him,
when the seventh day comes,
we will surely see disaster.
What can be done?
We should let him go
and leave the worry for later.”
The decision was made,
they came together to their son’s side,
each taking one of his hands,
Then they spoke to their son, saying:
"We will allow you to follow your will;
arise and return to eat."
Dàshī heard this
and immediately arose to have his meal.
When the meal was finished,
he immediately arose and went outside
and widely proclaimed a decree,
telling the people:
