"I now personally wish to enter the sea to gather treasures.
Who wishes to go?
We may proceed together.
I shall be the Sàbó,
and will provide the travel equipment myself."
At that time, in the kingdom,
there were five hundred people
who, having heard this decree,
all responded to the call.
They immediately prepared what was needed
and set a fixed date for departure.
When the day arrived, they loaded their gear,
bid farewell, and set out on the road.
The king and his ministers, along with his parents,
various princes, officials, and commoners,
numbering in the tens of millions,
saw them off along the way.
Each presented them with wonderful treasures
to provide for the journey's needs.
Their weeping was heartbreaking,
and they then departed.
After traveling for several days,
they stayed overnight in the wilderness
and encountered a band of thieves
who came looking to rob them.
The Púsà, feeling compassion,
immediately took all that he carried
and gave it all to them.
Proceeding forward, they reached a city;
the city was named Fàngbō.
In the city was a Póluómén
named Jiāpílí.
At that time, Dàshī
went to his place,
wishing to borrow three thousand ounces of gold from him.
This Póluómén
had a wonderful daughter
whose body was the color of purple-gold
and whose hair was deep blue;
she was of peerless uprightness,
without equal.
Eighty-four thousand kings of small nations
had all sought her for their princes,
but he had refused them all.
At this time, Dàshī
arrived at his gate
and asked Jiāpílí:
"I wish to see you."
The daughter was inside
and, hearing the voice from outside,
she joyfully and with surprise stood up
and said to her parents:
"The one outside
is my husband."
Then Jiāpílí
immediately went out to meet him.
Seeing his appearance,
he knew he was surely no ordinary man.
Hearing that he needed gold,
he promised to give it all.
Furthermore, with his left hand,
he held a golden washing pitcher,
and with his right hand, he held his daughter,
saying to Dàshī:
"Now this daughter of mine
has an extraordinary appearance.
Various kings sent envoys,
each seeking her for their sons;
now, seeing the Sàbó,
your uprightness is a match.
I ask that you take this daughter
to serve you."
Dàshī replied:
"I am now about to brave dangers and enter the sea;
how can I know if I will return safely?
To receive your daughter beforehand
is not appropriate."
Jiāpílí said:
"If you return safely,
you shall accept her for me."
At this time, Dàshī
immediately consented to this.
Then Jiāpílí was joyful
and gave him the three thousand ounces of gold and other necessities.
Thereupon they bid farewell,
and he proceeded forward to the sea.
He ordered the merchants to firmly prepare the ship,
making it seven layers thick.
They waited for the wind to arrive,
pushed the ship into the sea,
and with seven large ropes,
tied it to the shore.
Then, ringing a bell and proclaiming the decree,
he told the merchants:
"You all, listen to the dangers of the sea:
the black winds and Luóshà,
the swirling and surging waves,
the evil dragons and toxic vapors,
the mountains the color of water,
and the great Mójié fish;
the hardships are many.
Of a hundred companions who enter the sea,
only one returns safely at times.
Those who wish to withdraw
may stay here;
after the ropes are cut,
it will be too late for regret.
If you can have firm hearts
and disregard your lives,
renouncing parents, brothers, wives, and children,
and should you happen to return safely
having obtained the seven treasures,
for seven generations your descendants
will not exhaust their use."
After giving this decree,
he cut one rope,
and it was like this every day.
On the seventh day, after proclaiming the decree again, he cut the seventh rope.
Watching the wind, they raised the sails,
and the ship went as swift as an arrow.
Together with all the merchants,
they arrived at the place of treasures.
Dàshī was learned and clearly recognized various treasures,
their weight, value, appearance, and quality.
He showed the merchants, saying:
"Treasures of this color
are not heavy to carry,
yet they are of high price and should be taken.
Treasures of this sort
are heavy but of low price;
none of you should take them."
Furthermore, he commanded them
regarding the amount of treasure to take,
that they should take a moderate amount.
"If it is too much, the ship will be heavy;
if it is heavy, it will sink.
If it is too little, although the ship will be light,
it will not compensate for the toil."
When his warnings were finished,
each worked diligently at gathering
and stacked them upon the ship.
With the treasures sufficient and the ship laden,
they then wished to return.
At that time, Dàshī
did not wish to board the ship.
All the people gathered
and asked the reason for his intent.
Dàshī replied:
"I wish to proceed forward to the Palace of the Lóngwáng to seek the Wish-Fulfilling Pearl.
Even if it costs me my life,
I cannot return without it."
When the merchants heard this,
they were sorrowful and distressed,
and all said to him:
"We and our kind
rely upon you, Sàbó.
We abandoned what we held dear
and braved dangers to reach here,
hoping to depend on you
to return home safely.
How can you now
wish to abandon us?"
Dàshī replied:
"I shall make a vow and prayer for you,
so that you may return safely to your country."
When the merchants heard this,
their fearful hearts were settled.
The guide, Dàshī,
held an incense burner in his hand
and, facing the four directions,
he made a vow:
"I do not fear toil
in wading through the sea to seek treasures
to relieve the distress of all living beings' hunger and lack.
Amassing this merit,
I use it to seek the Fó-dào.
If I am sincere
and my wish is to be fulfilled,
let these merchants and the ship's treasures
encounter no evil hardships
and return safely to their country."
When the vow was finished,
the merchants came forward to embrace the guide's hands and feet,
weeping with sorrow,
as they bid farewell and returned to their country.
They cut the ropes and raised the sails,
returning to Yánfútí.
They all received safety
and were able to emerge from the great sea.
At that time, Dàshī,
After parting with the group,
he first entered into the water.
The water reached to his knees,
and he traveled for seven days.
Turning to move forward again,
the water gradually deepened
until it reached his thighs,
and he passed another seven days.
Advancing in this manner for seven days, it reached his waist;
for seven days, it reached his neck;
and for seven days, he constantly floated.
Arriving at the edge of a mountain,
he grasped the trees with both hands
and climbed up the mountain,
passing seven days
until he reached the summit.
Upon that mountain,
he walked on level ground for seven days,
then returned to descend the mountain,
taking seven days to reach the bottom,
where he arrived at the water's edge.
Within the water, there were golden lotus flowers,
and there were various poisonous snakes.
Their venom was extremely potent;
they all used their bodies
to entwine the roots of the lotus flowers.
When the Púshà saw this,
he immediately sat upright, focusing his mind and gathering his thoughts.
Entering the Sámmèi of Benevolence,
he contemplated that when these poisonous snakes were in their original lives,
it was because their anger and jealousy were doubly intense
that they were born here
to receive these evil forms.
With an ultimate heart of benevolence,
he felt pity and compassionate concern for them.
When his heart of benevolence was full,
the venom of those snakes
all naturally dissipated and ceased.
Dàshī then rose,
walked upon the flowers,
and after another seven days,
he was able to cross the snakes.
Turning to move forward again,
he saw various Luóshà.
Smelling the scent of a human,
they all came to search for him.
Dàshī, having seen them,
focused his mind on benevolent contemplation.
Among those Luóshà,
a respectful heart naturally arose.
They came to ask him in gentle words:
"Where do you wish to go?"
Dàshī answered in detail:
"I wish to seek the Rúyì Bǎozhū."
The Luóshà were delighted
and thought to themselves:
"This person of merit and virtue
is going to the Lónggōng,
but the way is still far.
How can we allow him to undergo such hardship?
We should carry him across the steep and difficult obstacles."
They immediately carried him away,
crossing four hundred yóuxún,
and then set him back on the ground.
"At this, Dàshī
turned to move forward on his own
and saw a silver city,
white, pure, and bright.
Knowing it was the Lóngchéng,
he happily approached it.
He saw that outside the city
were seven layers of moats.
Filled within all the moats
were poisonous snakes.
Their venom was fierce and potent;
they were hideous to look upon.
Dàshī the Guide
contemplated that these poisonous snakes
were all due to the intensity of anger and harm in their previous lives,
and thus they received such hideous forms.
He felt benevolence and pity for them as if looking upon an infant.
When his heart of benevolence was full,
the snakes' venom was completely removed.
He then rose and stepped upon them,
walking toward the Lóngchéng.
He saw two Lóng entwining the city with their bodies,
their heads meeting at the threshold of the gate.
Seeing Dàshī,
they looked up with startled glares.
Dàshī immediately
re-entered his heart of benevolence,
and the dragons' venom was then removed;
they lowered their heads and did not look at him.
Dàshī then went forward,
stepped over them, and passed.
Inside the city was a Lóng
sitting in a palace of seven treasures.
Seeing the Púshà from afar,
he rose in surprise and thought:
"Now outside my city,
within the seven layers of moats,
there are poisonous snakes,
other Lóng,
and Yèchā,
whom none dare recklessly cross.
Who is this person
who can come here?"
He immediately came forward to welcome and ask,
paying respectful homage
and inviting him to take a seat.
Sitting on a bed of seven treasures,
various kinds of delicious food
were used to make an offering.
After eating, they conversed,
and the dragon asked his reason for coming.
The Púshà replied:
"The people of Yánfútí
are poor and suffer hardship.
Seeking wealth and treasures to provide for clothing and food,
they kill, harm, and deceive,
performing all sorts of evil.
After their lives end,
they fall into the three evil paths.
My heart feels great pity for them,
and wishing to save them,
I have traveled a steep and long distance to come
and see the Great King,
to seek the Zhāntuó Móní
to use for their salvation.
By accumulating this merit,
I vow to seek the way of the Fó.
If you do not refuse,
I only ask that you grant it to me."
The Lóngwáng replied:
"The Zhāntuó Móní
is a rare treasure.
You have come from a long and difficult distance
specifically for this.
If you can open your heart
and stay for one month
to receive a small offering
and preach the Dharma for us,
the Zhāntuó Móní
can then be obtained."
The Púshà agreed.
Every day, the Lóngwáng
provided offerings of a hundred flavors
and performed various kinds of music
to make offerings to the Púshà.
The Púshà then fully explained the wisdom of the Sìnìanchù.
After the month had passed,
he took his leave to return.
The Lóngwáng was delighted,
untied the treasure jewel from his hair knot,
and presented it to him.
He then said:
"The Great Being's heart of benevolence
and universal salvation are difficult to match.
This resolve is powerful and fierce;
you will certainly attain the way of the Fó.
I wish to become your disciple of wisdom."
The Púshà agreed
and asked him:
"Now, this jewel of yours,
what power and ability does it have?"
He replied:
"This jewel can rain down all necessities for two thousand yóuxún."
The Púshà thought to himself:
"Although this jewel is excellent,
it still does not accomplish the great task of my vast salvation."
All the Lóng, great and small,
escorted him out the gate,
repeatedly expressing their farewells.
"At this, they parted,
and he moved forward again.
From afar, he saw a city
of pure blue Liúlí,
its color clear and clean,
and he again approached it.
Outside the city
there were also seven layers of moats,
and within the moats, it was also filled with poisonous snakes.
When the Púshà saw this,
he contemplated that these various snakes
were caused by anger and jealousy,
and thus they came to this place
to receive these poisonous forms.
Sitting upright, he entered benevolence,
adding ultimate compassion and pity.
When his heart of benevolence was intense,
the venom was all removed.
He stepped across them
and headed for the city gate.
He also saw two Lóng
entwining the city with their bodies,
their heads meeting at the threshold of the gate.
Having seen the Púshà,
they raised their heads and glared in anger.
The Púshà immediately
contemplated the heart of benevolence.
His compassionate mind being full,
their poison was again removed,
and they once more lowered their heads;
the Púsà then stepped over them.
At that time, in the city,
there was a Lóngwáng
sitting in a hall of seven treasures.
Seeing the Púsà from afar,
he rose in surprise and thought to himself:
“Considering that outside my city,
there are seven layers of snake moats
that various dragons and Yèchā
are unable to cross,
who is this person
who can come here?”
He immediately went down to welcome and inquire,
respectfully making obeisance,
and invited him to the hall,
where he sat on a bed of seven treasures.
He prepared a hundred flavors
and served delicious food.
After eating, he slowly conversed and asked for the reason for his visit.
The Púsà then answered with the intention of his coming:
“I only wish to beg for the Zhāntuó Móní.”
The Lóngwáng said:
“The Zhāntuó Móní
is extremely difficult to obtain!
If you wish to have it,
please accept my invitation
to stay here for two months
and also show and explain the practices of a Púsà.”
The Lóngwáng provided various kinds of food and drink,
performed various music and dance,
and made offerings.
The Púsà fully
explained for him the matters of the four bases of supernatural power.
After two months had passed,
he took his leave to depart.
The Lóngwáng then took out the precious jewel from his topknot
and offered it to him,
then making a solemn vow:
“Dàshì, your diligent mind
compassionately saves all living beings.
Your mind is vast;
you will certainly attain the Way of the Fó.
I wish to become your disciple with supernatural powers.”
The Púsà agreed, saying:
“As you wish.”
He then asked again:
“This precious jewel you gave me,
what is its power?”
The dragon then replied:
“This jewel can rain down all that is needed over four thousand yóuxún.”
The Púsà thought to himself:
“This jewel is even better;
although it is extraordinary,
it does not yet match my desire.”
The various dragons, great and small,
escorted him out the gate,
each harboring affection and regret.
“Then, after parting,
he proceeded further forward
and saw a golden city.
Its color was dazzling
and it was extremely wondrous and beautiful.
The Púsà went toward it.
He saw that outside the city
there were also seven layers of moats.
Within those moats,
they were also filled with poisonous snakes.
The Púsà thought to himself
that these poisonous snakes
were also because their practice of anger, hatred, jealousy, and harm in their former lives was intense;
thus they received these poisonous forms.
He sat upright and entered into compassion,
exercising extreme loving thoughts.
When his compassionate mind had reached them,
the snakes' poison was all removed.
He then stepped forward and trod upon them,
walking over them to cross.
Arriving at the city gate,
he also saw two dragons
coiling their bodies around the city
with their heads crossing at the gate's threshold.
Having seen the Púsà,
they raised their heads and stared in amazement.
The Púsà, according to the Dharma,
entered into the concentration of compassion.
The dragons' poison was removed,
and they lowered their heads and looked down.
He then stepped forward onto them
and crossed into the city.
At that time, in the city,
there was also a Lóngwáng
residing in a precious hall.
Seeing the Púsà from afar,
he thought to himself in amazement:
“Outside my city
there are seven layers of moats
filled with poisonous snakes.
Other dragons and Yèchā
are unable to cross them.
Now who is this person
who can come here?”
His mind was extremely surprised.
He immediately went down to welcome and inquire,
paying respect and making obeisance.
He invited him up to the hall,
provided a bed of seven treasures,
and offered it for him to sit.
After he was seated, he prepared various delicious foods.
After he had eaten, he slowly asked for the reason of his coming.
The Púsà answered:
“The people of Yánfútí
are of little merit and are destitute and suffering.
They labor their bodies and exert their thoughts,
killing and deceiving for the sake of clothing and food.
They possess the ten unwholesome deeds.
After their lives end,
they again fall into the three severe sufferings.
My mind is very much moved by pity and sorrow,
and I think of wanting to rescue them.
I heard that the Hǎi Lóngwáng
has the Rúyìzhū;
therefore, I have traversed distant and dangerous paths,
only hoping to obtain this.”
The Lóngwáng replied:
“The Rúyì bǎozhū
is a thing difficult to obtain.
Since the Dàshì has come for it,
I hope I should give it to you.
If you wish to obtain it,
stay for four months
to receive my humble offerings
and also teach and instruct me.”
The Púsà immediately agreed.
The Lóngwáng was delighted,
and every day he provided the finest food of a hundred flavors,
personally serving it
and offering sweet food.
He also commanded the performance of various music and dance.
The Púsà constantly explained for him the names, origins, and ends of all dharmas,
widely proclaiming their meanings.
The Lóngwáng respectfully admired him
and listened and received with single-mindedness.
Morning and evening, he inquired after him without missing the proper time.
Whatever was needed at any time, the dragon personally managed it.
When various dragons and Yèchā came wishing to see him,
whether they could enter or should depart,
he himself established the limits.
He served him for four months
and was well aware of what was appropriate for the time.
After the four months had ended,
the Púsà took his leave to depart.
At that time, the dragon untied the Rúyìzhū from his topknot
and offered it to him,
then making a vow:
“Dàshì, your vast vow
is to extensively save with a compassionate mind.
Pitying those living beings,
you do not fear toil and labor.
You will certainly be able to become a Fó
and rescue them from bitter suffering.
I wish to be your attendant and a disciple who upholds everything.”
The Púsà granted it.
Then he asked again:
“The jewel you have given,
how great is its power?”
The Lóngwáng replied:
“This jewel can rain down all necessities of seven treasures over eight thousand yóuxún.”
The Púsà was delighted
and thought to himself:
“The land of Yánfútí
is seven thousand yóuxún.
The virtue of this jewel
matches what I hoped for.”
Those obtained before and after
were altogether three jewels.
He tied them to the corner of his robe
and then rose and left the city.
The various dragons, great and small,
escorted him outside the city,
each harboring sorrow and affection,
and then they parted.
“The Púsà went forward,
held the jewels and made a vow:
‘If this is indeed the Zhāntuó Móní,
then may it cause my body to be able to fly through the empty void.’
Having finished making the vow,
he immediately lifted his body
and was then able to fly,
going out beyond the sea.
Having crossed the difficulties of the sea,
he took a short nap to rest.
At that time, in the sea,
there were various dragons
who discussed among themselves:
‘Within our sea...
"Only these three pearls,
their virtue is so great
that it is difficult to find any comparison.
This man has been able
to seek, obtain, and carry them away.
It would be a pity to lose these treasures;
they should be taken back."
When their discussion ended,
they secretly untied and took them away.
The Púsà woke from sleep
and saw the pearls were not there.
He immediately thought to himself:
"There is no one else here;
it must be the Hǎilóng
who has taken my treasures away.
For the sake of these pearls,
I have traveled through far and dangerous places.
Now, on the verge of returning to my country and fulfilling my wishes,
although he has taken my pearls,
I will never let them go.
I will certainly exert all my strength to drain this sea water,
vowing in my heart with fixed determination,
risking my life here.
If I do not get the pearls,
I will never return empty-handed."
Having finished his contemplation,
he went to the seashore,
found a turtle shell,
grasped it with both hands,
and was about to drain the sea.
The Hǎishén, knowing his intent,
came to ask him:
"The seawater is deep and wide,
spanning three million three hundred and sixty thousand lǐ.
Even if all types of people
came together to drain it,
they could not decrease it.
How much less can you, a single person,
accomplish this?"
The Púsà replied:
"If a person has a sincere heart
and wishes to do something,
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
When I obtain these treasures,
I shall use them to benefit all living beings.
With this merit,
I seek the path of the Buddha.
My heart does not flag;
why should I not be able?"
At that time, the Shǔtuóhuì Tiān,
seeing the Púsà from afar,
with one body and one mind,
working diligently alone,
wishing to provide relief, peace, and happiness to all.
"How can we not go and assist him?"
They spoke to one another
and came to his place.
The Púsà lowered his vessel,
and all the devas
used their heavenly robes
to soak up the water together.
When the Púsà drew out his vessel,
the devas lifted their robes
and cast the water elsewhere.
With one round of draining the sea,
it decreased by forty lǐ;
with a second round of draining,
it decreased by eighty lǐ;
with a third round of draining,
it decreased by one hundred and twenty lǐ.
The dragon was terrified
and came to his place,
saying:
"Stop, stop!
Do not drain the sea any more!"
The Púsà then stopped.
The dragon came and asked:
"You seek these treasures;
what do you intend to do with them?"
The Púsà replied:
"I wish to use them to provide for and save all sentient beings."
The dragon asked again:
"According to your words,
we have many sentient beings in our sea;
why not give them to us,
but insist on taking them away?"
The Púsà replied:
"The creatures in the sea are also sentient beings,
yet they do not have extreme suffering.
As for the people of Yánfǔtí,
for the sake of money and wealth,
they kill, harm, and deceive,
performing the ten non-virtuous acts,
and after death fall into the three miserable realms.
Because I am of the human race,
I understand the teaching of the Dharma.
Therefore I came to seek the treasures,
first to satisfy their needs,
and later with the ten virtues,
to exhort and instruct them."
Hearing his words, the dragon
brought out the pearls and returned them.
At that time, the Hǎishén,
seeing the deeds performed through his vigor and great strength,
made a vow:
"Since you are like this,
with unceasing vigor,
you will surely achieve the path of the Buddha.
I wish to become your diligent disciple."
"The Púsà obtained the pearls
and flew away once more.
Upon arrival, he first inquired about the merchant companions who had entered the sea with him,
and then descended to the ground.
When the companions saw him,
they were immeasurably surprised and joyful,
and all exclaimed together:
'How extraordinary! How unique!'
He proceeded further
and reached Fàngbō Chéng.
The Póluómén Jiāpìlí,
hearing that the Púsà had returned safely from the sea,
leaped for joy.
He went out to welcome and greet him,
and also invited the companions
to a gathering for guests.
He prepared various fine dishes and drinks.
After eating, they recounted the hardships and losses of their journey.
At that time, the Púsà held his precious pearls
and pointed them toward the house.
Within the Póluómén's house,
all the treasuries became full.
Those at the gathering witnessed this
and marveled that such a thing had never happened before.
Then Jiāpìlí
adorned his daughter
with various kinds of jewels
to decorate her body.
He personally held a golden jeweled washing pitcher,
first washing his own hands,
then taking his daughter's arm
and giving her to the Púsà.
The Púsà accepted her.
Jiāpìlí was delighted
and prepared five hundred singing girls,
selecting those talented and skilled in performance.
He also provided five hundred white elephants,
adorned with many treasures
to make them extremely magnificent,
to send off his daughter.
The Púsà instructed his companions
to mount their carriages and set out on the road.
Everyone in the city, young and old,
saw them off along the way.
With various kinds of music playing,
they were escorted back to his country.
"The parents of Dàshī,
since parting from their son,
had been knotted with grief and dazed with confusion.
Their weeping was excessively mournful,
and both their eyes became dark
until they were blind and could see nothing.
When the son returned to the country,
he bowed and greeted them.
The parents heard his voice
and felt him with their hands.
They then knew for certain that Dàshī had returned to the country.
Grief and joy took turns in them,
and they rebuked their son:
'You were truly heartless
to leave us and enter the sea,
causing us such hardship
that we barely clung to life.
In the great sea,
what kind of things did you get?'
The Púsà brought out the pearls
and gave them to his parents.
His parents held them in their hands
and said to themselves:
'Now in our treasury,
things comparable to these stones
are not few.
Why endure such hardship
just to get these?'
The Púsà took the pearls
and pointed them at his parents' eyes.
Their eyes suddenly became clear and bright,
like wind clearing away clouds.
Having regained their sight,
their hearts became joyful.
Moved by the virtue of these pearls,
they sighed and said:
'How extraordinary!
Though you suffered hardship,
your efforts were not in vain.'
The Púsà again held the pearls
and made a vow from them:
'If these are indeed Zhāntuómóní,
may they cause my parents...'"
Underneath his body, naturally,
there appeared a wondrous and rare throne of the seven treasures,
and above it was a majestic and pure great canopy of the seven treasures.
As soon as he finished speaking, it was immediately accomplished,
and everyone was joyful.
The Púsà again grasped the jewel and made a wish:
"May my father, mother, the king, ministers, and people,
have all their storehouses completely filled."
He then took the jewel,
passed through the four directions,
and all were filled according to his words;
there was no one who was not surprised and joyful.
He immediately sent people,
riding elephants capable of traveling eight thousand lǐ,
to inform all the people of Yánfútí:
"Móhē Shéjiāfán
has returned safely from the sea,
having obtained a rúyì jewel.
Its power is extraordinary.
Seven days from now,
he will make the jewel rain down all treasures, clothing, and food,
according to what people need,
to be taken as they please.
Let everyone observe the precepts,
and prepare
storage
in waiting."
"Once the announcement had been made everywhere
and the seven days arrived,
the Dàshī Púsà
bathed his body,
put on new, clean clothes,
went to a level ground,
then held the jewel,
placed it atop a high banner-pole,
held an incense burner in his hand,
and made a wish to the four directions:
'The people of Yánfútí
are poor and suffer hardships;
I wish to provide for them so they lack nothing.
If this is truly a Zhāntuómóní,
then it should rain down what the multitude needs in succession.'
When the wish was finished,
dark clouds formed in the four directions,
and immediately a wind arose,
blowing away all impurities,
flaws, filth, and sweepings,
removing them all.
Next, it rained a fine mist
to suppress the dust;
next, it rained food and drink
of a hundred superior flavors;
next, it rained the five grains;
next, it rained clothing;
next, it rained the seven treasures and various rare curios.
Within Yánfútí,
the various treasures accumulated and filled the land.
The people
took as they pleased;
superior and wondrous clothing and food
overflowed with abundance,
and they looked upon the treasures
as if they were tiles or stones.
At that time, the Púsà,
seeing the people were sufficient,
immediately sent officials to the four far regions
to announce throughout Yánfútí,
making it known to all:
'O you people!
Previously, because of poverty and lack,
you sought food, clothing, and various treasures,
deceiving one another,
killing and harming with extreme intent for self-interest while forgetting righteousness,
not considering sin or merit.
When your lives ended, you all fell into the Sāntú,
entering darkness from darkness,
suffering for many kalpas.
I always felt pity for you,
but had no way to save you.
Therefore, I forgot the suffering of my own body,
braved dangers to enter the sea,
obtained this precious jewel,
and came to rescue you.
Since you no longer have any lacks or shortages,
you should be mindful to discipline yourselves and diligently practice the Shíshàn,
restraining the body, speech, and mind,
being compassionate, benevolent, filial, and obedient,
with vigorous effort to control your thoughts,
and harbor no negligence.'
Using various skillful means,
he widely commanded the practice of good.
He then composed documents
to inform all kings and ministers,
conveying these dharma instructions
to make them known to all,
so they might encourage and supervise one another
and not recklessly commit wrongs.
At that time, everyone within Yánfútí,
having received this great kindness and the moistening of compassionate grace,
each thought of how
they might repay such supreme virtue.
Also having received the excellent teaching
commanding them to practice good,
they all longed for righteousness,
devotedly practiced compassion and respect,
restrained their body, speech, and mind,
did not recklessly commit wrongs,
and after their lives ended,
they all attained rebirth in heaven.
"In this way,
Shèlìfú!
If you wish to know who the father, the Póluómén Níjūlóutuó, was then:
he is my current father, King Jìngfàn.
The mother then
is my current mother, Móhē Móyē.
The one who was Dàshī then
is my current self.
The dragon in the Silver City
is now Shèlìfú.
The dragon in the Vaidūrya City
is now Mùjiànlián.
The dragon in the Golden City
is now Ānán.
The sea deity then
is now Líyuè.
When Ānán was a dragon king,
he served me
and well knew the appropriate times;
even until today,
he naturally knows the times.
As for Ānán's wish for these three vows,
I shall follow his intent."
When Ānán heard this,
he leaped with joy,
rose from his seat,
knelt down and said to the Buddha:
"I shall be the Buddha's attendant for as long as I live."
At that time, those in the assembly,
hearing what the Buddha said,
felt the great kindness,
single-mindedly disciplined themselves,
and contemplated the Four Truths and the essential ways of the dharma.
Some attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn.
Some planted the seeds of the roots of goodness for Pìzhīfó.
Some resolved their minds on the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Some attained the stage of non-retrogression.
All were joyful together
and respectfully followed the teachings.

Translated in Gāochāng Prefecture by the Shāmén Huìjué and others from Liángzhōu during the Yuán Wèi dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in Shèwèi Guó, at the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, a Shǒutuóhuì Tiān
descended to Yánfútí
and went to where the Shìzūn was,
requesting the Fó and the Sēng
to bathe and receive offerings.
The Shìzūn remained silent,
having already given permission.
He immediately prepared food and drink
and arranged bathing equipment;
a warm room and warm water
were adjusted to be comfortable for the body,
and fragrant oils and cleansing herbs
were all fully prepared.
When the arrangements were complete,
he said to the Shìzūn:
"The food and equipment are ready;
only the Holy One knows the time."
Thereupon, the Shìzūn and all the Bǐqiū
accepted his offerings,
all bathed together,
and enjoyed the food and drink;
the food was sweet and delicious,
a rarity in the world.
When the meal was over, they washed and rinsed,
and each returned to his original seat.
At that time, Ānán
knelt long with palms together
and said to the Shìzūn:
"What merit did this Tiān perform in the past
to have such a wonderful physical form,
such an extraordinary and majestic appearance,
and such a brilliant radiance,
like a great mountain of jewels?
I only wish that the Shìzūn
would explain this matter."
The Fó told Ānán:
"Listen carefully and keep it well!
I shall explain it.
Long ago in the past,
at the time of Pípóshī Fó,
this Tiān was in that life
the son of a poor family
who constantly worked as a hired laborer
to provide for his own needs.
Hearing Pípóshī Fó speak of the merit of bathing the Sēng,
he was joyful in his heart
and thought of making an offering.
He then worked diligently
and obtained a small amount of money and grain,
which he used to provide bathing equipment
as well as food and drink.
He invited the Fó and the assembly of Sēng
and offered them everything.
Because of this meritorious action,
after his life ended,
he was born in Shǒutuóhuì Tiān
and has this radiant appearance."
The Fó told Ānán:
"And as for this Tiān,
it is not only today that he has invited the Fó and the Sēng;
at the time of Shīqì Fó he also came to this world
to make offerings to the Shìzūn and the Sēng,
and even up to the time of Jiāshè Fó,
it was also like this."
The Fó told Ānán:
"This Tiān has not only served and made offerings to the seven Fó,
but in the future within the Xiánjié,
when a thousand Fó appear,
he will also wash each Fó and the Sēng,
just as he does today, without any difference."
At that time, the Shìzūn
then gave the Tiān a prediction:
"In a future world,
after the completion of an Āsēngqí and a hundred jié,
you shall become a Fó
named Jìngshēn,
complete with the ten titles.
The sentient beings you transform
will be beyond measure."
At that time, Ānán
and the fourfold assembly,
hearing what the Fó had said,
rejoiced immeasurably
and all spoke thus:
"The Rúlái's appearance in the world
brings great benefit;
from such a small gift,
one obtains such a vast reward."
The Fó told Ānán:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is as you say."
For the sake of the assembly,
he extensively explained the wonderful Dharma.
Among those who heard the Dharma,
some attained the level of Dàojì,
Wǎnglái,
Bùhuán,
or reached that of Yìngzhēn;
others resolved for the great enlightenment,
and each and every one rejoiced,
reverently accepting and practicing it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in Luóyuèqí on the Mountain Qíshéjué,
with a great assembly of Bǐqiū,
surrounding him as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, the Worthy Ānán,
seeing that Típódáduō,
toward the Rúlái,
always harbored jealousy and envy,
had driven drunken elephants
and pushed down a mountain to crush the Buddha,
using various means
wanting to cause him harm.
However, with the Buddha's heart of compassion,
he always had pity and empathy;
toward Luóhóuluó and Típódáduō,
he regarded them as equals without any distinction.
The Worthy Ānán,
seeing him like this,
always harbored resentment,
and pondering it in his mind,
he rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder,
knelt on both knees with palms joined,
and spoke of this matter with a sigh.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Típódáduō has not only directed evil toward me today;
in past lives, he also harmed me,
yet I have always thought of him with compassion."
The Worthy Ānán then said to the Buddha:
"I do not know of the past lives.
How Típódáduō
also caused harm,
and how there was compassion and pity then—
what were the circumstances?
I wish for you to explain it in detail."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In the distant past,
immeasurable, limitless, and inconceivable Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a king
named Lènàbámí,
which in the Jìn language means Bǎokǎi.
He ruled over five hundred minor kings
and had five hundred consorts and ladies-in-waiting,
but none of them had a child.
The king then prayed and made offerings to the various deities of the heavens, the sun, the moon, the mountains, the seas, and the trees.
Though years and decades passed,
he did not obtain any offspring.
The king was greatly worried and sorrowful,
and thought to himself:
'I have no son now.
If I should die suddenly,
the kingdom will have no successor,
and the world will surely fall into chaos.
Why is this?
The five hundred ministers
will not submit to one another
and will certainly contend by force.
The strong and the weak will slaughter one another, killing the innocent.
The kingdom will be destroyed and the people lost;
all will stem from this.'
Having thought of these matters,
his confusion and distress increased further.
At that time, a celestial deity,
knowing the king's sincere intent,
appeared in the king's dream
and spoke to him, saying:
'In the forest outside the city,
there are two immortals.
The first immortal
has a golden-colored body.
His merit and wise eloquence
are incomparable.
If you indeed need a son,
you may go and request of him,
and he will surely change his mind and come to be born in the royal house.'
The king soon startled awake
and had a look of slight joy.
He immediately ordered his carriage prepared,
and taking only a few people,
he searched everywhere for them.
Upon finding them,
he immediately sought their mercy
and explained in various ways
how the kingdom had no heir
and his worries and concerns were heavy.
'I humbly beg the Great Immortal
to be born in my house,
to succeed to the kingdom's throne,
and remove my anxieties.
If you do not find me unworthy,
please favor me with your regard.'
At that time, the immortal,
seeing the king's earnestness,
could not bear to refuse him
and thus consented.
The second immortal
also spoke to the king, saying:
'I shall also go and be born in the royal house.'
The king was greatly delighted
and then took his leave and returned to the palace.
After some time had passed,
the golden-colored immortal
reached the end of his life.
The king's primary consort,
named Sūmó,
immediately realized she was pregnant.
A clever woman
is able to have the wisdom to know she is pregnant
and distinguish whether it is a boy or a girl.
She then said to herself:
'What I am carrying
must surely be a boy.'
The king and those in the palace,
having heard these words,
were boundlessly joyful.
The king ordered the consorts and ladies-in-waiting in the palace
to all serve and provide for her together,
making her mind content and joyful.
The bedding and the food and drink
were made extremely fine and soft.
They protected her movements,
and she did not approach any danger.
When ten months were complete,
the primary consort
gave birth to a baby boy,
who was exceptionally handsome and extraordinary.
His body was of purple-gold color,
and his hair was deep blue-black.
He was complete with the marks of a man.
The king and those inside and outside the palace
never grew tired of looking at him.
Consequently, a physiognomist was summoned
to examine his features.
The physiognomist arrived immediately,
examined him from head to toe,
and was filled with exuberant joy.
He said to the king:
'This child's marks and features
are rare among men.
His wisdom and merit
are incomparable.'
The king was even more pleased upon hearing this,
and spoke again to the physiognomist,
asking him to give the child a name.
The physiognomist asked the king:
'Since this Crown Prince
was conceived,
have there been any unusual changes?'
The king immediately replied:
'The mother of this Crown Prince
was previously prone to jealousy and ill-will.
She delighted in the faults of others
and falsely accused them of wrongdoing.
When she saw the good in others,
her heart was not pleased.
Since she became pregnant,
her character and nature have transformed.
She has become compassionate and kind,
pitying the foolish and loving the wise.
She enjoys practicing charity and generosity,
and protects and nurtures all with an equal mind.'
Hearing this, the physiognomist
praised him, saying:
'How wonderful!
This is the child's own intent
being transmitted to the mother.'
He then gave him a name;
the name was Jiāliángnàjiālǐ,
which in the Jìn language means Shànshì.
The second consort,
named Fúbā—
the second immortal
also reached the end of his life
and was born in the second consort's womb.
When the months were full,
she gave birth to a baby boy.
His physical form and appearance
had nothing extraordinary about them.
Again, the physiognomist was summoned
to examine his features.
The physiognomist looked him over
and said to the king:
'As for this Crown Prince,
he is merely an ordinary person.
His merit and wisdom
are sufficient for him to manage himself.'
The king again ordered him
to give the child a name.
The physiognomist said again:
'Have there been any unusual occurrences?'
The king told the physiognomist:
'The mother of this Crown Prince
was originally of a loyal and good nature,
compassionate and compliant,
and she delighted in proclaiming the goodness of others.
Since she became pregnant,
she has conversely come to delight in evil,
becoming jealous of the worthy and capable,
and not being pleased when she sees goodness.'
The physiognomist spoke again:
"This is also the child’s own will,
which was placed within his mother;
that is why it is so."
Thereupon he gave him a name,
calling him Pōpójiālí,
which in the language of Jìn means 'Evil Deeds.'
At that time, the King
set his heart on loving and thinking of Jiāliángnàjiālí,
never failing to fulfill his wishes.
He immediately ordered the construction of palaces for the three seasons:
during the winter he lived in a warm palace,
in spring and autumn he lived in the middle palace,
and in summer he lived in a cool palace.
He arranged for music and dance
to entertain him.
As the Prince gradually grew older,
his intelligence and eloquence were extraordinary.
He studied all the secular classics
and the eighteen scriptures,
reciting and holding them with mastery
and excelling in their principles and meanings.
Later, he requested to go out for an excursion,
and the King granted it.
He ordered the roads and paths to be repaired,
and for impurities to be removed.
Riding a great white elephant
adorned with gold and silver,
with a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen
leading and following him,
through the streets and paths,
all the people
on both sides of the road
and on the various towers and pavilions,
countless onlookers,
all said of the Prince:
"How much he resembles Fàntiān!
His majestic appearance and features
are rare among men."
At that time, the Prince
saw many beggars
whose bodies were thin and haggard,
their clothing tattered and ruined.
In their left hands they held broken vessels,
and in their right they held broken staffs.
With humble words they pleaded for mercy,
begging for food from others.
The Prince asked:
"Why are you like this?"
The ministers replied:
"People of this sort
may have no parents,
are lonely, poor, and destitute,
with no one to rely upon.
Afflicted by infirmity, madness, or disease,
they cannot work;
without a single coin saved,
and hard-pressed by the needs of body and mouth,
that is why they are like this."
The Prince felt compassion,
and his heart was deeply moved with grief.
Moving further ahead,
he saw many butchers
killing animals,
cutting them into pieces and weighing them to sell.
The Prince asked:
"Why do you do this?"
They each replied:
"I do not necessarily enjoy it,
but since the time of my grandfather,
this has been my profession.
If I were to abandon this work,
I would have no way to support myself."
Upon hearing this, the Prince
sighed deeply and left.
Moving ahead, he arrived at the fields
and saw the various farmers.
As they tilled the earth, insects came out,
and frogs picked them up and swallowed them.
He then saw a snake
swallowing and eating a frog,
and a peacock flew down
to peck at and eat the snake.
The Prince asked the people:
"What is being done here?"
The farmers replied:
"This is my work;
I sow seeds in the ground,
so that later I may obtain grain
to provide food for myself
and to pay taxes to the King's house."
The Prince sighed:
"Because of food and drink,
they kill living beings,
toiling with body and strength;
the hardship is indeed great."
Moving further ahead,
he saw many hunters
approaching flocks of birds,
drawing their bows to shoot.
He also saw nets
spread out upon the ground,
and saw many birds and beasts
falling into them,
startled and crying out,
unable to escape.
The Prince asked:
"What are you all doing?"
They all replied:
"We capture various birds and beasts
to provide for ourselves."
Hearing this, the Prince
sighed deeply and left.
Arriving at the bank of a river and pond,
he saw fishermen
spreading nets to catch fish.
They lay in disorder on the ground,
leaping and twitching,
and the dead were countless.
The Prince asked again,
and they each replied:
"I rely on these fish
to provide for my food and clothing."
The Prince sighed deeply,
pitying all living beings.
"For the sake of clothing and food,
it should come to this:
killing living beings
to provide for the body and mouth;
as karmic offenses increase daily,
what will the future retribution be?"
He then returned to the palace,
worried and unhappy.
He went to tell his father the King:
"I wish to be granted one wish."
The King answered him:
"Whatever you desire,
I will not oppose you."
The Prince said to the King:
"I went out for an excursion
and observed the various kinds of people.
For the sake of clothing and food,
they deceive and kill;
their accumulated sins increase daily.
My mind is deeply grieved and compassionate,
and I wish to provide for them.
I hope the King will allow me
to use the royal treasury
to give charity as I please
to fulfill the needs of the people."
Because of the King's
intensified love for the Prince,
upon hearing his words,
he could not go against his wishes
and immediately granted it.
Thereupon the Prince
immediately issued a decree
to all the people:
"Prince Jiāliángnàjiālí
will give charity to those in poverty and need.
He will give to everyone;
let all come and take.
If anyone needs gold, silver, treasures, clothing, food, or anything else,
it shall be given to them."
He then opened the royal treasury,
brought out various treasures,
placed them at the city gates
and in the marketplaces,
and according to what people needed,
everything was provided.
At that time, from various countries,
Shāmén, Póluómén,
the poor, the lonely, and the elderly,
the disabled and the sick,
the strong and the weak supporting each other,
arrived in succession.
Those needing clothes were given clothes,
those needing food were given food,
and gold, silver, and treasures
were given freely as desired.
At that time, the people
spoke to one another,
and throughout Yánfútí,
they all gathered.
Of the King's treasury,
nearly two-thirds was gone.
At that time, the official in charge of the treasury
entered and spoke to the King:
"The Great King governs five hundred small countries.
There are envoys from these countries
coming and going,
and treasures are required for these matters
to be given as reciprocal gifts.
The Prince’s charity
uses the King's inner treasury;
of the three parts of its contents,
nearly two have been used.
The King should consider this,
lest there be regret later."
The King heard these words
and told the official,
“This Crown Prince of mine
loves to practice charity;
his heart is fervent
and cannot be turned back.
If he were to be forbidden or hindered and his will were crossed,
causing him to suffer and be distressed,
what then should be done?
Let him follow his will freely;
do not go against or fail him.”
After some time like this,
the Crown Prince gave in charity;
of the remaining items in the treasury,
he spent two parts out of three.
The official spoke to the King again,
“Of the items previously remaining,
through daily charity,
among the three parts,
two have been spent again;
only a small amount remains,
which should be kept for official needs;
it cannot be completely spent.
I wish the King to consider this carefully,
so that I may not be blamed later.”
The King then contemplated
and told the official,
“I love this son
even more than others.
I cannot bear to openly oppose his will.
If he comes to demand treasures,
avoid him slightly by making excuses;
if he demands them urgently,
then give them to him for now.
Sometimes he gets them, sometimes not;
this can delay things for some time.”
Then, the treasury official,
having received the King’s instruction,
when the Crown Prince on a later day
came to demand treasures,
the official made excuses
and went to other places.
Sometimes the Prince obtained them,
sometimes he did not;
his every need could not be satisfied.
The Crown Prince realized this
and thought to himself,
“This treasury official,
what power does he have
to dare go against me
and not follow my orders?
It must be the King’s intention
that has caused this.
Furthermore, by the etiquette of a son,
one should not exhaust and empty the storehouses of one’s parents.
Now in this treasury,
very little remains.
What should I do
to obtain wealth and treasures
to give in charity to everyone so they lack nothing?”
Having had this thought,
he immediately asked several people,
“In this world today,
what business can one do
to obtain much wealth to use as one wishes?”
One person said,
“If you do not avoid extreme hardships
and go far away to trade,
you can obtain much wealth.”
One person said,
“If you cultivate the fields,
not avoiding cold or heat,
and plant the five grains extensively,
you can obtain much wealth.”
One person said,
“If you raise many of the six types of livestock,
care for them throughout the seasons,
and they multiply in due time,
you can obtain much wealth.”
One person said,
“If only you disregard your life
and are able to enter the great sea,
reach the palace of the Lóng Wáng,
and seek the rúyìzhū,
if this matter is accomplished,
you will obtain the greatest wealth.”
At that time, the Crown Prince, hearing the words of the people,
thought to himself,
“Engaging in trade or farming,
or raising the six types of livestock,
is not suitable for me,
and the profit is meager.
Only entering the great sea
and going to the palace of the Lóng Wáng
suits my intention;
I must diligently seek this matter.”
Having had this thought,
he went to speak to his father the King,
“I wish to enter the sea
to seek treasures
to give to all living beings
so that they may use them without end.
I only wish that my father and mother
will grant me permission.”
The King and the Lady,
hearing the words of the Crown Prince,
were deeply worried and distressed
and asked the Crown Prince,
“What is your intention
in wanting to enter the sea?
If you wish to practice charity
and fulfill your original vow,
all that remains in our family’s treasury
shall be given to you
to use for charity.
Why do you abandon yourself
and say you want to enter the sea?
Furthermore, we hear that in the sea
there are many extreme dangers:
the black winds and luóchà,
waves and surging currents,
the great Mójé fish,
and mountains the color of water.
Among such numerous dangers,
few are safe.
When a hundred companions go together,
only one occasionally returns.
Why are you in such a hurry now
to plunge yourself into danger?
Your mother and I
are extremely worried,
and the kings, officials, and people
all harbor burning fears.
Think of abandoning this idea
and do not speak of it again.”
Then the Crown Prince,
having heard these words of the King,
his mind was set on the great plan,
his will was fixed on salvation.
Though the King tried to detain and stop him,
his intention was not moved.
Resolved to give his life
to accomplish the matter,
he threw his body onto the ground,
prostrating on his stomach before the King,
and said to the King,
“I only wish for your compassion!
Allow your son to fulfill his heart’s desire.
If you must refuse and oppose
and do not grant permission,
lying face down on this ground,
I will never rise.”
The King and the Lady
and everyone inside and out,
saw the Crown Prince’s intent
could not be turned back.
Having sworn to die there,
lying face down on the ground,
they all tried to reason with him,
persuading and apologizing to make him rise.
His words remained as before,
holding to his will without change,
from the first day to the second day,
and so on until the sixth day.
The King and the Lady
discussed among themselves,
“The Crown Prince has not eaten;
it has already been six days.
When the seventh day dawns,
his life will certainly not be saved.
This child, in all he does,
whenever he has an intention,
he must see it through
and cannot be turned back.
If we let him enter the sea,
there is still a possibility of return;
if we oppose his will now,
we will certainly cut off all hope.
We should simply grant him permission
and leave our worries for later.”
The King and the Lady,
having reached an agreement,
came forward together.
Each holding one of his hands,
with tears flowing,
they spoke to him, saying,
“We grant you permission to enter the sea.
You may rise and return to eat.”
At that time, the Crown Prince,
having heard the King’s words,
rose up with joy
and comforted his parents,
“Although I enter the sea,
I shall return before long.
I only wish that you do not worry too much about me.”
He prepared various fine foods and drinks,
and when finished, he went outside,
broadly issuing a proclamation,
“Jiāliángnàqiélí
wishes now to enter the sea.”
"Who wishes to go?
We should advance together."
At that time in the kingdom,
there were five hundred merchants,
who all came and gathered,
all saying they wished to depart.
At this time, there was a blind Dǎoshī in the kingdom,
who had previously several times returned from the sea.
When the Tàizǐ heard of this,
he immediately went to his side,
approached him with great earnestness,
and used gracious words to seek understanding:
"You must enter the great sea with me,
to show me the benefits and harms, and the way to come and go."
The Dǎoshī replied:
"I am already aged,
and blind with no sight.
Although I wish to go myself,
in my heart it is very difficult.
The Wáng loves the Tàizǐ
with a devotion many times beyond the ordinary.
If you leave his sight for even a moment,
he will be filled with melancholy and distress.
If he now hears that you
are entering the great sea with me,
and if I am then rejected,
the fault laid upon me will not be small."
At that time, the Tàizǐ,
after hearing these words,
immediately returned to the palace
and personally spoke to his father, the Wáng:
"Now in this kingdom,
there is a blind Dǎoshī
who has previously several times
been to the great sea.
I wish the Wáng would command and explain to him,
to make him go with me."
When the Wáng heard these words,
he personally went to that place
and spoke to the Dǎoshī, saying:
"This Tàizǐ of mine
has set his mind on entering the sea.
Despite various words of admonition,
his resolve is firm and does not turn back.
Since it cannot be helped,
I now permit him to go.
Considering he is young
and has not yet experienced hardship,
and having heard that you have traveled before
and know the ways of the sea,
I hope you will change your mind
and endure the toil to go together."
At that time, the Dǎoshī,
hearing these words from the Wáng,
immediately spoke to the Wáng, saying:
"I regret that I am aged
and blind with nothing to see,
but as it is the Dàwáng's command,
how would I dare to disobey?"
When the Wáng received these words,
he immediately returned to the palace.
At that time, the Tàizǐ
together with the Dǎoshī
fixed the day of departure.
Returning to the Wáng's place,
the Wáng asked those around him:
"Who respects and loves me
and can go together with the Tàizǐ to gather treasures?"
Pōpóqiélí
immediately spoke to the Wáng, saying:
"I wish to accompany my elder brother
and cross the great sea together."
When the Wáng heard these words,
he thought to himself:
"Now that the younger brother goes together into the midst of danger,
if he can help in a crisis,
it is better than someone else."
After having this thought,
he then permitted him to go.
"At that time, the Tàizǐ
brought out three thousand taels of gold:
using one thousand taels for provisions,
one thousand taels for the ship,
and another thousand taels for all necessary items.
When the preparations were completed,
he then wished to set out.
The Wáng and his Fūrén,
the various princes, ministers, and people,
wept as they saw them off,
parting at the roadside.
Thereupon the Tàizǐ,
with all his companions,
proceeded on the road and departed.
Arriving at the seashore,
they firmly repaired the ship,
making it have seven layers.
Waiting for the season of the wind,
they pushed it into the water.
Using seven great ropes,
they tied it to the seashore.
Shaking a bell and making a proclamation,
he spoke to the crowd, saying:
"Listen, all of you!
There are many dangers in the sea:
waves and churning waters,
evil dragons and Luóshà,
black winds that overturn,
mountains the color of the sea,
and the great Mójié fish.
There are other such dangers
still many in number.
Of those who enter the sea before and after,
few return safely.
If there are any who doubt,
you may return from here.
Who can have a firm mind,
give up their body and life,
disregard their parents,
and not long for their wives and children?
You shall enter the sea together
to reach the place of treasure.
If we obtain rare treasures
and return home in peace,
for seven generations of descendants,
the use of it will be inexhaustible."
After making this proclamation,
he then cut one rope.
Each day was like this,
until seven days had passed.
When the proclamations were finished,
he cut the seventh rope.
They raised the sails to catch the wind,
the ship swift as an arrow.
He went directly with the men
to that treasure isle.
The Tàizǐ was intelligent,
thoroughly versed in worldly classics,
recognized the appearance and colors of treasures,
and knew all their prices.
He showed the various merchants the quality of the treasures,
and commanded the merchants to take them as they pleased.
He again told the merchants
to take a moderate amount;
if they took too much, the ship would be heavy,
and there would be the worry of sinking;
if they took too little, the journey would be exhausting
and would not compensate for the suffering.
When the instructions were finished,
alone with the Dǎoshī,
he boarded a small boat separately,
and parting from the merchants,
he advanced further.
The Dǎoshī asked, saying:
"There should be a white-colored mountain ahead;
do you see it or not?"
The Tàizǐ said:
"I see it."
The Dǎoshī said:
"This is the Silver Mountain."
Advancing further,
the Dǎoshī asked again:
"There should be a deep-blue colored mountain;
have you seen it yet?"
The Tàizǐ replied:
"I have already seen it."
The Dǎoshī said:
"This is the Gànliúlí Mountain."
Advancing still further,
he again asked the Tàizǐ:
"There should be a yellow-colored mountain here;
have you seen it yet?"
The Tàizǐ said:
"I see it."
The Dǎoshī told him:
"This is the Gold Mountain."
Arriving at the foot of the Gold Mountain,
sitting on the golden sands,
the Dǎoshī said:
"I am now frail and weak,
and my life will surely not be saved.
Having already shown you the directions,
and the paths to proceed or stop,
you must go from here.
Ahead there will be a city;
that city is exceedingly wonderful,
with the seven treasures interspersed.
When you arrive at the city gate,
if the city gate is closed,
beside the city gate
there is a Jīngāngchǔ.
You then take the pestle
to strike the gate.
In the city there will be five hundred Tiānnǚ,
each bearing a precious pearl,
coming to offer them to you.
There will be one more maiden,
who is most exceptionally noble and superior;
the precious pearl she holds
is deep-blue in color,
It is named Zhāntuómóní.
This wish-fulfilling jewel,
once you obtain it, hold it fast;
do not let it be lost or slip away.
As for the others who give jewels,
you may also take them.
Restrain your senses,
and do not speak with them again.
I am now extremely exhausted,
with only a very little of my life remaining.
If, after my life ends,
you remember my kindness,
mourn for me
and bury me in this sand."
When the Guide finished speaking,
his breath ceased and his life ended.
Mourning him with great sorrow,
the Prince performed the burial for him,
and following his instructions,
he proceeded forward and departed.
He arrived at the City of Seven Treasures.
The city gates were tightly shut.
He saw a Jīngāngchǔ beside the gate.
As instructed, he took the pestle to strike the gate,
and the city gate then opened.
Five hundred celestial maidens,
each holding a precious jewel,
came to present them to the Prince.
The very first maiden
held a jewel in her hand
that was deep blue as described.
He took them in sequence,
wrapped them in the corner of his garment,
and then turned to return.
Previously, after the Prince had departed,
Pōpójiālǐ spoke to the crowd again:
"Traveling back and forth is not easy;
we should simply take many jewels."
The people were greedy for treasure
and took an excessive amount.
When the Prince returned,
their ship was already full.
They set sail to return,
but the ship then sank.
The merchants
were now sinking and now floating.
Because the Prince already possessed the wish-fulfilling jewel,
his body did not sink or drown.
Pōpójiālǐ called out to the Prince from afar:
"You must save me;
do not just abandon me!"
When the Prince heard these words,
he immediately pulled him along as they floated;
striving with effort to pull one another,
they were then able to emerge from the sea.
After emerging from the sea,
the younger brother spoke to the elder brother:
"We brothers
left our parents to come
into the great sea,
hoping not to return empty-handed.
But our circumstances were unfavorable;
we lost our wealth and treasures,
and to return alone and empty-handed
is truly shameful."
Jiāliángnàjiālǐ was by nature loyal and honest;
he immediately said to his younger brother:
"I have actually obtained a treasure."
The younger brother said to the elder:
"You should show it to me."
The elder then unwrapped his garment and showed him the jewel.
When the younger brother saw the jewel,
he then harbored this thought,
"I reflect that our father the King's kindness and mercy are not universal;
he is partial to my elder brother,
and I was not in his thoughts.
Now the two of us
have come into the sea together,
yet my brother has obtained a rare treasure
while I alone return empty-handed.
From this time forward,
he will surely treat me with contempt.
What shall I do?
I will take advantage of his sleep
to secretly kill my brother,
take his treasure,
and return to tell our father the King
that my brother died in the sea;
then he will surely love and care for me exceptionally."
After having this thought,
he secretly harbored a plan
and said to his brother:
"Human villages are getting closer.
We brothers
should not sleep at the same time;
we should take turns sitting and guarding the precious jewel."
The elder brother agreed to this,
and they constantly took turns guarding it.
When it was Pōpójiālǐ's
turn to rest and sleep,
he lay on the ground for a duration
far exceeding the usual measure,
and only then did he get up.
It was then the elder brother's turn to sleep.
Because he had been sitting for a long time,
his sleep was extremely deep.
Pōpójiālǐ
got up and went into the forest.
In the forest, there were trees
with extremely sharp thorns.
He took two of them,
each a foot and a half long,
and brought them to his brother's side.
His brother was sleeping very heavily.
Holding a thorn in one hand,
targeting his eye sockets,
he thrust the thorns in deep,
took the treasure, and left.
The Prince was in great pain
and cried out urgently in a loud voice:
"Pōpójiālǐ!
Pōpójiālǐ!
There is a thief here!"
He called out several times, but there was no response.
At that time, a tree spirit spoke to the Prince:
"Pōpójiālǐ
is your thief;
he has finished stabbing your eyes
and has taken your jewel away."
Thereupon the Prince rolled about in suffering and hardship,
crawling on his hands and knees,
gradually making a little progress,
and arrived at the Kingdom of Líshībádà.
Reaching a marshy area,
he encountered five hundred head of cattle coming to his side.
There was a bull-king
who, upon seeing the Prince,
felt pity and respect,
and extended its tongue to lick him.
All the other cattle gathered,
standing in shock and watching together.
At that time, a cowherd
came forward to investigate.
He then saw the Prince lying on the ground
and saw that in his eyes
were these long thorns.
Observing his appearance and bearing,
he also knew he was no ordinary person.
He immediately pulled out the thorns for him
and took him to his dwelling.
He constantly used clarified butter and milk
to apply to his wounds
and provided him with food and drink,
looking after and nourishing him accordingly.
After some time had passed,
the eye wounds gradually healed.
The host served him
without ever becoming negligent or weary.
At that time, the Prince
asked the cowherd:
"Living here,
what livelihood do you have?"
The cowherd replied:
"Living here,
I have no livelihood;
I rely solely on milk and curds,
which I sell to support myself."
The Prince thought to himself:
"I have encountered distress and hardship
and have troubled my host,
who has constantly provided for me.
Now that the wounds have healed
and I am slightly able to move about,
I should seek another place that is more suitable."
After thinking of this matter,
he spoke to the host:
"For such a long time,
I have troubled you.
I am deeply moved by my host,
and your kindness is difficult to repay.
I wish to move forward
to reach the city
and go about begging
to support my own life."
When the master of the cowherd's house
heard the Prince's words,
he feared that some weary words from his wife, children, or servants in the house had reached the Prince's ears.
"If it were not so,
for what reason would he take his leave?"
After having this thought,
he first asked those in the house:
"What displeasing thing have you all done
to make our noble guest take his leave and want to depart?"
Everyone in the house said:
"We treat him here as a brother;
we do not know for what reason he wishes to leave us."
Thereupon the master of the house
spoke to the Prince:
“I have served you
without anything being unsatisfactory;
you must not leave me to go begging elsewhere.”
At that time, the Prince,
hearing the host’s words
and seeing his earnestness,
wished to respect his feelings,
and so stayed for a short while.
After some time had passed,
he then said to the host:
“You have provided for me
without any lack at any time;
everyone in your household
has treated me with great generosity.
However, in my heart,
I wish to travel on to the city ahead.
I hope you will send one person
to go there together with me.”
Then the cattle herder,
seeing his persistence,
feared that opposing his will would make his heart sorrowful;
so he personally escorted and protected him,
and together they reached the city.
Having arrived at that city,
they were about to part and he was to return,
when the Prince said:
“If you have pity for me,
please buy a lute
for me to amuse myself.”
The cattle herder
immediately bought one for him.
They thanked each other,
and then they parted ways.
At that time, the Prince
was naturally gifted in many skills;
his songs, chants, and literary compositions
were exceedingly fine and ingenious.
In the streets,
he would raise his voice in song
and play the lute in harmony.
The sound was very pure and elegant.
When the people in the city
heard his music, they all delighted in listening and watching,
never growing weary.
Each brought food and drink
and vied with one another to give it to him.
At that time, there were five hundred beggars in the city
who all came to depend on him,
relying on him to eat their fill.
King Líshībá
had a garden warden
who guarded the orchard of *nài* fruit for the King.
When the *nài* fruit ripened,
parrots would come to eat it.
His labor was insufficient,
and he could not startle them away or block them.
Then the garden warden
carried the *nài* fruit to the King.
Among them, the good *nài* fruit
had been pecked and ruined by the parrots.
The King saw this and was enraged,
intending to impose punishment.
The garden warden was terrified
and explained himself to the King:
“My household lacks labor, which is why this happened.
I only ask for your leniency
to forgive the punishment.
I will seek a guard
so that this does not happen again.”
The King then forgave him
and did not press charges for his crime.
Having escaped, the garden warden
went out to search for someone.
He saw Jiāliángnàqiélí
begging by the roadside.
Observing his appearance,
he seemed to be an honest man.
He then said to him:
“Can you guard the garden for me?
If you can,
I will provide for all your needs.”
The Prince replied:
“My eyes cannot see;
how can I guard it?”
The garden warden said:
“If you truly wish to watch it,
though you have no eyes,
we shall use a clever method.
I will make many thin ropes
and tie them to the ends of the trees.
Using bells and such objects,
I will link them together
one after another, and you shall hold one end.
If you hear a sound,
you then jerk the rope,
and the parrots will be frightened and have no reason to stay.”
Hearing these words, the Prince
replied to him:
“If it is like this,
I can do it.”
Having reached an agreement,
he immediately went to serve as the guard.
Meanwhile, Pōpóqiélí
arrived at his father the King’s country.
The King, surprised that he came alone,
immediately asked for news.
Pōpóqiélí
spoke to the King, saying:
“Our group met with misfortune;
the ship was heavy and sank.
Jiāliángnàqiélí along with all the merchants,
together with all the treasures,
were all lost in the great sea.
I exerted my strength to swim
and barely managed to save myself.”
When the King and his Queen
heard these words,
they fainted for a long time,
losing all consciousness.
They sprinkled water on their faces,
and only after some difficulty did they revive.
The kings, ministers, and people inside and outside the palace halls,
upon hearing of this matter,
all felt deep sorrow and grief.
The King and his Queen
said to Pōpóqiélí:
“Prince Kālí has perished in the sea;
why have you come back?
Why did you not also die in the great sea?”
All the people of the land
felt bitter regret and loss,
weeping and longing for him day and night
as if they had lost their own parents.
While the Prince was in the palace,
he had always loved a certain goose.
The King said to the goose:
“The Prince raised you.
Now he went into the great sea,
was suddenly lost and has not returned.
Why do you not go and look
to find out where he is?”
He then wrote a letter
and tied it to the goose’s neck.
The goose immediately soared high,
searching far and wide.
Flying over that garden,
it recognized his singing voice.
It immediately descended to investigate
and saw the Prince.
It cried out in sorrow and joy,
unable to contain itself.
The Prince recognized it,
immediately untied and took the letter.
Since his eyes could not see, he was unable to read it.
He then sought paper and brush to write a letter to the King,
detailing how Pōpóqiélí had gouged out his eyes
and the places he had traveled through,
and all the bitter and painful trials.
He tied it to the goose’s neck,
and the goose then flew away.
King Líshībá
had a daughter
who was upright and exceptionally beautiful,
rare in this world.
The King loved and cherished her deeply
and never went against her wishes.
At that time, the daughter took leave of the King
to go out and tour the garden.
The King then allowed her to go.
When the daughter reached the garden,
she saw Prince Jiāliángnàqiélí,
his hair disheveled and his face dirty,
his eyes sightless,
wearing tattered and ruined clothes,
sitting among the trees.
The daughter observed him;
upon seeing his form and appearance,
her heart felt a deep connection toward him.
Not leaving his side,
she sat beside him
and conversed with him.
When mealtime arrived,
the King sent someone to call her.
The daughter sent the person back to say to the King:
“I wish for food to be sent here;
I want to eat in this place.”
The food was then sent,
and the daughter said to the Prince:
“I wish to sit and eat in one place together with you.”
The Prince replied:
“I am a man who begs for food;
you are a King’s daughter.
How can we eat together?
If the King hears of this,
my punishment will not be small.”
The daughter, with great sincerity,
said to the Prince:
“If you are not willing,
I shall not eat either.”
After returning several times like this,
and pressing her incessantly,
they eventually ate together.
Their words then became sincere and earnest,
their hearts gradually drew closer,
and their eyes did not leave each other.
As the day turned toward evening,
the King sent someone to call his daughter,
but the daughter sent someone back to tell the King:
"I wish to be the wife of this garden guardian;
I have no use for any other kings or crown princes.
Now my heart is devoted
and earnest in this way.
I only hope, Father King,
do not go against my wishes."
The messenger arrived at the King’s place
and reported the matter in detail.
After the King heard this,
he could not go against her feelings,
so he said to himself:
"This matter is disastrous and strange;
this daughter is unworthy.
To think it has come to this!
Great King Bǎokǎi
sent for his first prince, Jiāliángnàjiālǐ,
to come and seek her.
Now this prince
has entered the sea and not yet returned;
yet she wishes to be the wife of this beggar!
This brings shame to our name,
which is by no means a small matter.
Where should I cover my head and hide?"
After saying this,
he sent another messenger to call her.
The daughter spoke as before,
her will remaining firm and unmoving.
At that time, because the King loved her,
he could not go against her wishes;
he brought them both together,
placed them in the palace,
and then ordered them to be joined as husband and wife.
After several days had passed,
the wife constantly went out during the day
and returned only at night.
The husband, finding it strange, asked her:
"You said you would be my wife,
but you leave at dawn and return at dusk.
Your heart is not here;
is it because you have intentions for another that you act like this?"
The wife then made a vow:
"I am now single-minded
in honoring and serving you;
I have no other intention even as large as a hair.
If it is indeed so,
sincere and not false,
may your one eye be healed and whole as before."
As soon as the vow was completed,
the one eye immediately became as it was before.
He then asked the princess:
"Your parents,
in what country are they?"
The Prince said to his wife:
"Have you heard the name of Great King Lènàbámí or not?"
She replied:
"I have heard of him."
"He is my father.
And have you heard of that King’s prince, Jiāliángnàjiālǐ,
or not?"
She replied:
"I have heard of him."
"I am that person."
The wife then asked in shock:
"Why then have you suffered such hardships as this?"
The Prince then told her the whole story from beginning to end.
When the wife heard these words,
she sighed deeply,
and said to the Prince:
"Bōpójiālǐ
harbored malice against you;
from ancient times to the present,
there has never been such a case.
If you were to catch him,
how would you punish him?"
He replied:
"Even though Bōpójiālǐ harmed me,
regarding him,
I will never have anger or resentment."
The wife spoke again:
"This is hard to believe;
he troubled you so,
how could you not be angry?"
Jiāliángnàjiālǐ then made a vow:
"If I have no slight resentment as large as a hair
toward that Bōpójiālǐ,
and if my words are sincere
and not false or deceptive,
may my other eye also be restored to health."
After the vow was finished,
both eyes were clear and bright.
The wife saw her husband
with both eyes whole and pure,
and a dignified and majestic appearance
such as she had never seen before;
she was overcome with joy
and went to tell her father:
"Prince Jiāliángnàjiālǐ of Great King Bǎokǎi—
does Father King know of him?"
The King replied:
"I know of him."
The daughter then said:
"Do you wish to see him now?"
The King said:
"Where is he now?"
The daughter said:
"My husband
is that very man."
The King laughed and said:
"This girl is foolish and mad;
her mind is disordered and she has lost her senses.
Jiāliángnàjiālǐ entered the sea and has not returned;
you see a blind beggar
and call him by that name."
The daughter spoke again:
"I beg the King to go and see."
The King then went to look
and recognized that it was indeed the Prince;
his hair stood on end with awe,
and shame and fear filled his heart.
He prostrated himself before him
and spoke in repentance:
"I truly did not recognize you;
I hope you will forgive my fault."
He secretly took the Prince
and returned him to the border,
then announced publicly:
"Great King!
Prince Jiāliángnàjiālǐ
has returned from the great sea!"
He prepared all the necessary equipment,
adorned chariots with elephants and horses,
and accompanied by his officials,
went in person to welcome him.
Upon returning to the capital,
he held a grand banquet for the guests,
adorned his daughter,
and only then declared his intention to give her in marriage.
At that time, the wild goose returned
carrying the letter to the kingdom.
The Great King saw the goose,
opened and read the letter,
and for the first time received news.
He knew the Prince was alive
and learned in detail of all the bitter hardships he had undergone.
The King and his consort
were alternately grieving and joyful;
inside and outside the palace,
there was no one who did not feel sorrow, resentment, and fury.
They seized Bōpójiālǐ,
bound his body in chains,
and imprisoned him in a dungeon.
An edict was issued to King Líshībá:
"The Prince has suffered hardships
in your country;
why did you remain silent and not come to inform us?
When this letter arrives,
send him back with elephants and horses;
if anything goes against this,
I shall come myself."
The messenger then carried the letter
directly to that country.
King Líshībá
received it and read it.
Then the Prince
said to King Líshībá:
"The cowherd
has been kind to me;
I think of him now
and wish to see him;
you may send a messenger to call him for me."
The King immediately summoned him.
The Prince said to the King:
"My eyes were pierced,
and I relied solely on this man,
who provided for and nurtured me like my own parents.
If the King regards me with kindness,
he should reward him on my behalf."
The King was greatly pleased
and immediately bestowed upon him famous garments and fine robes,
elephants, horses, and chariots,
gardens, fields, and houses,
gold, silver, and precious treasures,
male and female servants,
and all the cattle he had tended—
giving them all to him.
The man was joyful,
beyond his expectations,
and thus obtained peace and lifelong wealth and honor.
He immediately returned and reported to the envoy,
and then presented a memorial explaining the situation:
"That the Crown Prince was here,
I truly did not know.
Regarding all the matters of bitterness and sorrow,
I humbly imagine the full details.
Now, the Crown Prince
has regained his sight.
I have immediately betrothed my humble daughter
to be the Crown Prince’s wife.
The ceremonial regalia and equipment are being prepared;
I, your servant, shall personally escort them."
Soon, he ordered the thorough preparation of five hundred white elephants,
