adorned with gold and silver
to make them exceptionally exquisite.
He selected five hundred people
to attend to the Crown Prince,
and further ordered the selection of five hundred handmaidens,
choosing those who were most upright, talented, and skillful.
With various treasures,
they were adorned.
Five hundred chariots,
decorated with precious objects,
were also made extremely wonderful
to escort his daughter.
King Líshībá,
personally with several hundred thousand chariots of ministers,
also accompanied and escorted them.
With music and songs of praise
surrounding them front and back,
and with boundless celebration,
they proceeded on the road back to the country.
At that time, the envoy
reached the Great King's place.
Upon opening and reading the memorial,
his joy greatly increased.
He announced to the various kings:
"All of you, come and assemble."
He immediately prepared elephants and horses.
The various ministers and officials,
and the ladies and palace women,
followed and led in front and behind.
He personally went to welcome the Crown Prince,
arriving at the border.
At that time, the Crown Prince,
seeing his father the King from afar,
descended from the chariot and advanced on foot.
He prostrated himself with his head to the ground
and inquired after his parents' well-being.
His parents also descended
and embraced him.
Long separated and longing to see their son,
they felt a mixture of sorrow and joy.
The various kings, ministers, and people,
seeing them thus,
were moved with feelings of joy
that could not be fully described.
After their conversation was briefly finished,
they returned to their carriages.
Striking bells and sounding drums,
and performing various music,
they joyfully praised the occasion
and escorted them toward the city.
Upon arriving outside the city gate,
the Crown Prince said to the King:
"Where is Pōpójiālí
now?"
The King answered him, saying:
"For such an evil person,
the world would not offer cover;
I could not bear to see him.
I have already confined him
within the prison."
The Crown Prince said to the King:
"He should now be released."
The King answered him, saying:
"His crimes are deep and heavy.
I have not yet finished investigating them;
how could he be released?"
The Crown Prince spoke again:
"If you do not release Pōpójiālí,
I will never enter the city."
The King immediately ordered his release
and sent word for him to come out.
Having been freed,
he came to see the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince embraced him
and comforted him,
and only then did they enter the city and go to the palace.
At that time, the parents,
the various kings, ministers, and people,
men and women, old and young,
saw that the Crown Prince
regarded his enemy
as if looking upon a newborn child.
Although Pōpójiālí had pierced his eyes,
he did not have the slightest resentment as large as a hair.
His respect, love, and compassion
were doubled compared to before.
The entire multitude
all joined in praising him:
"This is most extraordinary!
Among gods and humans,
there is truly no comparison."
When the Crown Prince arrived at the palace,
with Pōpójiālí,
his feelings of intimacy
and compassionate love were as of old.
He calmly asked about the jewel:
"Where is it now?"
Pōpójiālí
answered the Crown Prince, saying:
"When I came, I hid it in the earth by the roadside."
The Prince ordered people to go and retrieve it,
but they searched and could not find it.
The Crown Prince went together with them;
upon arriving, he saw it.
He collected the jewel treasure
and returned to the palace with them.
Using five hundred precious beads,
he bestowed them upon the various kings,
letting each take one.
The remaining Wish-Fulfilling Jewel
he kept for himself.
Holding the jewel in his hand,
he made a vow:
"If this is truly the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel,
may the place where my parents sit
have a throne of seven treasures,
and above their heads, let there be a great canopy of seven treasures."
Once he had finished speaking,
it was accomplished according to his words.
Again holding the jewel,
he made a vow:
"May the various treasuries within my parents' palace,
and all the treasuries belonging to the various kings and ministers,
which were previously used for giving,
all be filled once more."
He immediately held the jewel
and finished his rounds in the four directions,
and all the various treasuries
were filled again.
He again ordered the ministers
to announce to the various countries:
"Prince Jiāliángnàjiālí,
seven days from now,
shall rain down the seven treasures."
The announcement was immediately sent down,
and all heard and knew of it.
At that time, the Crown Prince
bathed in fragrant water,
erected a great banner,
and placed the jewel atop it.
Wearing new, clean clothes,
he held an incense burner in his hand,
bowed toward the four directions,
and spoke, saying:
"If this is truly the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel,
then it shall universally rain down all that is needed."
Once the vow was finished,
clouds and mist appeared in the four directions,
and a wind came
that blew away filth and excrement
and other impurities,
removing them all.
Next, it rained water
to settle the dust.
Next, it rained food of a hundred flavors and various delicacies.
Next, it rained the five grains.
Next, it rained clothes.
Next, it rained the seven treasures,
which piled up and filled the world.
At that time, the people
celebrated boundlessly,
looking upon the various jewels and treasures
as if they were tiles and stones.
Then, the Crown Prince
widely proclaimed an order:
"You have already obtained everything needed for your sustenance,
lacking in nothing.
If you can appreciate such kindness,
you should restrain your body, speech, and mind, and practice the Ten Paths of Goodness."
At that time, everyone
within Yánfútí
was moved by the Crown Prince’s infinite giving.
People heard his order,
exerted themselves in their hearts,
practiced the Ten Paths of Goodness,
and did not commit various evils.
After their lives ended,
they all attained birth in the heavens."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"If you wish to know who Prince Jiāliángnàjiālí was at that time,
it was my present self.
My father at that time, Lènàbámí,
is my present father, King Jìngfàn.
The mother at that time
is my present mother, Móhēmóyé.
King Líshībá at that time
was Móhējiāshè."
The one who was the wife at that time
is now Qúyí.
The one who was Bōpójiálí at that time
is now Típódáduō.
Those people of Yánfútí who received my grace
when I first attained the Way,
the eighty thousand devas,
and my disciples
who received the prediction of future enlightenment,
are these very people.
Ānán!
At that time,
I was harmed by him
and suffered to the absolute extreme,
yet I still used a compassionate heart
to pity and love him.
How much more so today,
having attained the Way of the Fó,
with all afflictions completely removed
and compassion widely spread—
being slightly harmed by him,
how could I not feel compassion and pity?"
After the Fó had said this,
those in the assembly,
hearing what the Fó had said,
were moved with gratitude for Shìzūn,
who, for the sake of all living beings,
had undergone intense suffering
without retreating or giving up.
They marveled at this unprecedented thing,
with sorrow and joy intermingled in their hearts;
they disciplined their minds and encouraged their wills,
contemplating the wondrous Fǎ.
There were those who attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
those who planted the good roots of a Pìzhīfó;
and those who gave rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed, correct, and true Way.
All together they respectfully revered it,
joyfully putting it into practice.
Xiányú Jīng, Volume Nine.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the country of Jiāwéiluówèi at the Níjūlútuó Saṃghārāma.
When the Buddha first returned to the country,
at that time, all the Shì people,
observing the Buddha's dignified bearing,
his marks and signs being extraordinary,
his body golden-colored,
with the thirty-two marks,
they never grew tired of looking at him.
They gathered together in groups in the streets, lanes, and marketplaces,
and with one voice,
they praised and spoke of the Rúlái:
"Among this multitude,
there is none of his kind;
he is truly worthy of respect!"
At that time, all the Bǐqiū,
having heard these discussions,
together spoke to the Buddha,
recounting the words of praise sung by those people.
At that time, the Shìzūn
told the Bǐqiū:
"You should know
that in the past,
among this multitude,
I was the most honored and most wonderful,
not only today."
Then the Bǐqiū
all together spoke to the Buddha:
"We do not know,
Shìzūn!
In past ages,
among this multitude,
how was it that you were the most honored and most wonderful,
and how did that happen?"
At that time, the Shìzūn
told the Bǐqiū:
"Listen closely, listen closely!
Keep it well in your hearts;
I shall for you
fully explain
the events of past ages."
They replied:
"Indeed,
we wish and desire to hear."
The Buddha then spoke for them:
"In the past, immeasurable,
inconceivable Āsēngqí Jié ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Lìngnú.
That king governed
eighty-four thousand minor kings,
ten thousand ministers,
five hundred princes,
and consorts and court ladies,
totaling twenty thousand.
The chief consort,
named Típóbápótí,
eventually became pregnant
and gave birth to a prince.
The child was handsome,
his body of purple-gold color,
his hair deep blue,
in the palms of both hands
were the marks of the thousand-spoked wheel,
on the sole of his left foot
was the mark of a horse,
and on the sole of his right foot
was the mark of a white elephant.
This child's merit
was singularly honored among men.
Following his parents' names,
he was given the name Típólìngnú.
Having been nursed and grown up,
the Great King Lìngnú
suddenly encountered a seasonal illness,
and his life was coming to an end.
The minor kings,
the ministers, and the princes
all came to inquire about his illness.
They asked the Great King:
'If you should pass away,
among the kings and princes,
who should succeed you?'
At that time, the king replied:
'If among my sons,
there is one who possesses the ten virtues,
then he shall be established as king.
What are the ten virtues?
First, his body is purple-gold in color,
and his hair is deep blue.
Second, in the palms of both hands,
there are marks of golden wheels,
complete and without defect.
Third, on the sole of his right foot,
there is the mark of a white elephant.
Fourth, under his left foot,
there is the mark of a horse.
Fifth, when he wears the royal garments,
they fit his body,
being neither too large nor too small.
Sixth, when he sits on the royal throne,
his majesty is towering,
and he sits in peace and stability.
Seventh, the kings and ministers
joyfully pay homage to him,
praising his goodness immeasurably;
when he enters the inner palace,
the consorts and court ladies
leap for joy
and pay respectful homage.
Eighth, if he is taken to a heavenly shrine,
the statues of the deities made of clay or wood
all pay homage to him.
Ninth, his power of merit
can cause seven treasures to rain down,
providing for all as requested.
Tenth, as for who his mother is,
he was born of the consort Típóbápótí.
If someone possesses these ten virtues,
he then shall be established
to serve as the Great King.'
Having finished giving his commands,
impermanence arrived,
and he then passed away.
"The kings, ministers, and people,
among the five hundred sons,
started from the eldest
and sequentially, using the ten criteria,
observed their bodies.
Among these princes,
their bodies were not golden-colored,
their hair was not deep blue,
their palms had no wheels,
and their soles had no marks of elephant or horse;
when wearing the royal garments, they did not fit;
when sitting on the throne,
the wooden lions
would startle and stand up,
wishing to strike or bite them;
the kings, ministers, and people
all did not pay homage;
when taken into the palace,
the consorts and court ladies
were not at all joyful,
and none paid respectful homage;
if they entered a heavenly shrine,
they themselves bowed to the heavenly statues,
while the various clay and wood heavenly statues
did not pay homage at all;
when told to make treasures rain down,
they were also unable to do so;
moreover, they were not born of the consort Típóbápótí.
Even up to all the five hundred great princes,
among the ten criteria,
they did not possess even one.
The youngest son,
his body was purple-gold in color,
his hair was deep blue;
looking at both his hands,
the wheel marks were complete;
observing the soles of his feet,
the elephant and horse marks
were as clear as a painting;
when he wore the royal dharma-garments,
they fitted his body;
when he sat on the throne,
his merit was towering;
among the kings, ministers, and people,
there was none who did not pay homage;
when he entered the inner palace,
the consorts and court ladies
respectfully paid homage;
when taken to the heavenly shrine,
the clay and wood heavenly statues
all paid homage to him;
when commanded to make treasures rain down,
as soon as the word was spoken, it rained;
when asked who had born him,
he was born of the consort Típóbápótí.
Possessing the ten criteria,
the kings, ministers, and people
then installed him as king.
On the fifteenth day,
at the first appearance of the sun,
a golden wheel treasure
came from the eastern direction.
The wheel had a thousand spokes,
and was one Yóujún in length and breadth.
The king then descended from his throne,
placed his right knee on the ground,
knelt and said:
'If my merit
is such that I should be king,
the wheel should respond to me.'
Immediately according to his words,
it came before the hall
and stayed in the empty air.
As for the white elephant treasure,
it came from Xiāng Shān.
Its hair and tail are strung with pearls;
if the king mounts it,
these elephants can all fly,
from morning until noon,
traveling throughout the Sì Tiānxià.
If it walks on foot,
the ground its feet touch
immediately becomes golden sand.
As for the Gànmǎ Bǎo,
its body is of a deep blue-green color;
the horse’s hair and tail
are all the color of pearls,
and they all rain down the seven treasures.
If the king mounts it,
in the time of a single meal,
it roams the Sì Tiānxià
without fatigue or exhaustion.
As for the Shénzhū Bǎo,
it arrives naturally;
the brilliance of that jewel
constantly illuminates one hundred and twenty lǐ day and night,
and from within it, it can further rain down the seven treasures,
providing for everyone’s needs.
As for the Yùnǚ Bǎo,
she arrives naturally,
upright and exceptionally wonderful,
fittingly suiting the king’s mind.
As for the Diǎncáng Chén,
whenever the king requires the seven treasures,
he provides them sufficiently as desired,
so they are never lacking or exhausted.
As for the Diǎnbīng Chén,
when the king desires the four types of troops,
in the time of a single glance,
all the troops assemble,
their ranks and formations disciplined and orderly,
with extraordinary power and majesty.
When the seven treasures were complete,
he sat and contemplated:
“I enjoy this position
all because of the merit and karma planted in past lives;
it is only because of this that I have attained it.
Now I must continue it so that it is never severed.”
He then used fragrant water
to bathe his body,
put on new, clean clothes,
and holding an incense burner in his hand,
he faced toward the Dōngfāng,
knelt, and said:
“Excellent ones of the Dōngfāng,
come and receive my invitation.”
Immediately, there were twenty thousand Bìzhīfó
who came to the royal palace;
toward the south, west, and north,
he invited them all in the same way.
At that time there were sixty thousand Bìzhīfó
who came to receive the king’s invitation.
The king and his ministers
provided the four kinds of offerings.
Those eighty-four thousand minor kings
had been away from home for a long time,
so they addressed the Great King,
wishing to take their leave and return to their countries.
The king immediately granted this.
They then addressed the king, saying:
“The excellent ones here
are very numerous.
We pray the king will show compassion
and spare a small number
for your servants to make offerings to,
wishing that we may share in this merit in the future.”
At that time, the Great King
then assigned the Bìzhīfó from the four directions
to the various minor kings
to make offerings to at appropriate times
for a period of eighty-four thousand years.
All the kings, ministers, and people,
after their lives ended,
were all able to be born in the heavens.”
The Buddha told all the Bǐqiū:
“If you wish to know who Lìngnú Wáng was at that time,
he is my present father, Báijìng Wáng.
She who was Típópátí Fūrén then
is my present mother, Móhē Móyé.
He who was Típó Lìngnú Wáng then
is my present self.
Those who were the five hundred Tàizǐ then
are these five hundred Shì.
Even at that time,
among all people,
I was the most honorable and wonderful.
Now that I have become a Buddha
with all the marks complete,
among this assembly,
I am the most extraordinary and wonderful.”
At that time, all in the great assembly,
hearing what the Buddha said,
some attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
some planted the causes and conditions for Bìzhīfó;
and some gave rise to the Púsà mind and attained non-retrogression.
Everyone in the assembly rejoiced,
and they received and practiced it with the highest respect.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in Shè-wèi-guó at the Qí-shù Jǐ-gū-dú-yuán.
At that time, Tí-pó-dá-duō,
although he had left the household life,
had a mind obscured by gain and offerings.
He committed three heinous crimes:
he pushed down a mountain to crush the Fó,
wounding the Fó’s toe;
he also let loose a black elephant,
intending to harm the Fó;
he caused a schism in the Sēng into two factions;
and he killed a Bǐ-qiū-ní who had ended all outflows.
Because he had thus killed living beings,
he was filled with doubt and fear regarding the future retribution he would receive.
At that time, there were the Liù-shī,
who went to question him.
The Liù-shī then spoke various false views to him,
saying:
"Doing evil brings no guilt,
and doing good brings no merit.
Should a mind of faith and respect arise,
one would lose and sever their roots of goodness."
At that time, Ā-nán,
whose love and respect for the Shì-zūn were profound as if for his own body,
felt deep regret and resentment.
Choked with sorrow and distress,
he addressed the Shì-zūn, saying:
"Tiáo-dá is so foolish!
He creates unwholesome karma,
destroys his roots of goodness,
and brings shame upon the Shì-zhòng-zǐ."
At that time, the Shì-zūn
said to Ā-nán:
"Tí-pó-dá-duō
has not only severed his roots of goodness for the sake of gain and offerings in this life;
in past lives, he also lost his life due to greed for gain."
Ā-nán addressed the Fó:
"Shì-zūn!
As for Tí-pó-dá-duō
in past lives
losing his life through greed for gain,
what were the circumstances of that?
We wish and long to hear of it."
The Fó told Ā-nán:
"Listen well, for I shall speak!
In the past, immeasurable and inconceivable Ā-sēng-qí-jié ago,
in this Yán-fú-tí,
there was a kingdom named Bō-luó-nài.
At that time, there was a Sà-bó named Mó-hē-yè-yí,
whose wife became pregnant.
She was naturally kind and good,
and her disposition was gentle.
When the months were full, she gave birth to a son.
His form was upright and handsome.
His parents loved him dearly.
They prepared fine food,
invited relatives and various Xiàng-shī,
and they celebrated together.
They held the child to show him to the assembly
and to give him a name.
The Xiàng-shī asked:
'Since this child was conceived,
what auspicious signs have occurred?'
The father replied:
'Since he was conceived,
his mother has naturally
been compassionate and kind.'
The Xiàng-shī then gave him a name,
calling him Shàn-qiú.
He was nursed and grew up,
fond of accumulating virtues
and having compassion for all living beings.
Later, she became pregnant again.
She naturally became ill-natured and wicked.
When the term was full, she gave birth to a son.
His form was ugly.
They immediately invited Xiàng-shī
to name him.
The Xiàng-shī asked:
'During this child's pregnancy,
what responses were there?'
They replied:
'Since she conceived this child,
her nature became ill-tempered and wicked.'
Thereupon, the Xiàng-shī
gave him a name,
calling him È-qiú.
He was nursed and grew up,
fond of doing evil deeds,
constantly giving rise to greed,
and harboring jealousy.
"When they had both grown up,
they wished to go together as merchants across the sea to seek treasures.
Each had five hundred attendants,
and they set out one after the other.
The road was long and distant,
and they ran out of food midway.
After seven days had passed,
they were not far from death.
At that time, Shàn-qiú
and the various merchants
all together with sincere hearts
prayed to the various deities,
wishing to be saved from hunger and deprivation.
In the empty marshes,
they saw a tree in the distance with lush branches and leaves,
and they immediately headed towards it.
There was a spring of water.
Shàn-qiú and the assembly,
all together with sincere hearts,
pleaded for mercy and protection.
Their sincerity moved the deity to respond,
who appeared and told them:
'Cut off one branch,
and what you need shall emerge.'
Everyone was joyful,
and they cut off one branch,
and delicious drinks flowed out.
They cut off a second branch,
and various foods emerged,
complete with a hundred flavors.
All of them received it
and each became full and satisfied.
They cut off a third branch,
and various wonderful clothes emerged,
of every kind and in great quantity.
They cut off a fourth branch,
and various treasures
were all provided,
fully adorned,
and all their needs were met.
È-qiú arrived later,
and his followers, just as before,
were all provided for.
Then he thought to himself:
'If these tree branches
can produce such various fine things,
how much more so its roots?
I should now fell it;
I will surely obtain the most wonderful and excellent things.'
Having made up his mind,
he ordered his men to fell it.
At that time, Shàn-qiú,
hearing these words,
was filled with indignation and distress,
and said to È-qiú:
'We were hungry and exhausted,
our lives hanging by a thread.
We received the grace of this tree
and were able to save our remaining lives.
How can you harbor such a wicked mind
as to wish to fell it?'
At that time, È-qiú
did not listen to his words
and immediately dug up its roots.
Shàn-qiú felt deep gratitude and respect,
and could not bear to watch it,
so he led his group back home.
After the tree had been felled,
five hundred Luó-shà appeared,
seized this È-qiú and the various merchants,
and devoured them all.
Their wealth and companions
were all lost."
The Fó told Ā-nán:
"The Shàn-qiú of that time
is my current self.
The father of that time
is my current father, Jìng-fàn-wáng.
The mother of that time
is my current mother, Mó-hē-mó-yē.
The È-qiú of that time
is the current Tí-pó-dá-duō.
Ā-nán!
Tí-pó-dá-duō
has not only done unwholesome things today;
for the sake of greed for gain and offerings,
he has done so throughout every lifetime.
In the past,
I frequently encountered him
and always taught him wholesome teachings,
but he would not follow them;
instead, he regarded me as an enemy."
At that time, Ā-nán
and the Sì-bù-zhòng,
hearing what the Fó had said,
were filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy.
They all encouraged one another,
and reverently practiced accordingly.
Xián Yú Jīng, Scroll Ten
Translated in Gāo-chāng-jùn by the Yuán Wèi Liáng-zhōu Shā-mén Huì-jué and others.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, in the Jǐshù Gěigūdú Garden.
At that time, the Bǐqiūs
all gave rise to doubts:
"The Worthy Ānán,
what deeds did he originally perform
to obtain this total retention,
so that upon hearing what the Buddha speaks,
he does not lose a single word?"
They all went together to the Buddha's place
and said to the Buddha:
"The Worthy Ānán,
what merit did he originally cultivate
to obtain such measureless total retention?
We only pray, Shìzūn,
that you would kindly give us an explanation."
The Buddha told the Bǐqiūs:
"Listen attentively and take it to heart!
This total retention
is entirely due to merit and virtue.
Long ago, in the past, an Āsēngqí of kalpas ago,
at that time there was a Bǐqiū
who kept a Shāmí
and constantly gave him strict orders,
instructing him to recite sūtras.
As for his daily lessons,
if the sūtra recitation was sufficient,
the teacher would be pleased;
if it was insufficient,
he would bitterly and severely reprimand him.
Thereupon, the Shāmí
was always full of distress.
Although he could recite the sūtras,
he lacked food and supplies.
If he went out to beg for food,
when he obtained food quickly,
his recitation would then be sufficient.
If the begging was slow,
his recitation would not be complete.
If the recitation was insufficient,
he would be severely reprimanded.
With a heart full of sorrow and worry,
he walked along weeping.
At that time, there was a Zhǎngzhě
who saw him weeping,
came forward, called to him, and asked:
'Why are you so distressed?'
The Shāmí replied:
'Zhǎngzhě, you should know!
My teacher is strict and demanding;
he commands me to recite sūtras
with a daily limit for the lesson.
If it is sufficient,
then he is pleased.
If it is incomplete,
I am bitterly and severely reprimanded.
I go out to beg for food.
If I obtain it quickly,
my recitation is then sufficient.
If the begging is slow,
the recitation is then incomplete.
If I do not complete the sūtra,
I am then severely reprimanded.
Because of these matters,
I am simply sorrowful.'
At that time, the Zhǎngzhě
immediately said to the Shāmí:
'From now on,
always come to my house.
I shall provide food and drink
so that you will not worry.
After eating, concentrate your mind and diligently recite the sūtras.'
At that time, the Shāmí,
having heard these words,
was then able to concentrate his mind and diligently recite and study.
The lesson limit did not decrease,
day by day according to the standard.
Because of this, the teacher and disciple
were both filled with joy."
The Buddha told the Bǐqiūs:
"The teacher at that time
was Dìngguāng Buddha.
The Shāmí at that time
is my current self.
The great Zhǎngzhě at that time
who provided the food offerings
is now Ānán.
Because he performed such deeds in the past,
he now possesses total retention
without any loss or forgetting."
At that time, the Bǐqiūs,
having heard this teaching,
rejoiced and accepted it with faith,
and received it with bowed heads to put it into practice.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi at the Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, in the Kingdom of Luóyuèqí,
there were two brothers who were merchants,
living together in one place.
The elder brother sought the daughter of a zhǎngzhě,
wishing to make her his wife.
The girl was young
and not yet of age to be married.
At that time, the elder brother
then went with many merchants
far to another country.
Years passed,
and he remained there for a long time, not returning.
As the girl grew older
and reached the age when she could be married,
[the zhǎngzhě] said to the younger brother:
“Your elder brother has gone far away
and has stayed there without returning.
You should now take my daughter.”
The younger brother replied:
“How could this be?
My elder brother is still alive;
I do not dare to go against him.”
At that time, the zhǎngzhě
repeatedly spoke of it,
but the younger brother’s resolve was firm
and he did not waver.
The zhǎngzhě did not stop there,
but forged a letter from afar
and entrusted it to various merchants,
saying that the elder brother had died.
When the younger brother heard of his brother's death, his heart was shocked.
The zhǎngzhě went to him again
and told him:
“Your elder brother is already dead.
What should the girl do?
If you do not take her,
I must consider another plan.”
Pressed by the urgency, the younger brother
then took the girl as his wife.
After some time had passed,
the woman became pregnant.
Later, the elder brother returned from the other country.
At that time, the younger brother,
hearing that his brother had returned to the country,
harbored shame and fear in his heart
and fled to Shèwèi.
After he had departed,
the various relatives and friends
pressed on the wife’s belly
and caused the fetus to be miscarried.
Through these turns of events,
[the younger brother] arrived before the Fó.
Driven by shame and regret,
he sought to leave the household life.
The Fó knew he could be saved
and immediately granted his permission.
Having received the Fó’s permission,
he then became a shāmén
named Yōupósī.
He upheld the disciplinary practices
with diligence and without sloth.
In due time, he attained the way of an āluóhàn;
his six supernatural powers were clear and penetrating,
and he was complete in all wisdoms.
When the elder brother arrived home,
he saw that the younger brother had already married his wife.
His heart was filled with jealousy and internal anger,
and he went in pursuit, wishing to kill him.
Seeking and inquiring after him,
he was told that he had gone to Shèwèi.
With poisonous hatred troubling his heart,
he immediately issued a great reward:
“To whoever can take my younger brother’s head,
I shall give a great reward of five hundred ounces of gold.”
At that time, there was a man
who came to answer the call:
“I can go and take his head.”
The elder brother immediately brought out the gold
to recruit the man,
and they set out together,
arriving in the Kingdom of Shèwèi.
Upon arriving there, they saw the younger brother
sitting in dhyāna meditation.
At that moment, that man
suddenly gave rise to a heart of compassion
and had this thought:
“How could I kill this bǐqiū?
If I do not kill him,
the gold will be taken back from me.”
He drew his bow, wishing to shoot;
while he was drawing the bow
and aiming at the bǐqiū,
when it came to releasing the arrow,
it struck the elder brother instead.
Harboring hatred, the elder brother
died in anger and distress.
Afterward, he took on another body,
in the form of a poisonous snake,
and was born within the door hinge of the dàorén’s dwelling.
His poisonous heart had not ceased,
and he planned to harm him.
As the door was frequently opened and closed,
his body was struck and he died.
After he had died,
he was still unable to change his disposition,
so he vowed to become a small poisonous insect.
He lived among the rafters of the dàorén’s house,
waiting for the time when the dàorén was sitting upright.
He descended from the rafters,
fell onto the top of his head,
and with fierce and potent venom,
he immediately killed the bǐqiū.
At that time, Shèlìfú,
having seen these events,
went to the place of the Fó
and said to the Fó:
“That deceased bǐqiū—
what were his past causes and conditions
that he could now attain the Way
yet be killed by poison?
I only wish, Shìzūn,
that you would grant an explanation.”
The Fó told Shèlìfú:
“Listen well and reflect well!
I shall explain it to you in detail.
In the distant past, throughout countless ages,
there was a pìzhīfó
who appeared in the world.
He lived in the mountain forests,
pursuing his purpose.
At that time, there was a hunter
who constantly caught birds and beasts,
using various methods and schemes,
hoping and waiting to make any catch.
The pìzhīfó
would startle the birds and beasts,
causing the hunter to be unable to catch them.
The hunter then harbored anger
and resentment,
and with a poisoned arrow,
he shot the pìzhīfó.
The pìzhīfó,
feeling pity for this man
and wishing to make him repent,
displayed spiritual powers for him—
namely, flying through the air and treading on the void,
bending and stretching, contracting and withdrawing,
appearing and disappearing at will,
with spiritual transformations.
At that time, the hunter,
having seen these things,
felt reverence in his heart.
Overcome with fear and self-reproach,
he sincerely apologized for his transgression
and begged for mercy in repentance.
The pìzhīfó
accepted his repentance.
After the repentance was finished,
he died from the poison.
When that man’s life ended,
he fell into hell.
After emerging from hell,
for five hundred lifetimes,
he was constantly killed by poison.
Down to the present day,
even though he attained the way of an āluóhàn,
he was still, by a poisonous insect,
stung to death.
Because he had given rise to an evil thought
yet immediately repented
and made a vow, saying:
‘May I in a future life encounter a holy teacher
and attain spiritual powers
like these,’
for this reason, he has now encountered me
and received the methods of the Way.”
At that time, Shèlìfú
and the whole assembly,
having heard what the Fó had said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, in the Jǐshù Gěigūdú Garden.
At that time, there was an old man
who had lost his wife early
and lived alone with his son.
Impoverished and without wealth,
he realized the world is impermanent
and thought of wanting to leave home.
He immediately went to the Buddha’s place
to seek entry into the Way.
Then the Buddha took pity on him
and immediately permitted him to leave home.
At that time, the father
then became a Bǐqiū.
Since the son was young at that time,
he became a Shāmí.
He always accompanied his father,
entering the village to beg for food
and returning to their dwelling at dusk.
At that time, there was a village
that was the most remote.
To go there to beg for food,
they had to return as dusk approached.
The father was old
and his pace was slow.
His son was afraid,
fearing various venomous beasts.
He hurriedly supported his father,
pushing him along the road.
His grip was not firm,
and he pushed his father to the ground.
Immediately, the father
died at his hands.
After the father died,
he went alone to the Buddha’s place.
Then the Bǐqiū
asked the Shāmí, saying:
"This morning, you and your master
went to the village to beg for food.
Where is he now?"
The Shāmí replied, saying:
"Earlier, I and my master
went there to beg for food.
When returning at sunset,
the master walked a bit slowly.
I was terrified at the time,
so I hurriedly pushed him.
I pushed him with too much force
and threw my master to the ground.
At that time, my master
immediately died on the road."
Then the Bǐqiū
rebuked the Shāmí:
"You are a very evil person!
You have killed your father and killed your master."
They immediately informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told them:
"Although this master died,
it was not with evil intent."
He then asked the Shāmí:
"Did you kill your master?"
The Shāmí replied, saying:
"I did indeed push him,
but it was not with evil intent that I killed my father."
The Buddha approved of his words.
"It is so, Shāmí!
I know your heart had no evil intent.
In a past life,
it was also just like this;
with no evil intent,
you killed each other."
At that time, the Bǐqiū,
having heard the Buddha’s words,
immediately spoke together to the Buddha:
"We do not understand,
World-Honored One!
In a past life,
what were the causes and conditions for this father and son
to then kill each other?"
The Buddha said:
"Listen carefully!
I shall tell you.
Immeasurable Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
a father and son
lived together in one place.
Then the father became extremely ill,
and while he was lying down asleep,
many horseflies and flies
frequently came to annoy and touch him.
The father then ordered his son to drive away the flies,
hoping to get peaceful sleep to relieve his fatigue.
Then the son hurriedly drove them away,
but the flies subsequently came back many times.
As they came back incessantly,
the son became angry.
He immediately took a large staff
and waited for the flies to kill them.
Then the horseflies and flies
vied to land on the father’s forehead.
He struck them with the staff
and immediately killed his father.
At that time,
it was also not with evil intent.
Bǐqiū, you should know!
The one who was the father then
is this Shāmí.
The son who struck his father’s forehead with the staff
is this dead Bǐqiū now.
Because at that time there was no evil heart,
though he struck and killed his father with the staff,
it was not with evil intent.
Now the retribution is returned,
and it was also not intentional killing."
At that time, the Shāmí
gradually cultivated and studied
with great diligence and without sloth,
and eventually became a Luóhàn.
Then the Bǐqiū,
having heard what the Buddha said,
all believed and understood in their hearts,
and joyfully practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Zhúyuán of Wángshè Chéng.
At that time, King Bōsīnuò of the Shèwèi Kingdom had a high official
named Xūdá,
whose family was immensely wealthy,
with limitless treasures.
He loved to practice charity
and relieved the poor and needy as well as the orphaned and the elderly.
People of that time, because of his deeds,
established a title for him,
naming him Gěigūdú.
At that time, the elder had seven sons.
As they each grew up,
he arranged marriages for them,
sequentially up to the sixth.
His seventh son was exceptionally handsome,
and he loved him with partiality.
When it was time to take a wife for him,
he wanted to find a woman of exquisite appearance, upright, and with auspicious marks
to seek her for his son.
He then spoke to various Póluómén, saying:
"Who has a fine daughter with perfect features?
Go and seek her for my son."
The Póluómén then searched for her,
traveling and begging from place to place,
until they reached Wángshè Chéng.
In Wángshè Chéng, there was a high official
named Hùmí,
with immeasurable wealth,
who faithfully respected the Sānbǎo.
Then the Póluómén went to his house to beg.
The law of the land for giving was that a young maiden must be ordered to hold the items for charity.
The elder Hùmí had a daughter at that time
whose appearance was upright
and her complexion was exceptionally beautiful.
She immediately came out holding food
to give to the Póluómén.
The Póluómén saw her
and were greatly delighted in their hearts:
"The one we were searching for, we have seen today."
They then asked the girl, saying:
"Has anyone come to seek you yet?"
She replied, saying: "Not yet."
They asked, saying: "Young lady!
Is your father in?"
The girl said: "He is."
The Póluómén said:
"Tell him to come outside,
for I wish to see him and talk with him."
Then the girl went inside
and said to her father:
"There are beggars outside
who wish to see you."
The father then went outside.
Then the Póluómén inquired after his well-being and whether he was at peace and well:
"The King of the Shèwèi Kingdom has a high official
named Xūdá.
Do you, Chancellor, know him?"
He replied, saying: "I have not met him,
but I have heard his name."
They responded, saying: "Do you know? This man is the most wealthy and noble in that Shèwèi Kingdom,
and you are the most wealthy and noble here.
Xūdá has a son
who is upright and exceptionally beautiful,
outstanding and full of wonder.
He wishes to seek your daughter.
Would this be acceptable?"
He replied, saying: "It is acceptable."
It happened that there was a merchant who wanted to go to Shèwèi.
Then the Póluómén wrote a letter and sent it with him to Xūdá,
explaining the matter in detail.
Xūdá was delighted
and went to the King to request leave to take a wife for his son.
The King immediately granted it.
Loading a great amount of precious treasures,
he headed for Wángshè Chéng.
Along the way, he gave relief to the poor and needy.
Arriving at Wángshè Chéng,
he reached the house of Hùmí
to seek a wife for his son.
The Elder Hùmí joyfully welcomed him,
arranged bedding and furnishings,
and he stayed the night at that house.
The household was bustling,
preparing food and drink.
Xūdá thought to himself:
"This Elder is preparing a great offering;
what does he intend to do?
Will he invite the King, the Prince, the Great Ministers, Elders and Laypeople, or marriage relatives
to hold a great assembly?"
He pondered the reason
but could not understand,
so he asked him, saying:
"Elder, this evening you are personally performing labor,
managing affairs,
and arranging offerings.
Is it because you wish to invite the King, the Prince, and the Great Ministers?"
He replied, "No."
"Is it to prepare a gathering for marriage relatives?"
He replied, "No."
"What then will you do?"
He replied, "I am inviting the Fó and the Bǐqiū Sēng."
At that moment, when Xūdá heard the names of the Fó and the Sēng,
his hair suddenly stood on end as if he had gained something.
His heart was filled with joy,
and he asked again, saying:
"What is meant by the name Fó?
I wish to understand its meaning."
The Elder replied:
"Have you not heard?
The son of King Jìngfàn, named Xīdá,
on the day of his birth, thirty-two auspicious signs descended from heaven,
and ten thousand gods guarded him.
He immediately walked seven steps,
raised his hand, and said:
'Above and below the heavens,
I alone am honored.'
His body is the color of gold,
with thirty-two marks
and eighty secondary characteristics.
He was destined to be a Jīnlún King ruling the four continents.
Seeing the suffering of old age, sickness, and death,
he did not enjoy staying at home,
but left home to cultivate the Way.
After six years of ascetic practices,
he attained All-Knowledge,
exhausted all fetters, and became a Fó.
He subdued eighteen hundred million demon hordes
and is named Néngrén.
With the Ten Powers and Fearlessness,
and the Eighteen Distinctive Qualities,
his radiance shines brightly,
and his Three Insights see far and wide;
therefore, he is called Fó."
Xūdá asked:
"What is meant by the name Sēng?"
Hùmí replied:
"After the Fó attained the Way,
Fàntiān entreated him to turn the marvelous Wheel of Dharma.
He went into the Lùyě Yuàn in Bōluónài
for the sake of Kūlín and the four others,
turning the Four Noble Truths.
Their taints were exhausted and fetters untied,
and they became Shāmén,
endowed with the Six Supernatural Powers.
Mastering the Four Applications of Mindfulness, Seven Factors of Enlightenment, and Eightfold Path,
they rose into the empty sky.
Eighty thousand gods
attained Xūtuóhuán,
and incalculable devas and humans
resolved upon the Supreme and Perfect Way.
Next, he saved the thousand people of the brothers Yùbēijiāshè;
their taints were exhausted and their minds liberated, just like those five people.
Successively, he saved the five hundred followers of Shèlìfú and Mùlián, who also attained the state of Yìngzhēn.
Such as these, with supernatural powers and ease,
are able to serve as a superior field of blessings for sentient beings;
therefore, they are called Sēng."
Hearing such marvelous things spoken, Xūdá
was filled with exuberant joy,
feeling thoughts of faith and respect.
He eagerly waited for dawn,
when he would go to see the Fó.
His sincerity moved the spirits to respond;
he saw the ground become bright as day.
Following the light, he immediately went
to the gates of Luóyuè city, which open three times at night:
at the beginning of the night, the middle of the night, and the end of the night.
These are called the three watches.
He went out the gate in the middle of the night
and saw a celestial shrine,
to which he immediately paid homage.
Suddenly, he forgot his thought of the Fó,
and his heart returned to darkness.
He then thought to himself:
"It is still dark tonight.
If I go,
I might be harmed by evil ghosts or fierce beasts;
I should return to the city."
He decided to wait for dawn before going.
At that time, there was a relative
who had died and been reborn in the Sìtiān.
Seeing that Xūdá wished to turn back,
he descended and spoke to him:
"Layman! Do not turn back!
If you go to see the Fó,
you will gain immeasurable benefit.
Even if you were now to obtain a hundred carts of treasures,
it would not equal taking one step toward the Shìzūn;
the benefit obtained is profound,
exceeding that of the treasures.
Layman! Go and do not turn back!
Even if you were now to obtain white elephants and treasures,
it would not equal lifting one foot to go toward the Shìzūn;
the benefit exceeds that.
Layman! Go and do not turn back!
Even if you were now to obtain the whole of Yánfútí filled with treasures,
it would not equal taking one step to the Shìzūn's place;
the benefit gained is vastly more.
Layman! Go and do not turn back!
Even if you were now to obtain the four continents filled with treasures,
it would not equal lifting one foot to go to the Shìzūn's place;
the profit obtained would exceed that by a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times."
When Xūdá heard the deva speak these words,
his joy increased even more.
Respectfully thinking of the Shìzūn,
the darkness immediately turned to dawn light again.
Following the road, he arrived at the Shìzūn's place.
At that time, the Shìzūn knew Xūdá was coming
and went outside to walk in meditation.
Then Xūdá saw the Shìzūn from afar,
like a mountain of gold.
His marks, characteristics, and majestic appearance
were solemn and radiant, exceeding Hùmí's description ten thousand fold.
Beholding him, his heart was delighted,
but he did not know the rules of etiquette,
so he simply asked the Shìzūn:
"I wonder, Qútán! How is your health?"
The Shìzūn immediately told him to sit.
At that time, a Shǒutuóhuì heaven deva saw Xūdá from afar and noticed that, although he beheld the Shìzūn,
he did not know the method of paying homage and making offerings.
He transformed into four people
who came in a line. Arriving at the Shìzūn's place,
they bowed to his feet,
knelt for a long time to inquire after him, asking if his health was vigorous,
circumambulated him three times to the right,
and then withdrew to stand on one side.
At that time, Xūdá, seeing them do this,
was amazed
and thought to himself:
"The method of showing respect
should indeed be like this."
He immediately rose from his seat,
paid respect like them,
inquired after the Buddha's health,
circumambulated him three times to the right,
and then withdrew to stand on one side.
At that time, the Shìzūn immediately preached the Dharma for him:
the profound Four Truths,
suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
Hearing the Dharma, he was joyful,
and was immediately imbued with the Holy Dharma,
attaining the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
just as a clean piece of white cotton is easily dyed with color.
Kneeling with palms joined,
he asked the Shìzūn, saying:
"In the city of Shèwèi,
among people like my companions, who are easily imbued upon hearing the Dharma, are there others comparable to me?"
The Fó told Xūdá:
"There is no second person like you.
In Shèwèi Chéng, most people believe in false teachings,
and it is difficult for them to be imbued with the Holy Teachings."
Xūdá said to the Fó:
"I only wish that the Rúlái would graciously descend
to visit Shèwèi,
to cause the sentient beings there to remove the false and follow the right."
The Shìzūn said:
"The ways of the renunciant are different from those of the laity,
and the places where they stay should be different.
There is no vihara there;
how could I go?"
Xūdá said to the Fó:
"Your disciple can build one;
I pray you will grant your permission."
The Shìzūn remained silent.
Xūdá took his leave to arrange his son's marriage.
After finishing, he took leave of the Fó to return home,
and said to the Fó:
"When I return to my own country,
I shall establish a vihara,
but I do not know the design or rules.
I only wish the Shìzūn would send one disciple to go with me and give instructions."
The Shìzūn contemplated:
"Within Shèwèichéng, the Póluómén believe in false and perverted views.
If others go there,
they will certainly not be able to succeed;
only Shèlìfú is of the Póluómén stock,
has been clever since his youth,
and possesses spiritual powers.
If he goes, it will surely be beneficial."
He then commanded him to go with Xūdá.
Xūdá asked, saying:
"When the Shìzūn travels on foot,
how many lǐ can he cover in a day?"
Shèlìfú said:
"Half a yóuxún a day.
Following the walking method of a Zhuǎnlúnwáng,
so too is the Shìzūn."
At that time, Xūdá, along the route, built a guest house every twenty lǐ.
Calculating the labor and costs,
he paid out money to hire workers,
stationed people there,
and ensured that food, drink, and bedding were all sufficient.
From Wángshèchéng to Shèwèiguó,
he returned to his home and, together with Shèlìfú, surveyed the lands to see which part was flat and broad,
so as to build a jīngshè.
They surveyed all around
but found no desirable place.
Only Prince Qǐtuó had a park
whose land was level and square,
its trees lush and dense,
neither too far nor too near,
and perfectly situated.
Then Shèlìfú said to Xūdá:
"In this park, a jīngshè should be built.
If it is built far away,
begging for food will be difficult;
if it is built close by, it will be noisy
and hinder the practice of the Way."
Xūdá was joyful
and went to the Prince's place,
saying to the Prince:
"I now wish to build a jīngshè for the Rúlái.
The Prince's park is excellent;
I now wish to buy it."
The Prince smiled and said:
"I lack for nothing.
This park is flourishing,
and I use it for amusement and relaxation."
Xūdá requested earnestly
even two or three times.
The Prince was attached to the park and reluctant to part with it.
Doubling the asking price,
he thought that by calling the price so high,
Xūdá would certainly be unable to buy it.
He said to Xūdá:
"If you can cover the ground with gold
so that there is no empty space between,
then I shall give it to you."
Xūdá said: "Agreed;
I shall pay that price."
Prince Qǐtuó said:
"I was only joking."
Xūdá said:
"According to the law of a Prince,
one should not speak falsely.
If one uses false words and deceit,
how can one succeed the throne
and care for the people?"
He then went with the Prince to settle the matter in court.
At that time, a Shǒuduóhuì Tiān, because a jīngshè was to be built for the Buddha,
feared that the ministers might be biased toward the Prince,
so he transformed into a person
to judge the matter. He said to the Prince:
"According to the law of a Prince,
one should not speak falsely.
Once the price has been agreed upon,
you should not regret it midway."
Thus it was judged to be given to him.
Xūdá was joyful
and commanded his servants: "Bring out gold on elephants."
Within the eighty qǐng, it was almost filled in a moment,
with only a small area of land remaining.
Xūdá pondered:
"Which treasury of gold is sufficient? Neither too much nor too little,
I must take enough to fulfill it."
Qǐtuó asked:
"Do you think it's too expensive and want to leave it?"
He replied: "No.
I am considering which gold treasury is sufficient
to fill the remainder."
Qǐtuó thought:
"The Buddha must be of great virtue
to make this man treat treasure so lightly."
He ordered him to stop there!
"Do not bring out more gold.
The land belongs to you,
but the trees belong to me.
I myself will offer them to the Buddha,
and we shall build the jīngshè together."
Xūdá was joyful
and agreed to it.
He then returned home
to begin the construction work.
The liùshī heard of this
and went to tell the King:
"The elder Xūdá has bought Qǐtuó's park
to build a jīngshè for the shāmén Qútán.
Let our followers compete in skills with them.
If the shāmén wins,
then allow the construction;
if they are not as good,
they may not build it.
Qútán's followers stay in Wángshèchéng,
while our followers stay here."
The King summoned Xūdá
and asked him:
"Now these liùshī say
that you bought Qǐtuó's park
to build a jīngshè for the shāmén Qútán,
and they seek to compete in skills with the shāmén's disciples.
If they win,
you may build the jīngshè;
but if they are not as good,
you may not build it."
Xūdá returned home,
wearing dirty and greasy clothes,
distressed and unhappy.
The next day at the proper time, Shèlìfú
put on his robes and took his bowl,
and went to Xūdá's house.
Seeing he was unhappy,
he asked:
"For what reason are you unhappy?"
Xūdá replied:
"I only fear that the jīngshè to be built will not be completed,
and for this reason I am distressed."
Shèlìfú said:
"What is the reason you fear it will not be completed?"
He replied:
"Now the liùshī have gone to the King to seek a competition.
If the honored one wins,
the jīngshè may be built;
if not as good,
they will block it and not allow its construction.
These liùshī have been renouncers for a long time,
their sincerity is well-established,
and in the skills they have learned, none can match them.
I do not know if the honored one's skills can compete with them or not."
Shèlìfú said:
"Even if these liùshī
filled the whole of Yánfùtí like a bamboo forest,
they could not move a single hair on my foot.
Whatever they wish to compete in,
let them do as they please."
Xūdá was joyful,
changed into new clothes,
bathed in fragrant water,
and went to tell the King:
"I have asked him.
The liùshī wish to compete;
let it be as they wish."
At that time, the King told the liùshī:
"I now allow you to compete with the shāmén."
Then the liùshī announced to the people of the country:
"Seven days from now,
at a wide and spacious place outside the city, we shall compete with the shāmén."
In Shèwèiguó, there were eighteen yì people.
According to the law of that country,
they beat drums to assemble the crowd.
If they beat the bronze drum,
eight yì people gathered;
if they beat the silver drum,
fourteen yì gathered;
if they beat the gold drum,
everyone gathered.

When the seven-day period was full, they went to the flat and broad place and beat the gold drum, and everyone assembled; the followers of the liùshī numbered three yì people. At that time, the people set up high seats for the King and his liùshī.
Then Xūdá set up a high seat for Shèlìfú.
At that time, Shèlìfú sat under a tree, silently entered samadhi,
his senses quieted,
wandering through various chándìng,
attaining thorough and unhindered understanding.
He thought:
"This great assembly has long practiced what is false,
they are arrogant and self-important,
treating the multitude of living beings like grass and weeds.
With what virtue should I subdue them?"
Having thought thus,
he would use two virtues.
He then made a vow:
"If, during countless jié, I have been filially devoted to my parents and have respected shāmén and Póluómén,
when I first enter the assembly,
may the entire great crowd bow down to me."
At that time, the Liù Shī, seeing that the assembly had already gathered,
and that Shèlìfú alone had not yet arrived,
they then said to the King,
“The disciple of Qútán, knowing himself to have no arts,
falsely claimed to challenge our abilities;
now that the assembly has gathered,
he is afraid and does not come.”
The King said to Xūdá,
“Your master’s disciple—
the time for the challenge has arrived,
he should come to speak.”
At that time, Xūdá went to where Shèlìfú was,
knelt down and said,
“Great Virtuous One!
The great assembly has gathered,
I wish for you to come to the meeting.”
Then Shèlìfú arose from his meditative concentration,
rearranged his robes,
placed his níshītán on his left shoulder,
and walked slowly and with composure,
like a lion king,
going toward the great assembly.
At that time, the people, seeing that his appearance and Dharma robes were extraordinary,
as well as the various Liù Shī, suddenly stood up,
like grass bending in the wind,
and unconsciously paid him respect.
Then Shèlìfú ascended the seat prepared by Xūdá.
Among the followers of the Liù Shī, there was a disciple
named Láodùchā
who was skilled in the knowledge of illusion.
Before the great assembly, he chanted an incantation to create a tree
that naturally grew large,
providing shade over the assembly;
its branches and leaves were lush and dense,
and its flowers and fruits were all unique.
The people all said,
“This transformation was indeed made by Láodùchā.”
Then Shèlìfú, using his spiritual power, created a xuánlán wind,
which blew and uprooted the tree,
toppling it to the ground
and smashing it into fine dust.
The people all said,
“Shèlìfú has won!
Now Láodùchā is not his equal.”
He then again chanted to create a pond,
the four sides of which were all made of the seven treasures,
and within the pond water, various flowers grew.
The people all said,
“This was made by Láodùchā.”
Then Shèlìfú transformed and created a great six-tusked white elephant,
on each of whose tusks were seven lotus flowers,
and on each of those flowers were seven jade maidens;
the elephant moved slowly and with composure
to the edge of the pond
and took the water into its mouth,
whereupon the pond immediately vanished.
The people all said,
“Shèlìfú has won!
Láodùchā is not his equal.”
He again created a mountain
adorned with the seven treasures,
with springs, ponds, trees, flowers, and fruits in lush abundance.
The people all said,
“This was made by Láodùchā.”
Then Shèlìfú immediately transformed and created a Jīngāng Lìshì,
who, using a Vajra pestle,
pointed at it from afar,
and the mountain was immediately destroyed,
with nothing remaining.
The assembly all said,
“Shèlìfú has won!
Láodùchā is not his equal.”
He again created a dragon
with ten heads on its body,
raining down various treasures from the void;
thunder and lightning shook the earth, startling the great assembly.
The people all said,
“This too was made by Láodùchā.”
Then Shèlìfú transformed and created a King of the Jīnchì Birds,
who tore it apart and ate it.
The people all said,
“Shèlìfú has won!
Láodùchā is not his equal.”
He again created an ox,
its body tall and large,
fat, strong, and powerful;
with thick legs and sharp horns, it pawed the ground and roared loudly, charging forward.
Then Shèlìfú transformed and created a lion king
that tore it apart and ate it.
The people said,
“Shèlìfú has won!
Láodùchā is not his equal.”
He then transformed his body into a Yèchā ghost,
its form tall and large,
with fire burning on its head,
eyes red as blood,
four long and sharp tusks,
and fire coming out of its mouth,
as it leaped and rushed forward.
Then Shèlìfú transformed his own body into King Píshāmén;
the Yèchā was terrified
and immediately wished to retreat and flee,
but fire arose on all four sides,
and there was no place to go.
Only around Shèlìfú was it cool and without fire;
he immediately surrendered,
prostrating with his five limbs to the ground
and pleading for mercy to save his life.
Once the feeling of humiliation had arisen,
the fire immediately vanished.
The people all shouted,
“Shèlìfú has won!
Láodùchā is not his equal.”
Then Shèlìfú ascended into the void
and manifested the four deportments:
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
emitting water from the upper part of his body
and fire from the lower part of his body;
disappearing in the east and springing up in the west,
disappearing in the west and springing up in the east,
disappearing in the north and springing up in the south,
disappearing in the south and springing up in the north;
sometimes manifesting a giant body
that filled the void,
and then manifesting a small one;
sometimes dividing his one body
into hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, or billions of bodies,
and then merging them back into one body;
from the void
he was suddenly on the ground,
walking on ground as if it were water,
and walking on water as if it were ground.
Having performed these transformations,
he withdrew his spiritual powers
and sat on his original seat.
The great assembly of the gathering, seeing his spiritual power,
were all filled with joy.
Then Shèlìfú preached the Dharma to them
according to their original conduct and past karmic conditions of merit;
each attained the traces of the Path:
some becoming Xūtuóhuán, Sītuóhán, Ānàhán, or Āluóhàn.
Three hundred million disciples among the followers of the Liù Shī left the home life to study the Path under Shèlìfú.
After the competition of skills was completed,
the fourfold assembly dispersed,
each returning to where they stayed.
The elder Xūdá, together with Shèlìfú, went to plan the monastery;
Xūdá held one end of the rope in his hand,
while Shèlìfú held the other end,
and together they measured out the monastery.
Then Shèlìfú smiled joyfully.
Xūdá asked,
“Honorable one, why are you smiling?”
He replied,
“As you have just begun to measure the ground here,
palaces in the Six Heavens of Desire have already been completed.”
He then lent him the eye of the Path;
Xūdá saw all the magnificent and pure palaces in the Six Heavens of Desire
and asked Shèlìfú,
“Among these Six Heavens of Desire, which place is the most blissful?”
Shèlìfú said,
“In the lower three heavens,
sensual desires are deep and thick;
in the upper two heavens, there is arrogance and self-indulgence;
in the fourth heaven, there are few desires and contentment,
and a Bodhisattva in the stage of one more birth always comes to be born there,
where the Dharma teachings never cease.”
Xūdá said,
“I should surely be born in the fourth heaven.”
As soon as he finished speaking,
all the other palaces vanished,
leaving only the palace of the fourth heaven appearing clearly.
They resumed following the rope,
but then Shèlìfú looked sorrowful and had an expression of worry.
He then asked the Venerable One, “Why do you have a look of worry?”
He replied,
“Do you see the ants in this ground now?”
He answered, “I have seen them.”
Then Shèlìfú said to Xūdá,
“In the past, during the time of Pípóshī Buddha,
you also built a monastery for that World-Honored One on this very ground,
and these ants were born among it.
In the time of Shīqì Buddha,
you also built a monastery for that Buddha in this place,
and these ants were also born among it.
In the time of Píshèfú Buddha,
you also built a monastery for the World-Honored One on this ground,
and these ants were also born among it.”
At the time of Jūliúqín Fó,
he was also a Shìzūn, and a vihāra was established in this ground,
and this ant was also born within it.
At the time of Jūnāhánmóuní Fó,
he was the Shìzūn, and a vihāra was established in this ground,
and this ant was also born within it.
At the time of Jiāshè Fó,
he was also a Fó, and a vihāra was established in this ground,
and this ant was also born within it.
Up to today, for ninety-one jié,
it has received this one type of body
and has not attained liberation.
Saṃsāra is long and far-reaching;
only merit is essential,
and one must not fail to plant it."
At that time, Sūdá felt deep pity and sorrow.
Having finished measuring the ground,
he built the vihāra,
making a cave-dwelling for the Fó.
Using exquisite zhāntán to make fragrant clay,
he built separate rooms for staying in twelve hundred places,
and in one hundred and twenty places, he separately hung jiānzhuī.
Having completed the arrangements,
he wished to go and invite the Fó,
but he thought to himself:
"There is a King above,
whom I should inform;
if I do not report to him,
there might be anger or resentment."
He then went to inform the King:
"I have built a vihāra for the Shìzūn;
I only wish that the Great King would send a messenger to invite the Fó."
When the King heard this,
he immediately sent a messenger to Wángshè Chéng to invite the Fó and the Saṃgha:
"I only wish the Shìzūn would grace Shèwèi with his presence."
Then the Shìzūn, surrounded by the sìzhòng, emitting great light and shaking the earth, arrived at the state of Shèwèi.
At every guest house he passed, he stayed,
and along the way, he liberated countless people.
Gradually approaching the outskirts of the city of Shèwèi,
the entire multitude held offerings
to welcome and wait for the Shìzūn.
When the Shìzūn arrived in the country,
he went to a spacious place,
emitting a great light that illuminated the three-thousandfold great thousand-fold worlds.
He pressed his toe upon the ground,
and the earth all shook.
The musical instruments in the city sounded by themselves without being struck;
the blind saw and the deaf heard;
the mute spoke and the hunchbacked straightened;
those with chronic illnesses or paralysis were all healed.
All the people, men and women, young and old, seeing these auspicious omens, rejoiced greatly
and went to the place where the Fó was;
eighteen hundred million people gathered together.
At that time, the Shìzūn administered medicine according to the illness,
preaching the wonderful Dharma for them.
Corresponding to their past karma,
each attained the path:
some became Sūtuóhuán, Sītuóhán, Ānàhán, or Āluóhàn;
some planted the causes for becoming a Bìzhīfó;
and some resolved their minds on the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Each and every one rejoiced and followed the Fó's words.
The Fó told Ānán:
"This garden land was bought by Sūdá,
while the trees, flowers, and fruits belong to Zhǐtuó.
Since these two people were of one mind in establishing this vihāra,
it should be named the Zhǐshù Gěigūdú Yuán of the Crown Prince;
let this name be spread and transmitted to future generations."
Then Ānán and the four groups, hearing what the Fó had said,
received it with reverence and followed it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Fó was at the Jiālántuó Zhúyuán in Luóyuèqí.
At that time, Ānán,
while among the trees,
sat in quiet meditation and reflection,
when suddenly this thought arose:
"The Rúlái, the Perfectly Awakened One,
is complete in all faculties;
his merit, wisdom, and brilliance
are exquisite and beyond measure.
In the past,
by what causes and conditions
did the Shìzūn first resolve his mind on this unsurpassed Great Vehicle?
What deeds did he practice
to attain such superior and wonderful benefits?"
After having this thought,
he immediately rose from meditation,
went to where the Fó was,
bowed his head in greeting,
and stepped forward to say to the Fó:
"Just as all Shìzūn
are among all humans and devas in the world
the most honored and exquisite,
with merit, wisdom, and brilliance
that are majestic and immeasurable.
I do not know,
Shìzūn,
by what causes and conditions in the past
did you first resolve your mind on this unsurpassed Great Vehicle?"
The Fó told Ānán:
"If you wish to know,
think upon it well.
I shall
explain it to you in detail."
Ānán said to the Fó:
"Yes, I shall listen well!"
The Fó told Ānán:
"In the far distant past,
immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable Āsēngqí jié ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Móhē Bōluópóxiū,
which in the Jìn language means Dàguāngmíng,
who ruled over five hundred small kingdoms.
At that time, the great king
went out hunting with his ministers.
The elephant the king was riding
had its lustful desires ignited.
Carrying the king, it galloped away,
chasing after a female elephant.
As it gradually approached a great forest
and rushed into the trees,
the elephant trainer said to the king:
'Grasp a tree and pull yourself up;
then you can save yourself.'
The king followed his words
and they both held onto a tree.
After the elephant had left,
the king was furious
and bitterly rebuked the elephant trainer,
wishing to kill him immediately.
'Because your training of the elephant was not up to standard,
you have nearly endangered my life today.'
The elephant trainer said to the king:
'I trained it according to the method,
but this elephant now
is deluded by desire.
Lustful minds are difficult to train;
it is not your servant's fault.
I beg for your forgiveness.
In three days,
the elephant will surely return of its own accord.
Watch your servant test it,
and if I fail, I shall not regret ten thousand deaths.'
The king then stayed his execution.
After the scheduled three days,
the elephant returned to the palace.
Then the elephant trainer
heated seven iron balls
until they were glowing red
and forced the elephant to swallow them.
The elephant did not dare to disobey,
and after swallowing them, it died.
The king's mind was opened to understanding,
and he, along with his ministers,
marveled at this unprecedented event.
He asked him again:
'Such a lustful mind—
who is able to tame it?'
At that time, a celestial deity inspired the elephant trainer
to answer the king:
'The Fó is able to tame it.'
When the king heard these words,
he resolved his mind, saying:
'Such sticky and stubborn
things that are difficult to subdue—
only the Fó can remove them.'
He then made a vow:
'I wish to become a Fó.'
Diligently practicing through jié,
never resting or ceasing,
until today,
he has finally attained the reward."
The Fó told Ānán:
"If you wish to know who that great king was at that time,
it is I myself."
At that time, the assembly,
hearing what the Fó had said,
all resolved their minds on the unsurpassed, right, and true path,
rejoicing greatly
beyond measure,
receiving it with reverence and following it.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in the Nígūlútuó Sēngjiālán in the kingdom of Jiāpíluówèi.
At that time, all the Shì people,
beholding the Shìzūn's radiant spiritual transformations
and the manifestation of his wondrous transformations,
which were most rare and extraordinary,
magnificent and majestic,
and beyond compare.
Furthermore, they praised the excellence of Jiāochénrú and the others:
"What past blessings do they have?
When the Rúlái appeared in the world,
and the drum of the Dharma first resounded,
they were the very first to hear it;
when the sweet dew first fell,
they immediately received its moisture,
forever leaving behind defilement and impurity,
their minds and bodies attaining the profound essence;
in cities, camps, villages, and towns,
crowds follow one another,
with different mouths but the same voice,
offering immeasurable praise?"
Then all the Bǐqiū,
having heard these words,
went to where the Buddha was,
prostrated with their heads at his feet,
and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"Now the people within this realm
have all gathered together,
with different mouths but the same voice,
to praise and sing of the Shìzūn's
various virtuous deeds,
and regarding these five people,
what past blessings do they have,
that they alone were the first to be delivered?"
The Buddha told the Bǐqiū:
"It is not only today that I have first delivered these five people;
in the distant past,
I also rescued them.
Using my body as a boat,
I saved them from drowning,
preserved their lives,
so that each attained peace and stability,
and reached the other shore.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood,
I deliver them first."
Then the Bǐqiū
immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not know,
Shìzūn!
In former times,
how did you deliver them
and cause them each to attain peace and stability?
We only pray that the Shìzūn
will speak of it for us."
The Buddha told the Bǐqiū:
"If you delight to hear it,
I shall speak of it for you."
They all said:
"Indeed."
The Buddha told the Bǐqiū:
"In the distant past,
in this Yánfútí, in the kingdom of Bōluónài,
at that time there was a king
named Fànmódá.
At that time in the kingdom,
there was a great Sàbó
named Lènàshéyé,
who traveled abroad,
and among the trees of a forest,
he saw a man
weeping and mourning bitterly,
who had tied a rope to a tree,
put his head into it,
and intended to hang himself.
He then went forward and asked him:
'Why are you doing this?
A human body is hard to obtain,
and life is fragile,
with countless declines and changes
that are always feared to arrive on their own.'
With various explanations,
he instructed him to cast away the rope.
The man replied:
'I have little merit,
and my poverty has reached its extreme limit.
My debts have piled up,
so many they are hard to count.
All my creditors
compete to strip and seize from me,
pressing me day and night,
and my worried heart finds no relief.
Although heaven and earth are wide,
there is no place to accommodate my body.
Now I wish to end my life to escape this suffering.
Although you, benevolent sir, advise me,
living is not as good as dying.'
Then the Sàbó
immediately promised him, saying:
'Sir, just release the rope.
However much you owe,
I will repay it all on your behalf.'
Having said this,
the man then stopped,
rejoicing and leaping with joy.
With immeasurable gratitude,
he followed the Sàbó,
and together they went to the marketplace,
proclaiming to all that he wished to repay the debts.
Then all the creditors
gathered like clouds,
coming to collect what was owed.
Those who came were without limit,
and his wealth was exhausted.
When his goods and wealth were gone,
the debts were still not fully paid.
His wife and children were impoverished and freezing,
begging for food to survive.
His clansmen and the people of the country and towns
all scolded and disliked him:
'This is a madman,
who has destroyed his own family estate.'
At that time,
there was a group of merchants
who urged the Sàbó,
wishing to go to sea together.
He immediately answered them, saying:
'According to the way of a Sàbó,
one must provide a ship and its gear;
I am now impoverished
and have nothing left.
By what means could I follow you?'
The crowd replied:
'We are five hundred people in all;
we will open our hearts and contribute money
to provide the ship and gear.'
Having heard these words,
he then granted permission.
The crowd agreed and combined their resources,
and they obtained much gold and treasure.
At that time, the Sàbó,
with three thousand taels of gold,
used one thousand taels to prepare the ship,
one thousand taels to prepare provisions,
and one thousand taels to provide whatever was needed on the ship,
with much remaining to support his wife and children.
Then at the seashore,
they constructed a large ship.
The ship had seven layers;
after the preparations were complete,
they pushed it into the water.
With seven great ropes,
they tied it to the shore,
struck a large golden bell,
and proclaimed to all:
'Who wishes to go to sea to obtain great and wonderful treasures, rare and unusual items that can be used without end?
You may now gather like clouds to go together to the place of treasures.'
He further told them:
'Only those who do not cherish parents, wife, children, the pleasures of Yánfútí, or their own lives
may go.
The reason for this is
that in the great sea,
hardships and dangers are many—
swirling waves and violent winds,
great fish and evil ghosts—
various things like these
that cannot be fully described.'
After saying this,
he immediately cut one rope.
Every day was like this,
until the seventh day,
when the ropes were all cut,
and the ship sped away.
Then while on the way,
they suddenly encountered a violent wind,
which broke the ship into pieces.
The people called out for rescue,
but had nowhere to turn.
Some were able to get planks, masts, or floating bags to save themselves,
while others fell into the water and drowned.
Among them were five people
who together addressed the Sàbó:
'We followed you to come here,
but now we are about to drown.
Danger is imminent;
we pray you will save us.'
The Sàbó replied:
'I have heard that the great sea
does not harbor a corpse overnight.
All of you now,
each catch hold of me.
For your sake,
I shall take my own life
to rescue you from your distress,
and I vow to seek Buddhahood.
In the future, when I attain Buddhahood,
I shall use the ship of the supreme Right Dharma
to deliver you from the suffering of the great sea of birth and death.'
After saying this,
he cut himself with a knife.
After his life ended,
The sea god raised a wind,
blowing them to the further shore;
they were able to cross the great sea
and all attained peace and security."
Fó told the Bǐqiū:
"If you wish to know who Lènàshéyé was at that time,
it is my current self.
The five people of that time
were Jūlín and the others.
In a previous life,
I saved the lives of those people from birth and death;
now that I have attained Buddhahood,
I have caused those five people to be the first to attain the undefiled true Dharma,
far removed from the great ocean of the long-flowing fetters."
At that time, all the Bǐqiū
together praised
Rúlái’s great compassion,
which is profound, wondrous, and immeasurable.
They all diligently exerted themselves;
having heard what Fó had spoken,
they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus I have heard:
at one time, the Fó was in the Zhúyuán of Mójíe Country.
At that time, the Shìzūn and the Bǐqiū
were heading toward Píshèlǐ
and arrived at the Líyuè Hé.
At that time, by the riverbank,
there were five hundred ox-herders
and five hundred fishermen.
Those fishermen
had made three kinds of nets,
differing in size:
the small one was pulled by two hundred people,
the medium one by three hundred,
and the large one by five hundred.
At that time, the Rúlái
stopped to rest not far from the river,
and all the Bǐqiū also sat down together.
Then the fishermen
caught a great fish in their net;
five hundred people pulled it
but could not bring it out.
They then called the crowd of ox-herders,
making a total of a thousand people,
and together they pulled it out.
They obtained a great fish
with a hundred heads on its body,
of various kinds,
such as donkeys, horses, camels,
tigers, wolves, pigs, dogs,
apes, monkeys, and foxes—
of such sorts as these.
The people were greatly amazed
and vied to gather and look at it.
At that time, the Shìzūn
told Ānán:
“What is happening there
that the great crowd has gathered?
Go and see.”
Ānán received the instruction
and immediately went to look.
He saw a great fish
with a hundred heads on its body;
he returned and told the Shìzūn
what he had seen.
The Shìzūn then,
together with the Bǐqiū,
went to where the fish was
and asked the fish:
“Are you Jiāpǐlí?”
It answered:
“I truly am.”
He solemnly asked three times:
“Are you Jiāpǐlí?”
It answered:
“I truly am.”
He asked again:
“The teacher who instructed you,
where is he now?”
It answered:
“He has fallen into the Ābí Dìyù.”
At that time, Ānán
and the great crowd,
not knowing the causes,
said to the Shìzūn:
“For what reason now
do you call the hundred-headed fish
Jiāpǐlí?
We only wish you would take pity
and explain this to us.”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Listen carefully, listen carefully!
I shall tell you!
Long ago, in the time of Jiāyè Fó,
there was a Póluómén
who had a son
named Jiāpǐlí
(in Jìn speech, called Huángtóu).
He was intelligent and brilliant;
among his kind,
he was first in learning,
yet he was still not as good as the Shāmén.
When his father was near death,
he earnestly cautioned:
‘You must be careful not to debate principles with the Shāmén of Jiāyè Fó.
Why is this?
The wisdom of the Shāmén is profound;
you will certainly not be their equal.’
After the father died,
his mother asked:
‘You have always been eminent and bright;
is there anyone now who is superior to you?’
He answered:
‘The Shāmén are far superior to me.’
The mother asked again:
‘In what way are they superior?’
He answered:
‘When I have doubts
and go to ask the Shāmén,
what they expound
causes one to understand.
If they ask me,
I cannot answer.
For this reason,
I know I am not their equal.’
The mother told him again:
‘Why do you not go and study their teaching?’
He answered:
‘To study their teaching, one must become a Shāmén.
I am a báiyī;
how can I study?’
The mother told him again:
‘Feign to be a Shāmén;
once you have mastered the study,
come back and stay at home.’
Following his mother's instruction,
he became a Shāmén.
After a short time,
he recited the Sānzàng
and mastered the meanings and principles.
The mother asked him:
‘Are you superior now?’
He answered:
‘Being superior in learning is not as good as zuòchán.
How do I know this?
When I ask those people,
they can analyze everything;
when those people ask me,
I do not know.
Because of this,
I am not yet equal to them.’
The mother told him again:
‘From now on,
if you talk with them
and happen not to be their equal,
you may then revile and insult them.’
Jiāpǐlí said:
‘The Shāmén who have left home
have no faults.
How can I revile them?’
She answered:
‘Just revile them,
and you shall be the victor.’
At that time, Jiāpǐlí could not bear to disobey his mother.
On a later day, when debating again,
if his logic was short or failed,
he would then revile them, saying:
‘You are all foolish!
You have no discernment
and are worse than beasts!
