What Dharma do you know?’
He compared them to the heads
of all the hundred beasts;
he did this repeatedly,
not just once or twice.
Due to these causes and retributions,
he now receives the body of a fish
and has a hundred heads.”
Ānán asked the Fó:
“When will he be able to escape this fish body?”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Within this Xiánjié,
even after a thousand Buddhas have passed,
he will still not have escaped.”
At that time, Ānán
and the people,
hearing what the Fó had said,
were disappointed and unhappy.
Filled with sorrow,
they all spoke with one voice,
saying:
“Actions of body, speech, and mind
must not be done without caution.”
At that time, the fishermen and the ox-herders
all together joined their palms toward the Fó,
seeking to leave home
and purely practice fànhèng.
The Fó immediately said it was possible:
“Welcome, Bǐqiū!”
Their hair and beards fell off on their own,
Dharma robes were on their bodies,
and they became Shāmén.
At that time, the Shìzūn
spoke the wonderful Dharma for them
with various hardships and urgencies.
Their defilements were exhausted and their bonds released,
and they became Āluóhàn.
He then extensively spoke various Dharmas for the assembled crowd,
distinguishing the Sìdì of Kǔ, Jí, Miè, and Dào.
Some attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit,
and some developed the resolve for the great path;
their numbers were very great.
At that time, the four assemblies, hearing what the Fó had said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Xiányú Jīng, Volume 10.
Xiányú Jīng, Volume 11.
Translated by the Shāmén Huìjué and others of Liángzhōu in Gāochāng Prefecture during the Yuán Wèi.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the country of Shèwèiguó, in the Jíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, the king of the country was named Bōsīnuò.
The king had a chief minister
who was intelligent and immensely wealthy.
His wife became pregnant
and gave birth to a son
whose appearance was upright and handsome
and whose physical form was extraordinary.
At that time, the chief minister,
seeing the child, was filled with joy;
he immediately summoned a physiognomist
and ordered him to read the child's signs.
The physiognomist looked and saw him,
and joyfully said:
“This child has signs of fortune;
he is outstanding among men,
intelligent, wise, and eloquent,
and possesses virtue that surpasses others.”
Upon hearing this, the father was delighted
and ordered a name to be given to him.
The physiognomist asked, saying:
“Since the child was conceived,
what unusual things have happened?”
The chief minister replied, saying:
“His mother's original nature
was not virtuous or kind,
but since she became pregnant,
it changed remarkably and unusually;
her character became respectful and submissive,
she delighted in praising the virtues of others,
she was compassionate toward those in suffering and distress,
and she did not like to speak of faults.”
The physiognomist said:
“This is the child's will;
we should name him
Āxìnzéiqí,
which in the Jìn language means Wúnǎo.”
As the child gradually grew up,
he became matchlessly robust
and possessed the strength of a powerful warrior.
One man could face a thousand;
he could leap up and catch flying birds
and run as fast as a galloping horse.
His father, the chief minister,
loved and cherished him deeply.
In that country,
there was a Pólāomén
who was intelligent and profoundly learned,
with broad knowledge and great insight.
He had five hundred disciples
who followed and studied under him.
At that time, the chief minister
took his son
and entrusted him to the teacher,
so that he might pursue his studies.
The Pólāomén agreed,
and accepted him for instruction.
Āxìnzéiqí
worked diligently day and night;
one day of his learning
surpassed a whole year for others.
Before he had studied for long,
he had thoroughly mastered everything.
The Pólāomén teacher
treated him exceptionally;
in every activity and movement,
he was always with him.
His fellow students
also looked upon him with great respect and admiration.
At that time, the Pólāomén teacher's wife,
seeing that his appearance and talent were outstanding and far surpassed the ordinary,
harbored lustful feelings and attachment for him,
and her desire for him would not leave her mind.
However, the various disciples
always surrounded him,
so he was never alone in his movements.
She had no opportunity to speak with him;
having a desire she could not fulfill,
she was constantly sighing in melancholy.
It happened that a Dányuè
came to invite the teacher and all the disciples
for a three-month period.
The Pólāomén teacher privately discussed this with his wife:
“I must now go to accept this invitation for three months,
and I should leave one person behind to manage things.”
At that time, the wife was secretly delighted
and devised a hidden plan.
She said to the Pólāomén:
“This is how it should be.
The household affairs are weighty
and require someone talented;
you may leave Wúnǎo and entrust him with the household matters.”
Then the Pólāomén
immediately commanded Wúnǎo:
“I am now going to the Dányuè's invitation.
The household affairs are many
and require someone to manage them.
You possess talent;
look after the household for me.”
Wúnǎo received the instruction
and stayed behind while the others left.
The teacher and the assembly of disciples
set off and departed.
His wife was immensely pleased and joyful;
she adorned herself elaborately
and put on many seductive airs.
She spoke with him,
attempting to stir his passions.
Wúnǎo’s resolve was firm,
and he had no intention of complying.
Her lustful heart grew even stronger,
and she spoke her true feelings to him:
“I have admired and loved you
for a long time,
but because of the presence of the others,
I could not express what was in my heart.
Before your teacher left,
I purposefully had you stay behind.
Now that it is quiet and we are alone,
you should follow my wishes.”
Wúnǎo reasoned with her and declined,
saying:
“According to my Fànzhì law,
I must not commit adultery with my teacher's wife.
If I were to violate this, I would no longer be a Pólāomén.
I would rather face death
than ever do such a thing.”
At that time, the teacher’s wife,
finding her great expectations thwarted,
felt ashamed and grew furious.
She then devised another secret plan.
Waiting until the teacher was about to arrive,
she tore her clothes,
scratched her face,
covered her body in dust,
and lay haggard on the ground,
saying nothing.
When the Pólāomén teacher and his disciples arrived,
the teacher immediately went inside.
Seeing his wife’s appearance,
he immediately asked for the reason:
“What caused you to be like this?”
The wife wept and said:
“It is not worth asking.”
The Pólāomén asked her again:
“What happened to you?
You must tell me.
Why do you not speak?”
The wife cried and said:
“The one you so admire and praise,
Āxìnzéiqí—
since you left,
he has repeatedly assaulted me.
Because I would not comply,
he tore my clothes
and harmed my body.
You keep such a disciple—
how could he be like this?”
Hearing this, the Pólāomén
was filled with great anger.
He said to his wife:
“This Wúnǎo
has the strength to face a thousand men.
He is the son of the chief minister,
and his clan is powerful.
Although I wish to punish him,
I must do so gradually.”
Having finished his planning,
he went to see Wúnǎo.
Using appropriate means,
he spoke comfortingly to him, saying:
“After I left,
you worked hard and labored.
Furthermore, all this time,
you have served me with complete loyalty.
I have always been moved by your devotion
and wished to reward you.
There is a secret method
that I have never spoken of before.
If you can accomplish it,
you will be born directly in Fàntiān.”
Wúnǎo knelt down
and asked what it was.
The teacher replied:
“If, within seven days,
you cut off the heads of a thousand people
and take one finger from each,
obtaining a total of one thousand fingers,
and make a garland out of them,
at that time, Fàntiān
will descend himself,
and after your life ends,
you will certainly be born in Fàntiān.”
Hearing this, Wúnǎo felt hesitant in his heart,
and said to his teacher again:
“This should not be so.
How could killing living beings
lead to birth in Fàntiān?”
The teacher said to him again:
"You are my disciple;
do you not believe my most essential words?
If you do not believe them, then our bond of righteousness is severed;
follow your own path and stay here no longer."
Then he cast another spell
and stood a knife in the ground.
Once the spell was spoken, an evil heart arose within the disciple.
The master, knowing his intent,
then handed him the knife.
Taking the knife, he ran outside
and killed whoever he encountered,
taking their fingers to make a garland.
When people saw him, they called him Āngchóumóluó,
which in the Jìn language means Zhǐmán.
He traveled about, killing and maiming, until the seventh day,
when he finally had nine hundred and ninety-nine fingers,
lacking only one finger.
If he could kill just one more person,
the number of fingers would be complete.
People all went into hiding,
and none dared to travel.
He went everywhere searching,
but could not find anyone else.
During those seven days,
he had neither food nor drink.
His mother felt pity for him
and sent people to bring him food,
but they were all gripped by fear,
and none dared to go.
His mother, carrying the food,
went there herself.
From afar, the son saw his mother
and ran toward her, intending to kill her.
His mother then spoke to him:
"Alas, you unfilial creature!
How can you harbor such rebellion and wish to harm me?"
The son then replied:
"I have received my master's teaching,
that within seven days
I must obtain a full thousand fingers,
and then I shall attain my wish to be born in Fàntiān.
The number of days is already full,
yet I can find no one else.
Since there is no other way,
I must kill my mother."
The mother spoke again:
"If it must be so,
then simply take my finger,
but do not kill me."
At that time, Shìzūn witnessed everything from afar.
Knowing that he could be delivered,
He transformed into a Bǐqiū
and walked near him.
Āngchóumóluó saw the Bǐqiū,
abandoned his mother, and leapt forward,
running to kill him.
The Buddha, seeing him coming,
walked slowly away.
Zhǐmán ran with all his might but could not catch up,
so he called out from a distance:
"Bǐqiū, stay a moment!"
The Buddha answered from afar:
"I am always at stay,
but it is you who do not stay."
Zhǐmán asked again:
"How is it that you are at stay while I am not?"
The Buddha replied:
"All my senses are tranquil and settled,
and thus I have attained mastery.
You follow an evil teacher
and have received false and inverted teachings
which have altered your heart;
you cannot remain settled
as you kill day and night,
creating boundless sin."
Hearing this, Zhǐmán’s mind suddenly awakened.
He threw the knife far away
and bowed from a distance to take refuge.
Only then did the Rúlái wait for him,
manifesting His Buddha-body,
radiant as the sun,
with the thirty-two marks
appearing brilliant and marvelous.
Zhǐmán, seeing the Buddha's radiant marks and majestic bearing,
threw himself to the ground
and repented with self-reproach.
The Buddha briefly preached the Dharma,
and he attained the purity of the Dharma Eye.
His heart became purely faithful,
and he requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha granted it, saying:
"Welcome, Bǐqiū!"
His hair and beard fell off of their own accord,
and Dharma robes appeared on his body.
According to what was appropriate for him,
the Buddha preached the Dharma again.
The impurities of his mind were completely exhausted,
and he attained the path of the Luóhàn.
The Buddha then took him
back to the Qǐtuó Lín.
At that time, within the kingdom,
the common people,
upon hearing the name of Zhǐmán,
were all struck with alarm and terror.
Pregnant women and animals
were so terrified they could not give birth.
At that time there was an elephant
that could not deliver its offspring.
The Buddha commanded Zhǐmán
to go and speak these true words:
"Since I was born,
I have not killed a single person."
Zhǐmán said to the Buddha:
"I have killed many since long ago;
how can I say I have not killed?"
The Buddha told him:
"Within the Noble Dharma,
this is when you were first born."
Then Zhǐmán adjusted his robes
and went to speak according to the instruction;
as soon as the words were spoken, all were delivered safely.
He returned to the Jīngshè
and sat in a room.
At that time, King Bōsī nì
assembled a great army,
intending to personally go and suppress Āngchóumóluó.
His route passed by Qǐhuán
as he set out to attack.
At that time within Qǐhuán,
there was a Bǐqiū
whose form was extremely short and ugly,
but whose voice was extraordinarily marvelous.
He raised his voice in loud chanting,
the sound being extremely harmonious and smooth.
The army leaned in to listen,
never feeling satiated.
The elephants and horses pricked up their ears
and stood still, refusing to move.
The King, finding this strange,
turned to ask his driver:
"Why is this so?"
The driver replied:
"It is because of the chanting
that the elephants and horses have stopped to listen."
The King said:
"Even animals delight in hearing the Dharma;
we who are human,
why should we not go and listen?"
So with his entourage,
he turned back into Qǐhuán for a while.
Arriving there, he dismounted his elephant,
unbuckled his sword, and put aside his parasol.
He went straight to where the Buddha was,
bowed respectfully, and inquired after Him.
That chanting Bǐqiū
had finished his chanting.
The King first asked, saying:
"Just now I heard the sound of chanting,
clear, marvelous, harmonious, and smooth.
My heart is filled with admiration;
I wish to meet and know him,
and will offer him one hundred thousand coins."
The Buddha told him:
"Give him the money first,
and only then should you see him.
If you have already seen him,
you will have no desire to give even a single coin."
Then the Buddha showed him the Bǐqiū.
Seeing his appearance,
which was doubly short and ugly,
the King could not bear to look at him,
and his mind had no thought of giving a single coin.
The King rose from his seat,
knelt down, and said to the Buddha:
"Now this Bǐqiū
is extremely short and hideous in form,
yet his voice is so deep and far-reaching.
What did he do in a past life
to receive such a retribution?"
The Buddha told the King:
"Listen well and take this to heart!
In the past there was a Buddha
named Jiāyè.
When He had finished delivering people,
He entered Bānnièpán.
At that time, the king of that country,
named Jīlǐpí,
collected the Shèlì
intending to build a Tǎ.
At that time, four Lóngwáng
transformed into human form
and came to see the King,
asking about the building of the Tǎ:
'Will it be made of jewels,
or will it be made of earth?'
The King then replied:
'I want the Tǎ to be large,
but I do not have many jewels;
how can it be completed?'
"Now I wish to build with earth,
and make it five lǐ square and twenty-five lǐ high,
so that it is extremely tall, prominent, and magnificent to behold."
The Lóngwáng said:
"I am not a human;
we are all Lóngwáng.
Hearing that the King is building a stupa,
we have come to inquire.
If you wish to use treasures,
we shall assist you."
The King said joyfully:
"If you can do so, it would be wonderful."
The dragon spoke again:
"Outside the four city gates,
there are four great springs.
Use the water from the spring to the east of the city
to make bricks,
and they will become dark blue lapis lazuli.
Use the water from the spring to the south of the city
to make bricks;
when those bricks are finished,
they will all become yellow gold.
Use the water from the spring to the west of the city
to make bricks;
once the bricks are completed,
they will change into silver.
Use the water from the spring to the north of the city
to make bricks;
when those bricks are finished,
they will turn into white jade."
Upon hearing these words,
the King's joy doubled.
He immediately appointed four overseers,
each in charge of one side.
While the work of the other three overseers was nearing completion,
one overseer was negligent and lazy,
and his work alone was not finished.
The King went to inspect and saw this,
and rebuked him with reason:
"You have not applied your mind;
you shall be punished."
That man harbored resentment
and said to the King:
"This stupa is too large;
when will it ever be finished?"
After the King left,
he ordered all the workers
to work diligently day and night,
and it was all completed at once.
The stupa was extremely high and steep,
adorned and carved with various brilliant treasures;
it was an extraordinary sight.
Seeing it, he felt joyful
and repented for his past fault.
Carrying a golden bell,
he placed it at the top of the stupa's pillar
and immediately made a vow:
"May the voice of my future births be extremely beautiful,
so that all sentient beings will delight in hearing it.
In the future there will be a Buddha
named Shìjiāmóuní;
let me see him and be delivered from birth and death."
"It is so, Dàwáng!
If you wish to know who that overseer was—the one who worked slowly and resented the stupa's size—
it is this bǐqiū.
Because of those words of hatred and his dislike of the stupa's size,
for five hundred lifetimes,
he was always extremely short and ugly;
because he later joyfully offered the bell to the top of the stupa,
seeking a beautiful voice and vowing to see me,
for five hundred lifetimes,
he had an extremely beautiful voice,
and now he has met me again
and attained liberation."
When the King heard this,
he took his leave to depart.
The Buddha asked the Dàwáng:
"Where do you wish to go?"
The King said to the Buddha:
"In my kingdom there is an evil bandit, Āngchóumóluó,
who harms and kills the people,
rampaging and committing violence.
Now I wish to lead my troops to attack and punish him."
The Buddha told the King:
"Āngchóumóluó
is now such that he would not kill an ant,
how much less anything else."
The King thought to himself:
"Has the Shìzūn already gone and subdued him?"
The Buddha told the King:
"Zhǐmán has now left the household, entered the path, and attained the stage of Āluóhàn;
all his evils are gone forever.
He is now in his room;
do you wish to see him?"
The King said:
"I desire to see him."
He immediately rose and went outside his room.
Hearing the sound of the bǐqiū Zhǐmán coughing,
and remembering the vast extent of his violent evil and harm,
he fell to the ground in terror and fainted, only reviving after a long while.
He returned to where the Buddha was
and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the King:
"Not only today did you fall to the ground and faint upon hearing his voice,
but in past lives, you also fainted upon hearing his voice.
Listen well, Dàwáng!
In the distant past,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great kingdom
named Bōluónài.
At that time in the kingdom,
there was a poisonous bird
that caught various poisonous insects
and always used them for food.
Its form was extremely poisonous
and could not be approached.
Wherever it passed over,
all sentient beings would die
and all trees would wither.
At that time, this bird
happened upon a forest
and perched upon a tree,
coughing as if about to cry out.
At that time in that forest,
there was a Bái Xiàngwáng
under a nearby tree.
Hearing the sound of the poisonous bird,
he fell to the ground and fainted, unable to move.
It is so, Dàwáng!
The poisonous bird of that time
is now Zhǐmán.
The Bái Xiàngwáng of that time
is now you, the King."
The King again said to the Buddha:
"Āngchóumóluó
was excessively violent and harmful;
he killed so many people,
and it is thanks to the Shìzūn that he was subdued and transformed to practice good."
The Buddha told the King:
"Āngchóumóluó
not only today killed many people
and received my subduing and transformation;
in past lives,
he also killed these same people,
and I also subdued and transformed him,
so that he again thought of good."
The King again said to the Buddha:
"I do not know how these people were harmed in previous lives
and how the Shìzūn subdued and transformed him.
How did it happen?
I wish for you to explain it."
The Buddha told the King:
"Listen well and take it to heart!
In the distant past, countless Āsēngqíjié ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great kingdom
named Bōluónài.
At that time, the King of the country
was named Bōluómódá.
At that time, the King
led the four kinds of troops
into the mountain forests
for travel and hunting.
The King arrived at a marsh
chasing after birds and beasts,
and riding alone on a single chariot,
he arrived by himself deep in the forest.
The King was then extremely exhausted
and dismounted to rest for a while.
At that time in the forest,
there was a lioness
who was overcome with intense desire
and was wandering in search of a mate.
Fatigued and unable to find one,
she happened to be in the forest
and saw the King sitting alone.
Her lustful intentions grew even stronger,
and she thought of following the King.
She approached his side
and stood with her tail raised and her back toward him.
The King knew her intent
and thought to himself:
'This is a fierce beast
whose strength can kill me.
If I do not comply with her wish,
I might meet with harm.'
Because the King was afraid,
he immediately complied with the lioness.
After the act of desire was completed,
the lioness went away.
His troops and followers
then arrived,
and the King together with the multitude
returned to the palace city.
At that time, the lioness
became pregnant from this,
and when the months and days were fulfilled,
she gave birth to a son.
His form was entirely like a human,
only his feet were spotted."
The lioness remembered and recognized him;
knowing he belonged to the King,
she then carried him in her mouth
and placed him before the King.
The King also reflected,
personally remembering previous events,
and knew this was his own son.
He immediately took and raised him.
Because his feet were mottled,
he was named Jiā mó shā bō tuó,
which in the Jìn language means Bó Zú.
As he grew up gradually,
he possessed heroic talent and a fierce will.
When the father King died,
Bó Zú succeeded to the rule.
At that time, King Bó Zú
had two consorts:
one of the royal lineage,
and the second of the Pó luó mén lineage.
At one time, King Bó Zú
went out of the city one day
to travel to the gardens for sightseeing.
He commanded the two consorts:
"Follow after me;
the one who arrives first
shall be granted one day
to enjoy the utmost pleasure with me.
As for the one who follows behind,
I will not see her."
After the King left,
the two consorts
adorned themselves exquisitely,
prepared their carriages and mounts,
and set out together at once.
Upon arriving midway on the road,
they saw a heavenly shrine.
The one of the Fàn zhì lineage
descended from the carriage to pay homage.
After finishing her homage, she hurried forward,
yet she still arrived afterward.
The King followed his original words
and would not receive her.
Thereupon the consort
was filled with anger and resentment,
blaming the heavenly deity:
"It was because I paid homage to you
that the King treats me with contempt.
If you have divine power,
why did you not protect me?"
Harboring hatred and distress,
she secretly formulated a plan.
After the King returned to the palace,
she served him with extra care.
After receiving his favor once again,
she requested a wish from the King:
"Allow me to have absolute authority in the kingdom for one day."
Meeting with the King's partiality,
he immediately permitted it.
She went out and ordered men to destroy the heavenly shrine,
leveling it to the ground,
and then returned to the palace.
The deity guarding the heavenly shrine
was aggrieved and vexed.
He went to the palace
intending to cause harm;
but the deity of the royal palace
blocked him and would not allow him to enter.
"There was a Xiān Rén
living in the mountain of the Xiān.
King Bó Zú
constantly provided offerings to him.
Every day at mealtime,
he would fly into the palace.
He did not eat fine delicacies,
but ate coarse food and humble offerings.
It happened one day that the Xiān Rén did not come.
The heavenly deity knew this
and transformed into his form
to enter the palace.
The palace deity still recognized him
and would not allow him to enter.
Standing far outside the gate,
he requested the King to allow him passage.
When the King heard the Xiān Rén was outside seeking an audience,
he wondered at the reason
and urgently ordered him to be let in.
At this time, the palace deity,
hearing the King's command, ceased and did not block him.
He went straight forward and gained entry,
sitting in the place where the Xiān Rén usually sat.
A meal was prepared as usual
to serve him.
The transformed Xiān Rén
refused to eat the food,
and then said to the King:
'This food is coarse and bad;
furthermore, there is no meat or fish.
How can it be eaten?'
The King immediately replied:
'Since the Great Xiān himself
has always eaten pure and vegetarian food,
I therefore did not have meat, fish, or fine delicacies prepared.'
The transformed Xiān further said:
'From this day forward,
do not provide coarse offerings,
but use only meat for food.'
It was prepared exactly as spoken,
and after eating, he departed.
When the next day arrived,
the old Xiān flew there.
Fine delicacies and various kinds of meat were prepared for him.
The Xiān Rén was enraged
and felt resentment toward the King.
The King said:
'The Great Xiān commanded me yesterday to do it this way.'
The Xiān Rén said:
'Yesterday I was ill
and fasted for a day;
I did not come here.
Who told you this?
You are merely mocking and testing me,
and thus it is so.
I cause the King, for the next twelve years,
to constantly eat human flesh.'
Having finished these words,
he flew back to the mountains.
After this, the kitchen supervisor
forgot to prepare meat.
At the time, he had no plan,
so he went out to seek meat.
He saw a dead child, plump and white, on the ground.
Thinking of the urgent need,
he immediately removed the head and feet,
carried it into the kitchen,
added various delicious spices,
and prepared the meal for the King.
When the King ate it,
he found it twice as delicious as usual,
and immediately asked the kitchen supervisor:
'Since I have been eating meat,
there has never been such deliciousness.
What meat is this?'
The kitchen supervisor was terrified
and prostrated himself before the King:
'If the King pardons my crime,
then I will dare to tell the truth.'
The King answered him:
'Just speak the truth;
I will not question your crime.'
The kitchen supervisor said to the King:
'The other day something happened,
and I did not have time to find meat.
I found a dead child
to meet the immediate need.
I did not expect Your Majesty
would actually notice it.'
The King said:
'This meat is exceptionally delicious.
From now on,
seek it out in this manner.'
The kitchen supervisor said to the King:
'Last time I just happened to find a child who died naturally;
finding another is impossible.
He who prepares the food
fears the laws of the land.'
The King again said:
'You just take them secretly.
If anyone finds out,
the judgment lies with me.'
The kitchen supervisor followed the order,
secretly capturing them,
and serving the King daily.
At that time, among the people in the city,
each went about weeping for their missing children,
asking one another:
'How has it come to this?'
The ministers gathered to discuss,
deciding to try keeping a close watch.
They placed people
everywhere in the streets and lanes.
They saw the King’s kitchen supervisor dragging away another child,
watched and captured him,
bound him and brought him to the King,
and reported all the matters of the children who had gone missing before and after.
When the King heard these words,
he remained silent and did not answer.
For the third time they said to the King:
'Now that the thief has been caught
and the crime is clearly exposed,
the matter should be judged and decided.
Why are you silent?'
The King then replied:
'It was I who ordered it.'
The ministers harbored resentment
and each withdrew.
Outside, they discussed together:
'The King himself is the thief
and eats our children.
How can we be ruled by a king who devours people?
We must remove him together and get rid of this calamity.'
All with one heart joined in a common plan:
"Outside the city in the garden,
there is a fine pond.
Its king goes every day
there to bathe.
The ministers should store weapons and
hide in ambush within the garden."
When the king went out to bathe and reached the pond,
the hidden soldiers suddenly surrounded him from all sides,
immediately encircling the king
to capture and kill him.
The king, seeing the soldiers gathered,
asked in alarm and fear:
"Why have you all surrounded and pressured me?"
The ministers replied:
"He who is a king
makes nourishing the people his business.
But you turn to the cook,
killing people for food.
The masses of people cry out in lament,
having nowhere to voice their grievances,
unable to bear the bitter cruelty.
Therefore, we wish to kill the king."
The king said to the ministers:
"I have indeed acted improperly.
From now on,
I will never do it again.
I only hope you will forgive and release me;
I shall reform myself."
The ministers said:
"We will never release you.
Even if today the heavens rained black snow,
and black poisonous snakes grew upon your head,
we still would not listen to you.
There is no need for further words."
At that time, King Bózú, having heard the ministers' words,
knew he would certainly die,
with no path to escape.
He then said to the ministers:
"Though you must kill me,
delay for a short moment;
allow me to stay a little while."
The ministers relaxed their hold.
The king then made a vow:
"By the good deeds
I have cultivated in my life,
by my righteous rule as a king,
by my offerings to the Xiānrén,
and by all the virtues I have gathered,
may they result in me becoming a flying Luóchà today."
After his words were finished,
they were immediately realized.
He flew into the void
and said to the ministers:
"You all joined forces,
wishing to kill me by force.
Fortunately for me,
I was able to extract myself.
From now on,
you all should take care,
for your beloved wives and children
will be the next for me to eat."
After speaking, he flew away
and stayed among the mountain forests,
flying and snatching people,
carrying them off to eat.
People of all kinds
hid in fear.
After this continued,
he had killed and eaten many people.
Other Luóchà
attached themselves as his followers.
His group gradually increased,
and the harm caused became even more widespread.
Later, the Luóchà
said to King Bózú:
"We serve you
as your followers, O King.
We wish for you
to hold a banquet."
At that time, King Bózú
promised them:
"I shall capture kings until they number one thousand
and give them to you
to be a banquet."
After making the promise,
he went one by one to capture them,
locking them in the deep mountains.
He had already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine kings,
with only one person remaining,
and the count was not yet full.
The kings thought:
"We are in dire straits;
where should we turn?
If he captures Xūtuó Sùmí,
Xūtuó Sùmí has great skillful means
and can save us."
After making this plan,
they said to the Luóchà King:
"If the King wishes to hold a banquet,
make it truly exceptional.
Take only kings,
without using common or lowly people;
Xūtuó Sùmí
has very high virtue.
If you can get him to come,
the King's banquet will be truly fine."
The Luóchà King said:
"What high virtue does he have?"
Immediately he soared up
and went, wishing to capture him.
He happened upon Xūtuó Sùmí,
who was leading his maidens.
In the morning, he wished to leave the city to go to the garden to bathe.
On the way, he saw a Suōluómén
begging from him for a gift.
The king said to the Póluómén:
"Wait until I return from bathing,
and I shall give you alms."
Once the king reached the garden,
he entered the pond to wash.
At that time, the Luóchà King
flew through the air to capture him
and carried him to the mountains.
Xūtuó Sùmí
was filled with sorrow and wept!
At that time, King Bózú
asked him:
"I have heard your name and virtue are supreme and foremost.
The will of a great man
should be able to withstand both adversity and success.
Why are you so sorrowful,
crying like a small child?"
Xūtuó Sùmí said to the Luóchà King:
"I do not love my body or begrudge my life.
But I reflect that since my birth, I have never spoken falsely.
This morning I left the palace
and saw a Dàoshì
in front of my carriage
begging from me for a gift.
I promised that after returning from bathing,
I would give him alms.
When I went out I met the Great King, who carried me here.
I reflect that I have now spoken falsely and broken my trust.
That is why I am sorrowful;
it is not out of concern for my life.
I beg for your compassion
to grant me seven days
to give alms to that Dàoshì.
I shall then return to meet my death."
Bózú, hearing this,
said to him:
"If you are allowed to go now,
would you actually return on your own to face death?"
He then asked again:
"Even if you do not return,
I myself can capture you."
He then released him and let him go.
The king returned to his country.
The Dàoshì was still there.
He joyfully made offerings
and gave alms to the Póluómén.
At that time, the Póluómén,
seeing that the king would soon return to face death,
feared he would be filled with sorrow due to his attachment to the country,
and for the king's sake,
spoke a verse, saying:
" 'When the cycle of kalpas reaches its end,
heaven and earth are utterly consumed,
Xūmí and the great oceans
all become ashes and embers.
Devas, dragons, humans, and ghosts
wither and perish therein.
If even the Two Primal Forces perish,
what constancy can a kingdom have?
Birth, aging, sickness, and death
cycle without end;
things go against one's wishes,
and sorrow and grief cause harm.
Desires are deep and calamities heavy,
afflictions are all-pervasive.
The Sānjiè are all suffering;
what reliance can a kingdom provide?
Existence originates from non-existence,
and all things are formed through causes and conditions.
That which flourishes must decline;
that which is solid must become empty.
Sentient beings are teeming,
all living as if in an illusory abode.
The Sānguǒ are all empty;
the land is also thus.
The conscious spirit has no form,
falsely riding upon the four snakes,
blindly cherishing them
as a carriage of pleasure.
The body has no permanent master;
the spirit has no permanent home.
Since even body and spirit must part,
how can there be a kingdom?' "
At that time, Xūtuósùmí,
hearing this verse recited,
reflected on its meaning and principles,
and felt boundless joy.
He immediately installed the Crown Prince
to take his place as king,
bid farewell to the ministers,
and prepared to return to fulfill his word.
The ministers spoke with one voice,
saying to the King:
“We pray that the King merely stays
and does not worry about Bózú.
We ministers have devised a plan
to prepare defenses and precautions.
We will forge iron to make a house,
and the King shall stay inside it for a time.
Though Bózú is fierce,
what would he be able to do?”
The King told the ministers and all the people:
“For a person living in this world,
sincerity and trust are the foundation.
To survive through falsehood
is something my heart cannot allow.
I would rather die with trust
than live with deceitful words.”
He further spoke of the various benefits of sincerity and trust
and extensively distinguished the sins of falsehood.
The ministers sobbed in grief,
and none spoke another word.
The King arose and left the city,
and everyone saw him off,
weeping and yearning along the road,
fainting and then reviving.
After the King finished consoling them,
he set out on his way and departed.
At that time, King Bózú
thought to himself:
“Xūtuósùmí
should arrive today.”
He sat on the mountain peak,
watching for him from afar,
and saw him following the path directly toward him.
When he arrived and saw him,
his expression was cheerful and pleased,
and his joy and relief
exceeded how he had been before.
The Rākṣasa King asked:
“You were able to come quickly!
Among people born in the world,
there are none who do not cherish their lives.
You are now about to die,
yet your joy is twice as much as usual.
After returning to your home country,
what good benefit did you obtain?”
Xūtuósùmí replied:
“The Great King showed broad mercy by granting me seven days for giving,
which allowed me to fulfill my sincere words.
Furthermore, I heard the subtle Dharma,
and my heart has been opened and enlightened.
Being as I am today,
my aspirations are fully satisfied.
Although I must face death,
my heart is as joyful as if I were alive.”
King Bózú said:
“What Dharma did you hear?
Try reciting it for me.”
Xūtuósùmí
recited the original verse for him,
and further used skillful means to extensively teach the Dharma,
distinguishing the sin of killing and its evil retribution,
and then spoke of the blessings of a compassionate heart and not killing.
Bózú was delighted and showed great respect,
accepting and following the teachings.
Having no more intent to harm,
he immediately released all the kings
to return to their respective countries.
Xūtuósùmí
then gathered his troops,
led Bózú back and settled him in his original kingdom.
The former vow to the immortal
was completed after twelve years.
From that time forward,
he no longer ate humans
and eventually returned to being a sovereign king,
governing the people as before.
“Thus it is, Great King!
If you wish to know who the King Xūtuósùmí was at that time,
it is my current self.
King Bózú
is the current Yāngchóumóluó.
The various people who, during those twelve years,
were eaten by King Bózú
are these various people
who were killed by Yāngchóumóluó.
These various people
have always been killed and harmed by Yāngchóumóluó life after life,
and I also, life after life,
have subdued him with goodness.
I recall that in the past,
when I was an ordinary person,
I transformed him so that he would not kill;
how much more so today, when I have become a Rúlái,
with all virtues universally complete
and all evils eternally ceased?
How could I not be able to subdue and transform him?”
The King again spoke to the Buddha:
“As for these people!
What past causes do they have
that they are always, life after life,
killed by him?”
The Buddha told the King:
“Listen carefully!
In a long-distant eon of the past,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great country
named Bōluónà.
At that time, the king of the country
was named Bōluómódá.
The King had two sons,
each possessing heroic talent
and extraordinary handsomeness.
The King loved and cherished them dearly.
At that time, the younger one
thought to himself:
‘If my father passes away,
my elder brother will succeed him as ruler.
Since I am the younger one,
I have no hope for the royal position.
Having been born into this life,
if I am not to be a king,
what is the purpose of remaining in the world?
It is better to seek the way of an immortal in solitude.’
After having this thought,
he went to speak to his father, the King:
‘I yearn for the deep mountains
to seek the way of an immortal.
I pray that you will grant me leave
so that I may fulfill my aspiration.’
He was so earnest
that his will could not be swayed,
so the father granted it
and allowed him to enter the mountains.
After several years had passed,
the father king died,
and the elder brother succeeded to the throne,
governing the people.
Not long after the elder brother began his rule,
he fell ill and died.
He had no son as an heir
and no one to succeed him.
The ministers gathered to discuss,
not knowing where to turn.
One minister said:
‘The King has a younger son
who previously petitioned the Great King
to enter the mountains to study as an immortal.
We should return and invite him back to succeed to the royal throne.’
The ministers joyfully said:
‘There is certainly such a person!’
They then led one another into the mountains to summon him.
Upon arrival, they fully explained the situation and their intent:
‘We only pray that you show pity
and take charge of our country.’
The immortal replied:
‘This matter is fearsome.
My life here is quiet and happy,
forever free from worry and hardship.
The people of the world are fierce and evil,
fond of cutting and killing one another.
If I become the king,
I might be plotted against.
I enjoy my life here very much now
and cannot do it.’
The ministers spoke again:
‘The King has died without an heir,
and there is no one else to succeed him.
Only the Great Immortal is of the King's lineage.
The land and the people
cannot be without a master.
We only pray that you show compassion
and look upon us with the intent to protect.’
With such sincerity
and earnest pleading,
his heart could not bear to refuse,
and he finally returned to the country with them.
Since the immortal had been young,
he had not practiced the affairs of desire.
Once he came to rule the country,
he gradually drew near to female charms,
and his indulgence in lust became deep.
He became reckless and dissipated,
day and night wallowing in debauchery, unable to restrain himself.
Consequently, he decreed throughout the country
that all women,
when they were to be married,
must first come to him,
and only after that
would they be allowed to go to their husbands.
As for all the beautiful women
throughout the country...
Those who caught his fancy,
were all humiliated.
"At that time, a woman,
on the road amidst a great crowd,
stood naked and urinated.
Everyone was shocked and laughed,
coming together to scold her:
'How can you have no shame to the point of doing such a thing?'
The woman immediately replied:
'Among women,
what shame is there?
You all urinate standing,
yet you are not ashamed.
You and I are no different;
what shame is there?'
The people replied:
'What does this talk mean?'
The woman spoke again:
'Only the King alone
is a man.
The women of the entire country
have all been humiliated by him.
If you were men,
would you allow it to be thus?'
Thereupon, the people
became mutually ashamed and embarrassed,
then discussed together:
'What this woman says
is indeed reasonable.'
They secretly harbored the woman's words,
passing them on in secret whispers,
and with one heart they conspired
to plot against the King together.
Outside the city in a garden,
there was a cool pond.
The King would often, with his attendants,
go to the pond to bathe.
The ministers and commoners
hid in ambush in the garden.
When the King came out to wash,
the hidden soldiers all came out,
surrounding him on all sides,
closing in to capture and kill him.
The King was startled and said:
'What do you intend to do?'
The ministers said:
'The King should govern justly, but you
have been excessively lewd and dissolute,
corrupting the customs
and defiling every household.
We have seen this
and can no longer endure it;
therefore we wish to remove the King
and seek another who is worthy and capable.'
The King was terrified upon hearing this
and said to the ministers:
'I truly did not mean to burden you;
I beg to reform myself,
and will never dare to do this again.
I wish for your leniency and release
to make a fresh start with the people.'
The ministers spoke again:
'Even if today
the heavens rained black snow
or venomous snakes grew from our heads,
we would never release you;
why say anything more?'
After the King heard this,
he knew he would surely die.
Filled with rage and indignation,
he said to the ministers:
'I was originally in the mountains,
uninvolved in worldly affairs.
You forcibly pressured me
and made me your King.
Before I had any great failing,
you conspired against me with one heart.
Now that I am solitary and weak
and have no power to save myself,
I vow that in future lives I shall always kill you.
Even when I am on the verge of attaining the Way,
I will still not let you go.'
Although he made this vow,
they still killed him.
Thus it is, Great King!
If you wish to know who the Hermit-King of that time was,
it is the current Āng-chóu-mó-luó.
The ministers and people who with one heart killed the King
are the people
who are now being killed by Āng-chóu-mó-luó.
From then on,
they have always been killed by him,
and even today,
he still harms them."
At that time, the King knelt
and addressed the Buddha:
"The Bhikṣu Zhǐ-mán,
having killed so many people,
now that he has attained the Way,
will he still receive retribution?"
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Actions must have retribution.
Right now this Bhikṣu
is in his room, and
the fires of hell
are emerging from his pores.
He suffers extreme pain and agony,
more excruciating than words can say."
At that time, the Tathāgata,
wishing to let the assembly know that evil actions must have retribution,
ordered a Bhikṣu:
"Take a door-bolt
and go to Zhǐ-mán's room,
and thrust it into the keyhole."
The Bhikṣu went immediately,
followed the instruction,
and as the bolt entered the door,
it immediately melted away.
The Bhikṣu was shocked
and returned to tell the Buddha.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣu:
"Retribution for actions is like this."
The King and the assembly
all believed and understood.
At that time, Ā-nán knelt and said to the Buddha:
"What past merit does Āng-chóu-mó-luó have,
that he is so favored,
his physical strength so robust,
with the power of a champion,
and that he is so vigorous and swift,
running as fast as a flying bird?
And how did he also encounter the Buddha
and cross over birth and death?
I only pray for your compassion
to explain it for the assembly."
The Buddha told Ā-nán:
"Listen carefully!
Long ago, in the time of Kā-shè Buddha,
there was a Bhikṣu
who served as a manager for the Saṃgha.
He was leading the Saṃgha's men and livestock
to transport grain and rice.
On the road, they encountered rain,
with no place to take shelter.
The sacks of grain and belongings
were all soaked.
At that time, that Bhikṣu
wished to pass through quickly,
but his strength was small and his pace was slow.
Having no way to fulfill his wish,
his heart was filled with frustration,
and he immediately made a vow:
'I vow that in a future life,
my strength will equal a thousand men,
my body will be light and my movement swift,
running as fast as a flying bird;
and when in the future there is a Buddha named Shì-jiā-móu-ní,
may I encounter him and eternally escape birth and death.'
Thus it is, Ā-nán!
The manager Bhikṣu of that time
is the current Āng-chóu-mó-luó.
Because in that life
he left home and upheld the precepts,
and because he managed Saṃgha affairs
and made that vow,
from then on,
in life after life he has been handsome, powerful, and swift,
all according to his vow.
He has also encountered me
and attained deliverance from birth and death."
At that time, Ā-nán,
the Bhikṣus,
the King, the ministers, and the people,
all those in the assembly,
hearing the Buddha's explanation of causes, conditions, and the retribution for actions,
were all moved and inspired.
They contemplated the Four Truths,
and some attained the stage of Xū-tuó-huán,
Sī-tuó-hán,
Ā-nà-hán,
or Ā-luó-hàn.
Some planted the roots of goodness for becoming a Pì-zhī-fó;
some gave rise to the aspiration for the Supreme, Perfect Way;
or some attained the stage of non-retrogression.
All guarded their bodies and speech, disciplined their minds to follow goodness,
and hearing what the Buddha said,
they joyfully put it into practice.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the state of Shèwèi, in the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, within the state,
there was a Póluómén named Bīntóulú Duǒdū,
whose wife was ugly and wicked,
and both her eyes were blue-green.
She had only seven daughters,
and no sons.
The family was naturally poor and destitute,
and the daughters were also impoverished.
The wife's nature was vile and evil,
and she constantly scolded her husband.
The daughters would come one after another to ask for what they needed,
and before they were satisfied with what was given,
they would glare with anger and weep.
The husbands of those seven daughters gathered at his house,
and to serve and provide for them,
for fear of displeasing them,
he had ripe grain in the fields,
but had not yet seen to its threshing.
He borrowed an ox from another,
and took it to perform the threshing,
but because he was not careful in guarding the ox,
he lost it in the marsh.
At that time, the Póluómén
sat and thought to himself:
"What sin have I sown
that bitterness and poison arrive together?
Within, I am scolded by a wicked wife,
pressured by seven daughters,
and the daughters' husbands gather,
with no way for me to provide for them.
Furthermore, I have lost another's ox,
and do not know where it is."
He searched far and wide,
but his body was exhausted and his heart weary.
In sorrow, depression, distress, and anxiety,
he happened to go into a forest,
where he encountered the Rúlái sitting beneath a tree,
his faculties serene and settled,
quiet and blissful.
At that time, the Póluómén,
leaning his cheek against his staff,
stood for a long time watching him,
and then had this thought:
"The Shāmén Qútán
is now most peaceful and happy,
without a wicked wife to scold or quarrel with him,
without daughters to vex and trouble him,
or the husbands of poor daughters
to cause him worry, loss, sorrow, and suffering.
Furthermore, he has no ripe grain in the fields,
does not borrow oxen from others,
and has no worry of loss."
The Fó knew his thoughts
and then spoke to him, saying:
"It is as you think.
As for me now,
I am quiet and without many troubles.
Truly, I have no wicked wife to curse or scold me,
no seven daughters to vex and trouble me,
nor do daughters' husbands compete to gather at my house.
Furthermore, I do not worry about ripe grain in the fields,
I do not borrow others' oxen,
and I have no worry of loss."
The Fó said to him:
"Do you wish to leave the household life?"
He immediately said to the Fó:
"As I am now, I see my home as a tomb,
and the various ties of wife and daughters as being among enemies and thieves.
If the Shìzūn in his compassion
allows me to leave the household life,
it would most suit my humble wish."
The Fó then said:
"Come, Bǐqiū!"
His beard and hair fell off of their own accord,
and the clothes he wore
were transformed into Jiāshā.
The Fó preached the Dharma for him,
and right there where he sat, all his defilements were forever exhausted,
and he became an Āluóhàn.
Ānán heard this
and sighed, saying:
"Excellent!
The Rúlái's skillful guidance is truly inconceivable.
This Póluómén,
what auspicious seeds did he sow in the past
to be able to escape so many troubles
and obtain such great benefit?
It is like pure wool, easily dyed with color."
The Fó told Ānán:
"This Póluómén
has not only today received my grace to escape suffering and obtain peace;
in a past life,
he also relied on my grace
to avoid many calamities
and again obtain peace and happiness."
Ānán said to the Fó:
"I do not know,
Shìzūn!
In that past life,
how was he rescued and delivered from suffering?"
The Fó told Ānán:
"Listen carefully, listen carefully!
Think on it well,
and I shall explain it to you in detail."
Ānán said to the Fó:
"Yes, I shall listen well!"
The Fó told Ānán:
"In the distant past, countless Āsēngqí Jié ago,
there was a great king
named Ābōluótímùqū,
which in the Jìn language means 'Upright'.
He ruled through the Way and its influence,
and did not wrong the people or their goods.
At that time, within the king's state,
there was a Póluómén
named Tánnìjī,
whose household was empty and poor,
with not enough food to fill his mouth.
He had a little ripe grain,
but could not process it,
so he borrowed an ox from another
and took it to perform the threshing.
When the threshing of the grain was finished,
he drove the ox back to its owner.
Having driven it to the owner's gate,
he forgot to entrust it to him
and then returned home.
Although the ox owner saw it,
he thought it was not yet finished being used,
and so he did not take it in.
Both parties neglected it,
and consequently the ox was lost.
Later the owner went to ask for it,
but Tánnìjī said he had already returned it,
and they slandered each other.
At that time, the ox owner
took Tánnìjī
to the king to demand the ox.
Just as they went outside,
they encountered a horse herder of the king's household.
A horse was running away,
and he called to Tánnìjī to block the horse for him.
At that time, Tánnìjī
reached down and found a stone,
which he threw at it,
hitting its leg and breaking it.
The horse official then seized him,
and they also went together toward the king.
Next, walking to the water,
they did not know where to cross,
and encountered a woodworker
who was holding an ax in his mouth,
with his clothes hitched up to cross over.
Then Tánnìjī
asked that man:
'Where is it possible to cross?'
In answering the location,
his mouth opened,
and the ax fell into the water.
He could not find it;
so he then came and seized Tánnìjī,
and together they went toward the king.
At that time, Tánnìjī
was being pursued by all the claimants,
being pressed by them,
and moreover was hungry and thirsty.
Along the road
at a wine-seller's house,
he begged for a little white wine
and climbed onto a bed to drink it.
He did not realize that beneath the quilt a small child was lying,
and his weight crushed the child's abdomen, causing it to burst.
At that time, the child's mother
also seized him and would not let go, saying:
'You are lawless
to have wrongly killed my child!'
Together they all held onto him
to take him to the king's palace.
Reaching a wall,
he thought to himself:
'My misfortune,
so many offenses have gathered against me.
If I arrive at the king's place,
he might kill me.
If I flee now,
perhaps I can escape.'
Having made this thought,
he leaped over the wall,
but below there was an old weaver,
and falling on him, the weaver died instantly.
At that time, the weaver's son
also seized him,
and together with the other people,
they took him to the king.
"Next, walking forward,
they saw a pheasant perched in a tree,
which asked him from afar, saying:
"You, Dánnìjī!
Where do you intend to go now?"
He immediately explained the previous circumstances to the pheasant.
The pheasant replied again, saying:
"When you arrive at that place,
speak to the King for me.
When I am in other trees,
my cry is not pleasant,
but if I am in this tree,
my cry is mournful and beautiful.
For what reason is it so?
If you see the King,
ask him for me."
Next, he saw a venomous snake.
The snake also asked him:
"You, Dánnìjī!
Where do you intend to go now?"
He then took the previous matters
and told them in detail to the snake.
The snake also replied, saying:
"When you arrive at the King's place,
speak to the King for me.
Every morning,
when I first emerge from my hole,
my body is soft and flexible
and I have no pains;
but when I return and enter in the evening,
my body is coarse, stiff, and painful,
getting stuck in the hole and making it difficult to move forward."
At that time, Dánnìjī
also accepted its request.
Next he saw a woman
who asked him, saying:
"Where do you wish to go?"
Again, regarding the previous matters,
he told her everything.
The woman told him:
"When you arrive at the King's place,
speak to the King for me.
I do not know for what reason, but
when I am at my husband's house,
I long for my parents' home;
when I stay at my parents' home,
I long for my husband's house."
He also accepted her request.
At that time, all the creditors
surrounded and guarded him together
and brought him before the King.
Then the owner of the ox
stepped forward and said to the King:
"This man borrowed my ox,
and when I demanded the ox from him,
he refused to return it to me."
The King asked him, saying:
"Why did you not return the ox?"
Dánnìjī said:
"I am indeed poor and destitute.
The grain was ripe in the fields,
and he, out of kindness,
lent me the ox.
When I finished using it for threshing,
I drove it back to the owner.
The owner also saw it,
and although I did not verbally hand it over,
the ox was at his gate.
I returned home empty-handed
and do not know how that ox was ultimately lost."
The King said to that man:
"Both of you
are in the wrong.
Because Dánnìjī did not hand it over verbally,
you should cut off his tongue;
because you saw the ox and did not take charge of it yourself,
we should gouge out your eyes."
That person said to the King:
"I beg to give up on this ox;
I do not wish to have my eyes gouged
or have his tongue cut off."
He then allowed a settlement.
The horse official then said:
"That man is lawless;
he broke my horse's leg."
The King then questioned Dánnìjī, saying:
"This is the horse of the King's household.
Why did you suddenly strike and break its leg?"
Kneeling, he said to the King:
"The creditors were taking me
along the road,
and that person called out to me,
ordering me to block the King's horse.
The horse was galloping and uncontrollable.
I reached down, found a stone, grasped it, and threw it,
accidentally breaking the horse's leg;
it was not intentional."
The King said to the horse official:
"Because you called him,
we should cut off your tongue;
because he struck the horse,
we should cut off his hand."
The horse official said to the King:
"I will provide for the horse myself;
do not carry out the punishment."
They each reached a settlement.
The woodworker also came forward and said:
"Dánnìjī lost my adze."
The King then asked:
"How did you also lose his adze?"
Kneeling, he said to the King:
"I asked for a crossing point,
and he answered me.
The adze in his mouth was lost and fell into the canal water,
and it could not be found despite searching;
it was truly not intentional."
The King said to the woodworker:
"Because he called you,
we should cut off his tongue.
As for the method of carrying things,
propriety dictates using the hands;
because you held it in your mouth, causing it to fall into the water,
I shall now strike and break your two front teeth."
When the woodworker heard this,
he stepped forward and said to the King:
"I would rather give up the adze
than have this punishment carried out."
They each reached a settlement.
Then the mother from the wine shop
also dragged him before the King.
The King asked Dánnìjī:
"Why did you wrongly kill her child?"
Kneeling, he said to the King:
"The creditors pressured me,
and I was also hungry and thirsty.
I asked her for a little wine
and sat upon the couch to drink it,
not realizing there was a small child sleeping beneath the covers.
After I finished drinking the wine,
the child had passed away.
It was not something I desired.
I only hope, Great King,
that you will show forgiveness and consideration."
The King told the woman:
"Your house sells wine
and your guests are numerous;
why did you place a sleeping child in a sitting area
and cover him so he could not be seen?
Now, both of you
are at fault.
Since your child is already dead,
take Dánnìjī
as your husband;
let him give you another child,
and then let him go."
At that time, the woman
then kowtowed and said:
"My child is already dead,
so let us each settle.
I do not want this starving Póluómén as a husband!"
Thereupon, the matters were resolved and a settlement was reached.
Then the weaver's son
also stepped forward and said to the King:
"This man is violent and reckless;
he stepped on and killed my father."
The King asked, saying:
"For what reason
did you wrongly kill his father?"
Dánnìjī said:
"Many creditors pressured me
and I was very terrified.
I leaped over a wall to escape
and happened to fall upon him;
it was truly not what I desired."
The King said to that person:
"Both of you are in the wrong.
Your father is already dead,
so take Dánnìjī
to be your father."
That person said to the King:
"My father is already dead,
and I will never take this Póluómén as my father!"
They were permitted to settle,
and the King allowed it.
At that time, Dánnìjī,
with all his matters resolved,
was immensely joyful and leapt for joy.
He remained before the King
and saw two women
disputing over one child,
approaching the King to state their cases.
The King was brilliant and clever;
using a wise stratagem,
he said to the two mothers:
"Now there is only one child,
and two mothers claim him.
I allow the two of you
to each pull one hand.
Whoever can get him
is the child's true mother."
The one who was not the mother
had no compassion for the child
and pulled with all her might,
not fearing that he might be injured;
the one who was the biological mother
had deep compassion for the child
and followed along to protect him,
unable to bear dragging him.
The King discerned the truth and the falsehood
and said to the one who exerted force:
"He is truly not your son,
yet you forcibly dragged another's child;
now before the King,
speak your true facts."
She immediately bowed her head to the King:
"I admit I was false and deceptive,
and falsely claimed another's child.
Great King, wise and sagely!
Please graciously forgive my false transgression."
The child was returned to his mother,
and they were each released.
There were another two people
disputing over a white woolen rug,
coming before the King in a confused clamor,
and the King again used his wisdom
to judge it as he had before.
At that time, Tánnìjī
spoke to the King, saying:
"These creditors,
when they were bringing me here,
by the side of the road,
there was a venomous snake
who earnestly requested me
to convey its message to the King:
'I do not know why,
when I come out from my hole,
I am soft and nimble,
but when I return into the hole,
it is obstructed and painful;
I do not know for what reason this is so?'"
The King answered him, saying:
"The reason it is so
is that when it comes out from the hole,
it has no afflictions;
its mind and mood are harmonious and gentle,
and its body is likewise.
Because the snake is outside,
matters regarding birds and beasts
disturb and provoke its body,
so that its anger and hatred swell up
and its body becomes thick and large;
therefore, when it enters,
it is obstructed by the hole and finds it hard to move forward.
You may tell it:
'If you are outside
and maintain a mind without anger,
as when you first came out, then you will not have this trouble.'"
He again spoke to the King, saying:
"On the road I saw a woman
who requested me to tell the King:
'When I am at my husband's house,
I long for my parents' home;
but if I am at my father's home,
I long for my husband's house;
I do not know for what reason it is so?'"
The King answered again, saying:
"You may tell her:
'Due to your deviant heart,
at your parents' home you keep another lover,
so when you are at your husband's house, you long for that other person;
but when you go there and become slightly weary,
you return to longing for your proper husband;
that is why it is so.'
You may tell her:
'If you maintain your heart,
abandoning the deviant and following the proper,
then you will not have this trouble.'"
He again spoke to the King, saying:
"On a tree by the side of the road,
I saw a pheasant
who requested me to tell the King:
'When I am on other trees,
my cry is not good,
but if I am on this tree,
my cry is sorrowful and harmonious;
I do not know the cause, for what reason is it so?'"
The King told that man:
"The reason it is so
is because under that tree there is a large cauldron of gold;
therefore, while upon it,
its cry is sorrowful and fine.
In other places there is no gold,
therefore when it stays on them,
its voice is not good."
The King told Tánnìjī:
"Though you had many faults,
I have already released you.
Your family is poor and in extreme hardship;
the cauldron of gold under the tree
ought to be mine,
but I shall use it to give to you.
You may go and dig it up."
He received the King's instructions
and answered the others one by one.
He dug up that gold,
traded for fields and property,
and all that he needed
was never lacking.
He thus became a wealthy man
and was happy for the rest of his life."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"The Great King of that time,
Abōluótímùqū,
who could he be other than me?
It was I myself.
The Brahmin Tánnìjī of that time
is the present Brahmin Bīntóulú Duǒshé.
In the past,
I spared him from many calamities,
gave him precious treasures,
and made him happy.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood,
I again pull him out of suffering
and bestow upon him the inexhaustible treasure of the Dharma."
The Venerable Ānán
and the whole assembly,
having heard what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Translated in Gāochāng Commandery by the Śramaṇa Huìjué and others of Liángzhōu during the Yuán Wèi dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in Shèwèi Guó, in the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, in the kingdom,
there was a Póluómén
named Shīzhì,
whose household was very wealthy,
but he had no children.
He went to the place of the Liùshī
to ask about the causes and conditions.
The Liùshī replied, saying:
“Your appearance shows you will have no sons.”
At that time, Shīzhì then returned home,
put on dirty and greasy clothes,
and was sorrowful and unhappy.
He thought to himself:
“I have no children;
once my life ends,
the household property and wealth
shall go to the King.”
Having thought this,
his sorrow and distress increased even more.
The Póluómén's wife
was an acquaintance of a Bǐqiūní.
At that time, the Bǐqiūní
happened to come to their house.
Seeing her husband
looking sorrowful and haggard,
she then asked her:
“For what reason does your husband
look so sorrowful and haggard?”
The Póluómén's wife
then answered her, saying:
“The family has no offspring.
He went to ask the Liùshī,
and the Liùshī divined his appearance, saying he would have no sons.
For this reason,
he is sorrowful and unhappy.”
At that time, the Bǐqiūní
spoke to her again, saying:
“The followers of the Liùshī
are not all-knowing.
How could they know the causes and conditions of a person's karmic actions?
The Rúlái is in the world;
He clearly understands all dharmas,
and regarding the past and future,
there is nothing that obstructs Him.
You may go and ask Him,
and He will surely be able to know fully.”
After the Bǐqiūní left,
the wife then told her husband what she had heard.
When the husband heard this,
his mind then became enlightened.
He changed into new clothes
and went to the Fó's place.
Prostrating at the Fó's feet,
he said to the Fó:
“In my physiognomy and fate,
will I have a son or not?”
The Shìzūn told him:
“You shall have a son,
possessing complete merit and virtue.
When he has grown up, he will delight in leaving the household life.”
When the Póluómén heard this, he was boundlessly joyful
and spoke these words:
“If only I have a son,
what does it matter if he studies the Way?”
He then invited the Fó and the Bǐqiūsēng
to a meal at his house the next day.
At that time, the Shìzūn silently accepted.
When the time came the next day,
the Fó and the assembly of monks
went to his house.
Once the assembly was seated,
the Póluómén and his wife, with one mind and purpose,
respectfully offered food and drink.
When the assembly had finished eating,
the Fó and the assembly of monks
returned to where they stayed.
On the way through a marsh,
there was spring water within it,
which was very clear and pleasant.
The Fó and the Bǐqiūsēng
then stayed there to rest.
The assembly of Bǐqiūs
each washed their alms-bowls.
A monkey
came to Ānán
and asked for his bowl.
Ānán feared it would be broken
and did not want to give it to him.
The Fó told Ānán:
“Quickly give it to him and do not worry.”
Receiving the instruction, he then gave it.
The monkey obtained the bowl,
carried it to a honey tree,
filled the bowl to the brim,
and offered it to the Shìzūn.
The Shìzūn told him:
“Remove the impurities within it.”
The monkey immediately
picked out the bees and insects,
making it extremely clean.
The Fó then told him:
“Mix it with water.”
As instructed, he added water,
and after finishing the mixing,
offered it to the Shìzūn.
Having received it, the Shìzūn
distributed it among the monks,
and they all drank it together
until it was shared by everyone.
The monkey was joyful,
leaping and dancing,
but he fell into a large pit
and immediately died.
His consciousness took conception in Shīzhì's household.
At that time, Shīzhì's wife
then realized she was pregnant.
When the months were complete,
she gave birth to a boy
whose face and head were handsome and upright,
with few equals in the world.
At the time of his birth,
the vessels inside the house
were naturally filled with honey.
Shīzhì and his wife
were overcome with joy.
They invited various physiognomists
to divine his fortune.
After the physiognomists finished their divination,
they told them, saying:
“This child has virtue
and is incomparably good.”
They then gave him a name,
naming him Mótóuluósèzhì,
which in the Jìn language means Mìshèng,
because on the day of his birth, honey appeared as an auspicious omen,
therefore he was named thus.
When the child had grown up,
he asked to leave the household life.
His parents, out of love and attachment, were unwilling to let him go.
The child again earnestly told his parents:
“If you insist on obstructing me and do not grant my wish,
I shall bring my life to an end,
for I cannot remain in secular life.”
The parents discussed it, saying:
“In the past, the Shìzūn
already foretold it,
saying he would leave the household life.
If we now stubbornly keep him,
he might seek death;
we should just let him do it.”
Having made their decision,
they told their son:
“Follow your aspiration.”
The child, greatly rejoicing, went to the Fó's place.
He prostrated, paid homage, and asked to leave the household life.
The Shìzūn said:
“Welcome, Bǐqiū!”
His beard and hair fell off by themselves,
Dharma robes appeared on his body,
and he then became a Shāmén.
He then extensively preached for him the wonderful Dharma of the Sìdì and various principles.
His mind opened, his bondages were exhausted,
and he attained the state of Āluóhàn.
Whenever he was with the Bǐqiūs
traveling and teaching among people,
if he became thirsty or exhausted,
he would throw his bowl into the air,
and it would naturally be filled with honey.
Everyone would drink it together,
and all would be satisfied.
At that time, Ānán said to the Fó:
“Shìzūn!
What merit and virtue did Mótóuluósèzhì
accumulate,
that not long after leaving the household life,
he attained the state of Yìngzhēn,
and whatever his mind requires,
he obtains according to his wishes?”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Do you remember when we previously accepted the invitation from Shīzhì?”
He replied:
“I remember it.”
The Fó said:
“Ānán!
Returning from that meal,
we reached an empty marsh.
At that time, a monkey asked you for your bowl,
filled it with honey to offer to the Fó,
and the Fó accepted it for him.
He danced with joy,
fell into a pit, and died.
Do you remember this as well?”
He replied:
“I remember it.”
The Fó said to Ānán:
“That monkey
is now this Mótóuluósèzhì.”
Because he saw the Buddha, rejoiced, and offered honey,
he was born into that family,
with an appearance that was upright and handsome.
He left home to study the Way
and quickly attained the state of no outflows. "
Ānán knelt for a long time
and again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what further reason
was he born among the monkeys?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In the distant past,
at the time of Jiāshè Fó,
there was a young bǐqiū
who saw another shāmén leaping across a canal and spoke these words:
'That person is so swift and agile, he is just like a monkey.'
At that time, after the shāmén heard these words,
he then asked him, saying:
'Do you know me?'
He replied, saying:
'I know you.
You are a shāmén from the time of Jiāshè Fó;
why would I not know you?'
Then that shāmén
spoke to him again, saying:
'Do not call me a shāmén in name only;
for the various fruits of a shāmén
I have already fully accomplished.'
When the youth heard this,
his hair stood on end,
and he prostrated himself on the ground
to plead for mercy and repent.
Because he repented of his transgression,
he did not fall into hell;
but because he mocked the appearance of an Āluóhàn,
he consequently spent five hundred lifetimes always as a monkey.
Because he had previously left home and upheld the prohibitions,
he is now able to see me,
be bathed in pure transformation,
and be able to end all suffering."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"The young bǐqiū of that time
is now Mótóuluó Sèzhì."
At that time, Ānán and the great assembly,
having heard what the Buddha said,
were filled with both sorrow and joy,
and they all spoke these words:
"The karmas of body, speech, and mind
must be guarded;
because this bǐqiū could not guard his speech,
he received such a retribution."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"It is as you say."
Thereupon, for the fourfold assembly,
he extensively expounded various dharmas
to purify the body, speech, and mind.
When the defilements of their hearts were cleansed and purified,
each attained the stages of the Way:
some attained Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
some developed the aspiration for the unsurpassed, correct, and true Way,
and some dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
The assembled crowd, having heard the Dharma,
were all joyful,
and they respectfully received and practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
at one time, the Fó was in the Zhúyuán of Wángshèchéng.
At that time, in the kingdom of Jūsàluó,
there was an elder
named Tánmóguànzhì,
who was noble and very wealthy,
but had no offspring.
He prayed and offered sacrifices to all the deities in the kingdom,
seeking to have a son.
His sincerity moved the spirits,
and his wife became pregnant.
When the full term of months and days was reached,
she gave birth to a son
whose body was handsome and dignified,
a rarity in the world.
They summoned many physiognomists
to divine his fortune.
The physiognomists examined him
and knew he possessed great merit;
they therefore gave him a name,
calling him Tánmǐlí.
Once he had grown up,
his father passed away.
At that time, Bōsīní Wáng
immediately conferred his father's rank upon him.
After he received the king's conferment,
his father's former residence
was transformed into the seven treasures;
within all the storehouses,
everything was completely filled
and all kinds of things were present.
At that time, Wángzǐ Liúlí
suffered from a severe fever
and became extremely exhausted.
The various physicians prescribed medicine,
requiring niútóu zhāntán to be smeared on his body
so that he would be cured.
The king immediately issued a decree,
proclaiming throughout the kingdom:
"Who has niútóu zhāntán?
Bring it to the royal household,
and I shall pay a price of one thousand ounces of gold for it."
Although the decree reached everywhere,
no one brought any.
Then there was a person
who informed the king, saying:
"The elder Tánmǐlí of Jūsàluó kingdom
has a great deal in his house."
When the king heard this,
he rode in a horse-drawn carriage
and went personally to seek it,
arriving at the gate of the elder Tánmǐlí.
Then the gatekeeper
immediately went in to inform him:
"Bōsīní Wáng has arrived and is outside the gate."
The elder rejoiced,
immediately went out to welcome him,
and invited the king to enter the palace.
First, they saw the outer gate,
which was made entirely of white silver.
Inside the gate was a woman
whose face and head were beautiful,
without peer in the world;
she sat on a silver bed
spinning silver thread,
with ten young girls
attending her on both sides.
The king then asked:
"Is this your wife?"
He replied:
"No,
she is the gatekeeping maidservant."
The king continued to ask:
"These young girls,
what are they for?"
Mǐlí replied:
"To convey messages."
Next, they entered the middle gate,
which was made entirely of deep-blue liúlí.
Inside the gate was a woman
whose features were upright and dignified,
even surpassing the previous one,
and her attendants on both sides
were double the previous number.
They proceeded to enter the inner gate,
which was made entirely of yellow gold.
Inside the gate was a woman
whose appearance was upright and beautiful,
surpassing those before.
She sat on a golden bed
spinning golden thread, with attendants on both sides
again double the previous number.
The king also asked:
"This woman,
is she your wife?"
He replied:
"No."
Entering into the house,
they saw a floor of liúlí
as clear as water.
Between the rooms were carvings of various animal shapes and images of aquatic creatures;
when the wind blew, it moved them,
and their shadows appeared upon the ground,
shimmering and swaying.
Seeing this, the king was suspicious and afraid,
thinking it was real water,
and he asked:
"Is there no other ground
that you must make a pool in front of the hall?"
Mǐlí replied:
"This is not water,
it is deep-blue liúlí."
He then removed a ring of the seven treasures from his finger
and threw it onto the floor;
it went straight to the other side,
stopping only when it hit the wall.
The king was delighted upon seeing this,
and together they entered further in,
ascending the hall of seven treasures.
Mǐlí's wife
was in that hall.
The bed she sat upon
was made of deep-blue liúlí.
There was another wonderful bed,
and he invited the king to sit.
Mǐlí's wife's
eyes immediately filled with tears.
The king asked her:
"Why are there tears?
Are you not happy to see me?"
The lady replied:
"It is wonderful that the king has come!
However, the king's clothes
have a slight scent of smoke,
which causes my tears to flow;
it is not out of dislike."
The king then asked:
"In your house now,
do you not light fires?"
She replied:
"No."
The king asked:
"With what do you cook food?"
She replied:
"When it is time to eat,
food of a hundred flavors
naturally appears before us."
The king asked again:
"In the darkness of evening, what do you use for light?"
She replied:
"We use mání beads."
They then closed the doors and all the windows
and brought out a mání bead,
its brightness surpassing the daylight.
Then Tánmǐlí knelt and said to the king:
"Great King!
For what reason have you troubled your noble self?"
The king told him:
"My son Liúlí
is gravely ill and needs niútóu zhāntán,
so I have come to seek it."
Mǐlí rejoiced,
leading him into various storehouses
to show him the goods.
Rare treasures of the seven gems
were as bright and pure as the sun.
Sandalwood was piled up
beyond measure,
and he said to the king:
"Take whatever you need."
Then the king replied:
"I need two ounces."
Mǐlí then broke off some and gave it to him,
the amount being just right.
The king had his attendants first send it back to the kingdom.
Then the king, with respect and mindfulness,
said to him:
"You should go to see the Fó."
Mǐlí replied:
"What is meant by 'Fó'?"
The king said:
"Have you not heard?
In Jiāwéiluówèi,
the son of Jìngfàn grew weary of old age, sickness, and death.
He left the home-life to study the Way;
when his Way was accomplished, he was called Fó.
With the thirty-two marks
and eighty secondary characteristics,
his spiritual powers and wisdom
are extraordinary and beyond compare.
He is the Honored One among humans and devas, and thus he is called Fó."
After Mǐlí heard this,
deep respect arose in his heart,
and he asked the king:
"Where is he now?"
The king replied to him:
"He is staying in the Zhúyuán of Wángshèchéng."
After the king departed,
Mǐlí immediately went to see the Fó.
Beholding the Buddha's majestic countenance,
which exceeded the King's praises ten thousandfold,
his heart was filled with joy.
He prostrated himself with his head to the ground
and inquired after the Buddha's well-being.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him,
and he attained the path of a Xūtuóhuán.
Kneeling for a long time with his palms joined,
he requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha immediately granted his request.
"Welcome, Bǐqiū!"
His hair and beard then fell away,
and Dharma robes appeared on his body.
Again, the Buddha preached for him the true Dharma of the Sìdì:
Kǔ, Xí, Jìn, and Dào.
