The defilements of his heart were completely exhausted,
and he became an Āluóhàn.
At that time, Ānán
and the other Bǐqiū
joined their palms and addressed the Buddha,
asking the Shìzūn:
"Bǐqiū Tánmílí,
what merit does he possess,
to be born among humans
and receive heavenly blessings and prosperity,
yet not delight in worldly pleasures,
and having not long left home, to immediately attain the fruits of the Path?"
The Buddha said to Ānán:
"Listen well, for I shall explain!
In the distant past,
ninety-one kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha in the world named Pípóshī.
After his Parinirvana,
during the period of the Xiàngfǎ,
there were five Bǐqiū
who made a mutual vow
to seek a quiet place
to practice the Path together.
They saw a forest marsh
where the spring water was clear and beautiful,
pure and delightful.
At that time, the Bǐqiū
all in one voice
spoke to and encouraged one person:
'This place is far from the city,
and begging for food is laborious.
You should perform the merit
of providing for us.'
At that time, the one person
immediately consented.
He went among the people
and encouraged the Tányuè
to provide food daily.
The four men were at ease
and practiced the Path with single-minded diligence.
Within ninety days,
they attained the fruits of the Path.
They then with one heart
said to this Bǐqiū:
'Because of you,
we have been at peace.
What our original hearts aimed for,
we have now attained.
What vow do you wish to make?
Ask as you please.'
At that time, the Bǐqiū’s heart was filled with joy,
and he spoke thus:
'May I in the future, among heavens and humans, be naturally wealthy and noble;
may the things I desire
be produced without effort,
all arising of their own accord;
may I encounter a Holy Teacher who surpasses you all a hundred, thousand, or ten thousandfold,
and upon hearing the Dharma, may my heart be pure and quickly attain the fruits of the Path.'"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"That Bǐqiū
is now Tánmílí.
Because he provided for those four Bǐqiū,
for ninety-one kalpas
he was born among heavens and humans,
noble, wealthy, and dignified,
never dwelling in poor or lowly households.
Now he has been able to see me, attain the Path, and cross over the world."
At that time, Ānán
and the other Bǐqiū,
hearing what the Buddha said,
each encouraged themselves
to practice the Path with diligence.
Some attained the first fruit or even up to the fourth fruit,
while others gave rise to a heart for vast salvation and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Each and every one was filled with joy,
and they bowed their heads to the teaching and practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi, in the Zhīshù Gěigūdú Yuán.
At that time, in the country of Mójié,
there was an Elder
who fathered a baby boy.
His appearance was perfect,
and he was most lovely and venerable.
On the day of his birth,
a golden elephant naturally emerged from the storehouse.
His parents were delighted
and so they invited a physiognomist
to give him a name.
At that time, the physiognomists,
seeing the child's merit and virtue,
asked his parents:
"On the day of this child's birth,
what auspicious omens were there?"
They replied, saying:
"There was a golden elephant
that was born together with the child."
Based on this omen, they gave him the name Xiànghù.
As the child gradually grew up,
the elephant also grew large accordingly.
Once he was able to walk,
the elephant also walked.
Whether coming in or going out, advancing or stopping,
they were never separated.
If he had no intention of using it,
it would remain inside.
The elephant's excrement and urine
were nothing but pure gold.
This Xiànghù
often went with five hundred sons of Elders
to play games together,
and each spoke of the extraordinary things in their homes.
One said:
"The houses, beds, and mats of my family
are all made of the seven treasures."
Another said:
"My family's houses and gardens
are also made of many treasures."
Yet another said:
"The storehouses of my family are always full of wondrous treasures."
Comparisons such as these
were many and varied.
At that time, Xiànghù
also spoke, saying:
"On the day I was first born,
inside the house, naturally,
a golden elephant was born.
As I grew older
and became capable of going and coming,
the elephant was also thus,
never disobeying me.
I always ride it,
wandering and sight-seeing in all directions;
it goes slow or fast according to my will,
and is very agreeable to my heart.
Its excrement and urine
are purely fine gold."
At that time, Prince Āshéshì
was also among them.
Hearing what Xiànghù said,
he thought to himself:
"When I become king,
I must seize it."
After he became king,
he summoned Xiànghù
and ordered him to bring the elephant to the king's palace.
At that time, Xiànghù’s father
said to his son:
"King Āshéshì
is violent and lacks the Way;
he is greedy and stingy.
He even mistreated his own father,
so how much more so with others?
Now that he has called for you,
he must be coveting your elephant
and it may be seized."
The son replied:
"As for this elephant of mine,
no one can take it by force."
Father and son immediately
rode together to see the king.
At that time, the gatekeeper
entered and informed the king:
"Xiànghù and his father
are at the gate riding an elephant."
The king told him:
"Allow them to enter riding the elephant."
Then the gatekeeper
went back out and told them.
Xiànghù and his father
rode the elephant straight forward,
and once they reached the inner palace,
they dismounted the elephant,
knelt and bowed to the king,
and asked after his well-being.
The king was greatly pleased,
ordered them to take their seats,
gave them food and drink,
and after some brief conversation,
in a short moment,
they took their leave of the king to depart.
The king said to Xiànghù:
"Leave the elephant here;
do not take it out."
Xiànghù complied joyfully,
following the order to leave it,
and walked out of the palace on foot.
Before long,
the elephant vanished into the ground
and surged up outside the gate.
Xiànghù was again able to ride it back home.
After a short while passed,
he thought to himself:
"The King is without the Way,
and his punishments are irrational.
Because of this elephant,
I might be harmed.
Now the Buddha is in the world,
bestowing his grace upon all living beings;
it is better for me to leave home and practice the pure life."
He immediately told his parents,
asking to enter the Way.
His parents gave their permission,
so he took his leave and departed,
riding his golden elephant
to the Zhīhuán monastery.
Having seen the World-Honored One,
he bowed his head in prostration,
and stated his original resolve.
The Buddha immediately granted his request, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
His hair and beard fell off naturally,
Dharma robes appeared on his body,
and he became a Shāmén.
The Buddha then preached the essential Dharma of the Four Truths to him.
His mind attained transcendent awakening,
and he attained Luóhàn status.
Whenever he was with the other Bhikṣus,
in the forests or under the trees,
contemplating and practicing the Way,
that golden elephant
was always before his eyes.
The people of the country of Shèwèi,
hearing there was a golden elephant,
vied with one another to gather and see it.
It was noisy and restless,
hindering and disrupting the practice of the Way.
At that time, the Bhikṣus
reported this situation to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Xiànghù:
"Because of this elephant,
there is disturbance and agitation.
You should now quickly dismiss the elephant and make it leave."
Xiànghù said to the Buddha:
"I have long wished to dismiss it,
but it is unwilling to go."
The Buddha said to him again:
"You should say to it:
'My births are now ended,
and I have no further use for you.'
Do this three times,
and the elephant will vanish."
At that time, Xiànghù,
obeying the World-Honored One’s instruction,
said to the elephant three times:
"I have no need for you."
At that moment, the golden elephant
immediately entered into the ground.
Then the Bhikṣus,
all marveled at this together
and said to the World-Honored One:
"Bhikṣu Xiànghù—
what virtue did he practice in the past,
and in what field of merit did he plant this root of goodness,
to receive such a majestic retribution as this?"
The Buddha told Ānán and the Bhikṣus:
"If there are living beings
who, within the field of merit of the Triple Gem,
plant even the smallest amount of goodness,
they will obtain boundless fruits.
In the distant past,
at the time of Kāyè Fó,
the people of that age
had a lifespan of twenty thousand years.
After that Buddha's teaching was complete,
his spirit entered Níhuán.
His sacred relics were distributed,
and many stupas and temples were built.
At that time, there was a stupa
which contained an image of the Púsà originally descending from Dōushuài Tiān riding an elephant,
to enter his mother's womb.
At that time, the body of the elephant
was slightly chipped and broken.
There was a man who,
while walking and circumambulating the stupa,
Seeing the body of the elephant statue was broken,
he then thought to himself:
“This is the elephant ridden by the Púsà;
now that it is damaged,
I should repair it.”
He took clay to patch it
and applied orpiment to paint it,
then he made a vow:
“May I in the future always dwell in noble and honorable positions,
with no lack of wealth and resources.”
When that person's life ended,
he was born in the heavens.
Having exhausted his heavenly lifespan,
he was born down into the human realm,
always born into noble, powerful, wealthy, and joyful families.
His appearance was upright and handsome,
distinct from the ordinary world,
and there was always a golden elephant
following and guarding him at all times.”
The Fó told Ānán:
“If you wish to know who the elephant-repairer of that time was,
it is this Xiànghù.
Because of his repairing the elephant in that past life,
from then until now,
whether in the heavens or among humans,
he naturally received rewards.
Due to his respectful heart
in honoring the Sānzūn,
he has now encountered me,
received the wonderful transformation,
his mental impurities are entirely exhausted,
and he has attained the state of an Āluóhàn.”
Huìmìng Ānán and the entire assembly,
hearing what the Fó said,
all reached understanding
and each attained their fruit;
some attained the stage of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
some gave rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed, correct, and true path;
and some attained the stage of non-retrogression.
There was no one who was not joyful,
and they reverently accepted and practiced the teachings.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in Wángshè Chéng on Jiùtóu Shān,
together with one thousand two hundred and fifty venerable disciples.
At that time, the King of Bōluónài,
named Bōluómódá,
had a chief minister
who fathered a son
with the thirty-two marks
and all the secondary beauties complete;
his body was the color of purple-gold,
and his appearance was outstanding and exceptional.
When the minister saw his son,
his joy was redoubled;
he immediately summoned a physiognomist
to examine him.
The physiognomist looked closely
and sighed, saying:
"How wondrous!
The marks and beauties are fully complete,
his merits are extraordinarily prepared,
his wisdom and eloquence are thorough,
and he surpasses all common people."
The minister rejoiced even more,
and for this reason gave him a name.
The physiognomist further asked:
"Since he was born,
have there been any unusual events?"
The minister replied:
"It has been most strange and extraordinary.
His mother's original nature
was not good or kind,
but since she became pregnant,
she has felt compassion for those in suffering and distress,
nourished the common people with kindness,
and cared for them with an impartial mind."
The physiognomist said joyfully:
"This is the child's aspiration."
Because of this, a name was established,
and he was called Mílè.
The parents celebrated with joy
with immeasurable hearts.
The child's exceptional reputation
spread throughout the entire land.
When the King heard of it,
he felt fear and said:
"I think of this small child,
whose name and appearance are so glorious;
if he possesses such lofty virtue,
he will surely seize my throne.
While he is not yet grown,
he should be eliminated beforehand,
for in time he will surely become a threat."
Having made this plan,
he immediately ordered the minister:
"I hear you have a son
whose appearance is unusual;
you should bring him here,
as I wish to see him."
At that time, the people within the palace,
hearing of the child's radiant reputation
and knowing the King intended to scheme against him,
were as distressed as if they were in boiling water or fire.
The child had a maternal uncle
named Bōpólí
in the kingdom of Bōlífúduōluó,
where he served as the State Preceptor;
he was intelligent, lofty, and broad-minded,
with thorough wisdom and extraordinary talent,
and five hundred disciples
always followed him for consultation and instruction.
At that time, the minister,
loving his son dearly
and fearing he would be harmed,
devised a secret plan
and sent people on an elephant to deliver him to his uncle.
When the uncle saw Mílè,
and observed his fine appearance,
he redoubled his care and affection,
regarding him with respect and holding him in his heart.
As he gradually grew older,
he was taught to study;
what he received in one day of instruction
surpassed what others learned in a whole year,
and before a year of study had passed, he was thorough in the common classics and scriptures.
At that time, Bōpólí,
seeing that his nephew
after not long studying
was thorough in all books,
wished to hold an assembly to praise his excellence.
He sent a disciple
to Bōluónài
to speak with the minister,
describing what the child had learned
and requesting precious treasures
to establish the assembly.
While that disciple was mid-journey,
he heard people speaking of the Buddha's immeasurable virtues;
longing and wishing to see Him,
he immediately went toward the Buddha,
but before arriving
he was devoured by a tiger.
By virtue of his wholesome mind,
he was born in the first of the four heavens.
Bōpólí exhausted all he owned
to gather wealth and goods
to hold a great assembly;
he invited the Póluómén,
all of whom gathered together,
and prepared various sweet and delicious dishes and foods.
After the assembly was concluded,
he gave great dá chèn offerings;
each person received five hundred gold coins.
When the giving was finished,
his wealth was completely exhausted.
There was a Póluómén
named Láodùchā
who arrived last of all
and saw Bōpólí:
"I have come after the others;
though I have not received food,
you should give me five hundred gold coins according to the proportion."
Bōpólí replied:
"My goods are finished;
truly, I do not withhold anything from you out of stinginess."
Láodùchā said:
"I heard of your offerings
and came with hope;
how can you see me empty-handed and not bestow your kindness?
If you surely refuse and do not give to me,
then in seven days
your head will split into seven pieces."
At that time, Bōpólí,
having heard these words,
thought to himself:
"The world has evil curses and other sorceries;
these matters cannot be taken lightly,
for perhaps this could happen."
His wealth was all gone,
and he suddenly had no means;
worrying about this
he was deeply afraid.
The disciple sent before who had died and been born in heaven
saw from afar his teacher's distress and helplessness;
he immediately descended from heaven,
came before him,
and asked his teacher:
"Why are you distressed?"
The teacher explained the circumstances in detail.
When the heavenly being heard these words,
he immediately said to his teacher:
"This person Láodùchā
does not know the supreme teaching;
he is an ignorant, deluded, and evil person;
what is he actually capable of?
And yet you worry about this.
Now there is only the Buddha,
who most understands the supreme teaching,
the infinite King of Dharma,
to whom you especially should go for refuge."
At that time, Bōpólí,
hearing the heavenly being speak of the Buddha,
immediately asked again:
"What kind of person is the Buddha?"
The heavenly being then said:
"The Buddha was born into the house of King Jìngfàn in Jiābǐluówèi,
born from the right side;
He immediately walked seven steps
and was proclaimed the Honored One of gods and humans.
With the thirty-two marks
and eighty secondary beauties,
His light shines upon heaven and earth,
with Fàn and Shì attending Him.
The thirty-two auspicious signs
manifest with shaking.
Physiognomists observed Him
and predicted two outcomes:
if He remained at home, He would be a Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng;
if He left home, He would become a Buddha.
Witnessing aging, sickness, and death,
He took no pleasure in the royal throne;
He leapt over the palace walls and left the country,
practicing austerities for six years.
Beneath the Pútí tree,
He defeated eighteen billion Maras,
and in the final watch of the night,
He universally perfected the Buddha-dharma.
The three insights and six transcendental powers,
the ten powers and fearlessnesses,
and the eighteen unique qualities
were all fully complete.
Arriving at Bōluónài,
He first turned the Wheel of Dharma;
Āruò Jiāochénrú and the other four became free of outflows,
eighty thousand gods
attained the purity of the Dharma Eye,
and countless gods and humans
gave rise to the aspiration for the Great Way.
Going again to Mójié,
He delivered Yùpíluó along with Shèlìfú,
Mùjiànlián, and others.
He led one thousand two hundred and fifty Bǐqiū as his followers,
called the Zhòngsēng.
Their merit, wisdom, and abilities
were beyond calculation.
To sum it up,
he is named Fó.
Now he is at Jùtóushān in Wángshè."
At that time, Bōpólí,
hearing the praise for the virtues of Fó,
thought to himself:
"There must certainly be a Fó.
My books record
that when the Fó star appears below,
and the heavens and earth shake greatly,
a Sage shall be born.
Now all these things are present;
it seems it must be he."
He immediately commanded Mílè and sixteen others:
"Go to see Qúután
and observe his physical marks.
If his various marks are complete,
then challenge him in your minds:
'My master Bōpólí,
how many marks does he have?'
As for me now,
my body has two marks:
first, hair that is dark blue;
second, a broad and long tongue.
If he recognizes this,
then challenge him in your minds again:
'My master Bōpólí,
how old is he now?'
As for my age,
it is now one hundred and twenty.
If he knows this,
then think and challenge him again:
'My master Bōpólí,
what is his clan and surname?'
If you wish to know my clan,
it is Póluómén.
If he answers and recognizes this,
then challenge him in your minds again:
'My master Bōpólí,
how many disciples does he have?'
As for me now,
I have five hundred disciples.
If he answers knowing the number,
then he must certainly be a Fó.
You must then become his disciples,
and let one person be sent to bring me the news."
At that time, Mílè and the others
proceeded toward Wángshè.
Approaching Jùtóushān,
they saw the footprints of Fó.
The marks of the thousand-spoke wheel were as clear as a painting.
They immediately asked a person:
"Whose footprints are these?"
Someone replied:
"These are the footprints of Fó."
At that time, Mílè and the others
felt deep admiration and longing.
They lingered by the side of the tracks,
with advance reverence and thirsty yearning.
At that time, there was a Bǐqiūní named Chàluó,
who held a dead insect and placed it on the site of Fó's footprint.
She showed it to Mílè and the others,
and they all looked at it together.
"You all admire, envy, and praise these footprints,
but what is so wondrous about treading upon and killing sentient beings?"
Mílè and the others
all went forward together to look.
Closely observing its form and appearance, they saw it was a naturally dead insect.
They then asked the Bǐqiūní:
"Whose disciple are you?"
The Bǐqiūní replied, saying:
"I am a disciple of Fó."
Then Mílè and the others
each said:
"Among the disciples of Fó,
there are such people!"
They gradually approached the place of Fó
and saw the Shìzūn from afar.
His light shone brilliantly,
and his various marks were glorious.
They immediately counted his marks
but did not see two of them.
Fó then extended his tongue to cover his face for them,
and further used divine power to let them see the concealed organ.
Seeing the full count of marks,
their joy increased.
They then followed their master’s command
and challenged him in their minds from afar:
"My master Bōpólí,
how many marks does he have?"
Fó then replied from afar:
"Your master, Bōpólí,
possesses only two marks:
first, hair that is dark blue;
second, a broad and long tongue."
Having heard these words,
they again challenged him in their minds:
"My master Bōpólí,
how old is he now?"
Fó replied from afar, saying:
"Your master, Bōpólí,
is one hundred and twenty years old."
Having heard this,
they again challenged him in their thoughts:
"My master Bōpólí,
what is his clan and surname?"
Fó replied from afar:
"Your master, Bōpólí,
is of the Póluómén clan."
Having heard this,
they again challenged him in their minds:
"My master Bōpólí,
how many disciples does he have?"
Fó replied from afar:
"Your master, Bōpólí,
has five hundred disciples."
At that time, those in the assembly,
hearing what Fó had said,
were very surprised that the Rúlái spoke these words alone.
At that time, the disciples
knelt and asked Fó:
"Shìzūn!
For what reason did you speak these words?"
Fó told the Bǐqiū:
"There is Bōpólí,
in the country of Bōpólífúduōluó,
who sent sixteen disciples
to come to my place
to observe my marks.
Because they challenged me in their minds,
I therefore answered each one accordingly."
Then Mílè and the others,
hearing Fó's answers to the challenges,
found everything to be just as it truly was,
without a single discrepancy.
Deeply feeling respect and admiration,
they went to the place of Fó,
bowed their heads in respect,
and sat to one side.
Fó preached the Dharma for them.
Those sixteen people
attained the purity of the Dharma Eye.
Each rose from his seat
and requested to leave the household life.
Fó said:
"Welcome!"
Their hair and beards fell off naturally,
Dharma robes appeared on their bodies,
and they immediately became Shāmén.
Again with skillful means,
he preached the Dharma for them,
and fifteen of them
became Āluóhàn.
Then Mílè and the others
discussed among themselves, saying:
"Our master Bōpólí
is far away and waiting anxiously;
it is time to send someone back to report the news."
Among the sixteen people,
there was one
named Bīnqíqí,
who was the son of Bōpólí's sister.
The group sent him to report the news.
He returned to the original country to the place of Bōpólí,
and based on what he had heard and seen,
he explained it extensively.
After Bōpólí heard this,
joy arose from his heart.
He immediately rose from his seat,
knelt and joined his palms
toward the city of Wángshè,
and spoke his sincere words:
"To be born and encounter a Sage's age,
which is very difficult to meet,
I long to behold the Honored countenance
and receive the pure transformation.
My years are already old and advanced,
and the strength of my feet is not great.
Although I have sincere devotion,
there is no way to reach him myself.
Shìzūn, with great compassion!
You know people's hearts in advance;
I only pray that you will bend your spirit
to come and receive and rescue me."
At that time, the Rúlái,
knowing his intent from afar,
in the time it takes to bend and stretch an arm,
arrived before him.
After bowing, Bōpólí raised his head
and immediately saw the Shìzūn.
Startled and filled with joy,
he bowed and inquired after him,
and invited him to take a seat,
He respectfully and solemnly attended the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him,
and he attained the state of Ānàhán.
At that time, the Shìzūn
soon returned to Jiùtóu Shān.
Then Jìngfàn Wáng,
hearing that the Buddha had attained the Way
and was traveling to teach and transform many people,
felt a heart full of yearning and admiration
and a desire to see him.
He told Yōutuóyé:
"Go to where the Buddha is
and convey my intentions
to Xīdá,
saying that you originally had an agreement that upon attaining the Way, you would return.
I hope you will honor your previous words
and come to meet me soon."
Yōutuóyé arrived
and fully announced the King’s wishes.
The Buddha soon agreed to it,
saying he would go in seven days.
Yōutuóyé was delighted
and returned to report the news.
When Jìngfàn Wáng heard this,
he told his various ministers:
"Yōutuóyé has come
and says the Buddha will return.
Within the city, decorate
and make it extremely clean.
Plaster and sweep the streets and alleys,
set up banners and pennants everywhere,
and prepare an abundance of flowers and incense
to await and make offerings."
When the preparations were complete,
he and his various ministers
went forty lǐ outside the city
to receive the Shìzūn.
At that time, the Rúlái
was together with a great assembly.
Eight Jīngāng Lìshì
stood on the eight sides;
then the Sì Tiānwáng
each led the way in front;
then Tiāndì Shì,
along with the gods of the Desire Realm,
attended and guarded his left;
then Fàntiān Wáng,
along with the gods of the Form Realm,
attended and guarded his right;
the Bǐqiū Sēng
were lined up behind him.
The Buddha was in the midst of the assembly,
emitting a great brilliance
that illuminated heaven and earth,
with a majesty exceeding that of the sun and moon.
Together with the great assembly,
they traveled through the air.
As they gradually approached the King,
they descended to the level of people's heads.
The King, the ministers, the commoners, the consorts, and the palace ladies
saw the great assembly, all shining brightly.
The Buddha was in their center like the moon among the stars.
The King was greatly overjoyed
and unconsciously knelt in prostration.
After finishing his prostrations and greetings,
he returned with them to the kingdom,
and they stayed at the Níjūlútuó Sēngqiélán.
At that time, the law of the land
required separation between men and women.
The King and the common men
listened to the Dharma every day.
Hearing the Dharma, they attained awakening,
and those who were liberated were many.
The various women
each harbored resentment, saying:
"Although the Buddha and his assembly
have returned to the kingdom,
only the men are fortunate enough
to see and hear him.
We women
do not receive his grace and protection."
The Buddha knew their thoughts
and immediately said to the King:
"From now on,
let the men and women of the kingdom
take turns listening to the Dharma for one watch each day."
From then on,
many were liberated.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Móhē Bōshébōtí—
after the Buddha had left home—
had personally spun and woven
a piece of golden woolen cloth.
With her heart concentrated on him,
she only waited for the Buddha.
Having now seen the Buddha,
joy arose from her very core.
She immediately took this woolen cloth
and offered it to the Rúlái.
The Buddha told Jiāotánmí:
"Take this cloth
and offer it to the assembly of monks."
Then Bōshébōtí
again said to the Buddha:
"Since the Buddha left home,
my heart has always thought of you.
Therefore, I personally spun and wove this,
intending it for the Buddha.
I only pray you will have compassion
and accept it for my sake!"
The Buddha told her:
"I know my mother’s devoted heart wishes to give this to me.
However, from a heart of personal affection,
the blessings are not vast.
If you give it to the assembly of monks, the reward obtained will be much greater.
I know this to be so,
and therefore I urge you."
The Buddha also said:
"If there is a donor
who makes specific invitations to sixteen kinds of people,
although they will obtain a blessed reward,
it will not be much.
What are the sixteen?
Bǐqiū
and Bǐqiūní
each have eight types;
this is not as good as
generally inviting four people from within the Sangha.
The merit obtained
and the blessings are greater than that;
the merit of the sixteen types
does not equal one part of it.
In the future final age,
when the Dharma is about to vanish,
even if Bǐqiū
keep wives and children,
if there are four or more
who are known as the Sangha,
they should be respected and viewed as if they were Shèlìfú
or Mùjiánlián."
Then Bōshébōtí's
heart was opened and enlightened.
She immediately took the garment
and offered it to the Sangha.
It was passed in sequence through the Sangha,
but there was no one who wished to take it.
When it reached Mílè,
he immediately accepted it.
Afterwards, the Shìzūn,
together with the assembly of Bǐqiū,
traveled to Bōluónài
to teach and transform.
At that time, Mílè,
wearing the golden woolen garment,
was handsome in appearance,
with a complexion like purple gold.
His inner and outer qualities matched,
and his bearing was dignified and orderly.
He entered the city of Bōluónài
intending to beg for food.
Arriving at the main street,
he held his bowl and stood still.
People of all kinds
beheld his appearance
and gathered around to watch
without ever feeling satisfied.
Although they all respected him,
none offered him food.
There was a bead-stringer
who happened to be on the road.
Seeing Mílè,
he felt great respect and admiration.
He immediately asked the Great Virtuous One:
"Have you obtained food yet?"
He answered:
"I have not."
The man then invited him to return home,
where he prepared and served food.
After eating and rinsing his mouth,
Mílè preached the wondrous Dharma for him.
His words were lofty and beautiful,
and the man listened without weariness.
At that time, there was a great Zhǎngzhě
whose daughter was about to be married.
He had previously given the man a bead
and hired him to string it.
If the stringing was finished,
he would be given one hundred thousand coins.
At that time, the Zhǎngzhě
sent someone to demand the bead.
The bead-stringer, hearing the Dharma,
felt sweet joy in his five senses
and said:
"Go away for now!
I will string it later."
The person said again:
"It is needed urgently now;
please set your hand to it immediately."
After giving the instruction, he left
and told everything to the Zhǎngzhě.
In a short moment,
Someone was sent again to demand the pearls,
but he was still listening to the Dharma,
and had not yet bored through them.
The messenger returned and told the Elder,
and the Elder spoke resentfully:
"Since I have hired you at a high price,
and did not employ you and entrust this to you in vain,
yet now you vacillate,
failing to meet my needs."
He sent a person again,
carrying money along:
"If they are not yet bored,
bring the pearls back."
The messenger arrived and asked,
but he was still listening to the Dharma;
knowing the pearls were not bored,
the messenger urgently demanded them back.
There was no choice,
so he immediately took them and returned them.
The master of pearl-boring,
before Mílè,
listened to the Dharma in sequence,
his mind feeling no weariness or withdrawal.
His wife was furious,
reproaching her husband, saying:
"A brief moment of labor
would have earned one hundred thousand coins
to provide for the shortage of clothing and food at home;
yet you only listen to the Shāmén's empty and beautiful talk,
losing such a great profit of wealth."
The husband heard her words,
and his heart felt regret and resentment.
Mílè knew his thoughts
and spoke to him, saying:
"Are you able to go with me to the Jīngshè now?"
He replied:
"It is possible."
They immediately went to the Jīngshè together;
bringing him into the assembly of monks,
he asked the assembly of monks:
"If there is a Tányuè
who invites one Shāmén who keeps the pure precepts
to his home to provide offerings,
how does the gain obtained
compare to someone getting one hundred thousand coins?"
At that time, Jiāochénrú
immediately spoke, saying:
"Suppose someone
obtains a hundred carts of precious treasures,
calculating its merit and profit,
it is not as great as the vast profit gained from inviting one pure-precept Shāmén to one's home for offerings."
Shèlìfú said:
"Suppose someone
obtains one Yánfútí full of precious treasures,
it is still not as great as the even more profit gained from inviting one pure-precept person to one's home for offerings."
Mùjiánlián said:
"Even if someone
obtains two worlds full of the seven treasures,
it is truly not as good as inviting one pure Shāmén
to one's home for offerings, obtaining extremely much profit."
The rest of the Bǐqiū,
likewise each
cited analogies
comparing the profits,
and all were greater than that.
Then Ānàlǜ further spoke himself:
"Even if one obtained the treasures filling the four worlds,
the profit would still not be as great as the many times superior profit of inviting one pure Shāmén to one's home for offerings.
The reason for this is,
I am the witness to it.
I remember in the past, ninety-one kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha in the world named Pípóshī,
after his Parinirvāṇa,
his teachings and Dharma had vanished.
At that time in Yánfútí,
there was a great kingdom
named Bōluónài.
In the kingdom at that time,
there was a Sàbó,
whose family was extremely wealthy,
lacking nothing.
He had two sons,
both of whom were handsome;
the elder was named Lèizhà,
and the younger was named Ālèizhà.
When the father was nearing the end of his life,
he instructed his two sons:
'I cannot escape death,
and shall soon enter the next life.
You brothers
must remember to support each other,
uniting your hearts and combining your efforts;
carefully avoid living separately.
The reason for this is,
it is like a single thread
which cannot bind an elephant,
but by gathering many threads,
one can control an elephant.
Like a single reed
which cannot burn alone,
but by grasping a bundle together,
once lit, it cannot be extinguished.
Now you brothers
are also like this;
relying on each other,
outsiders cannot destroy you,
and being internally harmonious and diligent in the household,
then your wealth and estate will increase daily.'
After giving these instructions and warnings,
his breath ceased and he died.
The brothers followed the teaching
and lived together for some time.
Later, Ālèizhà’s wife
thought to herself:
'Living together now,
we are constrained by the elder brother's family,
and guests and acquaintances cannot be properly hosted;
if we were to separate
and each exert our own efforts,
with no such difficulties, we could establish our own household.'
Having thought this,
she told her husband everything.
Ālèizhà heard what his wife said
and thought it was not right,
but the wife was persistent,
broadly citing reasons.
Ālèizhà’s mind changed,
and he informed his elder brother of the matter.
The elder brother again cited their father's dying words,
widely showing through analogies the reasons why it was not possible to separate.
Then Ālèizhà’s wife
frequently urged her husband,
until her husband's mind was set, and he urgently requested to live separately;
the elder brother, seeing his strong resolve,
divided the house and property with him.
After the separation,
Ālèizhà and his wife
indulged their desires and followed their whims,
gathering companions and parties,
drinking and eating luxuriously,
and not following proper etiquette.
Before many years had passed,
their household goods were exhausted,
and they were impoverished and without any resources.
He went to his brother to beg from him.
The elder brother pitied him again
and gave him one hundred thousand coins.
When it was used up, he asked again;
this happened six times,
and in total, he gave him six hundred thousand coins.
Later he came to ask again.
The elder brother scolded him:
'Our late father's instructions
you did not follow,
and before long,
you requested to separate.
You wasted resources without measure,
and cannot be supplied indefinitely;
I have already given you six hundred thousand coins,
yet you are not satisfied
and come again to ask.
Now I will give you another hundred thousand coins;
whether you have enough or not, do not come to ask again.'
The younger brother, having been scolded,
took the money with shame;
the couple changed their ways,
restraining themselves and being frugal,
diligently working on the family estate,
and their property increased daily.
Later they gradually became wealthy,
no longer lacking anything.
"The elder brother Lèizhà
suffered consecutive misfortunes;
experiencing ruin wherever he was,
his wealth scattered,
and the household suddenly fell into poverty with no plan.
He went to his younger brother's side
and recounted his hardships,
asking for a little money
to provide for his needs.
The younger brother was angry and resentful
and spoke to the elder brother, saying:
'I thought that in my brother's house
there was no such thing as poverty;
how is it that you have come again to ask of me?'
After saying this,
he would not even offer him food.
The elder brother then left,
feeling stunned:
'In the cycle of birth and death,
what is there to be feared?
Even brothers of the same body
do not recognize kindness and care,
how much less so others?'
As he pondered the principles of righteousness,
his mind became weary of the world;
he abandoned his home and entered the mountains,
sitting in stillness and contemplating the arising and ceasing of all phenomena,
and his mind immediately attained awakening.
He became a Pratyekabuddha,
with a dignified and impressive appearance,
and entered the city to beg for food.
Later, there was a year of famine,
and the people were hungry and lacking.
At that time, for the Pratyekabuddha,
it was difficult to obtain food through begging.
At that time, the younger brother Ālèizhà
later became poor.
Again encountering a year of famine,
his grain supply was not continuous.
Every day he went to collect firewood,
selling it to buy barnyard millet
for his wife and children
to support their lives.
One morning,
he went early into the marsh.
At the city gate,
he saw the Pratyekabuddha,
whose appearance was dignified and impressive,
entering the city to beg for food.
He then went to collect firewood.
Returning to the gate,
he saw the Pratyekabuddha coming out with an empty bowl.
He thought to himself:
"This is a noble man.
I saw him enter the city this morning,
yet now he comes back empty-handed.
If he would now return to my house with me,
I should share my food and offer it to him as alms."
After having this thought,
he left him and went on.
Then the Pratyekabuddha,
immediately knowing his intention,
followed behind him
and arrived at the doorway.
Ālèizhà saw him
and was filled with joy.
He immediately spread a mat
and invited him to sit.
He asked for his own portion of barnyard millet porridge
and, holding it with his own hands,
offered it to the Pratyekabuddha.
Then the Pratyekabuddha
said to Ālèizhà:
"You are also hungry and thirsty;
we should share and eat it."
Ālèizhà said:
"We laypeople
eat at no fixed times.
The Honored One eats once a day;
I only wish for you to accept it."
Having finished the food,
moved by his sincere heart—
encountering such a year of famine
where even fathers and sons cannot save each other,
yet he was able to cut from his own portion
to give as an offering—
the Pratyekabuddha decided to manifest a transformation to make him rejoice.
He then flew into the empty sky,
with water and fire coming from his body,
extensively showing supernatural powers.
Returning to stand before him,
he said to Ālèizhà:
"What vow do you wish to make?
It shall be as you desire."
Seeing the transformation, he was overjoyed and came forward with a sincere heart,
making a vow:
"All sentient beings
seek wealth in many ways.
I vow that in life after life,
I shall lack for nothing.
Whatever my heart desires
shall arrive according to my thoughts.
Furthermore, I vow that in the future,
I may meet a Superior Being
whose merit exceeds yours by a hundred thousand million times,
allowing me to attain the realization of the exhaustion of outflows through him,
and my supernatural powers and transformations will be no different from yours."
Having finished making the vows,
he was doubly joyful.
Then the Pratyekabuddha
returned to where he resided.
At that time, Ālèizhà
returned to the marsh to collect firewood.
There he saw a rabbit
and wished to catch it.
Chasing it and getting closer,
he threw his sickle from afar.
It immediately fell to the ground.
Just as he wanted to go forward to take it,
it transformed into a corpse, jumped onto his back, and tightly hugged his head.
He tried his best to push it off,
but could not do so.
His heart was filled with terror,
alarmed and distressed.
He wanted to enter the city
so that his wife could help remove it,
but feared people would see it and not let him enter.
He waited until dusk,
covered it with clothes,
and carried it on his back into the city to his house.
Once inside the house,
it naturally fell to the ground
and transformed into a pile of Yánfútán gold,
brilliantly shining
and illuminating the neighboring houses.
Word of it spread,
reaching the King.
The King immediately sent someone
to investigate the truth.
The messenger arrived and looked,
saw it was a corpse,
and immediately returned to tell the King:
"It is only a corpse."
The King asked other people,
who still said it was gold.
Finding the reason very strange,
he sent people to look again.
This happened seven times,
and the reports were inconsistent.
The King then went himself,
personally going to look at it.
He saw it was a corpse,
its form gradually becoming smelly.
He immediately asked Ālèizhà:
"What do you see this as?"
He answered:
"To me, it is truly gold."
He then took a small amount
and offered it to the King.
The King saw the golden color
and respected him as never before.
He asked for the cause:
"How did you obtain this?"
At that time, Ālèizhà
explained the whole story from beginning to end to the King:
"It must be because of the offering to the Pratyekabuddha."
The King heard his words
and sighed, saying:
"Excellent!
You have gained great benefit
by encountering this Superior Person."
He then gave him more gifts
and appointed him as a Great Minister.
Thus, O Honored Ones!
That Ālèizhà
was my former self.
In that lifetime,
I offered a little barnyard millet porridge to the Pratyekabuddha
and made a vow because of it.
Ever since then,
for ninety-one kalpas,
born among gods and humans,
I have lacked nothing,
being outstanding in three things,
being praised for my upright appearance.
Whatever my heart desired
arrived according to my thoughts.
Even in this current life,
when I was at home,
I always lived in leisure,
not liking worldly affairs.
My elder brother, Móhānán,
often had words of complaint.
My mother said:
"My son has great merit."
Móhānán said:
"I alone labor and worry
managing the household and the fields;
he eats while lying in leisure;
how is this merit?"
His mother wanted to test this,
and sent me to the field
to supervise the planting,
ordering that no food be sent.
I was surprised that the food was late
and sent someone to ask for it.
My mother sent someone to tell me:
"There is nothing."
I sent word back to my mother:
"I only wish for you to
send me 'nothing'."
At that time, his mother,
hearing these words from her son,
immediately took a jeweled tray
and ornate utensils,
covered them with a cloth,
and sent them to me,
asking Móhānán to follow and watch.
Having arrived before me,
he removed the cloth,
and food of a hundred flavors
completely filled the tray and utensils.
In other times as well,
whatever I thought of [appeared].
Even if one were to obtain treasures filling the four continents,
at the end of the kalpa,
they would naturally perish.
Again, it did not last long.
In this way, I gave a little gruel as an offering to a Pratyekabuddha (Bìzhīfó),
and for ninety-one kalpas,
the blessings and benefits have not diminished.
Moreover, by reason of this merit,
I met the Buddha and was delivered from suffering.
For this reason,
one should know that inviting one pure-precept Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū)
to one's home to make offerings yields benefits greater than the treasures of the four continents."
At that time, Ānālǜ,
having finished speaking these words,
the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) then
entered from outside.
Having heard Ānālǜ speaking of past events,
he told the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū):
"O you Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū)!
You speak of past events,
and I shall next speak of the coming age.
In this Yánfútí,
the land will be square and upright,
level and vast,
without mountains or rivers.
The ground will grow soft grass,
just like heavenly garments.
At that time, the people will live for eighty-four thousand years,
their bodies eight zhàng tall,
upright and exquisitely beautiful,
their natures benevolent and harmonious,
and they will fully practice the ten virtuous deeds.
At that time, there shall be a Wheel-Turning Holy King (Zhuànlún Shèngwáng),
named Shèngjiā
(in Jìn speech, meaning 'Complete').
At that time, a Brahman (Póluómén) family shall give birth to a son,
named Mílè.
His body will be the color of purple gold,
with the thirty-two marks,
and all the auxiliary signs fully complete,
his radiance extraordinarily brilliant.
He will leave the home life to study the Way,
attain the supreme perfect enlightenment,
and for the sake of all sentient beings,
turn the most honorable wheel of the Dharma.
At his first great assembly,
he will deliver ninety-three billion kinds of sentient beings;
at the second great assembly,
he will deliver ninety-six billion;
at the third great assembly,
he will deliver ninety-nine billion.
Thus, Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū)!
During the teaching of the Dharma at these three assemblies,
those who receive deliverance
are all sentient beings who planted blessings in my bequeathed Dharma—
or those who made offerings to the Triple Gem (Sānbǎo),
those who left home or remained at home and upheld the precepts,
those who burned incense, lit lamps, and performed prostrations—
all shall be among those at the three assemblies.
The three assemblies will deliver the remaining sentient beings from my legacy,
and afterward transform those with shared conditions."
At that time, Mílè,
hearing these words of the Buddha,
rose from his seat,
knelt down and said to the Buddha:
"I wish to become that Mílè Shìzūn."
The Buddha told him:
"It shall be as you say;
you shall be born there as Mílè Rúlái.
The one who teaches as described above
is none other than you."
At that time in the assembly,
there was a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū),
named Āshìduō,
who knelt down and said to the Buddha:
"I wish to become that Wheel-Turning King (Zhuànlún zhī Wáng)."
The Buddha told him:
"Throughout the long night, you only
crave the pleasures of birth and death;
do you not seek to escape?"
At that time, the entire great assembly,
seeing the Shìzūn give Mílè the prediction of future Buddhahood,
yet still naming him Mílè,
each had doubts
and wished to know the origin of this.
The Venerable Ānán then
rose and said to the Buddha:
"When Mílè becomes a Buddha,
he is still named Mílè.
I do not know from where this name originated."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Listen carefully and pay attention!
In the past, immeasurable Asaṃkhyeya kalpas (Āsēngqí jié) ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king named Tánmóliúzhī,
who ruled over Yánfútí,
with its eighty-four thousand kingdoms,
sixty thousand mountains and rivers,
eight billion villages,
twenty thousand wives and ladies-in-waiting,
and ten thousand ministers.
There was a small, prosperous, and happy kingdom;
the king of this kingdom
was named Bōsàiqí.
At that time, Fúshā Fó
had first appeared in the world,
and within this kingdom,
he was transforming and guiding sentient beings.
At that time, King Bōsàiqí and his ministers
were devoted to making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks (Sēng),
and they had no leisure to go and have an audience with the Great King;
their tributes and communications
had also completely ceased.
Then the Great King,
wondering at the interruption,
immediately dispatched an envoy
to go and demand the reason.
After the envoy arrived,
he proclaimed the King's command:
'In recent years,
both messengers and messages have been cut off.
You are a subject;
why have you departed from the norm?
Do you perhaps have different intentions
and harbor rebellion?'
At that time, Bōsàiqí,
receiving the Great King's instruction,
knew he had been remiss,
and not knowing what to do,
he immediately went to see the Buddha
and reported this matter.
The Buddha told the King:
'Do not worry.
Just send the envoy back and tell him truthfully:
"The Buddha is in my kingdom,
and I serve Him morning and evening.
Therefore, I have no leisure to go and see the Great King.
All the wealth within the kingdom
is used to provide for the Buddha and the Sēng,
and there is nothing remaining that can be offered as tribute."'
King Bōsàiqí,
having received the Buddha's teaching,
then replied to the envoy
just as the Buddha had said.
The envoy arrived and saw the King,
reporting these intentions in full.
When the Great King heard this,
he felt great anger,
and immediately gathered his ministers
to discuss this matter together.
The ministers all said:
'That king is arrogant and disrespectful,
perversely citing principles.
We should assemble troops and go to attack him.'
The King agreed,
and assembling the troops, he went in person.
When the vanguard drew near,
that king finally learned of it,
and feeling fear in his heart,
he hurriedly went to tell the Buddha.
The Buddha told the King:
'Do not worry.
Just go yourself to see him
and declare your previous words.'
King Bōsàiqí,
then along with his ministers,
went to the border.
Meeting the Great King,
and after finishing his polite inquiries,
he stood to one side.
The Great King questioned him:
'On what do you rely,
that you have been disrespectful and failed in your duties,
not coming for an audience?'
Bōsàiqí said:
'An age with a Buddha is hard to encounter,
and it is extremely difficult to behold Him.
He has recently been in my kingdom,
transforming and guiding the people and things.
Since I serve Him morning and evening, I have been remiss.'
Then the Great King
rebuked him even more severely:
'Even if it were so,
why have you cut off the tributes?'
Bōsàiqí said:
'The Buddha has followers
called the assembly of monks (Sēng),
whose virtue in precepts is pure,
and who are a supreme field of merit for the world.
Everything the entire kingdom possesses
is constantly used for offerings,
and there is no surplus that can be used for tribute.'
When Tánmóliúzhī heard these words,
he said:
'Wait!
I must see the Buddha first.
After seeing the Buddha and returning,
I shall then question your crime.'
He immediately, along with his ministers,
went to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Tathāgata (Rúlái)
was surrounded by a great assembly.
Each sat quietly and upright, entering meditative concentration.
There was a Bǐqiū,
who entered the Cí Sānmèi,
emitting a golden radiance,
like a great mass of fire.
Tánmóliúzhī,
seeing the Shìzūn from afar,
His radiance magnificent and brilliant, surpassing the sun,
surrounded by the great assembly,
like the moon among the stars,
paid homage to the Fó
and inquired after Him according to the Fǎ.
Seeing this Bǐqiū,
whose radiance was particularly prominent,
he immediately said to the Shìzūn:
"This Bǐqiū,
what kind of Dìng has he entered,
that his radiance is such as this?"
The Fó told the Dàwáng:
"This Bǐqiū
has entered the Cí Dìng and others."
When the Wáng heard these words,
his admiration increased manifold,
and he said:
"Since this Cí Dìng is so lofty,
I must surely practice this Cí Sānmèi."
Having made this vow,
his mind longed for the Cí Dìng,
his thoughts became very gentle and soft,
and he no longer had any harmful intent.
He then immediately invited the Fó and the Bǐqiū Sēng:
"I only wish that You would turn Your spirit
and come to the great kingdom."
The Fó then gave His permission and set a date to go.
"Wáng Bōsàiqí,
hearing that the Fó wished to go to the Dàwáng's kingdom,
felt great longing and regret,
sorrowful, fearful, and distressed,
and thought to himself:
'If I were a Dàwáng,
the Rúlái would always dwell in my kingdom;
it is because I am small that I do not have such freedom.'
Having thought this,
he immediately asked the Fó:
'Among all kings,
who is the greatest?'
The Fó told him:
'The Zhuǎnlún Wáng is the greatest.'
Wáng Bōsàiqí
then made a vow:
'I wish that through my long-standing
offerings to the Fó and the Sēng assembly,
and by this merit,
I vow to always be a Zhuǎnlún Wáng in every future life.'
Thus, Ānán!
The Dàwáng Tánmóliúzhī of that time
is now Mílè.
It was starting from that life
that he gave rise to this Cí Xīn,
and from then on,
he has always been named Mílè.
That Wáng Bōsàiqí
is now Qǐtuó;
because in that time
he always became a Zhuǎnlún Wáng,
from then on,
he has constantly been one in every life,
even until today,
his merit has not been exhausted;
that is why today,
he once again seeks to become one."
At that time, the pearl-piercing
master, having heard this,
immediately gave rise to the Wúshàng Zhèngzhēn Dàoyì.
The others in the assembly,
hearing what the Fó had said,
some attained the fruits of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
some gave rise to the Wúshàng Zhèngzhēn Dàoyì;
some attained the stage of Bùtuìdì;
each and all were filled with respect,
and joyfully followed the teachings.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in Shèwèi Guó, at the Qǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, the Zhǎngzhě Sūdá,
who revered and believed in the Fó Fǎ,
was a Tányuè for the Sēng,
and everything they needed,
he provided it all.
At that time, various Bǐqiū,
as they had need,
would come and go daily,
preaching the Fǎ and giving instruction.
Within Sūdá's household,
there were two parrots:
one named Lǜtí,
the second named Shēlǜtí;
by nature they were clever and wise,
and could understand human speech.
Whenever the Bǐqiū came or went,
they would always first announce it to the household so all would know;
they would dust and arrange the seats,
and joyfully go out to welcome them.
At that time, Ānán,
went to that house,
and seeing the birds were so intelligent and clever,
he felt affection for them in his heart,
and said to them:
"I wish to teach you the Fǎ."
The two birds were delighted,
and he transmitted to them the Sìdì Fǎ,
teaching them to recite and practice it,
and he spoke a verse:
"Dòuqū, Sānmóutíyé,
Nílóutuó, Mòjiā" (In the Jìn language, this is Kǔ, Xí, Miè, Dào).
In front of the gate there were trees;
two birds heard the Dharma,
and they rejoiced and practiced chanting it.
They flew up into the trees,
ascending and descending in sequence,
passing through seven rounds,
chanting the wonderful Dharma of the Four Noble Truths they had received.
That evening they nested in the trees
and were eaten by a wild cat.
On account of this virtuous mind,
they were immediately born in the four heavens.
When the time arrived the next morning, the Venerable Ānán
put on his robes and took his bowl,
entering the city to beg for food.
Hearing that the two parrots had been killed by a cat,
a feeling of pity and compassion arose in him.
He returned and said to the Buddha:
"Within the household of Xūdá,
there were two parrots.
Yesterday, I, your disciple,
taught them to chant the Four Noble Truths.
That night, their lives ended.
I do not know where their consciousness
has been born.
I only wish for the Rúlái
to show compassion and inform me."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Listen carefully, listen carefully!
Fix this well in your heart;
I shall speak for you,
to make you rejoice.
Because you taught them the Dharma,
and they received and upheld it with joyful hearts,
after their lives ended,
they were born in the Sìwáng Tiān.
Fifty years in this Yánfútí
is one day and one night in the Sìwáng Tiān;
there, thirty days make a month,
and twelve months make a year.
The lifespan in that Sìwáng Tiān is five hundred years."
Ānán asked the Buddha:
"When their lives end there,
where will they be born?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"They shall be born in the second heaven, the Dāolì Tiān.
One hundred years in this Yánfútí
is one day and one night in the Dāolì Tiān;
there also, thirty days make a month,
and twelve months make a year.
The lifespan in that Dāolì Tiān is one thousand years."
Ānán asked again:
"When their lives end there,
where will they be born?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"They shall be born in the third heaven, the Yánmó Tiān.
Two hundred years in this Yánfútí
is one day and one night in the Yánmó Tiān;
there also, thirty days make a month,
and twelve months make a year.
The lifespan in that Yánmó Tiān is two thousand years."
Ānán asked again:
"When their lives end there,
where will they be born?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"They shall be born in the fourth heaven, the Dōushuài Tiān.
Four hundred years in this Yánfútí
is one day and one night in that heaven;
there also, thirty days make a month,
and twelve months make a year.
The lifespan in that Dōushuài Tiān is four thousand years."
Ānán asked again:
"When their lives end there,
where will they be born?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"They shall be born in the fifth heaven, the Bùjiāolè Tiān.
Eight hundred years in this Yánfútí
is one day and one night in that fifth heaven;
there also, thirty days make a month,
and twelve months make a year.
The lifespan in that fifth heaven is eight thousand years."
Ānán asked again:
"When their lives end there,
where will they be born?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"They shall be born in the sixth heaven, the Huàyìngshēng Tiān.
One thousand six hundred years in this Yánfútí
is one day and one night in that sixth heaven;
there also, thirty days make a month,
and twelve months make a year.
The lifespan in that sixth heaven is sixteen thousand years."
Ānán asked again:
"When their lives end there,
where will they be born again?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"They shall return to be born in the fifth heaven.
In this sequence,
down to the Sìwáng Tiān.
Going up and down seven times,
being born among the six heavens of desire,
freely enjoying blessings,
exhausting the lifespan of those heavens,
without any premature death."
Ānán asked again:
"When their lifespan in the six heavens is exhausted,
where will they be born?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"They shall descend to Yánfútí,
be born among humans,
and leave the household life to study the Way.
Because of having previously chanted and upheld the Four Noble Truths when they were birds,
their minds will naturally open and understand,
and they will become Bìzhīfó;
one named Tánmó,
and the second named Xiūtánmó."
The Buddha told Ānán:
"All the Buddhas,
and the various worthies and sages,
and the categories of gods and humans,
the amount of blessings they receive
is all due to planting virtuous causes within the Dharma,
which causes each of them to subsequently obtain wonderful fruits."
At that time Ānán
and the great assembly,
hearing what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the Jǐshù Gǐgūdú Yuán in the country of Shèwèi.
At that time, among the trees of the forest,
there was a Bǐqiū
sitting in meditation and practicing the Way.
After eating, he was walking in meditation,
and while doing so, he chanted the sutras;
his voice was clear and elegant, wonderful beyond compare.
At that time there was a bird
that revered and loved his voice.
It flew into a tree
to listen to the sound.
At that time there was a hunter
who shot and killed it with an arrow.
Due to this virtuous mind,
it was immediately born in the second heaven, the Dāolì Tiān,
upon its parents' laps.
Suddenly it grew up
like an eight-year-old child,
with an upright countenance
and extraordinary, radiant features,
bright and without equal.
He then thought to himself:
"By what merit
have I been born here?"
Through the karmic reward of heavenly blessings,
he then recognized his past life.
Observing his former body,
he saw it was originally a bird
that, through the reward of merit from hearing the Bǐqiū chant sutras,
attained birth here.
He then took heavenly flowers
and went to Yánfútí,
arriving at the place where the Bǐqiū was.
He paid respects and inquired after him,
and with heavenly flowers and incense,
he made offerings and scattered them over him.
The Bǐqiū asked:
"What deity are you?"
He replied:
"I was originally a bird.
I loved your voice, Venerable One,
and came here to listen to the sutras.
I happened to be killed by a hunter,
and due to that virtuous mind,
I was born in the Dāolì Tiān."
The Bǐqiū was delighted
and immediately told him to sit,
preaching various wonderful and virtuous dharmas for him.
The heavenly being's mind opened and understand,
and he attained the fruit of a Xūtuóhuán.
Leaping with great joy,
he immediately returned to the heavens.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"The Rúlái's appearance in the world
brings very much benefit.
The various dharmas spoken
are truly profound and wonderful.
Even a flying bird,
because of loving the sound of the Dharma,
obtains immeasurable blessings.
How much more so for a person with firm faith who receives and upholds it?
The karmic rewards obtained
are difficult to compare."
At that time Ānán and the great assembly,
hearing what the Buddha said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Xiányú Jīng, Volume Twelve.
Xiányú Jīng, Volume Thirteen.
Translated in Gāochāng Jùn by the Śramana Huìjué and others from Liángzhōu during the Yuán Wèi.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the kingdom of Bōluónài.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
in the midst of a forest and marsh,
for the sake of the gods, humans, and the four groups of disciples,
was expounding the wondrous Dharma.
At that time, in the empty sky,
there was a flock of five hundred geese,
which heard the sound of the Fó's voice.
They felt deep love and joy in their hearts,
circling and hovering in flight,
soon wishing to descend to where the Shìzūn was.
At that time, there was a hunter
who had spread out a net.
The flock of five hundred geese
fell into that net
and were killed by the hunter.
They were reborn in the Dāolì Tiān,
upon the knees of parents.
Suddenly they grew
like eight-year-old children.
Their bodies were upright and majestic,
their countenances incomparable,
and their radiant features were bright and pure,
like a mountain of gold.
They then thought to themselves:
“By what cause
was I born into this heaven?”
The heavenly beings’ minds were sharp and their spirits discerning;
they immediately recognized their past lives.
Because they had loved the sound of the Dharma,
they received the karmic reward of rebirth in heaven
and should repay that kindness.
Immediately and at the same time,
carrying heavenly flowers and incense,
they descended to the kingdom of Bōluónài in Yánfútí
and went to the place of the Shìzūn.
Their heavenly light shone brilliantly,
like a grove of jeweled trees.
Simultaneously bowing their bodies,
they prostrated at the Shìzūn’s feet,
and with palms joined, they said:
“Having received the sound of the Shìzūn’s preaching of the Dharma,
we were born in this wondrous place.
We pray that you will again show us compassion
and reveal the essentials of the Way.”
At that time, the Shìzūn
then expounded the wondrous Dharma of the Four Truths for them.
The heavenly beings attained awakening
and achieved the fruit of Xūtuóhuán.
They then returned to the heavens.
They would not fall into the three miserable paths,
and following conditions through seven births,
they would bring all outflows to an end.
At that time, Ānán
addressed the Shìzūn, saying:
“Last night there were heavenly beings whose light shone brilliantly,
paying their respects to the Shìzūn.
I do not know the cause of this.
I pray that you will explain it to me.”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Think upon this well!
I shall explain it to you.
Yesterday, when the Shìzūn was in the forest and marsh,
for the assembly of the gods, worldly people, and the four groups of disciples,
he was expounding the wondrous Dharma.
There was a flock of five hundred geese
who loved and revered the sound of the Dharma.
With hearts full of joy and celebration,
they flew together
wishing to come to my place,
but they fell into a hunter’s net.
At that time, the hunter
immediately caught and killed them.
Because of this virtuous mind,
they were born in the Dāolì Tiān.
They recognized their past lives
and therefore came to repay the kindness.”
At that time, Ānán,
hearing what the Fó had said,
was filled with great joy.
He marveled at this unprecedented event
and said:
“The appearance of the Rúlái in the world
is truly marvelous!
He pours down the rain of the Dharma,
and there is none who is not moistened by it.
Even birds,
if they hear the sound of the Dharma,
can obtain such blessings.
How much more so for humans who receive and uphold it with faith!
If one calculates their karmic reward,
it would surpass theirs
by a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times;
it is beyond comparison.”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is as you have said.
When the Rúlái appears in the world,
he brings much moisture and benefit,
universally raining down ambrosia
to saturate all living beings.
For this reason,
one should with a single mind believe in and revere the Dharma of the Fó.”
At that time, Ānán
and the whole assembly,
hearing what the Fó had said,
rejoiced and put it into practice.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in the city of Wángshè Chéng on Mount Qíshéjué Shān.
At that time, Típódáduō,
who constantly harbored an evil mind
toward the Shìzūn,
wishing to harm the Rúlái
and claiming to be a Fó himself,
taught Āshéshì
to harm his father to become king.
"A new Fó and a new king
governing the world—
would that not be delightful?"
The prince believed and followed him,
then killed his father
and established himself as king.
At this time, the people of the world
all harbored evil minds;
toward the Bǐqiū,
they were averse and did not wish to see them.
At that time, when the Bǐqiū
entered the city to beg for food,
the people were angry and resentful
and all refused to speak with them;
they came out with empty bowls
and returned to the mountain,
where they addressed the Shìzūn, saying:
"Típódáduō
has done unwholesome deeds,
causing the fourfold assembly
to each give rise to an evil mind
toward the Shāmén."
At that time, the Shìzūn told Ānán:
"If there are sentient beings
who give rise to an evil mind
toward Shāmén or those who wear dyed garments,
you should know that such people
then direct their evil minds
toward all the Fó of the past,
the Pìzhīfó,
and the Āluóhàn;
toward all the Fó of the future,
the Pìzhīfó,
and the Āluóhàn;
and toward all the Fó of the present,
the Pìzhīfó,
and the Āluóhàn.
Because they give rise to an evil mind toward the worthies and sages of the three periods of time,
they will then incur immeasurable karmic retribution for their offenses.
Why is this?
Dyed garments
are all the emblems of the worthies and sages of the three periods of time.
If there are sentient beings
who shave their hair and beards
and wear dyed garments,
you should know that such people
will before long obtain liberation from all suffering,
attain undefiled wisdom,
and for the sake of all sentient beings,
act as a great protection and rescue.
If there are sentient beings
who can give rise to a mind of faith
toward those who have left the home-life and wear dyed garments,
the blessings they obtain are difficult to measure."
The Fó told Ānán:
"Because I, in the past,
toward those who had left the home-life and wore dyed garments,
deeply gave rise to a mind of faith
and revered and honored them,
I was able to attain Buddhahood."
Ānán addressed the Fó, saying:
"Shìzūn!
In the past, regarding the deep mind
that revered those in dyed garments—
what was the matter of that?
I wish to hear it."
The Fó told Ānán:
"Listen well, and I shall speak."
"Yes, Shìzūn!
I wish to hear it."
The Fó told Ānán:
"In the past, immeasurable Āsēngqíjié ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Típí,
who governed eighty-four thousand minor kings.
In that age there was no Fófǎ,
but there was a Pìzhīfó
who lived in the mountains and forests,
practicing meditation and the Path, and manifesting transformations such as flying through the air,
to bring blessings and deliverance to sentient beings.
At that time, all the wild beasts
all came to be close to him.
There was a lion
named Chānjiāluópí
(in the Jìn language, Jiānshì),
whose body was golden in color,
with bright and distinct marks of radiance, shining brilliantly.
He ate fruit and grass
and did not harm the various living beings.
At that time, a hunter
shaved his head and wore a jiāshā,
concealed a bow and arrows within,
and walked through the marshes.
Seeing the lion,
he was extremely joyful
and thought to himself:
'I have a great profit now.
Having seen this beast,
I can kill it and take its skin
to offer to the king,
which will be enough to escape poverty.'
At that time, the lion
happened to be sleeping,
and the hunter shot it with a poisoned arrow.
The lion woke up startled
and immediately wanted to charge and harm him,
but seeing him wearing the jiāshā,
he thought to himself:
'Such a person,
before long in this world,
will surely obtain liberation
and be free from all suffering and distress.
Why is this?
These dyed garments
are the emblem of the sages of the three periods of time—past, future, and present.
If I harm him,
then I will be directing an evil mind toward the worthies and sages of the three periods of time.'
Reflecting in this way,
his intent to harm subsided.
As the poison of the arrow spread
and his life was soon to end,
he then spoke a verse:
" 'Yē luó luó
Pó shē shā
Suō hē' "
"When these words were spoken,
heaven and earth shook greatly,
rain fell from a cloudless sky,
and the various devas were startled and alarmed.
They immediately used their divine eyes to look down upon the world
and saw the hunter had killed the Pú-sà lion.
In the midst of the void,
they rained down various celestial flowers
to make offerings to its corpse.
At that time, the hunter
skinned the lion
and took the skin home
to present it to King Tí-pí,
seeking a reward.
Then the King thought,
'The scriptures say:
"If there is a beast with a golden-colored body,
it must be a Pú-sà, a Great Being."
How can I now reward this person?
If I give him a reward,
it would be no different from being complicit in this killing.'
At that time, the hunter,
who was habitually poor and begged for mercy,
moved the King to pity,
and he gave him a small amount of wealth.
He asked the hunter,
'When the lion died,
what auspicious signs occurred?'
He replied,
'Its mouth spoke eight characters:
heaven and earth shook everywhere,
rain fell from a cloudless sky,
and the heavens rained down various flowers.'
Then the King,
having heard these words,
felt a mixture of grief and joy,
and his faith became even more resolute.
He immediately summoned his ministers, elders, and wise men,
ordering them to explain this meaning.
At that time, the crowd of people
were all unable to explain it.
In a deserted forest marsh,
there was an immortal
named Shē-mó,
who was well-versed in both characters and meanings.
The immortal was intelligent,
wise, and thoroughly experienced.
A messenger returned and reported to the King,
and the King immediately invited him to come.
At that time, the immortal
fully explained the meaning for the Great King:
'Yé-luó-luó:
its meaning is that only those who shave their heads and wear dyed robes
shall swiftly attain liberation from birth and death.
Pó-shē-shā:
it says that those who shave their heads and wear dyed robes
all possess the appearance of sages and saints
and are close to Nièpán.
Suō-hē:
it says that those who shave their heads and wear dyed robes
shall be seen and revered by all the devas and people of the world.'
At that time, after the immortal
had explained these words,
Tí-pí was filled with joy.
He immediately summoned eighty-four thousand minor kings
to gather in one place.
He made a high carriage of the seven treasures,
displayed the lion's skin,
showing it to everyone.
They all revered it together,
burning incense and scattering flowers
to make offerings
with the utmost sincerity.
Later, they hammered gold to make a coffin,
placed the lion's skin inside,
and built a pagoda for it.
At that time, the people,
because of this virtuous mind,
after their lives ended,
all attained birth in the heavens."
Fó told Ānán and the fourfold assembly:
"That lion at that time,
because it gave rise to a virtuous mind toward the person in dyed robes,
for ten billion kalpas,
was a Wheel-Turning Sage King,
providing for all sentient beings
and extensively planting meritorious deeds,
which led to the attainment of Buddhahood.
The one then named Shèn-jiā-pí-luó,
who else could it be?
It is I myself now.
At that time, King Tí-pí,
due to the cause of making offerings to the lion's skin,
for one hundred billion kalpas,
among heavens and humans,
was foremost in honor and nobility
and cultivated all roots of goodness.
He is now Mílè Pú-sà.
The immortal at that time
is now Shèlìfú.
The hunter at that time
is now Típó-dá-duō."
At that time, the fourfold assembly,
having heard Fó speak of these past causes and conditions,
felt joy in their hearts,
yet they deeply mourned and sighed with sorrow, saying:
"We were so ignorant!
We did not recognize the wise and sagacious
and gave rise to evil thoughts.
We only pray, Rúlái!
Have pity on our ignorance
and allow us to repent of our past sins."
Shìzūn, in His great compassion,
then spoke the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Four Truths for them.
According to their past conditions,
they all attained various fruits:
some attained the fruit of Shū-tuó-huán,
Sī-tuó-hán,
Ā-nà-hán,
and the fruit of Ā-luó-hàn;
some gave rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed, True, and Perfect Way.
At that time, Ānán
and the fourfold assembly,
having heard what Fó said,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Shìzūn was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, at the Jǐ-shù Gěigūdú-yuán.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
taking his attendant Ānán,
entered the city to beg for alms.
The robes that the Shìzūn wore on his body
were slightly worn and damaged.
Wishing to use this to transform and deliver sentient beings,
after completing his alms-round,
he intended to return to where he was staying.
There was a Póluómén
who came to the Shìzūn’s place.
He paid homage to the Shìzūn,
and observing that the Shìzūn’s countenance and radiant marks were extraordinary,
and seeing that the Shìzūn’s robes were slightly damaged,
he harbored a mind of generous giving.
Setting aside some from his household,
he obtained a small amount of white fine cloth
and brought it to offer to the Shìzūn:
“I only wish, Rúlái!
That you take this cloth and use it to mend your robes.”
The Shìzūn immediately accepted it.
At that time, the Póluómén,
seeing that the Shìzūn had accepted it,
felt joyful in his heart
and was doubly exuberant.
The Shìzūn, taking pity on this man,
immediately bestowed a prophecy upon him:
“In a future age, within two Āsēngqí and one hundred kalpas,
you shall become a Shìzūn.
Your divine powers and physical marks will be excellent,
and you will be fully endowed with the ten titles.”
Having received the prophecy, he departed joyfully.
The noble and virtuous elders and laypeople within the kingdom
all gave rise to this thought:
“Why did the Shìzūn
accept such a small gift from him
and repay it with such a great reward?”
After having this thought,
each for the sake of the Rúlái,
they tore fine cloth
and made various robes,
which they brought to offer to the Shìzūn.
Ānán asked the Shìzūn:
“What good deeds did the Shìzūn perform in the past
to be able to cause everyone to offer and bestow robes?
I wish the Shìzūn would speak of it
so that we may gain understanding.”
The Shìzūn told him:
“Listen attentively and take it to heart;
I shall speak for you of the past causes and conditions.”
Ānán said:
“Yes,
I shall listen well.”
The Shìzūn told Ānán:
“In the long distant past,
immeasurable and countless Āsēngqí kalpas ago,
at that time there was a Shìzūn
named Píbāshī,
who appeared in the world
together with his assembly of ninety thousand followers.
At that time there was a king
named Pántóu.
There was a high minister
who invited the Shìzūn and the monks
for three months of offerings,
and the Shìzūn consented.
Having received consent,
he returned to his home
and prepared all that was required.
At that time, King Pántóu
also wished to make offerings to the Shìzūn and the assembly of monks.
He went to the Shìzūn’s place
and said to the Shìzūn:
‘I desire to have the Rúlái and the Bǐqiū monks receive three months of offerings.’
The Shìzūn told Pántóu:
‘I have already accepted the invitation of that minister.
According to the way of a great man,
it is not appropriate to break one's word midway.’
The king then returned to his palace
and told his minister:
‘The Shìzūn resides in my kingdom;
I wish to make offerings,
but it is said that you have already invited him.
Now, you should yield to me;
after I have finished my offerings,
then you may invite him.’
The minister answered the king, saying:
‘If the Great King can guarantee my life,
and also guarantee that the Rúlái will always remain here,
and further cause the land to be always at peace and free from disaster;
if you can guarantee these matters,
then I shall rest my intent
and allow the King to make the first invitation.’
The king thought to himself:
‘These matters cannot be managed.’
He then enlightened him further, saying:
‘You shall invite him for one day,
and I shall invite him for one day.’
The minister then agreed to it.
They held the assemblies alternately,
and each fulfilled his wish.
At that time, the minister,
for that Rúlái,
prepared the three robes,
all in abundant supply.
He also, for the assembly of ninety thousand Bǐqiū,
made seven-strip robes,
giving one to each person.
Ānán, you should know!
The minister at that time,
who gave these supreme robes
and made offerings to the Shìzūn and the monks,
who else could it be?
It was I myself.
Through life after life,
I have planted blessings without weariness;
today I naturally receive them all,
and they are never in vain.”
At that time, Ānán and the others,
having heard this,
rejoiced and practiced diligently,
creating all manner of meritorious deeds.
With hearts full of exuberance,
they bowed and carried it out.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Shìzūn was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, at the Jǐ-shù Gěigūdú-yuán.
At that time, the Bǐqiū, having completed the summer retreat,
went to the Shìzūn’s place,
paid homage and inquired after his health.
The Shìzūn, with a compassionate heart, comforted and consoled them:
“While you were staying there, were you free from suffering?”
His compassionate heart was sincere and earnest,
harboring extreme pity.
Ānán, seeing this, said to the Shìzūn:
“Shìzūn! Your compassionate pity
and the sympathy you show are exceptionally profound.
I wonder, Shìzūn! Was the giving rise to such a mind
in the distant or recent past?”
The Shìzūn told Ānán:
“If you wish to know,
I shall speak of it for you.
Long ago in the past, for immeasurable and incalculable Āsēngqí kalpas,
there were two sinners together in hell.
The hell wardens drove them to pull an iron cart.
They stripped off their skin to use as the harness for the cart,
and further used iron clubs to beat them and make them run,
racing back and forth from east to west
without any rest.
At that time, one of them had little physical strength.
The hell warden pressured him,
and when he fell to the ground, he would immediately get up,
being extremely exhausted and weary,
dying away and then reviving.
His companion, seeing his hardship and suffering,
gave rise to a compassionate heart.
Pitying this man,
he looked back and said to the hell warden:
‘I only wish that you would allow me to personally take the place of this man and pull this cart alone.’
The hell warden was enraged
and struck him with a club.
He died instantly
and was reborn in the Dāolì Heaven.
