Ānán, you should know!
The person with the compassionate heart in hell at that time
was I myself.
It was at that time, while I was undergoing punishment in that hell,
that I first gave rise to such a heart of compassion and sympathy.
Toward all people, I have never retreated or abandoned it,
until today,
and I therefore delight in practicing
compassionate pity for all.”
At that time, Ānán, having heard what the Shìzūn said,
rejoiced and carried it out.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in Shèwèi Guó at the Qíshù Gǐgūdú Yuán,
together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty Bǐqiū.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
seeing that the various Bǐqiū
were greedy for fine ornaments,
attached to fame and profit,
kept many excessive possessions,
and accumulated them without satiety.
After the Fó had seen this,
he spoke to the Bǐqiū of the harms of greed:
"Now, those who have greedy desires
suffer damage to their bodies and lives in the present,
and in the end will fall into the Sāntú,
receiving immeasurable suffering.
Why is this so?
I myself remember that in a past life,
because of greed,
I fell away
and suffered various pains and afflictions."
At that time, Ānán
knelt down with joined palms,
stepped forward and said to the Fó:
"Shìzūn!
In the past, because of greed,
you fell away.
What was the nature of those events?"
The Shìzūn told him:
"In the distant past,
immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable Āsēngqí Kalpas ago,
in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Júsàlí,
who ruled over eighty-four thousand small kingdoms under heaven,
with twenty thousand consorts and maidservants,
and ten thousand high ministers.
At that time, a blister suddenly grew on the king's crown,
its shape like a cocoon,
pure and clear,
and yet it was not painful.
Later it grew larger and larger,
until it was like a gourd,
whereupon they split it open to look,
and found a young boy,
who was extremely handsome,
with hair of dark blue,
and a body of purple-gold color.
They immediately summoned physiognomists
to divine his fortune.
After the physiognomists had finished their divination,
they answered the king, saying:
'This child has virtue,
his majestic appearance is extraordinary,
and he will certainly become a Shèngwáng,
ruling over the four domains.'
They therefore gave him a name,
calling him Wéntuójié
(in Jìn speech, Dǐngshēng).
When he had grown up,
his heroic virtue became manifest,
and the king used one kingdom
to enfeoff him.
Later, the great king
became gravely ill,
and the various lesser kings
all came to visit him,
but he could not escape death,
and subsequently passed away.
The various vassal kings went together to Dǐngshēng,
and all said:
'The Great King has died,
wish you to succeed to the throne.'
Dǐngshēng replied:
'If I have the merit to be king,
I require that the Sìtiān and the honored Dìshì
come to welcome and install me,
only then shall I ascend the throne.'
Once he finished making this vow,
the Sìtiān immediately descended,
each holding a precious vase,
filled with fragrant water,
to pour over his head.
At that time, Tiāndì Shì
also held a precious crown,
and came to place it on him,
and then praised him.
The kings then urged him to go to the capital where the great king had ruled.
Dǐngshēng said again:
'If I have the merit to be king,
the kingdom should come to me,
and I shall not go to the kingdom.'
Just as he finished making this vow,
all the palaces,
gardens, groves, and bathing pools within the great kingdom
all came to the king.
The Golden Wheel,
the Elephant and Horse,
the Jade Maiden,
the Divine Jewel,
the Minister of Finance,
and the Minister of War,
all likewise gathered accordingly,
and he ruled the four worlds
as a Zhuànlúnwáng.
While patrolling the borders of his realm,
he saw the people
clearing the land and farming.
The king asked his officials:
'What are these various living beings
trying to do?'
They answered the king, saying:
'Creatures with form
exist because of food,
and therefore they plant grain,
wishing to sustain their lives.'
The king made a vow, saying:
'If I have the merit to be king,
there shall naturally be food of a hundred flavors,
to satisfy everyone
and cause them to have no hunger or thirst.'
Once he finished making this vow,
food immediately appeared.
The king went out to travel again
and saw the people
spinning and weaving.
The king asked again:
'Why are they doing this?'
The people replied:
'Food is now provided naturally,
but we have nothing to adorn our bodies,
and so we spin and weave to make clothing.'
The king made another vow:
'If I have the merit to be king,
marvelous clothes shall naturally appear,
to provide for the myriad people
and cause them to have no lack.'
Once he finished making this vow,
at that moment all the trees produced various marvelous clothes of different colors,
and all the people
could seek and obtain them without end.
The king went out to travel again
and saw the common people
preparing musical instruments.
The king therefore asked:
'Why are you doing this?'
The people reported:
'Clothing and food are now sufficient,
but we lack music,
and so we prepare these
wishing to amuse ourselves.'
The king made another vow:
'If I have the merit to be king,
various marvelous musical instruments
shall naturally arrive.'
Just as he finished making this vow,
at that moment, upon the trees,
many various musical instruments
hung from their branches,
and if anyone needed them,
they took them and played them,
the sounds being harmonious and smooth,
and among those who heard them,
there were none who were not delighted.
The king's virtue was most weighty,
and the myriad blessings gathered,
as the heavens rained the seven treasures,
throughout the borders of all the kingdoms.
The king asked his ministers:
'Whose virtue is this?'
The ministers replied:
'This is the King's virtue,
and also the fortune of the people.'
The king made another vow:
'If it is the people's fortune,
the treasures should rain everywhere;
if it is only my virtue,
they shall rain only within the palace.'
Just as he finished making this vow,
they ceased in all other places,
and rained only inside the palace,
for seven days and seven nights.
"That King Dǐngshēng,
in Yánfútí,
amused himself with the five desires
for eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, a Yèchā
surged up in front of the palace,
and cried out in a loud voice:
'To the east there is a land
named Fúpótí,
which is abundant and joyful,
pleasant and good beyond compare,
and the Great King may go to travel and see that realm.'
The King then consented.
Intending to patrol,
the Golden Wheel turned again,
and he advanced through the void,
The ministers and the seven treasures
all followed him.
Once he arrived at that land,
all the lesser kings
came to pay homage.
In that kingdom, the King
indulged himself in the five desires
for eight hundred million years.
A Yèchā then called out:
“In the west, there is a kingdom
named Qúyéní,
which is also joyful;
the King may go there.”
The King immediately agreed
and went to travel in that land,
eating the fruits of his merit and receiving joy for one billion four hundred million years.
The Yèchā called out again:
“In the north, there is a kingdom
named Yùdānyuē,
its land is peaceful and prosperous,
and its people are numerous;
the King may go there.”
The King immediately went there
and stayed within it,
indulging his heart and mind
to the limit with superior and marvelous five desires
for one billion eight hundred million years.
The Yèchā called out again:
“There is the place of the Four Heavenly Kings,
whose joy is immeasurable;
the King may travel there.”
The King, along with his ministers and the four types of troops,
mounted the void and ascended.
The Four Heavenly Kings saw them from afar
and felt great terror,
immediately gathering their military forces
to go out and resist him,
but they could do nothing against him
and returned to their dwellings.
Dǐngshēng stayed among them,
enjoying joy at his leisure
for several billion years.
Within his mind, he thought again:
“I wish to ascend to Dàolì.”
Immediately, with the multitude,
he tread on the void and ascended.
“At that time, there were five hundred xiānrén
living on the flank of Mount Xūmí.
The waste from the King’s elephants and horses fell down
and defiled the bodies of the xiānrén.
The xiānrén asked one another:
‘For what reason is there this?’
Among them was a wise one
who told the group:
‘I have heard that King Dǐngshēng
wishes to ascend to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
it must be that the elephants and horses have dropped this impurity.’
The xiānrén were resentful
and formed a spiritual curse,
causing King Dǐngshēng and his people
to all stop and be unable to move.
The King realized this
and immediately made a vow:
‘If I have merit,
all these xiānrén
should come to serve and attend to me.’
The King’s virtue was vast
and could cause an effect;
the five hundred xiānrén all came to the King’s side,
supporting the wheels and driving the horses,
together reaching the heavens.
Before they arrived,
they saw the heavenly city from afar,
named Kuàijiàn;
its color was pure white,
high, prominent, and extraordinary.
This Kuàijiàn City
had one thousand two hundred gates.
The devas were terrified
and closed all the gates,
fixing triple iron bars.
Dǐngshēng’s troops
headed straight for them without hesitation.
The King then took a conch and blew it,
drew his bow and plucked the string,
and the one thousand two hundred gates all opened at once.
Dìshì soon came out
to meet him,
then invited him into the palace
and shared his seat with him.
The Heavenly Emperor and the Human King
looked identical in appearance;
those who first saw them
could not distinguish them,
only by the speed of their blinking
could they know the difference.
“In the heavens, the King
enjoyed the pleasures of the five desires
through thirty-six Dìshì.
The last Dìshì
was Dà Jiāyè.
At that time, the Āxiūluó king raised an army and ascended to the heavens
to fight with Dìshì.
Dìshì was not as strong
and retreated his army into the city.
Dǐngshēng then went out,
blew the conch and plucked the bow,
and the Āxiūluó king immediately collapsed and fell.
Dǐngshēng thought to himself:
‘My power is such
that none are my equal;
why do I now
sit together with Dìshì?
It would be better to kill him
and rule alone as hegemon for pleasure.’
“An evil heart having arisen,
he immediately fell,
in front of his original palace,
exhausted and on the verge of death.
People came to ask:
‘If people of later generations
ask how King Dǐngshēng’s life ended,
how shall we answer them?’
The King replied to them:
‘If there is such a question,
then you may answer:
“King Dǐngshēng
died because of greed.
He ruled over the four realms
for four billion years,
with treasures raining for seven days,
and stayed in the two heavens,
yet without satisfaction or sufficiency,
he thus fell.”’
For this reason, Bhikṣus!
Material gain
is indeed a great affliction;
one should think of staying far from it and deeply seek the truth of the Way.”
Ānán said to the Buddha:
“What merit did this King Dǐngshēng
plant in his previous lives
to obtain such immeasurable great rewards?”
The Buddha told him:
“In the past,
countless eons ago,
there was a Buddha in the world
named Fùshā,
who, with his disciples,
traveled and transformed the world.
At that time, the son of a Póluómén
was about to take a wife
and held beans in his hand
to scatter over his wife;
this was the secular custom
of his household in that previous life.
He met the Buddha on the road
and his heart was filled with joy;
he then took these beans
and offered them by scattering them over the Buddha.
Four grains fell into the bowl,
and one grain stayed on the crown of his head.
Because of this cause and condition,
he received infinite blessings:
because the four grains fell into the bowl,
he ruled over the four continents;
because the one grain was on the crown of his head,
he received joy in the two heavens.”
At that time, all the disciples,
hearing what the Buddha said,
those who attained the first fruit, second fruit, third fruit, and Arhatship
were beyond counting.
They received and upheld the Buddha’s words,
and joyfully practiced them.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the Kingdom of Shèwèi, at Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, the Elder Xūdá
had a youngest daughter
named Sūmàn.
Her face and head were upright and regular,
and her appearance was most exquisite.
Her father loved and cherished her
especially among all his children.
Whenever he went out traveling,
he would always take her with him.
Then, the Elder
took her to the place of the Buddha.
When the girl saw the Buddha,
her heart was filled with manifold joy,
and she wished to obtain fine incense
to smear on the chamber where the Buddha stayed.
In this girl's hand
was a bīnpó fruit.
The Buddha asked her for it,
and following his instructions, she gave it to him.
The Buddha then, upon it,
wrote the names of incense and grains,
and gave it back to her.
The girl, together with her father,
returned to the city
and went about searching and buying various kinds of exquisite incense
as the Buddha required.
Bringing them, she went to Jǐhuán
and personally pounded and ground them,
doing so day after day.
At that time, the King of the Kingdom of Chíchāshīlì
sent one of his sons
on a mission to Shèwèi.
When he first arrived in that foreign land, he traveled widely to observe,
and gradually making his way around,
he reached the monastery.
He saw the girl Sūmàn inside grinding incense,
loved her appearance,
and desired to have her as his wife.
He immediately went into the city
and petitioned King Bōsīnuò:
"There is this girl
who suits my heart.
I wish the King to grant her to me
and not oppose my desire."
The King asked him:
"Whose daughter is she?"
He answered:
"She is from the house of Xūdá."
The King said:
"You should ask him yourself;
I cannot know of it."
He petitioned the King again:
"If the King permits,
I shall seek her myself."
The King said:
"You may do so."
That King's son
sent away his followers,
carriages, and various goods
to return to their original country first,
leaving only one elephant and himself behind.
He went to Jǐhuán,
seized the girl Sūmàn,
placed her on the mount, and left.
When Xūdá heard of this,
he sent men to pursue them.
The elephant ran very fast,
and they could not catch up.
He reached his home country
and made her his wife.
Later, she became pregnant
and gave birth to ten eggs.
The eggs later hatched,
and there were ten boys,
their appearances were beautiful
and differed from ordinary people.
As they grew older,
they were exceptionally brave and strong,
but they loved hunting
and harmed the lives of living beings.
Their mother, filled with pity,
taught them not to do so.
The sons said to their mother:
"The matter of shooting and hunting
is the greatest joy.
Now that Mother blocks us,
it will make us resent you."
The mother told them again:
"It is because I love you all
that I restrain you because of this.
If I were to hate you,
I would never say these words.
Why is that?
For the sin of killing living beings,
one shall enter Hell
and suffer various pains and afflictions
for tens of millions of years.
One will constantly be hunted and shot by Āpáng hell-wardens with the heads of deer, sheep, rabbits, and various beasts
for immeasurable years.
Even if one wishes for liberation,
by what means could it be attained?"
The sons said to their mother:
"What Mother says,
does it come from your own heart
or was it heard from someone else?"
The mother told them again:
"In the past, I heard these matters
from the Buddha."
The sons asked their mother again:
"What kind of person is the Buddha?
Please, we wish you to tell us everything."
The mother told her sons:
"Have you not heard?
The son of King Jìngfàn of Jiāwéiluówèi,
his physical marks are brilliant and prominent,
and he was destined to be a Shèngwáng.
Weary of aging, sickness, and death,
he left home to study the Way.
His vows and practices were perfected,
and he attained the supreme fruit.
His great body is sixteen feet tall,
his marks and signs are incomparable.
Possessing the Three Insights and Six Supernormal Powers,
his far-reaching vision has no limit,
his knowledge of the past is infinite,
and his knowledge of the future is boundless.
He observes and knows the three worlds
like a pearl in the palm of his hand."
When the sons heard this,
their hearts were filled with joy.
Therefore, they further asked their mother:
"Is the Buddha currently near or far?
Can he be seen?"
The mother then answered:
"He is currently in Shèwèi."
The sons petitioned their mother,
requesting to go and see the Buddha.
The mother immediately permitted it.
The sons all together
went to Shèwèi.
Their grandfather, Xūdá,
was delighted to see them
and his love and affection for them were redoubled.
He took them to Jǐhuán
to pay their respects to the Rúlái.
When the sons saw the Buddha,
his appearance and marks
exceeded what they had heard before
by tens of millions of times.
Their five senses were filled with joy,
and they could not contain themselves.
The Buddha, accordingly and appropriately,
preached the wondrous Dharma to them.
The ten of them simultaneously
attained the purity of the Dharma Eye.
They then spoke to the Buddha again,
requesting to leave home.
The Buddha asked them:
"Do your parents permit it?"
They answered:
"We have not yet consulted them."
The Buddha said:
"If the parents have not permitted it,
you cannot be ordained."
Xūdá then said:
"These are my grandsons;
I have authority over them.
I now release them,
and in principle, this is also acceptable."
The Buddha then consented
and permitted them to practice the Way.
Their hair and beards fell off of their own accord,
Dharma robes appeared on their bodies,
and they became Shāmén.
Diligent in the great work,
they all attained the state of Luóhàn.
These ten Bǐqiū
respected and admired one another greatly.
When walking, they advanced together,
and they lived in the same place.
The people in the kingdom
all revered and supported them.
Ānán said to the Buddha:
"These ten Bǐqiū,
what blessings and celebrations did they have
to be born into a noble family,
with extraordinary appearances,
to encounter the Shìzūn,
and to reach the end of suffering?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In the past, ninety-one eons ago,
there was the Buddha Pípóshī
who appeared in the world.
Having completed his teaching and transforming,
he entered Bānnièpán.
His Shèlì were distributed,
and immeasurable stupas were erected.
At that time, there was one stupa,
It was decayed and collapsed,
and there was an old mother
who was repairing and renovating it.
There were ten youths
who happened to see her while traveling
and asked the old mother, saying:
“What are you doing?”
The old mother replied:
“This is a venerable tǎ,
its merits are vast and grand;
therefore I am repairing it,
desiring to seek good fruits.”
The youths were joyful
and assisted in the work.
When the work was finished,
they vowed to be mother and sons,
and those ten youths
vowed to be born together.
From that time onward,
for ninety-one jié,
in the heavens and among humans,
they were always born together
and received blessings and happiness.
They always had three things
superior to other people:
first, their physical bodies were upright and handsome;
second, they were respected and loved by the multitude;
third, they always attained long life.
Having passed through such a time,
they did not fall into the sāntú.
Now meeting my era,
they were bathed in pure transformation,
all dust and defilements were exhausted,
and they all attained the state of yìngzhēn.
If you wish to know who the old mother of that time was,
it is the current Sūmàn nǚ.
The ten youths of that time
are the current ten Luóhàn.”
When the Fó spoke this,
among those in the great assembly,
there were those who attained the state of Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
or Āluóhàn;
those who gave rise to the aspiration for the Dàchéng and attained non-retrogression
faithfully accepted the Fó’s words
and joyfully put them into practice.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was at Luóyuèzhī on the Qíshéjué Mountain.
At that time, in this country, there was a wealthy Zhǎngzhě,
named Shīlìzhì,
whose family was very rich,
with the seven treasures overflowing.
His wife became pregnant,
and when the months were full, she gave birth to a boy,
whose appearance was dignified and exquisite,
with few peers in the world.
The parents rejoiced,
feeling deeply fortunate,
and then invited a Xiàngshī
to divine his fortune.
After the Xiàngshī finished the divination,
he spoke to the two parents:
"This son has such merit and virtue
that he will bring glory and brilliance to the clan."
The Zhǎngzhě became even more joyful,
his happiness being boundless,
so he further requested
that a name be given to him.
The Xiàngshī asked:
"Since having this child,
what auspicious signs have occurred?"
The Zhǎngzhě replied:
"His mother was originally
slow of speech and clumsy with words,
but since conceiving this child,
her conversation has become clever and skillful,
many times better than usual."
Then he named him,
calling him Póshìzhì.
When he grew up,
his intelligence and talent surpassed the crowd,
and with those of his own rank,
he went out to travel and sightsee,
and saw at the house of a Nàluó performer,
a young woman
whose face was pure and clean,
with a radiant appearance rarely seen,
and his heart immediately became attached,
desiring to marry her.
He returned and informed his parents:
"I wish for you to seek her for me."
His parents said to him:
"We are of a noble clan,
and they are common and lowly;
high and low are not a match,
how can we form a marriage?"
The son's love was deep,
and he could not release himself from it,
so he spoke again:
"Do not ask about family status,
only consider her person;
fortunately show me your compassion,
and out of pity, seek her for me.
If my wish is not fulfilled,
I will end my own life."
The parents complied with him
and sent someone to seek her.
That family replied:
"You are of a great clan,
and we are lowly people;
we have never been peers,
by what cause could this happen?"
The son was earnest,
and his feelings did not cease,
so he sent a messenger again,
repeatedly seeking her.
That family answered:
"If he can be like us,
learning various arts,
singing, dancing, and performing comedy,
making himself fully knowledgeable in all,
and before the King,
demonstrate his skills successfully,
only then shall we enter into marriage."
The son, captivated by her beauty,
was not ashamed of such lowly tasks,
and immediately went to that house
to learn the performing arts;
within a short period,
he had mastered them all.
At that time, the King
gathered all the Nàluó,
to climb poles and jump through windows,
and walk on ropes in mid-air,
along with many such various performances.
At that time, the Zhǎngzhě's son
also went to the King's side,
and when it was his turn to demonstrate his skill,
he climbed the rope and walked;
when the rope-walking was finished,
the King happened not to see it,
and ordered him to go up again;
following the command, he did so,
but his strength gradually weakened,
and midway he was about to fall,
his heart filled with terror,
having nowhere to turn for refuge.
The Venerable Mùlián,
soared through the air to his side
and spoke to him, saying:
"As for you today,
would you rather save your life
and leave home to study the Way?
Or would you rather fall to the ground
and marry that woman?"
He immediately replied:
"I wish to save myself;
I have no use for the woman."
Mùlián then,
in the midst of the air,
transformed it into level ground;
when the man saw this,
his fear immediately ceased,
and he descended by the ground,
keeping his body and head whole.
Having received safety and peace,
he was overjoyed beyond measure,
followed Mùlián,
and went to the Shìzūn,
paying homage and making offerings.
The Fó then, at that time,
extensively preached the wonderful discourse,
the so-called discourse
on giving,
on precepts,
and on being born in heaven,
that desire is impure,
and that the path to transcendence is the swiftest;
his mind became clear and understood,
and he immediately attained the first fruit.
He then said to the Fó:
"I wish to leave home
and practice the Right Dharma."
The Shìzūn granted this,
his hair and beard fell off naturally,
Dharma robes appeared on his body,
and he became a Shāmén.
The Bǐqiū concentrated diligently on meditation,
and following the correct practice,
all his taints were exhausted,
and he became an Āluóhàn.
The wise Ānán
came forward and said to the Fó:
"Regarding the Shāmén Póshìzhì,
in the past,
with that woman,
what was the cause and condition,
that his heart was so defiled and deluded,
almost leading to his death?
And with Mùlián,
what good cause did he create,
that he now receives his grace
and obtains safety?
Also by what cause and condition
did he himself attain the state of Yìngzhēn?"
The Fó told Ānán:
"In the past, immeasurable eons ago,
in the country of Bōluónài,
there was a great Zhǎngzhě
who had an only son born to him,
who was peerlessly handsome.
At that time,
someone in his family
who had come from the sea
brought a bird's egg
and presented it to the Zhǎngzhě.
The Zhǎngzhě accepted it,
and after a short time,
the egg hatched,
and out came a fledgling bird
with glossy feathers.
The Zhǎngzhě loved it
and gave it to his son to play with;
it gradually grew larger,
and they became fond of each other.
At that time, the Zhǎngzhě's son
would ride on the bird's back,
and the bird would carry him and fly,
traveling and sightseeing everywhere;
when his desire was satisfied,
they would return to their house,
being thus day after day.
After a long time,
that Zhǎngzhě's son
heard that the King of another country was holding a Nàluó performance,
so he rode this bird
to go there,
descending to watch,
while the bird stayed in a tree.
He happened to see the King's daughter,
and his heart was immediately filled with love for her.
At that time, he sent a messenger
to convey his feelings,
and the King's daughter consented,
so they then had an affair."
Their actions were not secret,
and they were discovered by the King (Wáng).
He sent people to investigate and capture them,
and they were caught in a short time.
They bound his body,
and he was to be executed.
The Son of the Elder (Zhǎngzhě zǐ) said:
“Gentlemen, why
exert yourselves to kill me?
Allow me to climb the tree and throw myself down to my death.”
The people granted his request,
and he then climbed the branches and ascended,
mounted the bird,
and flew into the void and departed.
Because of this bird,
he was able to prolong his life.”
The Buddha (Fó) told Ānán:
“The Son of the Elder at that time
is now Póshìzhì.
The King’s Daughter at that time
is now the daughter of the household of performers.
The bird at that time
was Mùlián.
In a past life,
he was deluded by beauty and fell into distress,
but was saved by the bird;
now again, he lusted after beauty
and was on the verge of death,
but because of Mùlián,
he attained peace and stability.
As for Póshìzhì,
his spoken intelligence and eloquence,
and his becoming one who is Wúlòu (without outflows),
in the distant past,
in the kingdom of Bōluónài,
there was a Lay Devotee (Jūshì),
who saw a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó)
coming to beg for food.
The Lay Devotee immediately
gave him food as an offering,
and then further requested
that he preach the sutras and the Dharma (Fǎ).
That Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó)
declined, saying he could not,
threw his bowl into the void,
and leaped up and vanished.
The Lay Devotee thought:
‘This man has spiritual powers
and his transformations are without limit,
yet he cannot proclaim the path or its transformation.
I vow that in my future births,
I may encounter a Holy Sovereign (Shèngzūn)
who surpasses this man
by billions of times,
to expound and spread the meaning of the Dharma (Fǎ),
without end or limit,
and let my person
also attain the realization of the fruits.’
Because of these causes and conditions,
in this life he is intelligent
and has attained the fruit of an Arhat (Luóhàn).”
When the Buddha (Fó) said this,
everyone was delighted.
There were those who attained the fruit of Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán),
Sakridāgāmin (Sītuóhán),
Anāgāmin (Ānàhán),
and Arhat (Āluóhàn);
some planted the good roots of a Pratyekabuddha (Yuánjué);
some gave rise to the Bodhisattva (Púsà) mind.
They all believed the Buddha’s (Fó) words,
bowing in reverence and carrying them out.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Fó was in Shèwèi Guó in the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, in this country there was a fànzhì,
named Ābājútí,
who was intelligent and widely learned,
drawing from the ancient and understanding the modern.
He went to the place of the Fó,
seeking to become a shāmén,
and further addressed him, saying:
"If I leave home,
and my wisdom and eloquence
are equal to those of Shèlìfú,
then my heart will be willing and joyful;
if they are not as good,
I shall then return home."
The Fó immediately replied, saying:
"You will not be equal to him."
At that time, that fànzhì
stopped and did not pursue the Way,
and returned to his home.
The Shìzūn afterwards
told the assembly:
"After my extinction,
within one hundred years,
this póluómén
shall be profoundly transformed,
attaining the six supernatural powers,
his wisdom being high and far-reaching,
and he will teach and transform sentient beings,
in numbers as many as the dust."
When the Fó was about to enter nièpán,
he said to Ānán:
"After my extinction,
all the collections of Sūtras
are entrusted entirely to you;
you should receive and maintain them and cause them to be widely distributed."
After the Shìzūn had passed away,
Ānán maintained the Dharma.
Later, when Ānán
wished to discard his body,
he told his disciple Yéshìjī:
"After I leave the world,
all the essential scriptures
you should protect and maintain."
He then further told him:
"In the country of Bōluónài,
there will be a jūshì named Jútí;
this man has a son
named Yōubōjútí.
You should carefully seek him out
and deliver him to the Way;
if your life ends,
entrust the Dharma to him."
After Ānán passed away,
this Yéshìjī
reverently maintained the Fófǎ,
traveling and teaching throughout the world,
delivering very many people.
He then went to Bōluónài,
went to visit the jūshì,
became acquainted with him,
and visited him frequently.
That jūshì
gave birth to a son
named Ābājútí
when he was still at a young age.
At that time, Yéshìjī
went to ask for him,
wanting him to enter the Way.
The father replied:
"I have only one son,
who must succeed the family line;
it cannot be so.
If another is born later,
I shall then give him to you."
Later, another son was born,
named Nántuójútí.
At that time, Yéshìjī
went again to ask for him,
but the father replied:
"The eldest son manages the outside,
and the second son manages the inside;
only by residing in the house
can it prosper.
In my heart, I am attached and reluctant,
and cannot yet grant your request;
if there is another later,
I will certainly offer him to you."
This Yéshìjī
was an Āluóhàn,
fully possessing the three insights
and able to know people's spiritual faculties.
Observing these two children,
they had no affinity for the Way,
so he ceased his efforts
and did not seek them diligently.
At that time, that jūshì gave birth to another son,
whose appearance was upright and wonderful
and whose form was extraordinary.
At that time, Yéshìjī
went again to ask for him.
The father replied:
"The child is still small now
and cannot yet serve you;
furthermore, the family is poor,
and we have nothing to send with him.
For now, I wish to keep him;
when he is older, I shall give him to you."
As he gradually grew older,
his talents and capacity became more abundant;
the father entrusted him with goods
to sell in the marketplace.
At that time, Yéshìjī
went to his side
and preached the Dharma to him,
teaching him to bind his mindfulness,
using white and black pebbles as counters;
for a good thought, put down a white one,
and for an evil thought, put down a black one.
Yōubōjútí reverently received his teaching,
and regarding his good and evil thoughts,
he would always throw down a pebble.
Initially, the black ones were mostly dominant
and the white ones were very few,
but through gradual practice,
the white and black became equal.
With unceasing mindfulness,
there were no more black stones,
but only white ones.
Good thoughts having become abundant,
he attained the first fruit.
At that time, in that city,
there was a courtesan
who sent her servant girl with money
to go and buy flowers.
Yōubōjútí,
being honest and upright in character,
gave her many flowers
so as not to let her have regrets.
The servant girl brought the flowers back,
and the courtesan was very surprised,
asking her servant girl:
"The other day when you bought flowers,
you used the same amount of money;
why were they few then?
Why are there so many now?
Could it be that you were cheated or shorted before?"
The servant girl replied:
"Today's flower-seller
is compassionate, kind, and observant of propriety;
he gave them fairly,
which is why I obtained so many.
Furthermore, that man's
physical form is extraordinarily wonderful;
if my lady were to see him,
you too would have no regrets."
Hearing this, the courtesan
sent a messenger to invite him.
Yōubōjútí
restrained himself and did not go;
she invited him again,
but he ultimately did not comply.
At that time, the courtesan
had relations with the son of a royal family,
interacting with him;
coveting his clothing made of many treasures,
profit arose and righteousness declined;
she killed him and hid him.
The royal family searched for him
and found him in her house.
They immediately seized the courtesan,
cut off her hands and feet,
cut off her ears and nose,
hung her from a high post,
and stood her in the burial ground.
Although she suffered this misery,
she had not yet died.
Yōubōjútí
went to her place;
the courtesan said:
"In the past when I was beautiful,
you were unwilling to see me;
today my body is mangled,
what is there to look at?"
He immediately replied:
"I do not love physical beauty,
and have come here
out of compassion for you;
that is why I have come."
He then proclaimed the Dharma of the four impermanences:
"This body is impure, suffering, empty, and without a self.
Observe each of these carefully;
what is there to rely on?
Deluded and confused people
falsely give rise to defiled thoughts."
The courtesan heard the Dharma
and attained the purity of the Dharma Eye.
Yōubōjútí,
to become an Ānàhán.
At that time, Yéshìqī,
again went to the householder
to ask for this youth
to serve as a Shāmí;
he followed the instructions and gave him over.
Bringing him to the jīngshè,
he conferred the ten precepts upon him;
when he reached twenty years of age,
he then conferred the full ordination.
After the Báisi Jiémó was completed,
he attained the path of an Āluóhàn,
and the sānmíng liùtōng
were all fully complete.
His speech was skillful,
and his expositions were inexhaustible;
he then gathered the people,
desiring to preach the Dharma for them.
At that time, the demon Mó Bōxún,
at the place of the assembly,
rained down gold coins.
The people competed to pick them up,
and in the end did not hear the Dharma.
On the second day,
he again gathered the great assembly;
the demon rained down flower garlands
to disturb the minds of the people.
On the third day,
he once more gathered the great assembly;
the Demon King then transformed into a great elephant,
deep blue lapis lazuli in color,
with six tusks in its mouth.
Upon each tusk,
there were seven bathing pools;
within those bathing pools,
there were seven lotus flowers;
upon each and every lotus flower,
there were seven jade maidens.
All these jade maidens
performed music and dance;
the elephant strolled slowly and leisurely by the side of the assembly.
The people turned their eyes to look,
and their minds were not on the Dharma.
On the fourth day,
he again gathered the great assembly;
the Demon King again transformed into a woman,
upright and beautiful,
standing in attendance behind the Zūnzhě.
The people fixed their gaze on her,
and suddenly forgot the Dharma service.
At that time, the Zūnzhě
immediately transformed that woman,
causing her to become white bones;
after the people saw this, they focused on listening to the Dharma,
and those who attained the Way were many.
The Zūnzhě originally
had a dog;
day after day, at its ear,
he secretly preached the Dharma to it.
When the dog’s life ended,
it was born in the Sixth Heaven with Mó Bōxún,
sitting together on one couch.
The Demon King thought to himself:
"This Great Virtue of Heaven,
who is equal with us,
from where did he pass away to come be born here?"
He immediately observed him,
and knew he came from a dog’s body.
"That Shāmén
has insulted me thus."
Watching from afar for when the Zūnzhě entered chándìng,
he took a jeweled crown
and placed it on his head.
Once he arose from concentration,
he felt there was a crown on his head;
he immediately reflected and observed,
knowing it was the demon’s doing.
He then used his spiritual power
to compel the demon to come,
and transformed his dog’s corpse
to look like a hair ornament,
then said to the demon:
"You left me a crown;
I deeply thank you for your intention.
Now with this hair ornament,
I present it to you in return."
After the Demon King received it,
he returned to the heavens,
but saw that what he was wearing was actually a dead dog.
In his heart, he was disgusted and wanted to remove it,
but even exhausting his spiritual powers, he could not get rid of it.
He then went to Dìshì,
seeking to remove the impurity.
Dìshì replied:
"He who made this,
that person can cast it off;
it is not within my power to dismiss it."
The Demon King left again,
inquiring widely among the heavens, even up to the Fàntiān,
saying to them joyfully:
"I wish to remove this filth."
Each answered as before,
that it was not what their power could manage.
Having no other choice,
he came to the Zūnzhě
and said to him:
"The Fó is truly of Great Virtue,
his compassionate heart is boundless;
but you shēngwén,
are truly fierce and malicious.
How can this be proven?
In the past,
I led demon armies totaling eighteen hundred million
to attack and surround the Púsà,
desiring to defeat his path;
yet he still maintained compassion,
and did not regard it with resentment.
Now I have merely provoked you slightly,
and you trouble me thus."
The Zūnzhě replied:
"The logic is indeed such.
The Fó compared to me
is a hundred, thousand, ten thousand times greater—
it cannot be illustrated by metaphor.
It is like Xūmí Shān compared to a mustard seed,
like the water of the great ocean compared to a cow’s hoofprint,
like the shīzi wáng compared to a jackal;
the forms of great and small
truly cannot be compared."
The Zūnzhě said to the demon:
"I was born in the final age
and have not seen the Rúlái.
I hear your spiritual power can transform into a Fó;
try to manifest once,
for I wish to see it."
The Demon King replied:
"I shall now manifest;
be careful not to bow."
He replied:
"I will not bow."
At that time, the Demon King transformed his body into a Fó,
sixteen feet tall,
the color of purplish-burnished gold,
with the thirty-two marks
and eighty secondary characteristics;
his radiance was brilliant,
surpassing the sun and moon manifold.
The Zūnzhě was joyful
and stepped forward to prostrate himself.
The demon returned to his original form
and said to the Zūnzhě:
"Earlier you said you would not bow;
why did you bow just now?"
The Zūnzhě replied:
"I was bowing to the Fó,
not bowing to you."
The demon again apologized, saying:
"I only wish for your pity
to remove this dead dog."
The Zūnzhě told him:
"If you give rise to a compassionate heart
and protect all living beings,
then this dead dog
will turn into a jeweled ornament;
if you harbor malicious intent,
then it will be a dog’s corpse."
Because the demon was afraid,
he constantly generated virtuous thoughts.
At that time, after the Zūnzhě attained the Way,
the sentient beings he transformed
who attained the four fruits
each had one tally;
each tally was four inches long.
Tallies such as these
filled an entire room;
the room was sixty feet high,
and its length and width were the same.
Thereupon the people said to the Zūnzhě:
"The Zūnzhě’s merit and virtue
are truly vast and extensive;
your transforming and delivering of the masses
is beyond calculation."
The Zūnzhě told them:
"When I was an animal,
I also transformed sentient beings,
enabling them to attain the sagely fruits;
how much more so today?"
The assembly said:
"We do not know of that former life;
what was delivered then?"
The Zūnzhě told them:
"Long ago in the past,
in the kingdom of Bōluónà,
there was an Immortal Mountain,
where five hundred Pìzhīfó
dwelt within.
At that time, there was a macaque
which came daily to make offerings,"
Having received and gazed upon the dignified appearance.
All the Pìzhīfó,
later entered Nièpán.
There were also five hundred Fànzhì
who continued to dwell in their midst.
These Fànzhì:
some served the sun and moon,
and some served fire.
Those who served the sun and moon
stood on one leg toward them;
those who served fire
lit it morning and evening.
At that time, that macaque,
seeing them standing on one leg,
would then pull them down;
seeing them lighting the fire,
would then extinguish it.
The macaque at that time
sat upright in contemplation.
The Fànzhì, seeing this,
said to one another:
"This macaque
is showing us this dignified bearing."
Soon each adjusted their posture
and carefully observed the true reality;
their hearts and minds attained realization,
and they all achieved the way of the Pìzhīfó.
That macaque
was I myself."
The assembled multitude spoke again:
"By what causes and conditions
did you receive the body of a macaque?"
The Zūnzhě told them:
"Long ago, ninety-one kalpas past,
there was Pípóshī Fó
who appeared in the world.
There were many Bǐqiū
dwelling in the Xiānshān of Bōluónài.
At that time, there was an Yìngzhēn
who climbed to the mountain peak,
moving his legs with light speed.
There was a young Dàorén
who spoke these words:
'His movement is so swift,
just like a macaque.'
Due to these causes and conditions,
for five hundred lifetimes,
he was always a macaque.
For this reason,
all within the Four Groups
should guard their own mouths
and not recklessly utter words."
When Zūnzhě Yōubōjútí
spoke this Dharma,
within the entire great assembly,
those who attained Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
and Āluóhàn;
those who planted the roots of goodness of a Yuánjué;
and those who gave rise to the Dàshèng mind and attained the stage of non-retrogression
were beyond counting.
They believed and accepted his teaching,
rejoiced, and practiced it.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was on Mount Qíshéjué in Luóyuèqí.
At that time, by the city side,
there was a pool of water,
filthy with mud and impure,
full of much excrement and filth,
a stinking place of feces and urine.
The people of the country,
of the common and lowly sort,
constantly took discarded filth
and threw it into it.
There was a large creature,
whose shape resembled a snake,
and furthermore had four feet.
Within that pool of water,
it scurried east and west,
sometimes sinking and sometimes emerging.
Passing through years and years,
it always remained within it,
suffering immeasurable pain.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
leading the Bǐqiū,
surrounded by them in front and behind,
arrived at the place of that pit,
and asked the Bǐqiū:
“Do you all recognize the deeds this creature committed in its past lives as its original cause?”
At that time, the Bǐqiū
all pondered it,
but none were able to know the deeds it had committed.
Together they addressed the Buddha,
all saying:
“We do not know.”
Then the Buddha told them:
“You all should listen!
I shall explain to you the deeds it committed.
In the past there was a Buddha
named Pípóshī,
who appeared in the world.
After his teaching and transformation were complete,
he entered Nièpán.
Within the Dharma of that Buddha,
there were one hundred thousand Bǐqiū,
who purely cultivated the Brahman-conduct,
lived in leisure and delighted in stillness,
relying on a certain mountain.
On the left and right of that mountain,
there were fine groves of trees,
with flowers and fruits lush and incomparably dense.
Among those trees,
there were flowing springs and bathing pools,
cool and delightful.
At that time, the Bǐqiū
dwelt there in admiration,
following the good and practicing the Way,
diligently practicing without laziness.
All attained the first fruit,
up to the fourth fruit;
none were ordinary people.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants
who gathered together,
wishing to enter the great ocean.
Setting out on their journey,
they passed by this mountain
and saw the Bǐqiū restraining their hearts and being diligent.
Internally they felt joy and respect
and thought to provide offerings.
At that time, the merchants
joined together
and went to invite the assembly of monks,
seeking to make offerings;
but they encountered other Dányuè
who had each already invited them,
day after day in succession,
so their wish could not be fulfilled.
Immediately they went to the assembly of monks
to bid farewell before entering the great ocean.
‘If our group
returns safely,
we shall provide offerings;
we pray you will compassionately grant us this.’
At that time, the monks remained silent,
consenting to accept the invitation.
The merchants entered the ocean,
gained many precious treasures,
and returned safely.
Arriving at the place of the assembly of monks,
they selected the most precious and highest-priced of the treasures
to give to the assembly of monks,
intending them for food and drink,
and if there was more than enough for food,
they could be used as desired.
At that time, the assembly of monks received their treasures
and handed them over to the monk Mómótì.
Later, the assembly of monks
found that the food supplies were almost exhausted,
so they sought from him the treasures of that time
to be used to continue the food supply.
At that time, Mómótì
replied to the assembly of monks, saying:
‘Previously, the merchants
gave the treasures to me themselves;
for what reason do you now ask for them?’
The Shàngzuò and the Wéinà
said to Mómótì:
‘Previously, the Dányuè
gave the treasures as offerings to the monks
and had you keep them.
Now the monks’ food is exhausted
and they should be used to supplement it.’
At that time, Mómótì
said in anger:
‘You people should eat feces!
This treasure is mine;
for what reason do you now ask for it?’
At that time, the assembly of monks,
seeing that Mómótì had already given rise to evil intentions,
immediately dispersed.
Because he had deceived the monks and cursed them with an evil mouth,
when his body was destroyed and his life ended,
he fell into Ābí Hell,
his body constantly tossing and turning in boiling feces.
Passing through ninety-two Jié,
he only then emerged from the hell.
Now he has again fallen into this pool of feces and urine,
passing through years and years,
having not yet attained liberation.
Why is this?
In the past there was a Buddha
named Shīqì,
who leading the Bǐqiū,
passed by this pit,
showed it to his disciples,
and explained its origin.
Furthermore, there was a Buddha
named Suíyè,
who also led the assembly of Bǐqiū
to this place,
and explained its causes and conditions.
When his life ended there,
he returned to hell,
passing through several trillion years,
and after his life ended there, he was born again in this place.
Next there was a Buddha
named Jūliúqín,
also with a crowd of followers,
who surrounded him and came to this pit,
instructing the Bǐqiū
and explaining its origin.
Next was the Buddha named Jūnàhánmóuní,
who also with his disciples
came to this pit.
Next was Jiāyè Buddha,
who also came here,
and for all his disciples
explained its causes and conditions.
Next, as the seventh Buddha,
I, Shìjiāmóuní,
now show you the causes and conditions from beginning to end;
observe this creature.
In this way, all future Buddhas of the Xiánjié
will each do the same,
leading their disciples
to the place of this pit,
to point out this creature
and explain the causes and conditions it created in the past.”
At that time, the Bǐqiū,
hearing what the Buddha had said,
were shocked and their hair stood on end.
They admonished each other
to carefully guard the karma of body, speech, and mind,
faithfully accepted the Buddha’s words,
and joyfully put them into practice.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi, in the Jǐshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, the Venerable Shèlìfú,
during the three periods of the day and night,
constantly used his divine eye
to observe the world
to see who should be delivered,
and would immediately go to deliver them.
At that time, there were some merchants
who wished to go to another country.
Those merchants
brought along a dog together
until they reached the middle of their journey.
The merchants stopped to rest,
and waiting for a quiet moment when people were not watching,
the dog then stole the merchants' meat.
At that time, the people were filled with anger
and together they beat the dog,
breaking its legs,
abandoned it in the empty wilderness,
and left it behind.
Then Shèlìfú,
from afar with his divine eye,
saw the body of this dog,
crippled and lying on the ground,
suffering severely from hunger,
its life hanging by a thread and near death.
Putting on his robes and holding his bowl,
he entered the city to beg for food.
Having obtained it, he carried it out and flew to where the dog was.
With a heart of compassion and pity,
he gave the food to it as a gift.
The dog received the food,
its remaining life was saved,
its heart was very joyful,
and it became even more elated.
Then Shèlìfú
immediately for the sake of that dog
fully explained the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
The dog then ended its life
and was born into a Póluómén family in the country of Shèwèi.
Then Shèlìfú
was walking alone to beg for food.
The Póluómén saw him
and asked him, saying:
"Venerable, you walk alone;
do you have no shāmí?"
Shèlìfú said:
"I have no shāmí.
I hear that you have a son;
you should give him to me."
The Póluómén said:
"I have a son named Jūntí.
He is still a young child
and is not fit for service.
When he grows older,
I shall give him to you."
Then Shèlìfú,
having heard those words,
kept them in his heart
and returned to Jǐhuán.
When the child reached seven years of age,
he came again to ask for him.
At that time, the Póluómén
immediately took his son
and entrusted him to Shèlìfú
to have him leave home.
Then Shèlìfú
received the boy,
brought him to Jǐhuán,
and allowed him to become a shāmí.
Gradually, he fully explained various wondrous Dharmas to him.
His mind was opened and awakened,
and he attained Āluóhàn-ship.
His six divine powers were clear and penetrating,
and his merits were all complete.
At that time, the shāmí Jūntí,
having just attained the Way,
used his own power of wisdom
to observe his past lives,
seeing what actions he had originally performed
to come and receive this form,
and how he met a holy teacher
and attained the realization of the fruit.
He observed and saw that in his previous life,
he was a hungry dog.
"I received the kindness of my Héshang Shèlìfú,
and now I have obtained a human body
and also attained the fruit of the Way."
Joy arose within his heart,
and he thought to himself:
"I have received my teacher's kindness
and escaped all sufferings.
I should now spend my entire life providing for his needs,
always serving as a shāmí,
and not receive the full precepts."
At that time, Ānán
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not know what evil actions
in the past
this person committed
to receive this dog's body?
And what roots of goodness did he create
to obtain liberation?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Long ago, in the time of Jiāshè Buddha,
there were several bǐqiū
gathered in one place.
At that time, there was a young bǐqiū
whose voice was clear and elegant,
and who was skillful at chanting praises,
which people delighted to hear.
There was another bǐqiū
of advanced age and seniority,
whose voice was hoarse and dull,
and who was not able to chant the sutras.
Whenever he made a sound,
it was only for his own amusement.
That old bǐqiū
had already attained Āluóhàn-ship;
his shāmén merits
were all complete.
At that time, the young bǐqiū with the beautiful voice,
seeing that the old shāmén's voice was dull and hoarse,
relied on his own good voice
and scolded him, saying:
'Now you, Elder,
have a voice like a dog barking.'
Having finished his slight and scolding,
the old bǐqiū
then called to the young one:
'Do you know me?'
The young one replied:
'I know you well;
you are a bǐqiū from the time of Jiāshè Buddha.'
The Elder replied:
'I have now already attained the path of the Āluóhàn,
and the shāmén disciplines
are all complete in me.'
Then the young bǐqiū,
hearing what he said,
was shocked and his hair stood on end.
Terrified, he blamed himself,
and immediately before him,
repented of his error.
At that time, the old bǐqiū
then accepted his repentance.
Because of his evil words,
for five hundred lifetimes,
he constantly received the body of a dog.
Because of his leaving home and upholding the pure precepts,
he is now able to see me
and has received liberation."
At that time, Ānán,
hearing what the Buddha said,
joyfully believed and accepted it,
and bowed in respect to practice it.
